title: Ancestors and Teachers Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Koun Ejo, Dogen's successor and the last ancestor listed in Keizan's Denkoroku, as the first individual figure in a series on ancestors and teachers. Kanho follows Ejo from Mount Hiei and the burning of his Daruma school to years as Dogen's attendant, recording the Shobogenzo Zuimonki, and then to leading Eihei-ji after Dogen's death. The North Star serves as the image for a teacher who gives direction, until eventually the student has to walk. Kanho reads the "one hair goes through myriad holes" exchange from Cleary's translation and from a heavily footnoted edition, then ends by telling the sitters they are the ancestors future people will look to, before sending them into triads.

title: Dongshan Liangjie
speaker: Junka Ken Oates
summary: Junka Ken Oates introduces Dongshan Liangjie, founder of the Chan school that became Soto, after the sangha chants the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, a chant attributed to him. Junka traces his life from the child who touched his own face while reading the Heart Sutra, through the awakening with Yunyan over non-sentient beings expounding the Dharma, to the poem written after he glimpsed his reflection in a stream. Junka reads his exchange with a monk about the bird path, which Dogen echoes in the Sansuiko, and his deathbed "delusion banquet." Junka ends with scholars' view that the chant dates from the late twelfth century, young enough when Dogen heard it to come in paperback rather than hardcover.

title: Shantideva: Working with Anger
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Shantideva's chapter 5, "The Guarding of Awareness," and his chapter 6 on patience (kshanti), reading the verses that tell an arrogant or irritated mind to remain like a block of wood. Nomon tests the teaching on anger against the previous day, when a nationwide grounding of flights stranded travelers and indignation at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy rose in Nomon's own mind. Shantideva's answers include conditioning, shared delusion, and the child wailing over a broken sandcastle, until the chapter arrives at longing for an enemy like a treasure found at home. Nomon closes with tomorrow's Shosan and precepts ceremonies, in which Katie and Trish receive new Buddhist names.

title: Shantideva: Calling for Help
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the legend of Shantideva, the monk at Nalanda nicknamed Busuku for eating, sleeping, and pooping, who recited the Bodhicharyavatara from a teaching seat built to embarrass him and then floated out a window. Nomon reads from chapter two, "Confession of Faults," where Shantideva admits harm done and calls for help to Samantabhadra, Manjushri, Avalokiteshvara, and Jizo. Nomon then describes a restless night when a vision of teaching in the Zendo came to mind and calmed body and mind into sleep. Chapter three turns back to light with the prayer "May I be medicine for the sick," and Nomon closes on its last line about inexhaustible delusions and the question of how to end them.

title: Ancestors and Teachers Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart begins a series on Zen ancestors and teachers by asking what it means to chant the names of Dharma ancestors from India, China, and Japan, and who the lineage chart leaves out. Kanho treats the flower sermon and the Platform Sutra verses of Shen Xiu and Huineng as stories that carry religious truth without being reliable history. The chart is one surviving thread: the 845 persecution under Emperor Wuzong closed thousands of monasteries, and women like Mahapajapati Gotami and Dhammadinna never appear on it. Kanho closes by saying the ancestors have done their part and now it is the listeners' turn, then poses triad questions about honored teachers and teachers' mistakes.

title: Dharma talk with Juriki Samuel Senerchia at Samish Sesshin
speaker: Juriki Samuel Senerchia
summary: Juriki Samuel Senerchia reads two of Juriki's own poems from the previous weekend, one set at a river and a family farm, the other on longing and the mother as fresh water. Between them, Juriki speaks of the memorial service for Laura that evening and of Juriki's work as a palliative care chaplain. Juriki then returns to the class on embodied Zen and the Twelve Step recovery, guiding the room through the spine from sit bones to crown. Along the way Juriki cites Sojun Mel Weitsman's advice to keep looking for upright posture and Edward Brown's call for a soft belly. Juriki closes by picturing the spine as the cross on the wall, rooted in earth and reaching up with two arms, then introduces kinhin.

title: Dharma talk with Kanshin Allison Tait at Samish Sesshin
speaker: Kanshin Allison Tait
summary: Kanshin Allison Tait takes up Huineng's Formless Repentance in the Platform Sutra alongside the repentance of the Twelve Steps, then turns to Gateless Barrier case 13, Deshan carrying his bowls. Kanshin opens with Terence's line "Nothing human is alien to me" and Norman Fischer's remark that the problem with San Francisco Zen Center is that everyone there is a human being. Huineng's line "forever to engage in no action is called repentance" meets the GRIP program at San Quentin, where twelve men's 623 years of sentences trace to under two minutes of violence. In case 13, Deshan accepts the Tenzo's rebuke, and Yantou whispers a turning word that changes Deshan's next talk. Kanshin closes by reading a Tiger's Cave passage on crying and laughing with emptiness in the heart.

title: Koans of Recovery
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first meeting of Sengcan and Daoxin from the Jingde Chuandeng Lu, where Daoxin begs for liberation and Sengcan asks, "Who is binding you?" The question runs through Sengcan's verse about the flower seed, Keizan's poem in the Denkoroku, and Rosemerry Wahtola Trommer's poem "One Morning," with Huike's offered arm and Bodhidharma's pacified mind alongside. Nomon suggests thinking of awakening as forgetting to feel separate, and asks sesshin participants to look at what binds them without treating the teachings as a shortcut. Nomon closes with thanks to the shuso and a memory of Laura, the camp cook who bought the Moosewood cookbook to feed a Buddhist group vegetarian meals.

title: Feeding our Hungry Ghosts
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Halloween ceremony for feeding hungry ghosts, explaining the Buddhist cosmology behind it. Nomon describes the six realms, from the hell realms up through the hungry ghosts, with their bloated bellies and pencil-thin necks, to the animals, the rare human realm, and the heavens, where the first sign of death is starting to smell bad. Teachings are the best food for the gaki, so the ceremony is raucous, with instruments, the room turned away from the Buddha toward a back altar, and a closing offering of merit to a name or quality such as "my fear." Nomon ends with Kobun Chino Roshi's words on expanding awakening into the darkness, and an invitation to come raw rather than cleaned up.

title: Addicted to Clinging
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects during sesshin on Juriki's shuso choice to present the twelve steps, then re-expresses each step in Buddhist language, from admitting the power of ignorance and conditioning to taking up the bodhisattva vision. Nomon notes that people in recovery never say they have graduated, and that precepts work the same way. The root addiction is the belief in a separate self, and Nomon connects this to Dogen's Genjokoan line "to forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things." Nomon closes by reading Shantideva's passage on faith from the Precious Lamp Dharani Sutra, which begins "plant the root of faith."

title: Remembering Les Kaye
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett remembers Les Kaye, priest of Kannon Do in Mountain View, who has just died and whom Nomon first met at 18 on a high school class visit. Nomon recalls the settled feeling of that small converted church, then reads from the book of Les's talks, I Had a Good Teacher: the silent lunch with Suzuki Roshi, the tape measure for ordination robes, and Roshi's words to Les's late-arriving mother, "You came at the right time." A passage from You Have to Get Wet, with Yaoshan's silent lecture and the ocean image, leads Nomon to a theory that zazen works when we finally tire of our own figuring. Nomon closes with Les bowing one by one with people at the door after sitting, a custom Nomon now repeats once a year.

title: Two Darts and One Arrow
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Sallatha Sutta's two darts and the parable of the poisoned arrow, beginning with a man Kanho watched pound the roof of his car in a traffic jam after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. The first dart is the pain itself, the second is the resistance and blame the mind adds, and the arrow is the demand for an explanation before the wound gets attention. Kanho reads the opening verses of the Dhammapada, which name the harm plainly and say hatred ends through non-hatred. Kanho then reads the Daniya Sutta, setting the cattleman's secured roof beside the Buddha's freedom from needing one, and suggests that refuge means discovering we can stand in the rain. Kanho closes with the vow that Buddha's way is unsurpassable and two questions for triads about what the moment asks when suffering arrives.

title: Poems of Emptiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the relationship between teachers and students, starting from Norman's essay "There Are No Teachers of Zen" and the Book of Serenity case "Huangbo's Dreg Slurpers." Nomon moves to priests and lay people as a play of form and emptiness, then reads Naong's fourteenth-century Korean poem "The Human Route" and asks what sesshin teaches about emptiness. A sobbing breakdown after an unsigned note about announcements, a gaze at a Douglas fir at Loon Lake, and a mistaken sighting of Satian's car show how people get boxed in by labels. Nomon ends with the poem's question about the one pure and clear thing.

title: Accepting Things as They Are
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up acceptance through a failed errand to replace AirTag batteries and through teachings from Eihei Dogen, Pema Chodron, and Norman Fischer. The errand sends Seishu from Fred Meyer to the Apple Store to a battery shop, until a red light prompts the question "what's happening right now?" and shows how much of the irritation was extra. Seishu then turns to the Four Noble Truths, right view, and the blue lotus opening in fire from Dogen's Shobogenzo. A second story, about a medical test canceled after a drive to Seattle, ends with Pema Chodron's advice to collaborate with your life.

title: Metta Sutta Talk 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Metta Sutta on page 13 of the chant book, chanting it and then reading its second and third paragraphs slowly. Nomon points out that Metta has no direct English equivalent, and tells the story of the Dalai Lama's confusion when asked about self-hatred. The group tries substituting "I" for "all beings" in the chant. Nomon links the sutta's "strenuous, upright and sincere" to a run with a talking watch, where longer strides brought both effort and relaxation. A guided loving-kindness meditation follows, moving from a loved one to "we" to oneself, and listeners share what they noticed. Nomon closes with the sutta's last line, freedom from birth and death, which the original frames as freedom from rebirth.

title: Metta Sutta Talk 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Metta Sutta on pages 13 and 14 of the chant book, an early text that Western teachers added because Zen's own literature says little about compassion. Reading the opening lines, Nomon sets "strenuous, upright, and sincere" beside Bobby McFerrin's "Don't Worry, Be Happy" and finds both seriousness and joy in the Dalai Lama's laughter. Nomon tells of monastics who flee a haunted forest and return chanting the sutta to the unsettled spirits. The word suka, usually rendered "happy," becomes grounded joy, the savoring of what has arrived. The evening closes with groups of three taking four-minute turns on what supports offering love unconditionally and what gets in the way.

title: The Three Doors of Liberation
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up the three doors of liberation (emptiness, signlessness, and aimlessness) as the second part of a series that began with the three dharma seals. Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh and the Diamond Sutra, IkuShun explains emptiness as being empty of a separate self and full of everything else, and illustrates signlessness with a sunflower and a plant labeled a weed. For aimlessness, IkuShun tells of a man who longed for a toy train in a store window, played with it for a few days, and then forgot it. IkuShun closes on stopping, samatha in Pali, as the ground for insight, and sends the group into triads to talk about IkuShun's own practice.

title: The Three Dharma Seals
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up the Three Dharma Seals (impermanence, no self, and nirvana or suffering) as the first of a two-part seminar, drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh and the Five Remembrances. She begins with the Two Truths, using the image of waves and the ocean, then tells how a blackberry hedge and her father's remark about buying underwear exposed her belief in permanence. A microscope and a drop of her own blood show her red blood cells as herself. For the third seal, IkuShun recounts waiting up for her son, who was home asleep and quiet all along, and the fisherman whose angry rival turns out to be an empty boat. She closes on Chris's question: where do you abide right now?

title: Entering the Mirror Part 5
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan close their five-part seminar by setting Huineng's Platform Sutra beside Dogen, Dongshan, and Shunryu Suzuki. Seiu recalls Huineng's non-dual mind and his answer to Shenxiu's mirror-polishing poem, then tells of a bird's trill during sesshin and of choosing a fruit and nut cup outside habit. Kanho reads Suzuki's chapter "Don't try to figure out who you are," with Dongshan's line "wherever I turn, I meet myself," and explains Dogen's Jijuyu Zanmai as life receiving and expressing itself. The evening ends with triad discussion questions, including what dust remains to be polished.

title: Entering the Mirror Part 4
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan take up the formless precepts in Huineng's Platform Sutra, in Red Pine's translation, during the fourth seminar pairing Huineng with Dogen. Kanho moves through the three bodies of the Buddha as chanted at meals, the four boundless vows, and the verse of repentance, recalling nine daily prostrations during years of self-hatred as an alcoholic. Seiu reviews the earlier seminars, then describes the precepts as awakening taking shape in a human life, using the mirror image, a person who drops a heavy box, and a friend who sits with a grieving person over tea. The session ends with four minutes of pair discussion on why precepts are needed if Buddha nature is already complete.

title: Entering the Mirror Part 3
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan continue their five-part series on Huineng and the Platform Sutra, bringing Dogen alongside. Seiu retells Huineng's story, from the woodcutter who hears the Diamond Sutra to the argument over the flag and the wind, then reads his words on prajna, paramita, and no thought. Kanho turns to Dogen's Bendowa and Genjokoan, asking why anyone sits if wisdom is already present, and compares thoughts to baited hooks and a social media feed that keeps pulling us in. Kanho closes with a memory from Tassajara, where a red-lit safe deposit box opens in the wall and takes in thoughts during long hours of zazen.

title: Entering the Mirror Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan continue their study of the Platform Sutra and Dogen, following Huineng from the poetry contest into flight. Seiu retells the midnight transmission, Weishun's failure to lift the robe and bowl on Taiyu Ridge, and the question about the original face before parents were born, then recalls a minute of sudden insight on a mountain trail. Kanho stays with Huineng's eight months of pounding rice and the line "simply practice with a straightforward mind," reading it beside "practice and realization are one" in Bendowa and "reality studying reality" in Shoho Jisso. Kanho ends by asking where practice stops and ordinary life begins, with scrubbing the bathroom and folding laundry as examples.

title: Entering the Mirror Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan open a five-class seminar, Entering the Mirror, that pairs the Platform Sutra in Red Pine's translation with Dogen's teaching. Seiu tells the story of Huineng, the illiterate wood seller who awakens on hearing a line of the Diamond Sutra, and of the rival mirror poems he and Shenxiu write for Hongren. Kanho asks what practice becomes if awakening was never absent, turning to Fukanzazengi, Bendowa, and Genjokoan, and cautions that "no dust" does not excuse careless conduct. The session closes with three practice questions, about where the mind abides, what it tries to fix, and how to stay with a hard feeling, followed by triads of four minutes per person.

title: Mountains, Waters and Sesshin, Part 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells how the Samish Island sesshin came to include a spirit-settling ceremony, then turns to Dogen's "Mountains and Waters Sutra," sections 14 and 15, with Su Dongpo's poem "Mount Lu." The story begins with Florence Caplow's frightening vision during the first retreat in 1993. It continues through a Samish elder's question, "Are you the ones that have been calling to us?", and a ceremony where a strong pull in Nomon's gut leads to a warning broadcast during zazen. Norman phones afterward to suggest ending the ceremony, and Nomon answers by writing the quieter version the sangha did the day before. In the Dogen reading, standing in the middle of the mountain hides its true face, and the passage closes on mountains belonging to those who love them.

title: The Reality of All Things
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Dogen's essay Shoho Jisso, "The Reality of All Things," after Katagiri Roshi's poem "Peaceful Life" and a word of love for everyone gathered at the end of sesshin. Kanho observes that Dogen offers clouds and rain, sadness and joy, pine and bamboo where a reader expects definitions, and reads "reality studying reality" as transmission by participation. The Yogacara storehouse consciousness becomes a field where a gardener arrives with weed killer, set against Dogen's invitation to become intimate with every seed. Kanho asks where the body stops, describes a quiet feeling of companionship in sitting, and closes with Rumi's "Come, come, whoever you are."

title: Mountains, Waters and Sesshin, Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues the history of Samish sesshin into the 2000s, tracing how Richard Baker's fall at San Francisco Zen Center sent former students back to practice with Norman Fischer, then turns to sections seven through ten of Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra. Along the way Nomon describes an orthodox rabbi who prayed by the gazebo during morning service and the 2008 mini practice period, when Norman opened each talk by appreciating the previous evening's. Dogen's passage on water, which dragons see as a palace and hungry ghosts see as pus and blood, leads Nomon to community as the place where people are left alone to work through their stuff. Nomon closes with John Wiley's remark that he noticed how beautiful it is here.

title: Insentient Beings Speaking Dharma
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Dogen's fascicle Mujo Seppo, "Insentient Beings Speaking Dharma," through the exchange between Dongshan and Yunyan, ending in Dongshan's verse that "the ears never hear it, only the eyes do." Kanho asks what counts as sentience and where the boundary falls between a feeling subject and an inert world, then turns to sesshin, where the bell, the light, and the grief that surfaces are already teaching. The story of Nagarjuna's bowl of water and Kanadeva's needle shows communication without explanation. Kanho closes on Tusi's answer to the monk, "Don't badmouth them," and a passage from Emerson's Nature.

title: Mountains, Waters and Sesshin, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with memories of 1990s sesshin at Samish with Zoketsu Norman Fischer, then turns to section four of Dogen's "Mountains and Waters Sutra" and its line "Green mountains are always walking." Among the memories, Heidi Epstein sews a rakusu for her daughter, killed in a car crash, and Norman prepares one for the daughter too, with a name and lineage paper. Norman also answers Nomon's worries about sesshin with "Keep it simple." Reading Dogen's warning not to slander the mountains, Nomon hears advice against slandering ourselves, and tells Blanche Hartman's story of Suzuki Roshi hollering "Only Zazen does Zazen." Nomon closes with Yaoshan, who sits silent on the teaching seat, then goes back to his quarters and shuts the door.

title: Mountains, Waters and Sesshin, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra, read in Kaz Tanahashi's translation, to begin a Samish Island sesshin. First comes a recollection of the early retreats with Norman Fischer, who no longer comes: a borrowed cabin on Lummi Island, and an incense bowl that breaks when Norman and Nomon carry the altar to the middle of the room. Then Nomon turns to the phrase "abiding in its condition," the saying about mountains being mountains again, and Daokai's line "the green mountains are always walking." That line becomes a way to practice kinhin, each step the whole mountain walking. The sesshin session ends with a chanted reading of the sutra's walking-mountains sections.

title: Sandokai Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the Sandokai, "The Merging of Difference and Unity," the eighth-century poem by Shitou on page eleven of the chant book, and takes up its second page on light and dark. Nomon tells of the Dalai Lama greeting an exhausted new arrival from Tibet, joking one moment and weeping with her the next, as an example of joy and sorrow held together. Einstein's passage calling separateness an "optical delusion of consciousness" joins the poem's image of the front and back foot in walking. Nomon reads through the closing lines on mountains and rivers and on not passing days and nights in vain, then sends everyone into groups of three to speak about the light and dark in their own lives.

title: The Six Paramitas
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up Bodhidharma's Outline of Practice, the three-page text also called Contemplation of Four Practices for Entering the Mahayana Path, on the last Sunday before summer break and the close of a series on the six paramitas. Joden sketches Bodhidharma's life, from the Daruma doll in Cloud Hall that gets its second eye painted to the meeting with Emperor Wu, where the answers are "No merit" and "I don't know." Joden then reads through the four practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, wanting nothing, and practicing the dharma. Ryokan's lines on meeting disaster, Harada Roshi's invocation, and an old New England proverb about using it up and wearing it out come along the way. The last words are the morning's chant: "The Buddha's way is unsurpassable; I vow to become it."

title: Sandokai Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up "Merging of Difference and Unity," Shitou's poem in the chant book, as part of a year of talks on the book's short texts. Nomon introduces Shitou as a student of Huineng who lived in a hut on a boulder and received the Dharma name "stone head," then reads the first half of the poem line by line. Light and dark, branching streams, and the senses come alive through tree-gazing, where the tree is you and still keeps its place, and through Nomon's delight at seeing Nomon's own eyebrows for the first time. After small groups of three share what the lines stir up, Nomon closes on the poem's last line, "Don't waste your time in vain," and wonders whether the laughter in the room comes from the darkness or the light.

title: Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom, the chant that follows the Heart Sutra and comes from chapter seven of the Prajnaparamita in 8,000 lines. Nomon begins with a Portland pizza dinner where a senior colleague asks "What's your vow?", which leads to two braided paths, healing and transformation. Nomon then reads a sample dialogue between Subhuti and Sakra, and dwells on the hymn's key line, that wisdom knows the own being of all dharmas and does not stray from it. A college student's question about prayer brings up a 2007 prayer by Norman Fischer, whose footnote offers other names to call on: Guanyin, Tara, Prajnaparamita.

title: Prajna Paramita
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up prajna, the sixth of the six bodhisattva practices, after a quick tour of generosity, ethics, patience, energy, and concentration. Nomon draws on Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise and John Welwood's poem "Forget About Enlightenment," read twice. The main story is Mazu polishing a tile with Nanyue, who asks how sitting can make a Buddha if rubbing can make a mirror. Nomon describes gripping the steering wheel on an errand day, then bringing the body down to make space. Nomon closes with five suggestions, ending on smiling so deeply that the smile fills the universe.

title: Muscle Memory and the Practice of Daily Life
speaker: Junka Ken Oates
summary: Junka Ken Oates takes up the Six Paramitas, which the sangha has studied in Sunday talks for months, and asks what happens to them once everyone leaves the temple and gets into traffic. Junka compares kata in karate to chanting in the zendo, noting that some practitioners learn over a hundred forms, though memorizing them is not the point. Bodhidharma's Bloodstream Sermon, the Bruce Lee finger-and-moon image, and the "too many mind" scene in The Last Samurai all point to training that works without thinking. Junka closes by sending the sangha outside to the beautiful day, likening practice to sanding furniture and noting that the sangha sometimes rubs off sharp edges too.

title: Jewel Mirror Samadhi Part 4
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up three passages from the Jewel Mirror Samadhi in the seminar's final session: Yi the archer, the lines on ministers and children, and the closing advice to practice like a fool. Yi's arrows meeting point to point become a picture of effort that cannot force the result but must still loose the arrow. Serving and obeying turn into call and response, illustrated by the national teacher calling his attendant three times and by the Blue Cliff Record monk Huichao, who is told "You are Huichao." The host within the host, tied to Dongshan's five ranks, lands on washing dishes and painful joints, and the evening closes with triads.

title: The Ground of Energetic Joy
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up virya, the fourth paramita, usually translated as joyful effort or energetic joy, and opens with George Eliot's line from Middlemarch about the "hidden life" of people who rest in unvisited tombs. IkuShun describes daruma dolls that pop back up when pushed over, then draws on Ringu Tulku Rinpoche's three kinds of laziness: procrastination, filling time with busyness, and insulting ourselves before trying. Bodhicitta and right view become the ground for sustained energy, shown through the relative and ultimate truths and the image of the right arm helping the left without hesitation. IkuShun closes with a poem, "Ordinary Things."

title: Flower Garden Buddhism
speaker: Ben Connelly
summary: Ben Connelly takes up the Flower Garland Sutra through Weisong's Ocean Seal Chart, the 210-character Korean poem behind Ben's book Inside the Flower Garland Sutra. Ben reads lines on abundance, where a rain of jewels represents skillful means, and on interdependence, where one mote of dust holds the ten directions. Stories from Minneapolis carry the teaching: a grocery-delivery spreadsheet that grew into Neighbors Helping Neighbors and raised $5.7 million for rent, the offerings tended at George Floyd Square, and a silent Buddhist walk of 700 people. Sudhana's 53 teachers in the Gandavyuha Sutra frame the variety of practice. Questions about rage lead Ben to objectlessness.

title: Responding to the Cries of the World Retreat
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up Avalokiteshvara and the paralysis that can block compassion, turning to Pema Chödrön's When Things Fall Apart and Start Where You Are for the teaching that compassionate action grows from working with one's own unwanted feelings. Myoki tells of a blocked artery found weeks ago and a stent placed two weeks ago, and of reaching for blame when the pharmacy lost a prescription, because vulnerability is harder to feel. Myoki then describes the four stages of Tonglen as Norman Fischer first taught them and guides a sitting round of breathing in a difficult feeling and breathing out healing. The last stretch suggests brief on-the-spot Tonglen, such as while washing dishes after an angry exchange with a boss, and opens the floor to questions.

title: Compassion
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up the six paramitas as six ways that compassion (karuna) moves in the world, moving through generosity, ethics, patience, enthusiastic effort, concentration, and wisdom. Bob Ross stands for enthusiastic effort, and Martin Luther King's words "Until all men are free, I cannot be free" mark Seiu's first meeting with the bodhisattva vow. Seiu then asks how to feel compassion for someone whose ethics seem abhorrent, naming three barriers: confusing compassion with approval, tribalism, and threat to identity. Seiu draws on parenting a person with a mental health disorder. The paramitas become an inhalation and compassion an exhalation, with a breath-pause between them that a women's retreat participant described as exquisite, and triads close the session by sharing how each person responds to a clashing viewpoint.

title: Responding to the Cries of the World Retreat
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan introduces Avalokiteshvara, the archetype of compassion who hears the cries of the world, and traces how the figure shifts from male to female as Buddhism moves through India, China, Japan and Tibet. Seiu shows images of Kuan Yin and Kannon, including the legend of the eleven heads and thousand arms and a pot holder with an iron and a toaster in the hands. Seiu then turns to the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, which Norman Fischer discussed at the Samish sesshin. Seiu tells of chanting it while holding a crushed arm on the way to the ER after an e-bike fall, and closes with Pema Chödrön on welcoming uncomfortable feelings.

title: Jewel Mirror Samadhi Part 3
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up part three of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, beginning with its line that reality is naturally real yet inconceivable, beyond delusion and enlightenment. The repeated number five leads Kanho to Dongshan's five ranks, ending in a fully blacked-out fifth position, and to the ox-herding return to the marketplace. For the trapped rat and tethered colt, Kanho offers a hatching gecko, a mouse frozen by fright, and a kayaking storm where the question "What is it I'm worried about when I worry about anything?" arose. Kanho reads Zoketsu Norman Fischer's poem "Responsibility," then sends the group into triads to talk about being outwardly still and inwardly moving.

title: Jewel Mirror Samadhi Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart returns to the Jewel Mirror Samadhi and picks up the invitation from last week to live with a line rather than analyze it. Kanho reads the lines about filling a silver bowl with snow and hiding a heron in the moonlight, where white on white shows that difference remains even when contrast fails. After a round of triads on the "inquiring impulse," Kanho tells how Dongshan, leaving his teacher Yunyan, asks what to say of the teaching and hears "just this is it." Years later Dongshan sees his reflection in a stream and recognizes "you are not it, in truth it is you." The evening closes with "inquiry and response come up together" and Dongshan's Five Ranks poem as the week's reminder.

title: The Jewel Mirror Samādhi
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Jewel Mirror Samādhi, the ninth-century poem by Dongshan Liangjia, and has the sangha chant it at the start of each seminar for four weeks. Kanho asks listeners to sense into the poem the way they would listen to birdsong, and to let go of translating it into "non-duality" or "emptiness." Close readings of "Now you have it, so keep it well" lead to a question: if it is already here, what gets overlooked? Triads of three minutes each follow. The line "Turning away and touching are both wrong, for it is like a massive fire" leads to homework: when something is strongly liked or disliked, neither move toward it nor away. Kanho closes with Dongshan's poem of the old woman and her mirror.

title: Joyful Effort and the Energy of Sangha
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the paramita of joyful effort, working with Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara and the Sangarava Sutta. Heigaku opens with a flare of anger at work over who should update the life safety drawings, then moves through effort, perfection, and joy. In the sutta, the Buddha compares the five hindrances to a bowl of water that is boiling, clouded, overgrown with algae, rippled by wind, or muddy, so that a face already there cannot be seen. Sangha members describe the joy of painting, laying floors, and sewing together in the room. Heigaku ends on doubt and faith, which dance like protons and electrons to form matter.

title: Heart Sutra, Part 7: The Good News
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the last pages of the Heart Sutra chant, from the list of "no" lines through the closing mantra. Nomon proposes the Chinese word for sky in place of emptiness, since sky has room for all of the mind's weather, even storms. The "no" lines point to the twelvefold chain and the Four Noble Truths, and Nomon sets Dan Harris's 10 Percent Happier beside the Buddha's claim of full freedom from suffering. Nomon then explains the four inverted views, which no longer arise, much as a winged rabbit never comes to mind, and the mantra "gate, gate, para gate, parasam gate, bodhi svaha." The evening ends with trio conversations about what struck people in the sutra.

title: Dhyana Paramita
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the paramita of dhyana, setting the Anapanasati Sutra's sixteen contemplations of breathing beside Dogen's Fukanzazengi. Myoki walks through the sutra's four sets (body, feelings, mind, wisdom) and Dogen's posture instructions and his line "Think of not thinking," noting how detailed the Buddha's guidance is next to Zen's bare-bones shikantaza. Breath counting, learned from Norman Fischer at Green Gulch, had become autopilot, so Myoki now recites the sutra's verses in personal wording. One morning's sit moves from a rapid breath to rehearsing this very talk to nervousness in the body. A short guided meditation with the first four contemplations closes the morning.

title: The Paramitas in Daily Life
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the six paramitas in daily life, drawing on Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise and Dale Wright's The Six Perfections. Seishu recounts Norman's answer that his first priority as abbot was his own happiness, then describes how a long meditation practice has opened a small space before speaking, using a moment of irritation over Seishu's wife's physical therapy visit. Suzuki Roshi's phrase "shine one corner of the world" frames the rest, along with two airport scenes: a patient ticket agent during mass cancellations, and a mother calmly containing two boys beside a pacing, angry man. Seishu closes with Robin Wall Kimmerer's words on choosing joy because the earth gives it daily.

title: Heart Sutra, Part 6: Empty Marks, Empty Chains
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with remembrances of three people who recently died, Luba, David Chadwick, and Anka Rick Spencer, then returns to the Heart Sutra's third paragraph. Luba hides the chainsaw of loggers cutting trees in a green belt near her home. David, an early student of Suzuki Roshi, shows up hung over at Tassajara, and Suzuki Roshi tells his critics to leave him alone. Nomon reads "all dharmas are marked by emptiness" alongside the three marks of existence and the wave and ocean image, then takes up the repeated "no" before eyes, ears, and the other senses as an invitation to look again. The twelve nidanas, glimpsed in the last lines, wait for next time.

title: Heart Sutra, Part 5: Making Friends with Emptiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues a Heart Sutra series by taking up emptiness through the five skandhas and a long reading from Thich Nhat Hanh's The Heart of Understanding. Nomon describes how body, feeling tone, perception, mental formations, and consciousness change when reactive and when open, then reads Thich Nhat Hanh on a sheet of paper that is empty of separate self yet full of sunshine and cloud, and on waves and water. Nomon turns to Cesar Chavez, whose labor organizing sits beside Dolores Huerta's recent account of abuse, as a case of holding opposites. Nomon closes by setting up an exercise in groups of three.

title: Manifesting Kanzeon
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up dana, the perfection of generosity, through Kanzeon and the koan of her thousand hands and eyes, found in the Blue Cliff Record (Case 89) and the Book of Serenity (Case 54). Joden recalls a four-day stay at San Francisco Zen Center, where chanting the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo with Joan Amaral and Zenkei Blanche Hartman began a habit of chanting it everywhere. Dawu's answer in the koan, that Kanzeon acts like a person reaching for a pillow in the dark, becomes a picture of giving without thought. Joden then turns to Allen Ginsberg's poem "Who Be Kind To?" and a Zen colleague worn out by her daughter's alcoholism, and ends with a seven-round chant and three questions about what keeps us from giving freely.

title: Heart Sutra, Part 4: Form is Emptiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra's line "form does not differ from emptiness," after a review of the five skandhas as a way to loosen the grip of "everything is happening to me." Nomon explains emptiness as emptiness of separateness, and offers a seed that becomes a tree only through sun, water, and undisturbed habitat. An old Volkswagen bus that broke down and brought help from strangers shows what happens when we expect form to stay solid. Nomon points to Thich Nhat Hanh's chapter "Long Live Emptiness," leads a space-seeing exercise around the room, and closes with a meditation on Jeff Foster's poem "Peeling Off the Label."

title: Interconnectedness of the Paramitas
speaker: Junka Ken Oates
summary: Junka Ken Oates takes up the six paramitas, drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching and Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise, where paramita means "gone to the other side." Junka tests the list against personal habits: a miser's inheritance from Depression-era parents, including a kitchen drawer of newspaper rubber bands, a yearly giving budget that turns the precepts into generosity, and a phone checklist with a box labeled sit. Sailing aboard a boat named Kshanti shows what full presence in an activity looks like. Each paramita turns out to contain the other five, with wisdom as the well-baked container that holds them. Junka closes by asking everyone to name the biggest wedge of their own pie chart and find the rest inside it.

title: Dana Paramita
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up dana paramita, looking at generosity in how we interpret the intentions of others. An out-of-date hospital schedule sparks anger at a coworker who had in fact updated it, and a college philosophy paper earns a professor's rebuke for skipping the generous reading of its author. Heigaku then turns to Nancy Mujo Baker on fault-finding and Jack Kornfield's practice of imagining that everyone acts as a Buddha for our benefit. A second paramita, dhyana, follows, with Norman Fischer's passage in The World Could Be Otherwise on meditation as returning. The session ends with listeners pairing up for discussion.

title: Heart Sutra, Part 3: The Skandhas
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the opening of the Heart Sutra, where Avalokiteshvara perceives that all five skandhas are empty and so relieves all suffering. Nomon walks through the five aggregates (form, feeling tone, perception, mental formations, and consciousness) as an alternate model of a person that needs no "me in the middle." A guided meditation finds earth, water, fire, and wind in the body, and Lisa Feldman Barrett's story of a soldier who sees a boy's herding stick as an AK-47 shows the mind building what it sees. Nomon closes by previewing emptiness as a reality too large for any bucket of concepts, the skandhas included.

title: Practicing the Six Perfections
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Six Perfections, the year's theme, and draws on Dale Wright's book The Six Perfections and on Dogen's writings. Kanho compares the paramitas to learning the Native American flute, where fingers miss the holes and the same mistakes keep returning. Kanho invites listeners to examine their own relationship to the word "perfection" and to swap in another word if it hurts. A walk through generosity, ethical conduct, patience, effort, meditation, and wisdom follows, with Dogen's line about giving a flower or leaf to the wind and Jack Kornfield's joke that anyone who stays calm through everything is probably a dog. Kanho closes with Mary Oliver's "Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it."

title: Heart Sutra, Part 2: Avalokiteshvara
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who speaks the Heart Sutra, and opens with a short video of the Theravada monks' Walk for Peace and Red Cedar's own silent walk on Sunday. Nomon then traces the names Guanyin and Kanzeon, tells how Avalokiteshvara's head burst from the world's suffering and was rebuilt with ten faces, and retells the fable of Miao Shan, who gives her eyes and arms to cure her cruel father. Nomon closes by reading John Blofeld's account of a statue of Guanyin in a Chinese monastery answering him: "Seek it with your mind."

title: Paramita of Ethical Conduct: Metta
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the paramita of ethical conduct through the sixteen bodhisattva precepts, which Myoki reads aloud with the sangha, quoting Norman Fischer's description of them as the lifeblood of the Buddhas. Myoki distills the three pure precepts into one vow to loving kindness and describes the literal, compassionate, and ultimate levels of practice, including the white lie at a dinner party and a lie told to a Nazi soldier to protect someone hiding in an attic. Myoki notes that metta was dropped from the original ten paramitas, then leads a guided Theravadan metta practice moving from a loved one to Myoki, a neutral person, a difficult person, and the whole world. Myoki closes by introducing Tonglen, using Myoki's own divorce and the feeling of betrayal as the example.

title: The Second Paramita: Sila
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up sila, the second paramita of ethical conduct, through Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise, which describes ethics as a joyful path that comes naturally from the fullness of the heart. Seiu recalls turning down an offer to smuggle cocaine from South America after thinking of a grandfather who would be hurt. Seiu then recites the three refuges, three pure precepts, and ten clear mind precepts, using a starving family and a loaf of bread to read the precept against stealing at concrete, compassionate, and absolute levels. After a look at karma, repentance, and forgiveness, Seiu sends listeners into groups of three to ask where ethics challenges them and how it helps.

title: Heart Sutra, Part 1: Overview
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the Heart Sutra, the most commonly chanted text in Zen temples, and spends the evening on its origins and its theme of emptiness. Nomon traces how the prajnaparamita literature shrank from a hundred thousand lines to the Heart Sutra's few dozen, and uses the ancient image of a cart losing its wheels and handles to ask when a cart stops being a cart. A morning of unexpected compassion for ICE agents, after reading news of two people killed in Minnesota, becomes Nomon's example of emptiness at work, alongside Thich Nhat Hanh's "interbeing." Nomon then reads the longer Sanskrit prologue in Edward Conze's translation, where Shariputra asks Avalokiteshvara how to train, and begins the five aggregates. The evening closes with an assignment to spend a long time with a tree.

title: Is Patience a Four-Letter Word?
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up the Buddha's saying that nothing in a life is more beautiful than patience, reading it through Gil Fronsdal's teaching on the Pali word khanti. IkuShun traces a lifetime of impatience and hidden anger to childhood physical limits, and to declining help from a fellow hiker on a retreat. A rescue dog who senses aggression in a loving pat and another dog who sits only to earn a treat show the gap between gentleness and endurance. Practices follow: the phrase "nothing to do, nowhere to go," white space in the schedule, and letting others tell their stories without adding one's own. IkuShun closes with three aspects of patience: accepting reality, perseverance rooted in Buddha nature, and patience under insult.

title: Living in a world we Did Not Design
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the patience chapter of Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara alongside Sheri Huber's essay "A Project for Saving the World," after opening with a poem, "Feel It All." Shantideva's image of wearing shoes instead of covering the whole earth in leather anchors a look at anger. An ex-partner vacationing in Hawaii with an umbrella drink shows what drinking poison to harm an enemy looks like. Huber's imagined group, which saves the world by blaming no one and involving no one, supplies the willingness that carries on after outrage fades, much as first-retreat eagerness fades around day three when the knees start to hurt. Kanho closes by asking listeners to put a little leather on their own feet.

title: Dana Paramita
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up dana paramita, the first of the six paramitas, using Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise. Myoki starts from the habit of watching out for number one, then asks the room to close their eyes and feel what it is to sit in the lap of the Buddha. Life's generosity appears in the next inhale after each exhale and in plants pushing up through cracks in cement. Myoki also tells of writing a way-seeking mind talk as shuso and coming to see a sad childhood as part of what brought Myoki to the temple. The recording ends as Myoki turns to the Genjokoan line about leaping clear of abundance and lack.

title: With our Whole Hearts - Taking Refuge
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the three refuges of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, starting from a Dhammapada verse about false and true refuge. Nomon tells how the Buddha ordained his son Rahula with the three refuges, which prompts the Buddha's father Suddhodana to object and the Buddha to make one of the first monastic rules. Nomon then goes through the Pali chant, where gacchami carries a sense of going with understanding, and the Chinese characters behind "I take refuge," which say "return and rely." Groups of three close the evening by asking what taking refuge means for each person.

title: Tend to Your Spirit
speaker: Zenshin Florence Caplow
summary: Zenshin Florence Caplow takes up virya (energy, or joyful effort) and shraddha (faith) through twenty-five years of chronic illness, beginning with coho salmon leaping the cascades of the Sol Duc River. Zenshin describes retreats adapted for a body that cannot get through a full sesshin, and Darlene Cohen's way of teaching from living with pain. Blue Cliff Record case 87 follows, in which Manjushri sends Sudhana to find something that is not medicine, and Sudhana finds nothing. Vimalakirti's illness leads into the five remembrances, chanted in call and response. Zenshin ends by reading "Can I Love the Life I Have?" from the book Tend to Your Spirit.

title: Joyfully Impossible - The Bodhisattva Vows
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Four Bodhisattva Vows, the verse chanted at the end of the evening, starting with a memory of flipping open a book in a Palo Alto bookstore at fifteen or sixteen and being stopped by those four lines. Nomon admits how impossible the vows sound, then traces their roots from a Lotus Sutra passage through Zhiyi's earlier version to the Platform Sutra, where "I will cause" becomes "I vow." The Chinese character translated as "save" originally means "to measure" and carries the sense of helping across a river, so Nomon suggests "crossing together." Nomon closes by setting up groups of three, where each person speaks for five minutes on what the vows mean while the other two listen.

title: The Three Refuges—Coming Home and Living by Vow
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up the three refuges, drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Reb Anderson's Being Upright, and Thich Nhat Hanh's Plum Village verses. IkuShun opens with an image of a traveler closing the door of a hut and lighting a fire against a storm, then recalls Dogen hanging the words Buddha, Dharma and Sangha on his sickroom pillar and circumambulating while chanting the refuges. Taking refuge begins as shelter and coming home, then deepens into vow, as Thay's teaching that the Buddha takes refuge in me makes the practice reciprocal. IkuShun closes on Reb's image of the Buddhas and ancestors saying "Welcome home," then sends everyone into small groups.

title: Vow of Repentance
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up the verse of repentance, "All my ancient twisted karma," which comes from Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's fourth vow in the Avatamsaka Sutra. Seiu recalls a long stretch of nine prostrations each morning and a Dokusan conversation with Peter Levitt, who pointed to the words "ancient" and "beginningless" as a reminder that no one invented this karma. A story from a 12-step program about falling into the same hole on the same street leads to walking down a different street. Seiu separates formal repentance, such as apologizing to someone harmed, from formless repentance, which is zazen itself, and closes with Kodo's rhyming poem of zazen instruction and a Samantabhadra Sutra line about misdeeds melting like frost and dew in the sun of wisdom.

title: Rohatsu
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Rohatsu, the day marking the Buddha's awakening, through Xuansha's line in the Shobogenzo that the entire world of the ten directions is one bright pearl. Kanho describes each period of zazen as a reenactment of the Buddha sitting under the Bodhi tree, and reads Mara as the inner voice that says to quit, bringing anxiety, comparison, and bitterness. The Buddha touches the earth and lets the visions rise and fall, so the pearl includes even fear. Generations of practitioners sit behind the room, from Mahapajapati to lay people who kept altars in kitchens and barns. Kanho closes with Gina Poirot's poem "My Courage Is a Wild Song."

title: Opening the Dharma
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Opening the Dharma verse chanted before each teaching, reading it line by line through its Chinese characters and their Sino-Japanese sounds. Nomon traces the first line to chapter two of the Lotus Sutra, where the Buddha answers Manjushri after the opening scene of light streaming from the Buddha's forehead, and defines a kalpa as the time it takes to empty a huge storehouse of poppy seeds at one seed per century. The third line's word "now" sets the vastness of the dharma beside the feeling of coming home, which Nomon links to a remark from Norman Fischer that the dharma is both mysterious and right here. Nomon ends on the fourth line, where the character for treasure is the one once reserved for imperial treasures.

title: Taking Refuge
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up taking refuge at the close of the first practice period in the new temple, working from the Ugra Paripriccha Sutra and a chapter on refuge in Suzuki Roshi's Becoming Yourself. Suzuki's image of a basket sunk in water, which has no holes while it stays there, becomes Nomon's picture of letting ourselves be ourselves. Nomon adds the story of Chinook salmon reaching the upper Klamath River in October 2024, the first season after four dams came down, and compares their return across some twenty generations to our own remembering of the way home. Nomon closes with the afternoon ceremony in which Ken moves to the Buddha seat, then drops back to sit with everyone else.

title: Sutra Book 2 - Dedication of Merit
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Universal Dedication, the short chant at the bottom of page one in the chant book, sung at the end of nearly every Zen ceremony and chanted tonight in Sino-Japanese. Nomon recalls learning it at the Suzuki family temple in Japan, then reads the chant line by line as three treasures: all Buddhas of ten directions and three times, Bodhisattva Mahasattvas, and Maha Prajnaparamita. Merit is described as the underlying energy of the universe, and waves on the ocean serve as the image for separateness and interconnection. Nomon compares the literal Chinese with the looser Halifax and Tanahashi translation, and ends on letting go of the merit as it is given away.

title: Chanting the Robe Chant
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the robe chant that opens each evening of practice, a verse chanted with the kesa held on top of the head. Nomon reads Dogen's account of weeping with joy on first seeing Chinese monks chant it, then goes through the verse line by line. The characters for "liberation" turn out to mean unraveling and undressing, and two English renderings of the second line, "field far beyond form and emptiness" and "a formless field of benefaction," are set side by side. Nomon offers three ways to meet the chant: intellectual, devotional, and as practice. The closing caution is that the robes are optional, and that people wearing more special things are not more special.

title: Fall Sesshin-Buddha, Occam, Danish Architects&British Grandmothers
speaker: Junka Ken Oates
summary: Junka Ken Oates tells how the Buddha's plain teaching of dissatisfaction, change, and interconnection grows into lists, among them the eighty-five Robert Thurman counts in his Vimalakirti Sutra translation, as it travels through China, Korea, Japan, and America. Thich Nhat Hanh's hammer striking the other hand shows how suffering is shared. Junka asks lay people, the receivers in the three wheels of giver, receiver, and gift, to share the teaching, citing a karate teacher's advice to do it "another thousand times." Compassion then gets its own turn: karuna is set apart from metta and pictured as a down feather whose quill stays sharp. Junka closes with the advice to keep the sharp end pointed at oneself.

title: Fall Sesshin
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up how to practice seriously as a lay person, working with the Buddha's conversation with the lay follower Ugra and the Zaikei Tokudo half of the Jukai ceremony the next morning. Nomon begins with a sesshin practice of not controlling anything, then recalls the unlikely chain of zendos, a Jewish poet teacher, and a Christian church camp that made this retreat possible. Zaikei, the word for layperson, and Tokudo, "become a monk," lead to Suzuki Roshi's title Becoming Yourself, set beside Kokyo Henkel's 30-day solo sesshin. Nomon closes on Sangha as the solid face of Buddha and Dharma, practiced through the precepts.

title: Finding Zen in the Ordinary
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Eihei Dogen's Bendowa and Fukanzazengi, where practice and realization are one, and asks what that means off the cushion. Kanho recounts Dogen's young question about why beings with Buddha nature must still practice, and admits to sitting in sesshin with painful knees, telling Dogen's "Dharma gate of repose and bliss" that it has been understood. Kanho then turns to Norman Fischer's reminder that awareness runs through washing dishes and driving to work, and to Sherry Huber's teaching that the voice in your head is conditioning speaking. Kanho closes with Gina Puro's poem "Stillness," which ends on breathing into each question without needing the answer.

title: Dogen's Genjokoan - at Bozeman Zen Group
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's Genjokoan at a Bozeman Zen Group sesshin, reading from the chant book through the opening paragraph, the line "blossoms fall and in aversion, weeds spread," and the teaching to study the self and forget the self. Nomon connects these to daily life: whatever the mind rehearses grows stronger, and good therapy and self-forgetting both belong in practice. Nomon then retells the story of Mayu fanning himself when a monk asks why fan if wind reaches everywhere, reading wind as Buddha nature and fanning as practice. Nomon closes with the sixth-century master Zhiyi's advice to count breaths, then simply follow them, with buckets of humility.

title: Dogen's Vow - at Bozeman Zen Group
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Eihei Koso Hotsugan Mon, the vow chant drawn from Dogen's writings, at a Bozeman Zen Group sesshin. Beginning with two members starting precept study, Nomon resolves to sit in vigil at a naval air base gate over the US boat strikes in the Caribbean, then teaches the sixth-century Chan master Zhiyi's breath instructions: anchor the mind in the belly, soften the body, and visualize breath moving through the pores. In the vow, Dogen's line that "we in the future shall be Buddhas" sits beside "already Buddha," and confession becomes a practice that melts obstacles at the root. Nomon closes by previewing the next morning's shosan ceremony, where Reb Anderson once allowed Nomon to say simply, "I have no question."

title: Exploring Four Themes of Dogen's Teachings
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a four-part Lion's Roar article in which contemporary teachers take up themes from Dogen: being time, practicing together, being the Buddha you are, and being awakened by all phenomena. Shinshu Roberts pictures walking into a meeting with a difficult co-worker, and Chimyo Atkinson recalls sharing a cramped room with seven other nuns at the Aichi women's monastery. Nomon adds a memory of a monk at Eiheiji straightening an okesa, then swaps "love" for "Buddha" in Koun Franz's closing paragraph. A question from Aiden about Dogen's admiration for ascetic practice leads Nomon to the Tendai marathon monk from the Japan trip, who says he feels unchanged.

title: Finding Your Middle Way
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett asks whether Zen practice should favor intensity or flexibility, and tells of meeting Dai Ajari Mitsunaga Endo, a Tendai monk who completed the seven-year Kaihogyo marathon practice on Mount Hiei. Nomon describes the nightly 25-mile runs past 260 shrines, the nine-day Do-Iri retreat without food, water, or sleep, and the humble rice-growing life that follows. Beside him Nomon sets Tom Kirschner's Rinzai training in Kyoto and a first sesshin at San Francisco Zen Center that was both the hardest and the best thing Nomon ever did. Nomon closes with healing and transformation as two paths that inter-be, and with the seven years of running that add up to the circumference of the earth.

title: Zazen
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the basic practice of zazen, opening with Pablo Neruda's poem "Keeping Quiet" and the Buddha sitting under the Bodhi tree. Kanho follows Bodhidharma's exchange with Emperor Wu, who asks what merit he has gained and hears "No merit," before Bodhidharma sits facing a wall for nine years. Practical instruction on posture comes next: the tripod of stability, the straight spine, the tucked chin, and the cosmic mudra, which Abbot Steve at Green Gulch once called out. Kanho then turns to thoughts, which are never stopped, and to counting the breath like loosely holding a puppy's leash. Two more Neruda poems close the evening, the last asking how long the rhinoceros lasts after being moved to compassion.

title: No Gaining Idea
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Suzuki Roshi's passage on practice without gaining ideas from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, read alongside the Heart Sutra's line that form is form and emptiness is emptiness. Nomon sets the book against the earlier Zen of D.T. Suzuki and Philip Kapleau's Three Pillars of Zen, with its dramatic awakenings, and adds the Three Doors of Liberation, especially wishlessness. The story of Baoshou fanning himself from Genjokoan asks why practice continues when the wind already reaches everywhere. Nomon ends with a flash of jealousy on Facebook over a friend's retreat at Hollyhock, which tightens, then releases into freedom again.

title: Sesshin Opening Sesshin
speaker: Hoka Chris Fortin
summary: Hoka Chris Fortin takes up the Vimalakirti Sutra through Joan Sutherland's commentary on the eve of an ordination, beginning with Vimalakirti sick in a ten-by-ten room that holds 32,000 beings. Hoka recalls Norman Fischer's three points for ordination (humility, service, seeing each person as Buddha), then reads Suzuki Roshi's story of the boy Oka Sotan, who runs back to the tofu shop shouting "give me" for a hat already on his head. A verse from Katagiri Roshi, Blanche Hartman's comments on it, and Dogen's four methods of guidance follow. Hoka closes with a Soto Zen Buddhist Association living statement and the question of what the robes, the ritual, and the practice period are for.

title: Practice Period Opening Sesshin at Sansui-Ji Temple
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the practice period by taking up its theme of committed lay practice, reading the start of the Ugra Paripriccha Sutra in Thich Nhat Hanh's The Bodhisattva Path, where the Buddha tells the lay practitioner Ugra how to take refuge in Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Nomon reworks each refuge, hearing "remember that you are Buddha" and finding that sharing the Dharma completes it, and admits that the sutra's dig at the Śrāvaka path mirrors the small judgments Zen practitioners make of one another. Nomon then tells of Maggie Weisberg, who began meditating in her 90s at the Willows retirement community in Bellingham, turned construction noise on her deck into an orchestra of sound, and died at 101 by her own chosen date. Nomon closes with the last paragraph of her reflections, ending on the cactus on the windowsill and the sunset painting the sky.

title: Self Power and Other Power
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the self-power and other power pair, jiriki and tariki, to ask why Zen keeps chanting and bowing when meditation looks like the practice that does the work. Nomon then hands out a worksheet and goes character by character through the Chinese of the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, from the title and the name Kanzeon to the lines "with Buddha, I cause" and the repeated nen, thought or mindfulness. Small groups draft their own English versions, including one that plays on the character for joy also meaning music. Nomon closes by comparing five published translations, the Zen Community of Oregon's among the freest, and settles on its last line, "Time after time there's nothing but this."

title: A Temple of Paramitas
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the six paramitas (generosity, ethics, patience, energy, concentration, and wisdom) and finds them at work in the newly remodeled Bellingham building where the sangha is sitting. Nomon looks closest at four: the donors and volunteer hours, a six-month construction estimate that ran into late August, and the image of one hand pulling a splinter from the other without deciding to give. Along the way Nomon notes that Norman Fischer calls energy "enthusiastic energy" and Reb Anderson calls it "heroic effort." In the discussion, a participant asks where ethics and wisdom live, and another tells of giving away a jade ring bought for herself.

title: What are your intentions? (Opening the Temple)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to a set of Dogen poems for the opening of the new temple, going through them one by one with brief comments. The waterfowl leave no ripples, waves break on a pale moon, a white heron hides in snowy grass, and a scarecrow guards a mountain rice paddy without knowing its worth. Nomon ties the white heron to the Lojong slogan "Don't expect applause," and the scarecrow to the five remembrances, offering "My actions light up the world" as a gentler last line. The Lotus Sutra poem leads to Costco as a place where the Dharma is preached. The evening closes with the seasons poem, the question of why each person came, and groups of three.

title: Despair and the Bodisattva Vow
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up despair and the bodhisattva vow as a tribute to Joanna Macy, reading from the "Despair Work" chapter of Macy's World as Lover, World as Self and a poem, "The Healing Time" by Pesha Gertler. IkuShun names IkuShun's own steps: acknowledging fear and sorrow, accepting the state of the planet, keeping joy alongside grief, and resting on the vow. IkuShun recalls Thich Nhat Hanh taking his monks and nuns to the ocean after 9/11, and a Jataka tale of the Buddha as a plumeria tree, which IkuShun's teacher answered with "you're a bodhisattva now." IkuShun closes with the Elm Dance, which Macy carried to grieving women in Novozybkov after Chernobyl, and gives the dance's basic steps.

title: A Tribute to Joanna Macy
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up "The Hidden Lamp" poem by Laywoman Chen, who sees old woodcutters on the high slopes with the spirit of the knife and axe while mountain flowers glow red in the water, and pairs it with Joanna Macy's commentary, offered in tribute days after Macy's death. Seiu describes Macy's outrage and opposition, then Chen's turn toward what the woodcutters are missing. Seiu brings in an Auckland Zen Center talk on the three poisons and Peter Coyote's June 18 post on staging a protest with discipline, quiet, and clean clothes. Small groups take up a prompt: can we witness wilderness without taking something away from it?

title: Precept Eight - Non-Being Stingy
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the eighth precept, non-being stingy, through Nancy Baker's word "tight" and a body exercise in which listeners squeeze themselves shut and try to reach out, soften the heart, and take a breath. Myoki names the many forms of stinginess (money, time, heart, gratitude, receiving compliments) and pairs this precept with non-greed, using Diane Rosenblum's merged wording and Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise on life's abundance, such as a weed pushing through a sidewalk crack. Myoki closes the precept series with the literal, relative, and absolute levels of practice, then sends everyone to breakout rooms with two questions: "Tell me your way you're stingy" and "What do you believe is lacking?"

title: Precept Ten - Non-Abusing the Three Treasures
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the sixteenth Bodhisattva Precept, non-abusing the three treasures, through Nancy Mujo Baker's chapter and Bodhidharma's line about not raising a distinction between Buddhas and sentient beings. Nomon offers "rejoicing" as the positive side of the precept, then describes a grouchy, hunched work party at the temple under construction, where the tension eases by the next morning. Upstairs, the stored boxes of dusty, jumbled belongings become a heap of gold, the aspirations and generosity of thousands of people. Nomon suggests catching yourself being Buddha, the way a parent catches a child being good. The session ends with a monologue exercise in groups of three about times of closeness to the three treasures.

title: Invisible Scars and the Dharma of Women
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens with a Gina Puorro poem, then describes a 1980 study by Kleck and Strenta in which subjects wearing a fake facial scar, secretly removed before they met strangers, reported negative reactions that never happened. Kanho connects this to the Matilda effect, citing Trota of Salerno, whose books were credited to men, and to a childhood with a mother who wanted an invisible, obedient daughter. Quoting Dogen on carrying the self forward, Kanho names zazen as the place where invisible scars find space to speak, sometimes as months of tears. The closing returns to the poet's line "fire is sparking from my tongue," with the dharma's answer: let it burn.

title: The Womb and the Sword
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up women, the womb, and the sword, opening with Maya Angelou's poem "Phenomenal Woman." Kanho sets the childbearing role of women beside Mahapajapati Gotami, who walked hundreds of miles with 500 women to ask the Buddha for ordination. Kanho then tells of warrior women including Boudica, Tomoe Gozen, Grace O'Malley, and Nakano Takeko. These stories work like koans, and Kanho asks how to meet them without clinging or aversion. After closing with Oriah Mountain Dreamer's poem "The Invitation," Kanho takes questions on violence and nonviolence, and recounts how Grace O'Malley divorced a husband under Irish law by throwing his clothes out the window.

title: Precept Six - Non-talking about Others' Errors and Faults
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the sixth precept, non-disparagement of others, opening with Dogen's line about getting dirty to embrace beings mired in the mud. Myoki describes growing up in a critical household and taking on a home practice from Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise: noticing each critical thought, which turns up hundreds of times a day. Along the way come Nancy Baker's four ways of practicing with the precept, Diane Rizzetto's idea of "freezing" a person after a friend stands you up for coffee, and the habit of assuming others' motives. Myoki closes with Reb Anderson's Being Upright, where facing one's own afflictions kindly and staying upright reveals interdependence, and trust follows naturally.

title: Precept Seven - Non-Elevating One's Self and Blaming Others
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Precepts Six and Seven, not disparaging others and being humble, as two sides of one coin rooted in comparison and ranking. Nomon draws on a yoga class where the teacher says not to look around, Paul Warrick's advice to see oneself as neither better, worse, nor the same as others, and a student's remark that "it's difficult when I want." Norman Fischer's advice to new priests (be humble, try to help, see everyone as Buddha) and poems by David Budbill and Derek Walcott join a story of silent-retreat judgments that vanish when the person finally speaks. The session closes with a breakout exercise on the question "What makes you do it?"

title: Reflections of the Mind
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens with a Gina Poro poem, "The wild will call you back," then takes up Yogacara and the Lankavatara Sutra, telling of a crashed OpenOffice file that took Kanho's written talk and every backup with it. Kanho lays out the eight consciousnesses, with Manas as the clinging "I" maker and Alaya-vijnana as the storehouse that can become great mirror wisdom, and compares that change to a compost heap turning into dark soil. Kanho's example of aliens who watch Monty Python's Holy Grail and arrive expecting killer rabbits shows how projection works. Kanho closes with Lankavatara practices, including compassion for other people's projections, and a second poem.

title: Taking the Backward Step
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens by reading Mary Oliver's poem "Have You Ever Tried to Enter the Long Black Branches," then takes up Dogen's instruction to "learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself." Kanho admits to reading the line many times without understanding it, until one evening it opened. Kanho describes the "forward step" of chasing outcomes, reacting from habit, and seeing separation everywhere, and sets it beside the Genjokoan image of a boat on an ocean that only looks circular. Zazen becomes the backward step, with practice and enlightenment as one word and the map never the territory. A closing poem, "Peaceful Life," ends on practicing right here, now, as living in vows.

title: Blanche Hartman, Woman Ancestor
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells stories about Zenkei Blanche Hartman, a teacher from San Francisco Zen Center, and reads from the book of her collected teachings. Nomon recalls meeting Blanche at Green Gulch Farm, her story of Suzuki Roshi's rage when she said she was learning to do zazen, and her sharp answer that zazen has nothing to do with friendliness when asked whether the cushions should face in or out. That exchange leads Nomon to describe two paths in Zen, healing and transformation. At Tassajara, Blanche takes off her robes and says "Hand me a wrench" to help fix the failed water system, missing a period of zazen. Nomon ends with her words on cultivating kindness and on waking up again and again.

title: The Wisdom of Kanzeon
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the ten-line Kanzeon Sutra through Uchiyama Roshi's commentary, starting with the line "permanent, blissful, self, undefiled," which seems to reverse impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Norman links the chant to Thanksgiving, since praising Buddha and giving thanks both remember that everything is a gift, and reads "thoughts arising from life" as every thought already being Kanzeon. Space becomes the next image: zazen lets suffering be held in spaciousness, as at Samish, where the open lawn and a circling bald eagle fill the sky. Norman closes with the deaths of Layman Pang's family, the daughter going first during an eclipse and the son dying standing at his hoe.

title: Opening the Hand of Thought
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads Molly Bloom's closing soliloquy from Ulysses on Bloomsday, then turns to Uchiyama Roshi's forthcoming book The Sound That Perceives the World. Starving and frozen while making charcoal in the wartime mountains, Uchiyama suddenly finds himself chanting "Namo Kanzeon Bosatsu," a practice rooted in the Lotus Sutra's Kannon chapter. Norman links that chant to Uchiyama's phrase "opening the hand of thought," where the robin hears you as you hear it and self and other stop standing apart. For anyone who cannot manage zazen, Norman offers the breath as Kanzeon, and ends with breathing through the dentist's pulling of a wisdom tooth.

title: Miaozhong on Silence
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen returns to Miaozhong, the 12th-century Chinese Buddhist nun and abbess, reading from her first address as an abbess and from her verse commentaries on koans such as "The World Honored One Ascends His Seat." Miaozhong's line that sages transmit nothing leads Myoki to Dogen's backwards step in Fukanzazengi and to silence as the heart of practice. Two examples illustrate it: years of sitting with a sangha known only in silence, and a wordless hug with a Dharma brother at a sesshin in Arizona. Myoki also separates the external silence of sesshin from the inner quiet of zazen. Reb Anderson's advice to take refuge in the silence, which Myoki copied onto cards placed around home and office, leads into small-group questions about seeking or avoiding silence.

title: What do you call the world?
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up case 12 of the Book of Serenity, in which the monk Xiushan asks what can be done about the world and Dizang, who plants fields and cooks rice, answers, "What do you call the world?" Norman sets the case beside the An Lushan Rebellion, when burned monasteries sent the Chan ancestors to the mountains to sit and plant, and beside a large protest the sangha skipped to sit in silence. Norman lists what a person can do, from running for office to making protest signs, and then describes the Buddhist three worlds of desire, form, and formlessness. Norman closes on sesshin's one shirt and simple food, where nothing is missing.

title: Breathing Deeply, Master Zhiyi's Meditation Instructions
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Book of Serenity Case 3, in which the ancestor Prajnatara answers a king's question about reading scripture by describing his breathing, and turns to Master Zhiyi's meditation manual for its first two dharma gates, counting and following.
