Nomon recalls learning breath counting as a young man, and Zenkei Blanche Hartman's suggestion to count down from ten to one. Blanche's own story follows: she tells Suzuki Roshi she is getting the hang of zazen, and he cuts her off with "You don't do zazen. Zazen does zazen." Zhiyi's remedies for sinking and floating come next, with awareness raised to the tip of the nose or lowered to the navel. Nomon closes by saying the bell does not end zazen.

title: Precept Five - Non-Misusing Intoxicants
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells how a missing copy of Nancy Baker's precepts book, which turns out to be propping up a projector in the office, sets off a blaming mind state that Nomon recognizes as an intoxicant. Baker's chapter on non-misusing intoxicants centers on addictive mind states, and Nomon pairs it with a Costa Rica retreat where a student in recovery skipped the last-night party, plus Nomon's own pull toward a beer. Norman Fischer's wedding-ceremony line that sharing spirits moderately "may be all right" frames the flexible reading, and the Three Marks of Existence point to the self as the deepest intoxicant. Nomon closes with the kalpa image of a bird wearing down a granite mountain with a silk scarf.

title: Moshan Liaoran
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Moshan Liaoran, a ninth-century Chinese woman teacher, through her encounter with the monk Guanxi, who arrives at her mountain refusing to bow or remove his traveling hat, as told in The Hidden Lamp. Seishu reads the exchange along with Shinshu Roberts's commentary on meeting life as it presents itself, then adds similar words from Jetsunma Tenzin Palmo and Charlotte Joko Beck. A surprise tax bill in February becomes Seishu's example: Seishu and Carolyn pay it from savings and mail the check, skipping the old round of blaming the accountant, the IRS, and corporations that dodge taxes. Seishu credits those teachers and years of daily sitting for catching sooner the moment a reaction is making things worse.

title: Kisa Gotami and Patacara – Grief, Suffering and the Path Forward
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose tells the stories of two first-generation women disciples of the Buddha, Kisa Gotami and Patacara, drawing on the Therigatha and the Dhammapada commentary. Joden recounts Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed, then Patacara's story: eloping from a seven-story tower, then losing her husband to a cobra, her sons to an eagle and a river, and her parents and brother to a collapsed house, until she wanders naked and mad to the Buddha. She calms, ordains, and awakens while pouring water from a pot over her feet and watching a lamp go out. Joden closes by asking how the Buddha listened and how practice helps with grief, then sends the group into small discussions.

title: Life, Death, Time, Place
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny reads "Today," a poem written long ago, and uses it to trace how life, death, time, and place led to Bellingham. The path runs through Emerson and Thoreau's call to spend a day deliberately, a 1980 road trip that ends at Green Gulch, and a Bodhidharma sticker on Tim's van dashboard. Reizan recalls the first sitting group on Harris Street, the sauna shack, and the 1993 Lummi Island retreat where Norman served food to each mat. Thirty-five years on this land bring Tammy's paintings, the idea of sleeping on the ground, and the bow hunter's still hunting, moving slowly like a deer. Reizan closes by inviting everyone into zazen and asking them to sneak back when the han sounds.

title: Precept Two - Non-Stealing
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the second precept, non-stealing, beginning with Nancy Baker's line that sitting meditation is the practice of "nothing to get." Myoki pairs it with the giving-and-receiving of the yin yang symbol and the meal chant's "emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver and gift." Everyday stealing gets a long list: pirated movies, padded bills, wasted time, extra napkins grabbed for the car. Beneath the grabbing, Myoki finds fear of scarcity and a sense of lack, and also the stinginess of holding back. Myoki tells of folding yoga blankets with a teacher after Yin yoga, and closes by setting up paired questions, "Tell me something you steal" and "Tell me a way you experience lack."

title: Precept Three - Non-Misusing Sex
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the precept of non-misusing sexuality through Diane Eshin Rizzetto's book Waking Up to What You Do, which phrases it as "I take up the way of engaging in sexual intimacy respectfully and with an open heart." Nomon reads a student's version that meets craving and the fear of craving, closeness and the fear of closeness, and sees this precept drawing on all the others. Along the way come a prayer for survivors of sexual violence, the remark that sex takes eighty years to learn, and a drop in teenage pregnancies from sixty-two per thousand in 1991 to thirteen in 2022. A guided meditation on sexual energy leads into paired sharing, five minutes each, with three sentence starters in the chat.

title: Chinoyo
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up Chiyono, the thirteenth-century Japanese nun credited as the first woman abbess in Japan, and a second nun at Tokeiji who meditated on Chiyono's poem. Chiyono, grieving her husband, awakens when the bottom of a mended bucket gives way and the moon's reflection drains out with the water. The second nun's poem finds the moon multiplied in every rain puddle, which leads Shin-yu to the false self and to a 7-Eleven stop where a big man in a huge pickup turns out to want only to ask about the mileage on a Toyota Yaris. Shin-yu closes by reading Dogen's passage on the original face from Shobogenzo Zuimonki twice, followed by quiet sitting and small-group discussion.

title: Miaoxin and the Characteristic of Confidence
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up the story of Miaoxin, the ninth-century student of Yangshan, as Dogen tells it in the "Raihai Tokuzui" fascicle of the Shobogenzo. Seventeen monks lodging at her office argue over Huineng's wind and banner, and Miaoxin calls them blind donkeys, then asks them to "come forward" before she answers. IkuShun draws on Grace Schireson's commentary, including Grace's leap into the ocean to reach a frightened boy while adults shouted from shore. IkuShun adds a missed answer in dokusan about a bird song, and the chanting advice of Sojun Mel Weitsman. The evening closes with two questions for small groups: what moves me, and how to meet the ancient teachings so they stay alive.

title: Precept One - Non-Killing
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first of the ten grave precepts, non-killing, through Nancy Mujo Baker's chapter on the precepts. Nomon points out that the Chinese character behind "clear mind" actually means grave or weighty, and that Baker's preference for "non-killing" over "not killing" makes it a practice. Nomon moves from the impossibility of living without killing, such as eating, weeding the garden, and burning fossil fuels, to Baker's view that the precept concerns separation and connection. Judging others or diminishing their spirits counts as killing too. Nomon offers Norman Fischer's wording, "protects life," alongside "nourishing life," and closes with a guided reflection on welcoming every part of oneself, including the part that messes up.

title: Maiozong's Fearlessness and Vulnerability
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up Miaozong, the twelfth-century Chinese Buddhist nun and abbess, and reads her story "Miaozong's Dharma Interview" from The Hidden Lamp. Myoki first sketches her life: a scholarly family, an arranged marriage, a reply to a questioning master asking whether the Dharma is divided into male and female forms, and Dahui's remark that she is like a ship blocked in a harbor. In the interview, Miaozong lies naked before the disapproving monk Wan'an and says all the Buddhas came out of this place. Myoki links that nakedness to zazen and to Suzuki Roshi's "Zen is Zen when you are you," then closes with the paramita of fearlessness and asks how each listener practices it.

title: The Warrior in All of Us
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up Kakusan Shidō, the thirteenth-century founder of Tokeiji Convent, whose story from The Hidden Lamp has her drawing a ten-inch dagger before her teacher during the transmission ceremony. IkuShun reads Laura del Valle's commentary on that story, including del Valle's boot-camp Rinzai training in Mexico City and the day she drove a mother to bring her children back from the father. From there, IkuShun recalls speaking up for patients as a diabetes educator and asks where courage comes from, returning to del Valle's line about cutting off the fear of self-concern. IkuShun closes with a conversation with a teacher about Rosa Parks, whose clarity may have left no room for choice.

title: Baddha Kundalakesa
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan tells the story of Baddha Kundalakesa, a woman ancestor from the Therigatha who lived in Magadha around 500 BCE, as part of Seiu's continuing practice of honoring women ancestors. Baddha falls for a thief she has pardoned, survives his attempt to throw her off a cliff for her jewelry, and becomes a Jain renunciate whose hair grows back curly. Over fifty years of wandering she becomes a famed debater who marks each town with a sand pile and a rose apple stick. Seiu connects this to Zen mondo and shosan. Baddha falls silent when Shariputra asks "What is the one?" and he takes her to the Buddha. Seiu closes with her death poem about kissing every inch of every road, then offers two questions for small groups.

title: Women Ancestors, Known and Unknown
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart reads from the Therigatha, the poems of the elder nuns, and tells the stories of two women, Ambapali and Kisa Gotami. Kanho describes Ambapali, the celebrated courtesan of Vesali, who wins the Buddha's meal over the Licchavi nobles because she was there first, then reads her poem cataloguing the losses of age, each verse closing on the refrain that the truth speaker's words do not change. Kisa Gotami carries her dead child from house to house in search of a mustard seed from a home untouched by death, and finds none. In the discussion that follows, one participant hears Ambapali's refrain as a victory song.

title: The Three Pure Precepts
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett and Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett and Myoki Raizelah Bayen open a precepts class built on Nancy Baker's Opening to Oneness and the Three Pure Precepts. Myoki describes the precepts as intrinsic to awakened reality, and recalls telling Norman Fischer before Jukai that they were impossible and hearing that practicing them is like walking toward the horizon. Nomon tells the Yunmen koan, "an appropriate response," traces the three precepts to Dhammapada verse 185 and Reb Anderson's reading of embracing forms and ceremonies, and leads the sangha in chanting the Red Cedar wording three times. Small groups then work with two repeated questions, beginning with "Tell me a way you hide from yourself and stay unconscious."

title: Women in Zen: Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells the story of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī asking the Buddha three times to let women go forth, and being refused each time. Kanho begins by passing around the women's lineage document, which came about after a weeping student asked Zoketsu Norman Fischer in dokusan where the women ancestors were. Gautamī cuts her hair and arrives with swollen feet, Ananda pleads her case, and she is admitted on eight conditions. Kanho then reads from the Therigatha, with verses by Kema, Visakha, Upalavanna, and Soma, and closes with Sona, Mother of Ten, who spits on old age, and Kanda the beggar, ordained by Patacara.

title: Taking Refuge in the Triple Treasures
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the practice of taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha at a one-day sitting retreat, drawing on Okumura's Living by Vow and John Daido Loori's The Heart of Being. Myoki traces refuge to the Pali sarana gamana, a return to a safe place like a child running into a parent's arms, and reads a refuge statement written fifteen years ago that still sits on the home altar. Loori's three views of the treasures (unified, manifested, abiding) lead to Nancy Baker's point that we take refuge as the three treasures. Myoki closes with Dogen in his death room, walking around a pillar and chanting Buddha, Dharma, Sangha.

title: Everyday Vowing: Renunciation and Repentance
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up the bodhisattva vow and the vow of repentance on a day named On Vows. Seiu opens with the troubles of the present moment, recalling Edward R. Murrow in the film Good Night and Good Luck, then turns to Seiu's teacher Kathy's view that vow is who we already are, and to Ruth Ozeki's image of letting others onto the elevator first. Seiu offers self-care for hard times: walking to the water, playing with a pet, and remembering Seiu's cat Angie, who rested against Seiu's neck after Seiu's ankle replacement. Seiu then reads Suzuki Roshi on taking vows moment by moment and describes formal and formless repentance, closing on the line "Come, even if you have broken your vow a hundred times."

title: Practicing in Troubled Times
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the USAID funding freeze, which reaches Nomon through photos and news from Marcy Okumu, Nomon's Kenyan daughter, whose Save the Children job is suddenly in doubt. Nomon recalls visiting her brother Maxwell's farm, where withered corn grew 50 yards from a canal until the sangha raised about $600 for a pump, and reads Atul Gawande's account of the programs the freeze halted. Turning to how to respond, Nomon describes an upset that shifted from righteousness to curiosity, recalls the three reminders given at ordination (be humble, see everyone as Buddha, try to help), and reads Wendell Berry's poem "The Real Work." Nomon closes by asking how each listener is already responding, just before the sangha chants its bodhisattva vow.

title: Ananda Says Yes! Keizan's Denkoroku, talk3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the third story in Keizan's Denkoroku, the case of Ananda and Kasyapa, in which Ananda asks what was transmitted beyond the gold brocade robe. Kasyapa calls "Ananda," Ananda answers "Yes," and Kasyapa tells Ananda to topple the flagpole in front of the gate. Nomon first describes the women patrons who supported Keizan, then Ananda's long yearning and his tears before the first council. Nomon recalls working with this "Yes" for years with Norman Fischer, until a flagpole clinking at Samish Island and Norman's sudden "Tim" in dokusan. The evening closes on a silent sit with the question "When do you listen?"

title: Everyday Tea and Rice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the opening of Dogen's Kajo, which names drinking tea and eating rice as the activity of the Buddha ancestors, and offers bagels and coffee as a stand-in. Nomon then walks through the koan in which Daokai asks Touzi whether there are teachings beyond everyday tea and rice, and Touzi covers the student's mouth with a whisk and announces thirty blows. A hug or a cup of tea that stops an argument becomes an image for how a physical interruption brings someone back into the body. Nomon closes with Domyo Burk's two mindsets about practice and Dogen's advice to leap clear of both the ordinary and the special.

title: Our Ancestor, Keizan
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces Keizan Jokin, the second founder of Soto Zen, and opens a year of study on Keizan's Transmission of the Light (Denko Roku) by reading its first chapter, on Shakyamuni Buddha, in full. Nomon explains why the book stayed obscure for centuries, kept as a sacred object on hidden altars, and tells of a young monk at Eiheiji whose job was bringing Dogen's spirit a meal each day. The chapter's line about awakening together with the great earth leads into Keizan's play on "I" and "together with," which Nomon calls mind yoga. Nomon closes on suffering as the sign of a sticky "I," and the relief when the penny drops again.

title: Valley Sounds, Mountain Colors
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Dogen's fascicle Keisei Sanshoku, "Valley Sounds, Mountain Colors," from the sangha's Dogen reading group. Kanho reads Su Dongpo's poem about hearing the valley stream as the Buddha's long broad tongue, then the stories of Xiangyan, who burns his books and wakes when a swept pebble strikes bamboo, and Lingyun, who sees peach blossoms in bloom. Following Dogen, Kanho says that sounds and colors are the teaching itself, and that chasing a dramatic awakening overlooks it. Kanho suggests pausing each day to hear traffic, birds, and breath, and closes with Dogen's vow to hear the true Dharma in every birth.

title: Practicing with Love in a Broken World
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Alberto Rios's poem "Something is always broken," then plays a short talk by Hogen Bayes of Great Vow Zen Monastery that offers four perspectives for meeting the fallout of a national election: calm the body, understand causes, respond in the present, help others. Nomon adds what Hogen's words leave out: deep not-knowing, our own blind spots, and the insult of telling trauma survivors to calm down. Nomon then turns to the rakusu ceremony from Sunday, and to a doctor's remark about never having gone to graduate school. Nomon ends hoping that ritual steps heal and never divide.

title: Practice is Everywhere (Fall Samish Sesshin talk two)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up two practices that happen outside the zendo, dokusan and oryoki, and turns to Dogen's essay on the tenzo, the head cook. At the center is Dogen's story of meeting the sixty-one-year-old tenzo of Mount Ayuwang on a ship in China, where the old cook buys mushrooms and refuses to stay for tea because tomorrow's meal needs him. Nomon recalls Edie, bent by scoliosis, answering "if not me, who?" when asked to sit down, and thanks Bob Rose as three assistant tenzos take up the ladle. Prajnatara's practice of exhaling without following conditions and inhaling without dwelling leads to tomorrow's Jukai ceremony for six students.

title: Practicing with What's Here (Fall Samish Sesshin talk one)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's dharma hall discourses from the Eihei Koroku to ask what sesshin shows about practicing with whatever is here. Nomon describes how the quiet makes judgment, the longing to be seen, and the clouds of theory easy to see through, and how a week of sitting makes impermanence felt rather than merely agreed with. Dogen's address on returning to his monastery after months teaching a samurai patron, his verse on the ox herder coming home, and a prayer for clear skies during endless rain follow. Nomon closes on that last piece: the record never says whether the rains stopped, and Buddha's way is Buddha's activity.

title: Dogen's Japan Journals, Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns for the third and last time to the journal of Dogen's years in China with his teacher Rujing, found undated among Dogen's papers after his death by his attendant Ejo. Nomon reads practical instructions on the tongue, the open eyes, and walking in a straight line beginning with the right foot, then Rujing's teaching that the zazen of Buddha ancestors carries compassion and the vow to awaken all beings, which arhats and shravakas lack. Rujing's poem "Windbell," about a mouth hanging in emptiness, follows, along with Dogen's beginner question about what emptiness is and Rujing's answer that emptiness is prajna, not a lack of form. Nomon closes with Ejo's colophon, in which Ejo copies the draft in tears in 1253, and then opens the floor for discussion.

title: Dogen's Japan Journals, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the second installment of Dogen's Hokyoki, the journal of Dogen's exchanges with the Chinese teacher Rujing, opening with a newsletter by Ryan Dowd about tending the small fire of hope and a dark morning jog through Cornwall Park, where owls and migrating snow geese become Nomon's kindling. Nomon reads Rujing's long list of things to avoid, from onions and music to staring at big fish, and Katagiri Roshi's poem "A Peaceful Life." Dogen's question whether the nature of things is good, bad, or neutral gets Rujing's answer that the Buddha Dharma goes beyond all three. The evening closes with small groups asking how to practice in the dark.

title: Dogen's Japan Journals, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Hōkyōki, Dogen's record of his years in China, in the translation by Kazuaki Tanahashi and Norman Fischer. Nomon traces the text's uncertain history, from Eijo finding it after Dogen's death to the question of whether it was written late in life. Nomon then reads Dogen's letter asking Rujing for informal access, and Rujing's replies on "transmission outside the teaching" and on future births, including the land of Uttarakuru, where unrelenting pleasure keeps anyone from hearing the Dharma. Nomon pairs these with the Genjokoan story of Baoche fanning himself though wind reaches everywhere, then sends small groups of three off to talk about asking for help.

title: If It Is Without Love, It Is Not The Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the precepts as Jukai approaches, reading Tenshin Reb Anderson's translation of the three collective pure precepts and the ten grave precepts from Being Upright. Wise words received at a time of need anchor the evening: "if it is without love, it is not the precepts." Kanho admits that the precepts get broken all the time, then turns to the okesa and rakusu, Dogen's Kesa Kudoku, and Ben Conley's account of Tomoe Katagiri bringing robe sewing to America in 1971. A participant is puzzled by such reverence for a robe first sewn from rags. Kanho answers that taking refuge makes any clothing Buddha's robe, and that a practitioner in blue jeans and a t-shirt is no less a practitioner.

title: Opening to Joy
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan tells of a 2016 trip to Rinso-in in Japan, where Hoitsu, son of Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, recalls a father who threw him in the pond for forgetting his schoolwork, then ends with the words "Practice with joy." Seiu brings in James Baraz's picture of the brain as Teflon for good experiences and Velcro for bad, and asks the room to call out what brings them joy. The center is mudita, sympathetic joy, one of the four Brahmaviharas, along with Seiu's memories of measuring up against others and a guided practice that moves from oneself to a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person, and all beings. The closing names Dogen's three minds and Kate, who shows joy in how she appreciates others' good fortune.

title: The Verse of Repentance
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the Verse of Repentance, chanting it with the group three times. Myoki reads "beginningless greed, hate, and delusion" as the karma of everyone before and after, and tells of writing an apology email to an ex-husband after seeing a habit of blame and criticism learned in a harsh, perfectionist household. Drawing on Reb Anderson's Being Upright, Myoki distinguishes formal repentance, an apology to another person, from formless repentance, which addresses the separate self's work of protecting itself. The verse becomes an acknowledgment of being human, though being human excuses nothing. Groups of three follow, with five-minute monologues on a hurtful act and what repentance would look like.

title: Mountains and Waters
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra, chanted on a trail below Mount Baker, and then tells the Native story of Jumping Mouse. A group member, Kit, connected the sutra to that story, which Nomon first heard from Gary Bacon, a teacher in a small alternative high school program. In the story, a mouse who hears a roaring no one else notices meets Raccoon and Frog, sees the sacred mountains, and is renamed. Along the way he gives both eyes to a dying buffalo and a forgetful wolf, and ends as an eagle. Nomon invites the room to circle up and ask where the story mirrors their own lives.

title: Dogen's Places
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells the story of Dogen's life by place, moving from Mount Hiei and Kennin-ji to China, Koshoji, and Eiheiji. Mary Oliver's poem about setting out to save the only life one can save frames the telling, and Kanho reads from Dogen at each stop, including Valley Sounds, Mountain Colors, One Bright Pearl, Old Mirror with Guotai's answer "An old mirror," and Continuous Practice with Facang's hut. Along the way come the twelve-year-old Dogen running off to the monastery, the lord Hatano Yoshishige giving land for Eiheiji, and Kanho's admission that no record explains why Dogen left Kyoto. Dogen's death poem, written on a follower's wall in 1253, leads into a second Oliver poem about goldfinches in a field of thistles.

title: Dogen's Instructions to the Cook
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up Dogen's Tenzo Kyokun, the instructions to the cook, and reads it through Joden's own eight years as tenzo for Red Cedar Zen. Joden draws on Uchiyama Roshi's commentary How to Cook Your Life, then tells two stories: the Ayuwang tenzo who walks fourteen miles to buy mushrooms and back so the next meal is made well, and the sixty-eight-year-old monk Lu drying mushrooms in the scorching sun. Joden sets Dogen's distress at the neglect of meals in Japan beside a week in a monastery kitchen with no altar or blessing, then turns to big, parental, and joyous mind. It closes with a question for groups of three: how do you make the best of whatever greens you have?

title: Fascicle Number 93 - Birth and Death
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Dogen's short fascicle "Birth and Death" from the Shobogenzo, reading all of it aloud, including the closing paragraph copied into the Zen notebook of Seishu. Seishu draws two themes from it: face whatever arises without avoiding or clinging, and find nirvana inside ordinary day-to-day life, which Seishu links to Suzuki Roshi's quotes and a remark by Norman Fischer. Seishu then describes Seishu's father, born in 1912 and raised Catholic, who stayed kind and calm in traffic and content through dementia and a walker. The father's last words to Seishu were "It's okay to die if you've had a good life." Seishu closes by reading Uli Kay's poem "Particles of You" twice.

title: The Self That is Only the Self
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up Dogen's Bendoa through Uchiyama Roshi's commentary, translated by Shohaku Okumura, and asks what "the self that is only the self" means. IkuShun reads on Jijuyu Zanmai, self-fulfillment dharma joy samadhi, and describes sitting on a mountain deck beside a spouse, each living in a different world of pines and wind. Thich Nhat Hanh's hamburger shows how distraction fills a life with concepts, and the four days after IkuShun's mother died reveal a deeper place of love that arrived unasked and passed. Dogen's questions about why the Buddha and Bodhidharma kept sitting lead to Uchiyama's closing line that practice and enlightenment are one.

title: Zazen, Non-duality and Interconnectedness
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up three Dogen fascicles, Fukanzazengi, Zazenshin, and Zenki, to look for what they share: the central place of zazen, the oneness of practice and enlightenment, and the interconnection of all things. After opening with care for Zelda's family and friends, Kanho reads the start of Zazenshin, where Yao Shan answers a monk's question about what to think in steadfast sitting with "Think not thinking," and Dogen criticizes students who treat zazen as mere calmness. From Zenki come life and death as each complete in its moment, along with the boat and shore image from Genjokoan. Kanho ends with the poem "The Wild Will Call You Back" and the four vows.

title: Mountains and Waters
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra from the Shobogenzo, dedicating it to the sangha's wilderness program and its hikers. Seiu reads the opening verses, including "the green mountains are always walking" and the stone woman who gives birth at night, beside the Su Tung Po poem said to have inspired the fascicle. Wendy Johnson chanting the sutra on the walk from Tassajara to Green Gulch, Qingyuan Weixin's mountains-as-mountains passage, and a short turn to water and "blue mind" fill out the middle. Seiu closes with Gary Snyder's poem "Atomic Dawn," in which a young Snyder on Mount St. Helens in August 1945 reads of Hiroshima and vows to fight against atomic destruction.

title: Limitation is a Doorway to the Unbound Self
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up a line from Dogen's Genjokoan, "in attachment, blossoms fall and in aversion weeds spread," and tells of noticing a preference for spaciousness over contraction while serving as Co-Eno at the Samish sesshin. Constant talk about a COVID policy and about coordinating with the other Co-Eno leaves Myoki feeling critical and controlling, and a breathing gatha for letting go backfires. In dokusan, Norman points to the bodhisattva heart beneath the critic, and Myoki connects this to Dogen's Fukanzazengi, Suzuki Roshi's Not Always So, Joan Sutherland's "endarkenment," and the yin-yang symbol. The session closes with a guided reflection and four-minute triads on the good intention beneath a contracted place in one's own life.

title: Dogen's Time and Reality
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up two fascicles from Dogen's Shobogenzo, Genjokoan and Uji, to look at reality and time. Kanho begins with Genjokoan's opening lines on studying the self and forgetting the self, then reads the opening of Uji, where "for the time being" runs from the highest peak to the sixteen-foot Buddha body. Dogen's claim that time and being are one is set against the clock-and-watch way of seeing past, present and future. Kanho reads a passage from the foreword to the Treasury of the True Dharma, where a dewdrop's depth is the moon's height and yesterday flows into today. Kanho closes by asking who we are beyond thoughts and feelings.

title: Trust in Mind - Part 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the teaching of no preferences from the Xinxin Ming and works with Case 43 of the Blue Cliff Record, where a monk asks Dongshan how to escape cold and heat. Norman reads Dongshan's five ranks poems in Thomas Cleary's translations, and the lotus in the fire leads to the messy reality of eating and the septic tanks at Norman's own house. Norman then sets the ranks aside and urges close study of one's own preferences, along with plain attention to body and breath. Norman closes with Sojun Roshi's image of crossing a desert, setting down baggage one step at a time and finding that everything needed lies under each footstep.

title: Points to Watch in Practicing the Way - Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Points to Watch in Practicing the Way
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the fourth chapter of Dogen's Gakudo Yojinshu, "Do Not Practice Buddha Dharma with a Gaining Mind," in Shohaku Okumura's translation. Nomon opens with the 1862 smallpox ship at Victoria and a study in which imagining someone's favorite vegetables restores the sense of that person as human. Dogen's advice to refrain from clinging and rejecting leads to the practice of noting, which Nomon applies to judgment, and to Dogen's warnings about fame, heard as comparing mind and hunger for validation. Using the Two Truths, Nomon asks whether to help a sobbing person in sesshin, and finds that walking past to the dining hall can be the kindest act, echoing the Xinxin Ming line "The wise do nothing at all."

title: Trust in Mind - Part 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads the whole Xinxin Ming in Red Pine's translation on Juneteenth, after Zhaozhou's challenge to a monastic who couldn't recite it, and then draws out a few lines. Norman recalls Layman Pong, his wife, and their daughter Lingzhao answering "difficult," "easy," and "neither" about the way, and offers "What is this?" as a practice to replace saying "not two." Presence turns out to be ungraspable, and the Dharma works like music, which Norman hears best in a language not Norman's own, as with the German Magic Flute. Norman closes with a poem written on returning to Tassajara in May.

title: Points to Watch in Practicing the Way - Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Points to Watch in Practicing the Way
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up chapters one through three of Dogen's Gakudo Yojinshu, "Points to Watch in Practicing the Way," after a morning of standing in the rain during sesshin. Chapter two borrows a line from Confucius about a loyal minister and a wise emperor, and Nomon reads the emperor as the stubborn conditioned mind, offering a story of letting go of resentment and unused zingers. Chapter three holds practice for its own sake alongside its rewards. Suzuki Roshi's "Mind Waves" in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind supplies the advice to make effort and then forget about it.

title: Trust in Mind - Part 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the opening lines of the Xinxinming (Trust in Mind) by Sengcan, "The true way is without difficulty, just avoid picking and choosing," and follows them through four Zhaozhou cases in the Blue Cliff Record. Norman traces suffering to grasping and rejecting, then offers equanimity as the way to meet each moment as it is. In case 57, Zhaozhou answers a monastic with the baby Buddha's words, then gets angry at the monastic's disrespect for himself. In case 59, Zhaozhou tells a monk who recalls only one line of the poem that the line is enough. Norman closes with a story in which one sits, one stands, and each sees the other.

title: Eihei Dogen's Kindness and Compassion
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Dogen's kindness and compassion, starting from the Zen saying "Drinking a cup of tea, I end the war," which Kanho now reads as ending a personal war with what is. Kanho admits to being lost on first reading Dogen, offers Steven Heine's five-step hermeneutic loop as a way to keep reading, and sets Hongzhi's poem Zazenshin beside Dogen's reinterpretation of it. Examples of compassion follow: Dogen's instructions for the cook, where no rice kernel is left behind, and the Buddha answering the same question with eight points for one listener and 108 for another. Kanho closes by reading Gina Poro's poem "Oh Death," in which Death invites a woman to dinner.

title: Points to Watch in Practicing the Way - Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Points to Watch in Practicing the Way
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the opening paragraph of Dogen's Gakudo Yojinshu, "Points to Watch in Practicing the Way," in Shohaku Okumura's translation, on the first day of sesshin. Nomon starts with the roles people hold in the zendo, telling of a devoted timekeeper who was upset at being rotated out, and of Fu, a fierce ino who became a gentle shuso. After a sketch of Dogen's life and the centuries his writings sat on altars unread, Nomon reads the chapter on arousing Bodhi mind as the mind that sees impermanence, and describes a Tendai marathon monk who stood for 49 days. Enjoying Laura's cooking is fine, since nobody needs a jar for the evening breeze.

title: The Dharma of Zen Poetry
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads "The Dharma of Zen Poetry," a talk by Deirdre Asho Peterson of Red Rocks Zen Circle in Sedona, which Nomon found while preparing retreat talks on the poet Ryokan. Peterson finds the three marks of existence running through poems by Han Shan, Ryokan, Isa, Li Po, Ikkyu and Basho. Isa's poem on his daughter's death ends with "This world is a dewdrop world. And yet." Nomon adds asides on Ryokan playing with children using string balls, and on Han Shan's invitation to "leap the world's ties." Peterson closes by urging Zen students not to put practice off.

title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 6)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster close their six-week class on the Surangama Sutra with its final section on the fifty demonic states that arise as practitioners loosen their hold on the five skandhas. IkuShun reads samples from each aggregate, including the "excess of severity in one's practice," where a meditator weeps over mosquitoes and worms, and ties it to a childhood scream over a squashed mosquito. Kanho adds a memory of sobbing through sesshin for no particular reason. Both return to the Buddha's calm in the face of Mara and to the warning against believing oneself a sage. Kanho describes a craving for a cookie that lasts only as long as it keeps getting refreshed, and IkuShun ends by posing right view as the question for discussion.

title: Dogen's Heart of the Way
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's short essay Doshin, "The Heart of the Way," from the Shobogenzo, after a run of announcements about a one day sit, a priest training completion ceremony for Ryusin Kate, and Dokusan. Nomon reads it in sections: seek out friends who have the true heart of the Way, keep impermanence in mind without obsessing, and chant the three refuges through the intermediary realms, in the womb, and at death. Nomon notes how conventional the text is, since Dogen leaves out the Pure Land chant, and then turns to the kashaya as a robe everyone wears, seen or unseen. Ryokan's poem about weeping over Dogen's records closes the reading, followed by small-group sharing on what the Dharma heart feels like.

title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 4)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster take up the closing chapters of the Surangama Sutra in this fourth class. IkuShun reads Avalokiteshvara's account of turning hearing inward, with its 32 forms and thousand arms, and connects those forms to skillful means and to meeting each patient where they are as a dietitian. IkuShun then reads Manjushri's verse and Xuan Hua's commentary, and sends the class to breakout rooms to compare reversing hearing with Dogen's backwards step. Kanho plays a recording of the Surangama mantra, then reads the Buddha's teaching that sexual desire binds beings to birth and death. Kanho closes by asking how sexual desire differs from hunger and tiredness.

title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 3)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster take up part four of the Surangama Sutra in the third class of their series. IkuShun reads the Buddha's account of how the world of illusion arises from adding understanding to understanding, and the parable of Yajnadatta, who runs madly from home after he loses his face in a mirror. IkuShun also tells of looking through a microscope with a young son and feeling more care for the creatures from the planter than for the blood cells. Kanho plays a gorilla video to show change blindness, then turns to Ananda's reliance on his senses and the Buddha's bell test, where the sound ends while hearing goes on.

title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 2)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster continue their class on the Surangama Sutra, with IkuShun working through Master Xuan Hua's commentary on visual awareness and Kanho turning to the matrix of the Thus Come One. IkuShun reads the image of the visitor and the innkeeper and the dust bobbing in a sunbeam, then sings a short song about a clear blue sky and passing clouds. Kanho reads Dogen's ocean passage from Genjokoan, explains why mindfulness falls short of true mind, and closes with Ananda's vow to wait while even one being has not become a Buddha. A participant's question about awareness sitting among the seven primary elements stays open.

title: Just As It Is
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up a passage from Dogen that begins "Thusness is the body and mind right now," reads it line by line, and then turns to Ruth Fuller Suzuki, whose Kyoto temple the group visited in Japan. The verb "arouse" signals active engagement, and a blade of grass or a speck of dust becomes a golden Buddha body or a shrine. Ruth, a wealthy Chicagoan turned Rinzai priest, led a translation team that included Gary Snyder and left the Rinzai Roku unfinished when she died in 1967. Tom Kirchner spent ten years completing it, then showed Nomon's group the room where the work happened. Nomon closes with Suzuki Roshi's grandson, who thanked the group for the chanting and bowing and never mentioned the zendo.

title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 1)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster open a multi-week class on the Surangama Sutra, with Kanho covering background and IkuShun reading from Part One. Kanho compares the sutra's red-pill question to a clip from The Matrix, sketches Buddha nature and Yogacara, and tells the sutra's opening, where Ananda is lured onto a woman's bed by a spell, as a reason scholars think it was written in China. IkuShun reads Ananda's proposals for where the mind sits, from inside the body to the middle, each refuted by the Buddha. The reading ends with the Buddha telling Ananda that the mind that makes distinctions is not his true mind, and the assembly falls silent.

title: Opening The Heart
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the opening lines of the Heart Sutra in an older talk, offered after a headache prevented writing a new one. Kanho goes through the unfamiliar terms one at a time: Avalokiteshvara, who becomes Kuan Yin in China; prajnaparamita, with perfection heard as contentment in practice; emptiness as empty of a separate, independent self; and dukkha as unease, illustrated by the Buddha's list from birth to the five clinging aggregates. Shariputra, the fall guy of Mahayana sutras, and the two meanings of dharma follow, then a "decoded" reading of the full opening passage. Kanho ends by asking how each listener will unfold the heart of the Heart Sutra.

title: Declaration of Interdependence
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart reads two poems, one that calls on us to release the myth of independence and one that imagines a woman sharing a last dinner with Death. Between them, Kanho describes a week of sesshin with the Everyday Zen community, led by Norman Fischer, where meditation kept circling interbeing and the blackened teeth on a bronze Manjushri's lion kept turning into an obsession with flossing. Plums from a neighbor, shipped from Chile, can't be returned to any tree, and a pig never needed lipstick. Both images lead to gratitude and to a body replaced every seven years. Kanho ends by saying the second poem means a new book of poems to buy.

title: The Teachings of Sojun Mel Weitsman
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the teachings of Mel Weitsman, drawing on Weitsman's book Seeing One Thing Through and his writings on Zen forms, bowing, and the balance of active and passive effort in meditation. Seishu describes a five-day retreat where thoughts tripled the pain in Seishu's knees, and a three-day airport delay met with patience. Weitsman's instruction to pick up a cup of tea with both hands leads into small practices of full attention at meals, driving, and listening. Seishu also relays Gil Fronsdal's account of Weitsman staying calm through the 1983 San Francisco Zen Center scandal, and closes on Norman Fischer's words: "always reliable, always kind, always patient."

title: Fukanzazengi, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Eihei Dogen's Fukanzazengi, the short zazen manual in the chant book, and reads its opening section line by line. Nomon first traces why Zen wrote almost nothing about sitting until the 11th century, and how handwritten copies of Dogen's text drifted into an early and a late version. The reading moves from "the way is basically perfect" to the phrase "and yet," then to the Buddha's six years and Bodhidharma's nine years of sitting. Nomon recalls being shocked at Green Gulch Farm when a senior practitioner admitted not liking zazen much. The evening closes with groups of two or three asking what the backward step feels like.

title: Closing Sesshin Reflection
speaker: Hoka Chris Fortin
summary: Hoka Chris Fortin returns to Dogen's Genjokoan at the close of the practice period, reading from Suzuki Roshi's first lecture on it at Sokoji in 1966, where the whole woven textile appears alongside its separate threads. Hoka then reads the koan of Mayu fanning himself, who answers a monk's question about the wind's permanence by simply continuing to fan. From there Hoka turns to Dogen crossing stormy seas to China while calling out to Avalokiteshvara, then to Zhaozhou's "non-zazen" and Yunmen's "an appropriate response." Hoka ends at Vulture Peak, where pilgrims from Myanmar invite Hoka and a husband to press gold leaf onto the rocks, a moment that brings Hoka to tears.

title: Closing Sesshin Reflection
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen reflects on the eight weeks of practice period and Myoki's time as Shuso, centering on Dogen's Genjokoan. Myoki opens by remembering Myoki's Dharma friend Edie Norton and reading from Edie's book on sitting with a group and not giving up. Myoki then circles through the opening lines of the Genjokoan, leads a short facial self-massage as a way to settle into the body, and reads Okumura's line that we should manifest these views with our actions. Myoki shares a poem stitched together from the class's own poems and closes with Okumura's poem on the present moment.

title: Closing Sesshin Reflection/Birth and Death
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's passage in Genjokoan on firewood and ash, where firewood abides completely as firewood and birth and death include each other. Nomon then tells stories of birth and death from close to home: Mercy, the Kenyan girl Nomon sponsored through school for twenty years, who has just given birth to a son, and two sangha members who recently died. Michael Kalbarer comes to Zen with intense curiosity, receives the precepts two months before his death, and quizzes his doctors about cancer. Edie Norton meets Kobun Chino in a community college class, ordains at seventy-eight, plans her own memorial, and speaks her last words: "Access the light, for this is a solemn moment."

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 7
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen returns to the fan koan of Zen Master Baoche at the end of the Genjokoan, reading Uchiyama on waving the fan to actualize the wind of life. The earth is gold but becomes gold only through the process of making it so, and river water has no taste of milk until practiced. Okumura's rendering of Dogen's word for practice, as actualized awakening, shows practice as a verb. Myoki names the lines that spoke most over the months of the class, including "Get out of the way" beside leaping clear of the two and the one, and "You are the dewdrop." Participants then write their own lines, answer each in a few words, and shape the answers into a short poem. Desiree closes by offering the koan "Wanting I am lost, being here, I am found."

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 6
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the Genjokoan passage on the fish in the water and the bird in the sky, opening with a confession that sharing joy and wonder feels more exposing than sharing struggles. Myoki reads Judith Regier on Dogen's paradoxes and the mud of samsara, then links the fish and bird to zazen and to the word "practice" slipped into the text's first line. Andrea's story of a grizzly bear fishing for salmon prompts the question of how to be completely human while washing dishes or folding laundry. Myoki sends everyone into dyads with one repeating question: what would be an authentic expression of yourself right now?

title: Zen Alive!
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the Genjokoan, which Ryushin calls the one koan of Soto Zen, and shares personal stories from Ryushin's own life, drawing on a study of it at Berkeley Zen Center. Ryushin's first image is a scrawny grizzly at a Kodiak Island fishing river who keeps fishing in his own awkward way, actualizing his fundamental point. Ryushin then tells of finding Ryushin's birth mother's photograph and seeing that nothing was wrong with her, only a Greek nose and a way of moving. Ryushin describes the hatred heard from a neighbor after October 7th and the grumpiness it stirred. Opening to the sorrow under the rage, Ryushin asks what Genjokoan means in the listeners' lives.

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 5
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the Genjokoan passage on the moon reflected in a dewdrop, reading it alongside Judith Regier, Nishijima, and Okumura. Okumura's call to express the height and depth of the moon in all activities leads Myoki to the precepts as the place where absolute and relative meet, and to the chills of retaking them at a July wedding. Myoki also describes the four views of water: a palace to a fish, a jewel to a heavenly being, fire to a hungry ghost. The group chants the precepts together, then talks in breakout rooms about how precept practice shows up now. Ariel closes by saying the cushion and the precepts together complete her circuit.

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 4
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen returns to Dogen's Genjokoan at the midpoint of practice period, taking up the boat-and-shore passage and the firewood-and-ash passage through Okumura's Realizing Genjokoan. Myoki opens by asking what the practice period has brought forth, describing five weeks of COVID as practice with the koan Moonface Buddha, Sunface Buddha, and recalling Norman Fischer's answer to a complaint about exhaustion: "So you're a tired Buddha." Breakout groups and a repeating question, "What do you take to be true right now?", follow, along with Myoki's years in the Diamond Approach, where that form of inquiry was learned. Okumura's point that the present moment has no length frames the firewood passage, and a participant closes by reading Dogen's Zenki lines on the boat.

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 3
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen takes up the next section of Dogen's Genjokoan, "To study the Buddha way is to study the self," alongside Okumura's Realizing Genjokoan and Hakuun Yasutani's Flowers Fall. Myoki describes a mantra practice of asking "who am I right now?" while washing dishes or pushing a son on a swing, a practice Norman Fischer read aloud, anonymously, at two Everyday Zen practice period openings. Triads and a repeating question, "What are you holding on to right now?", give the group a chance to try self-study. Yasutani's "pure white sheet of paper" leads to small awakenings: letting go of being right in a disagreement, or of perfectionism during four weeks of COVID. Suzuki Roshi's line that enlightenment is there even in imperfect practice meets Dogen's "no trace continues endlessly."

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 2
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen returns to Dogen's Genjokoan in the second talk of a series, reading its opening lines alongside commentary from Okumura, Nishiari, Suzuki Roshi, and Norman Fischer. Myoki tells of a Rohatsu one day sitting where a posture of childhood fear softened after belting out an unfamiliar chant as Kokyo. Myoki then traces a life of well-timed accidents, from teaching massage to Steve Stuckey's spa garden to reconnecting with Tim. A dyad exercise asks whether listeners push upstream or let the current pull them. Myoki closes by asking what leaping clear looks like in listeners' own lives.

title: Dōgen's Points of Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō Zuimonki, the informal talks given at Kōshōji and recorded by Ejō, read here in Shohaku Okumura's translation, and follows four themes through it. Aspiration comes first, with a student of the Buddha who could not remember a single verse yet attained verification within one summer practice period. Impermanence follows through Norman's grief when his friend Alan Lew died on a morning jog, and through a visit with Edie Norton, now on hospice, to choose a name for a November Jukai. Generosity brings Eisai breaking up the copper meant for a Medicine Buddha's halo to feed a starving family. Nomon ends by linking that story to the man who slept under a table in the old downtown space and was nicknamed MUTA.

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Workshop
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen leads a writing workshop on Dogen's Genjokoan, opening with several translations of the title and the meaning of koan as a public case that can be touched and practiced with for a lifetime. Myoki reads passages from the text, including the lines on forgetting the self and the boat that moves while the shore seems to, and invites participants to pick a line and write for five minutes, three times. Each person then gathers three lines into a poem and reads it aloud in small groups. Participants say the exercise felt freeing, and Myoki credits Sue Moon as its source. The session closes with one line from everyone assembled into a group poem that may appear anonymously in the Red Cedar newsletter.

title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 1
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen opens a seven-week course on Dogen's Genjokoan, naming Okumura's Realizing Genjokoan and a second book with commentary by Nishijima, Suzuki Roshi, and Uchiyama as companions. Myoki studies the title word by word: Gen as appearing, Jo as completing, Ko as a public case, and An as the hand that presses and kneads, which Myoki has the class feel by pressing hands to face and heart. Then comes a slow reading of the first four lines, with Thich Nhat Hanh's sheet of paper for emptiness and Uchiyama's translation of "leaping clear," which Myoki tries by actually leaping and landing in not knowing. The class closes with a repeating-question exercise in breakout rooms: "What keeps you from fully showing up right now?"

title: We Have Everything We Need
speaker: Hoka Chris Fortin
summary: Hoka Chris Fortin takes up Dogen's practice-period teaching and the story of Chiyono, a servant in a thirteenth-century Japanese convent. After Tim reads the opening of Daigo, Hoka names snow, shovels, and a bout of COVID as everything the sangha needs, then reads Rujing's poem about splashing in pitch-black lacquer and Dogen's line that the more mud, the bigger the Buddha. Chiyono asks an elderly nun whether a woman with no skills can attain the way, and the nun answers that each person is already complete. Chiyono's old bamboo-bound pail gives way at the well, and Hoka closes with Nyozo's poem of the pale moon of dawn caught in the rain.

title: The Tripitika
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Tripitaka, the Three Baskets of Sutta, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, after opening with a Mary Oliver poem and the December 28th death of a friend, John Michael Kelbera. Kanho describes a beautiful sunrise and a sad heart held together, and says "and" is truer than "but." Each basket gets a brief sketch, along with the old quarrels over whether Mahayana sutras belong, and Kanho wonders what Western sanghas miss by studying only the Sutras. Most of the time goes to the Vinaya. A peasant ordained before a prince stays senior to him forever, the robber and murderer Angulimala outranks later ordinands, and the four defeats bring expulsion. Kanho spares listeners the 92 Pacittiya rules and says the Abhidhamma comes in a future talk.

title: If Only You Do Not Pick and Choose
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the Faith in Mind poem, attributed to the Third Ancestor Jianzhi Sengcan, on the night of the winter solstice. Nomon starts from the shifting length of day and night, then turns to the poem's first line, "The great way is not difficult, simply set aside picking and choosing," and to the Merging of Difference and Unity, where light and dark oppose each other like the front and back foot in walking. After a full reading, Nomon comments on the lines about love and hate, about stopping activity by passivity, and about the phrase "not two." A sidebar describes sangha member Michael Calbera in his last days, as an example of not accepting or rejecting life and death.

title: Impermanence
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up impermanence, starting with the three marks of existence (anicca, dukkha, anatta) from the Pali Canon and then drawing on Norman Fischer, Dogen, and Gil Fronsdale, who treat impermanence as the path itself. Seishu describes watching clouds, an itchy nose, and the breath come and go, then tells of an eight-day retreat on Samish Island where a story about a long, sleepy day produced exactly that day, until dropping the story revealed alternating sleepiness and alertness. Seishu's mother, who lived to nearly 103 and longed to die after years of blindness and deafness, anchors the point that grief is healthy and accepting impermanence is not passive. A Sri Lankan monk's remark closes the teaching: impermanence is innocuous and harms only when we grasp.

title: The Silent Woman
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up "The Silent Woman," the Gateless Gate koan in which Manjushri arrives late to a gathering of the Buddhas and finds a young woman still in samadhi beside Shakyamuni. Manjushri cannot wake her, and the Bodhisattva of Delusive Wisdom, who rises from the earth, wakes her with one finger snap. Nomon recalls an early sangha member who stayed motionless after a Samish sesshin evening until Norman touched her shoulder, then reads Manjushri's jealousy and the messy Bodhisattva as invitations to bring our own mess to practice. Nomon also hears the woman's silence as restraint, and closes by setting up small groups to explore jealousy and showing off, starting with an urge to stare down the fluorescent lights.

title: More Stories - Women in Buddhism
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells stories of women in Buddhism, starting with Mahaprajapati leading the women on a long walk to ask the Buddha for ordination, and Ananda's argument that wins the Buddha over. Nomon recounts the Lotus Sutra's dragon girl, who answers Shariputra's list of five obstacles by awakening before the assembly, and reads Dogen's essay Raihai Tokuzui on refusing to discriminate between men and women. Nomon then reads from Geshin Claire Greenwood's Bow First, Ask Questions Later, which describes work in a 35-degree nunnery kitchen in Japan, and plays a video featuring the nunnery's abbess. Nomon closes with Red Cedar's ten practice leaders, exactly five men and five women.

title: Swimming in a Sea of Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the eight great events of the Buddha's life, drawing on Bernard Faure's The Thousand and One Lives of the Buddha, as a way of enacting the story during Rohatsu. Starting from the silent light that opens the Lotus Sutra, Nomon moves through Queen Maya's dream of the white elephant, Mara's armies, the monkey's offering of honey, the elephant Nalagiri calmed by the fearless mudra, and the mango-tree miracle at Shravasti. Nomon observes that Western scholars and modernizing Asian leaders cut the miracles and kept the meditation, and that every generation retells the story. Nomon closes by asking listeners to notice their own stories, since it was all a story to begin with.

title: The Lotus Sutra (Fall Class Part 6)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett leads a guided imagining of a traveler who leaves home to find what is missing, meets a kind companion, and reaches a shimmering city that vanishes. Nomon then reads the Lotus Sutra's chapter seven parable of the Phantom City, where a guide conjures a resting place for exhausted travelers, and the chapter eight parable of the jewel sewn into a drunk man's robe. Participants answer with their own stories, including an ashram in India that resembled the phantom city. Nomon asks whether the guide's trick is dishonest or skillful means, and closes on Paula Arai's line that we pray to Kanzeon and realize we had always been healed.

title: The Lotus Sutra (Fall Class Part 5)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up chapters three and four of the Lotus Sutra, opening with a guided meditation on a time of settling for less and then reading the parable of the burning house. Shariputra receives the first prophecy of Buddhahood, and the Buddha tells of a father who lures his absorbed children out of a blazing house with promised goat, deer, and ox carts, then gives each a great white ox carriage. Nomon then reads the prodigal son, who shovels dung for twenty years before his father names him heir. Class members connect both stories to their own lives, including a pottery studio, a stripped-down San Francisco apartment, and a therapist's question about settling. The evening closes with the question of skillful means versus the ends justifying the means.

title: Not Making Things Worse
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up two early Buddhist suttas, the Sallatha Sutta and the Culamalunkya Sutta, both built around the image of an arrow. In the first, the Buddha separates the untaught worldling from the well-taught noble disciple: both feel the first dart of pain, but only the worldling throws a second dart of resistance, blame, and "this shouldn't be happening." In the second, a monk demands answers to cosmic questions, and the Buddha answers with a man who refuses to have a poisoned arrow removed until he knows the archer's clan, the bow, and the feathers. Nomon leads a reflection on a personal upset, then timed speaking and listening in small groups.

title: Master Shitou
speaker: Sokaku Kathie Fischer
summary: Sokaku Kathie Fischer takes up Shitou Xiqian's Sandokai through Suzuki Roshi's Tassajara lectures, Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness, and the idea of "warm hand to warm hand." Sokaku tells short exchanges among Huineng, Xingse, and Shitou, including Shitou's answer "I don't understand either" when a monk asks about Bodhidharma. Sokaku compares the disappearing "I" to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and describes Sokaku's own half-asleep sentences as a kaleidoscope of mind. Sokaku reads Suzuki Roshi on sharing another's suffering, notes that Sokaku's husband's toothache is not Sokaku's to feel, and closes with Thich Nhat Hanh's poem "Please Call Me by My True Names."

title: History of the Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart traces the history of the precepts for a Jukai celebration on Samish Island, framing it with Mary Oliver's poem "When Death Comes." Kanho follows the rules from the Buddha's time, when the Sangha could not agree which to drop and kept even the one against slurping soup, through the Vinaya in India, the Chinese Brahma Net Sutra with its 58 precepts, and Saicho's ordination platform in Japan. Dogen's reformulation into the 16 Bodhisattva precepts follows, understood as practice-realization with no gap between them. Kanho ends by reading the ten grave precepts with the commentaries of Bodhidharma and Dogen, then rereads the tenth when a participant asks.

title: Holding Opposites
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up gratitude and sorrow together at a sesshin, working with the Lotus Sutra and Thich Nhat Hanh's commentary on the paramita Kshanti. Nomon gives thanks to the lineage, the Samish Nation, and parents, reading an early Buddhist passage about carrying one's mother and father on one's shoulders for a hundred years. Nomon then tells how smallpox reached Victoria in 1862, how sick people were forced home to their villages, and how a newspaper that year dismissed Indigenous people. The Lotus Sutra scene of golden bodhisattvas springing from the earth leads to Thich Nhat Hanh's reading of Kshanti as a heart large enough to embrace the sharp thing.

title: The Lotus Sutra (Fall Class Part 3)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett leads the third fall class on the Lotus Sutra, opening with a meditation that sets a mountain or ocean beside a butterfly or flower, then taking up the Verse of Remembrance in small groups. Nomon reads chapter 17 in verse with the class, where the Buddha's immeasurable lifespan outweighs eons of flawless practice, and chapter 20, where Bodhisattva Never Disparaging bows to everyone and gets stones thrown at him. Nomon adds a Chinese sect that bowed to stray dogs and an American folk song about the bodhisattva. The class ends on how to accept others' aggression without inviting abuse, with the reflection "this person wants to be happy and doesn't want to suffer."

title: The Lotus Sutra (Fall Class Part 2)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up chapters 15 and 16 of the Lotus Sutra in Gene Reeves's translation, after opening with Dogen's "Only a Buddha and a Buddha" and its line on the self-power of jiriki and the other-power of tariki. Nomon compares several English renderings of the Chinese four-character phrase, then reads aloud with the class as bodhisattvas spring from the earth and Maitreya wonders how a Buddha of forty years could have taught them. The Buddha's answer is the parable of the physician whose poisoned children take the medicine only after hearing he has died. Participants share turning points, including a young woman sent back to San Francisco by Tartang Tulku, and Nomon offers historical, devotional, and practical ways to read the sutra's dizzying numbers.

title: Mindfulness and Peace
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Satipatthana Sutta as a tool for peacemaking, beginning from grief over the war in Israel and Gaza. Nomon reads statements from Alan Senauke, Chozen Bays, and Chagdud Tulku Rinpoche, whose peace prayer offers the peacock that eats poisonous plants and turns them into bright feathers. Nomon then walks through the four foundations of mindfulness: body, feeling tone (vedana), mind, and patterns such as the five hindrances and the seven factors of awakening. Noticing "anger is arising" loosens a grip that "I am angry at so and so" tightens, and Nomon closes by wondering why no one calls a friend to say, "I am not angry right now."

title: The Lotus Sutra (Fall Class Part 1)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the fall class on the Lotus Sutra by asking students to notice how they do zazen, then offers three ways to read the text: historical, devotional, and practical. Nomon tells of reading the Diamond Sutra in a Zurich hotel the night before meetings with Swiss bankers, and sketches the sutra's history and the paths of Shravaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva. Students then read chapter 2 on skillful means in Gene Reeves's translation, where the Buddha twice refuses Shariputra's request to teach and five thousand listeners walk out. The homework is to look for one's own limited views and for the skillful means the universe is offering, and to read chapters 15 and 16.

title: Advice Given to Anathapindika
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster offers the Anathapindika Advice Sutra, found in the Ekottara Agama, the Majjhima Nikaya (number 143), and the Madhyama Agama, as part of a fall series on the early discourses. After a short history of Anathapindika, the wealthy merchant who bought the Jeta Grove by covering its grounds with coins, IkuShun recalls first hearing the sutra read by Sister True Emptiness at a Thich Nhat Hanh retreat. IkuShun then reads the Plum Village version as a meditation, moving through senses, elements, aggregates, and the three times, and closes by comparing it with the Majjhima Nikaya wording "I will not cling to the eye." IkuShun suggests reading several translations and considering each translator's background.

title: Mountains and Rivers Sutra
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up Dogen's Mountains and Waters fascicle, fresh from the sangha's Mount Baker pilgrimage, where wildfire smoke turned the hike into a retreat at the farm. Working from Kaz Tanahashi's translation, with Nishijima's stanza numbers and Brad Warner's casual rendering, Heigaku follows four threads: the dissolving of separateness, the way study widens ignorance, Dogen's harshly dualistic language, and a text meant to change its reader. Two workplace stories carry the teaching, a co-worker whose communication style upends everything and a blood bank temperature problem whose cause, misaligned valves, was plain from the mechanical room doorway. Heigaku ends with Dogen's "mountains hidden in hiddenness: this is how we study."

title: One Day Sitting - Perfect Just As You Are
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the story of Suzuki Roshi telling a room of students that they are perfect just as they are and could use a little improvement, then teaches the six Dharma gates of Master Zhiyi. Nomon reads Blanche Hartman on the sailors told to put down their buckets in fresh water off the Amazon Delta, and recalls the ordination instruction to see everyone as Buddha, including oneself. Breath counting gets the most time. Suzuki Roshi returns to it after nearly drowning at Tassajara, and Blanche tells Nomon to count backward from ten when the practice turns rote. The morning ends with Dorianne Laux's poem "Anti-Lamentation."

title: Foundations of Mindfulness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Sutra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipatthana), opening a series on early Buddhist teaching in the Pali collection. Nomon reads the sutra's opening lines in Analayo's translation, draws on Joseph Goldstein's commentary, and notes how the sutra shaped Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction class. Nomon then walks through the four qualities named before any practice instruction: ardent, clearly knowing, mindful, and free from desires and discontent. Three contemplations support ardency: the preciousness of the Dharma, impermanence, and karma. The evening closes with small groups of three, where one person speaks for four minutes on what motivates their practice while two listen.

title: Trungpa's Path of Liberation and Right Mindfulness
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up right mindfulness, the piece missing from the series on the Eightfold Path, and then turns to Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche's book The Truth of Suffering and the Path of Liberation. After Mary Oliver's poem "The Swan," Kanho lists the four Satipatthanas (body, feelings, mind, phenomena), quotes the Buddha telling a monk that the world is whatever disintegrates, and describes mindfulness as a supervisor keeping right effort on course. Kanho names Trungpa's controversial conduct plainly, then walks through his four qualities of the path: path, insight, practice, and fruition. Kanho closes with the bodhisattva vows and a second Mary Oliver poem about saving the only life you can save.

title: Kaizen and Zen
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Kaizen, the post-World War II industrial idea of continuous improvement, and sets it beside Dogen's fascicle Gyoji, "continuous practice." Kanho opens with Mary Oliver's poem "Dogfish," then describes joining a Soto Zen group in 2001 expecting koan fireworks and finding a path of slow change, which Shunryu Suzuki compares to getting wet while walking in fog. Kaizen asks for steps so small they seem laughable: five minutes of zazen, the 2,000 words a day that Stephen King writes, a ride around the block on the way back to 100k. Kanho ends by reading the opening of Gyoji, where continuous practice is the circle of the way.

title: Right Speech
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up right speech, the final talk in the summer series on the Noble Eightfold Path, drawing on the Pali Canon's abstentions and the Buddha's five questions. Seiu recalls adolescent gossip and Seiu's brothers' satire, then describes a post office visit where harsh thoughts about a clerk gave way to talk of his sewing once he saw Seiu's rakusu. Seiu's dad's heated arguments end when Seiu suggests changing the conversation. Seiu reads Norman Fischer on language as dialogue and Thich Nhat Hanh on deep listening, then sends the group into small breakout rooms to share where right speech has been present or absent.

title: Right Livelihood
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up Right Livelihood, the fifth element of the Eightfold Noble Path, drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching, the Metta Sutta, and the Buddha's image of a goldsmith holding a balance scale in the Anguttara Nikaya. Joden tells of a stepdaughter's aunt, a state prosecutor who died surrounded by hoarded purchases, then traces a path from pre-med studies through boatbuilding, forest conservation, and farmland protection. Small groups take up questions about what in their own work embodies Right Livelihood. One group reports that it is okay to say no, and a member recalls telling a boss that thinking about work in the shower is against their religion.

title: The Social Psychology of Compassion
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Numbers and Nerves, the book by Paul and Scott Slovic, and its research on why people stop responding to suffering at large scale. Starting from the wildfires in Oregon and the burning of Lahaina, Reizan describes Paul's findings: psychophysical numbing, shown with candles lit in a dark room, then compassion fade, the drowning-child question, and the prominence effect. Reizan closes with Annie Dillard's instruction to multiply yourself by 1,198,500,000 and Zbigniew Herbert's poem "Mr. Cogito Reads the Newspaper." In the discussion, Reizan answers questions on hope and numbness by describing sitting practice as staying alive to sensation, and the great vows as "just one more step in that direction."

title: Right Livelihood
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up right livelihood through a thought experiment prompted by a house guest, who asked how a career military man can be a Buddhist. Shin-yu imagines being a 25-year-old Buddhist in the 1960s deciding whether to join the Air Force, and reviews the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path along the way, with readings from the Pali Canon and the story of the Buddha's last student, Subhadda. Shin-yu notes that the sources on right livelihood name only making or shipping arms, never using them, and adds a saying that pilots have big egos and big watches, plus warm memories of Iranian colleagues. The thought experiment ends with a resolve to refuse any order that amounts to a war crime.

title: Right View and the Three Doors of Liberation
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up Right View, the first factor of the Noble Eightfold Path, through the Three Doors of Liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and aimlessness. For emptiness, IkuShun draws on Thich Nhat Hanh's teaching that a self is made of non-self elements, and on watching IkuShun's son grow up as a reminder that nothing stays in one form. For signlessness, IkuShun describes how a dandelion becomes a weed in the mind, and how an overheard complaint in a restaurant about a Prius blocking a horse trailer reveals the complainer's views. Aimlessness loosens the pull of status and wealth, and IkuShun closes on the word transparency: seeing through concepts a little more clearly while still living among them.

title: Right Understanding
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up right view, or right understanding, from the eightfold path, recalling how no self, nirvana, enlightenment, and emptiness confounded early practice in the 1970s. Shuko tells of asking Kobun Chino to explain emptiness and being handed Nagarjuna's book on it, which made no sense at all, then describes decades of slowly seeing emptiness as impermanence and interbeing, with help from Thich Nhat Hanh and B. Alan Wallace. Zazen, as Kobun taught it by silently adjusting each sitter's posture, does most of the work. Shuko closes with the practice of saying "don't know," learned at Tassajara in 2013, which drops anger in the moment and lets old habits of body and mind fall away.

title: Right Effort
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up Right Effort, the sixth step of the Noble Eightfold Path, by way of IkuShun's recent trip to Tassajara and the excerpts Sojun Mel Weitsman's writing that IkuShun's teacher brought there. IkuShun tells of a lifelong dream IkuShun nearly let go of, then reached with a walker and a fretting mind IkuShun learned to set aside. IkuShun reads Sojun's image of the rabbit, the horse, and the elephant, and names aspiration, commitment, inspiration, joy, ease, love, and creativity as what sustains effort. IkuShun closes with Gil Fronsdale's line on choosing satisfaction over pleasure and two questions for small groups.

title: Right Effort on the Eightfold Path
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Right Effort, the sixth step of the Eightfold Path, while Tim is away, and asks what separates it from Right Action. Seishu tells of a "goddamn Canadian" thought that arose after a driver cut in front of the car in Bellingham, then gives the Buddha's four-part answer to how to live: avoid unskillful states of mind, abandon them, cultivate skillful ones, and maintain them. Two recent episodes test the path. A board-meeting suggestion that left some members feeling dismissed shows its absence, and a patient ninety-minute call about a new modem shows its use.
