Seishu ends by comparing the abandoning of unskillful thoughts to pulling weeds in a garden.

title: Precepts and the Path
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens with a passage from Genjokoan, then tells about Tony Long, who joined the 2022 precepts class on Zoom, saying, "I'm here because I'm dying." Kanho recounts traveling to Yakima with Hannah Sullivan to hold the precepts ceremony for Tony, with Red Cedar members joining by screen, and explains the Zen names "completely rooted" and "peaceful way." Dainin Katagiri's poem "Peaceful Life" sits beside the news that Tony died the day before, and his wife Rosemary wrote of how much the precepts meant to him. Kanho then reads Blue Cliff Record case 55, Daowu's condolence call, and ends with Jianyuan searching with a hoe for his dead teacher's remains while Shishuang answers with roaring waves washing the sky.

title: The Intersection of the Noble Eight-fold Path and the Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Noble Eightfold Path and the Zen precepts, opening with a Mary Oliver poem about giving up worry and singing. Kanho traces how the Buddha's first small group of friends needed only the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, until a growing sangha brought 250 rules for monks and 348 for nuns. Kanho then describes the Bodhisattva precepts, drawn from the Brahmajala Sutra, as lifetime koans that can only be applied to oneself. Right speech, livelihood, effort, and concentration are each set beside the precepts, with the Eightfold Path as the large umbrella and the precepts as day-to-day steps. Kanho closes with Oliver's "Invitation," in which goldfinches sing in a field of thistles.

title: The Lotus Sutra, Part 5
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up chapters 15 and 16 of the Lotus Sutra, the last session of a two-month class, reading closely with participants taking turns aloud. Bodhisattvas spring from the earth, and Maitreya asks how a Buddha who taught for only forty years could have trained so many, comparing it to a twenty-five-year-old pointing to a hundred-year-old and calling him his child. Chapter 16 answers that the Buddha's life is immeasurably long and the announced death is skillful means. Nomon reads the parable of the physician father whose poisoned children take the medicine only after hearing he has died. Small-group sharing follows, including one participant's memory of tiny English daisies on the lawn at Samish.

title: Katagiri Roshi's Peaceful Life
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to Right View, the first factor of the Eightfold Path, through a poem by Dainin Katagiri that opens "Being told that it's impossible, one believes in despair." Nomon sketches Katagiri's life as a Soto priest sent to serve Japanese congregations in California, then Minnesota, and recalls a 1986 sesshin where Katagiri said "Full moon in the autumn sky." The sketch includes the sexual misconduct that came to light after Katagiri's death. Reading the poem line by line, Nomon dwells on "knowing how to walk with people" and on vowing to practice what looks impossible. Nomon ties that line to walking across the lawn at Samish to bring each person to practice discussion.

title: The Lotus Sutra, Part 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up chapters 12 and 13 of the Lotus Sutra, opening with a reflection on awe and a Templeton Foundation summary of its science. Nomon retells Devadatta's three attempts to kill the Buddha before the sutra prophesies his buddhahood. The group then reads the eight-year-old dragon princess answering Shariputra's claim that a woman's body cannot become a buddha, and discusses her instant change into a male body and the silence of the doubters. Nomon adds Maha Prajapati's barefoot walk to ask for ordination and closes with a Therigatha poem by the nun Muta about being free.

title: Great Expectations - Or Not So Great
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up expectations as a way into the Beginner's Mind retreat, reading Shunryu Suzuki Roshi's lines from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind about sitting without gaining ideas. Heigaku shares a laundry-room moment when the cat demands food, and a four-step account of sitting that adds naming what pulls attention away, such as "planning" or "expecting." A story from The Hidden Lamp follows, in which a woman answers fire, a drowning son, and her own awakening with "Let it be." Heigaku describes letting go of expectations after Diane's death, and a thought at Samish that returned about a hundred times in one sitting before it finally stopped coming back.

title: Right Effort & Action
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Eightfold Path, focusing on Right Action and Right Effort. Nomon reads the early story of the monastic Sona, who walks until his soles bleed, then learns from the Buddha's vina image to tune his persistence neither too taut nor too loose. Right Action widens from the precepts against killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct into everyday cases, such as the office supply closet and a polite visit from two Bible-carrying women at the door. Nomon then describes the four practices of Right Effort: preventing, overcoming, arousing, and maintaining. Marshall Rosenberg's feelings and needs inventories lead into a small-group exercise on a recent less-than-wholesome action, which runs out of time.

title: Right Speech
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up right speech, the third item on the Eightfold Path, and starts with how holding someone below or above ourselves bends what we say, using Nomon's own struggle to support a person who bristles at Nomon's advice. Nomon turns to the Zen precepts on praising oneself and denigrating others, then to the Buddha's three questions of true, beneficial, and well timed, and the ten-step checklist for correcting someone. Gil Fronsdal's Steps to Liberation invites curiosity about our own bad speech. Tonan O'Connor tells of exploding at her two sons in 1969 and coming home to three balloons, three bottles of Coke, and a note reading "We love you all the time." The evening closes with groups of three sharing a difficult communication.

title: The Lotus Sutra, Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with a guided meditation in which participants bring to mind a loved one, someone they admire, and someone they quietly hold below themselves, offering each the wishes "may you be well, accepting, kind to yourself." The class then reads chapter four of the Lotus Sutra, the parable of the poor son who flees his wealthy father and shovels dung for twenty years before being named heir. Nomon and the group puzzle over the shifting timelines and the father's long delay, then turn to chapter five's parable of the plants, where one rain falls on large and small plants alike and none can know its own rank. Erica connects this to the Tenzo Kyokun's remark that high things belong in high places without being better.

title: The Lotus Sutra, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up chapter three of the Lotus Sutra, "A Parable," and the burning house story inside it, after a guided sit that settles the breath like a feather falling. Shariputra receives a prophecy that he will become the Buddha Flower Light, and small groups reflect on life events no one could have predicted. Nomon then reads the burning house story, where a father lures his absorbed children out with promised carts. Nomon links the children's playthings to the mind's own, and tells of replaying a mishap at a January sesshin, where a sewing project and a dryer broke the rules. The class ends on the question of why the children need carts at all.

title: The Lotus Sutra, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a class on the Lotus Sutra in Gene Reeves's translation with a guided meditation set on a mountaintop, where the Buddha sits among disciples, bodhisattvas, and dragons. Nomon then reads chapter one, in which Manjushri tells Maitreya about 20,000 Sun and Moon Light Buddhas and reveals Maitreya as the former Fame Seeker Bodhisattva. After slides on the sutra's history and its three paths, the class reads chapter two aloud, where the Buddha refuses Shariputra's request twice and 5,000 followers walk out. Nomon closes by assigning Dogen's "Dharma Flowers" and suggesting a cloth for wrapping the sutra book.

title: The First Noble Truth is About Happiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a series on the Eightfold Path with the Four Noble Truths, reading the first as the truth of happiness as much as suffering. Nomon retells the Buddha's first teaching, including the merchant who walks off mid-explanation, then turns to Robert Waldinger and the Harvard study of adult development, which finds that caring for the body and keeping close relationships matter most for happiness. Nomon reads Norman Fischer's essay from When You Greet Me I Bow, with the story of Yunyan and Daowu on the many hands and eyes of the Bodhisattva of compassion. The evening ends with groups of three taking four-minute turns on what truly makes each person happy.

title: The Path of Relationship
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's "Ango" chapter from the Shobogenzo, which treats the practice period as peaceful abiding, as the close of the winter practice period nears. Nomon recalls the Buddha's monsoon-season retreats and Sharon Salzberg's account of wading through flooded Kolkata streets, then reads Dogen's quotation of Ru Jing's poem about piling up bones in an open field. Dogen's line that the practice period "requires unstinting support" leads to a silent reflection on how each person has been supported over the last ninety days. Listeners then divide into groups of four or five for a round of speaking and deep listening, and the evening closes with chants and announcements about learning the bells.

title: The Satipatthana (Mindfulness) Sutra
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Satipatthana Sutta, the Middle Length Discourse on the four foundations of mindfulness, reading its opening and explaining "Thus have I heard" and "Bhikkhus." Kanho tells of falling in love with the Pali Canon twice, through Carl Eugen Neumann's German translation and later in mindfulness teacher training, then traces the secular mindfulness movement through Joseph Goldstein, Thich Nhat Hanh, and Jon Kabat-Zinn. The Buddha's story of the two darts separates plain pleasant or unpleasant feeling from the ego's liking and disliking, and Kanho connects it to a partner's recent stroke and hospital stay. Kanho closes by noting that mindfulness courses leave out the precepts and the Brahma Viharas.

title: Bringing the Dharma Home
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster returns to the Dharma tools from IkuShun's class series, asking how teachings such as the Noble Eightfold Path, the two truths, and the three doors of liberation work in everyday life. Thich Nhat Hanh's image of the wave and the water frames IkuShun's examples. A disagreement with IkuShun's partner Bert over pruning the last branch of an apple tree shows IkuShun catching IkuShun's father's beliefs about order, then asking "Are you sure?" IkuShun tells of crumpling up slips of paper naming traits IkuShun disliked, and of the story of the empty boat. IkuShun ends with IkuShun's dog Kenji's death, and a morning when Chris bumps heads with IkuShun in greeting and IkuShun feels Kenji right there.

title: Noble Truth
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the word "noble" in the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Noble Path, beginning with a childhood memory of Ryushin's mother calling two passing nuns "a noble life." Ryushin describes the seriously ill patients from a physician's practice, whose ordinary, difficult lives carry a quiet nobility near the end. Then Ryushin turns to Mumonkan Case 19, "Ordinary mind is the way," and Linji's "true person of no rank." Sojun Mel Weitsman's ease, Blanche Hartman's lighthearted smile at her own tightness, and Suzuki Roshi's wartime vegetable garden show a life that does not cling. Ryushin ends with playing the cards life has dealt and trusting all of what life has been.

title: The Three Doors of Liberation
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Three Doors of Liberation (emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness) as Thich Nhat Hanh presents them in How to Love and The Heart of Buddha's Teaching. Nomon reads from Itsudo Patty Krall's essay in Seeds of Virtue, Seeds of Change, including her Starbucks encounter with a woman who quit the zendo after being asked to help put away cushions, and her line about her small sangha's future: "Don't know. Doesn't matter." Drawing on Northwest Trees, Nomon describes western hemlocks waiting in the shade for a Douglas fir to fall, then recalls placing both hands on an old-growth Douglas fir on the Ridley Creek Trail and feeling a tingling in the palms. Nomon ends by offering thank-you, said and meant a little more fully, as another way to practice the three doors.

title: The Buddha Taught Nirvana
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the first noble truth, prompted by a listserv complaint that "suffering" is a downer, and ties it to the practice period's study of Thich Nhat Hanh's heart of understanding. Ryushin retells the two arrows: the first is a Rinzai master wailing at his son's death, and the second is the story added on top, like the "nobody loves me" Ryushin catches while walking in the back door after work. Impermanence and no self then open into a sense that nothing is lacking, shown through a koisaku whack in a Berkeley sesshin that loosens the hold of Ryushin's father's karma, and through a former student's wedding photo. Ryushin ends by asking how each person responds.

title: Effort and Ease
speaker: Jonathan Prescott
summary: Jonathan Prescott takes up Right Diligence, or Right Effort, as a dynamic balance between effort and ease. Jonathan tells of sitting alone on a curb at age three, of two years spent on an introductory koan, and of Anne Aitken's thirteen years on hers. Zen is strong on effort, which can solidify the ego, while Jonathan's own Plum Village tradition can turn into summer camp and settle for ease. Jonathan works the balance through sitting posture, through breathing, where little John makes the effort to breathe in and Buddha nature breathes out, and through concentration, beginning with an entering-the-hall gatha and closing with Ajahn Chah's line about letting go a little, a lot, or completely.

title: Getting to Zero
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach opens the practice period at Red Cedar by taking up "getting to zero," a phrase from Ryushin's old teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman for resetting life and clearing the slate. Ryushin introduces Ikushen Desiree as Shuso and describes the Shuso as a mirror for everyone's practice. Inspiration and aspiration run through the evening: Okumura Roshi's gentleness, and Ryushin's habit of raising the intention to be kind before entering each patient's room in a busy emergency department. Zazen is where zero is felt in the body, and Suzuki Roshi's image of spring in the grasses among the snow comes near the end, followed by practice suggestions on time, breath, and meeting people eye to eye.

title: Show up in a good way – On Zen and Solidarity with Indigenous Water Protectors
speaker: Ben Connelly
summary: Ben Connelly tells of a prayer circle at the Treaty People Gathering in northern Minnesota, where Anishinaabe elder Great Grandmother Mary Lions asks a mostly non-indigenous crowd to "show up in a good way" as they oppose the Line Three pipeline. Ben recites a poem about woodcutters beside the roaring drill rig, then ends up swinging an axe at a work party cutting maples for a prayer lodge, after being asked who has the spirit of the knife and the axe now. Dogen's line in the Genjokoan that water is life, with the fish and the bird, grounds a turn toward interdependence and toward fear, rage, and despair as things to show up for. Ben ends with a leatherback turtle laying eggs in front of the lakeshore zazen.

title: Meditation - Revisiting the Basics
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Pema Chodron's book How to Meditate: A Practical Guide to Making Friends with Your Mind, reading it as a tune-up for the basics of Seishu's own sitting. Seishu returns often to coming back to the breath, and tells of a 1970s group therapy marathon where Seishu realized having heard nothing the partner said. Seishu describes learning to accept sleepiness during a seven-day Samish sesshin, after which the worst part was being upset about it. Seishu then tries four of her suggestions: a longer body scan, a check of emotions and thoughts, watching breath and body with the storyline dropped, and making brushing teeth or walking one block the object of attention.

title: Ancestor Bodhidharma
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Bodhidharma, beginning with his meeting with Emperor Wu in Case 1 of the Blue Cliff Record, where the answers are "Empty, no holiness" and "I don't know." Kanho opens with grief over the war in Ukraine on Easter morning, then moves to the legends of nine years of wall sitting, including the eyelids that become tea plants. Kanho reads from the Outline of Practice and its four practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing, and practicing the Dharma. The koan of skin, flesh, bones, and marrow follows, with Dogen's reading that each student's answer expresses the Dharma fully. The story ends with Bodhidharma's tomb, opened to reveal a single sandal.

title: Reflections on Our Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's Zazenshin and its opening koan, in which Yaoshan tells a monk to "think not thinking." Nomon reads the active verb "think" as an invitation to engage thoughts without getting stuck in them, then follows Dogen's warnings against treating zazen as calm rest or as practice only for beginners. The story of Mazu and Nanyue polishing a tile into a mirror leads to Suzuki Roshi's "nothing special" and a mother's ordinary, astonishing children. Nomon closes with Dogen's poem, which ends on a fish swimming like a fish and a bird flying like a bird.

title: On Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the precepts, reading the Everyday Zen version of the threefold refuge, the three boundless precepts, and the ten clear mind precepts, followed by an excerpt from Norman Fischer's book Taking Our Places. Kanho describes three levels for understanding a precept (literal, compassionate, and ultimate) and cautions that "the cup is already broken" is no reason to swing a baseball bat at fine crystal. Having grown up Catholic in Germany, Kanho compares the precepts with the Ten Commandments, finding that several commandments concern how to feel about God, and calls the precepts a lattice that helps bean sprouts grow into the sky. Kanho closes with Jane Mead's poem "Concerning That Prayer I Cannot Make," which ends on the words "I am holy."

title: Three Ways To Practice With Emptiness
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up three ways to practice with emptiness, beginning with the Anattalakkhana Sutta, in which the Buddha tells the group of five monks that each of the five skandhas is non-self. Faith comes next, through Tenshin Reb Anderson's instruction to rise at the wake-up bell and the meeting of the nun Chi-Kwang with a 102-year-old Korean nun in The Hidden Lamp. The third way, holding boundlessness as an attitude, is illustrated by a coworker furious over a delayed request for lightbulbs, where everyone involved is acting out of care for patients. Heigaku ends by describing mourning for the dead as joyous and asking whether this practice is better called an attitude or a perspective.

title: How Do We Practice in the Middle of Hellfire?
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart asks how to practice in the middle of hellfire, starting from sadness over the war in Ukraine, and turns to the bodhisattva Samantabhadra through a Hongzhi poem from the Complete Enlightenment Sutra. Kanho describes a habit of fixating on outcomes when urgency rises, which narrows attention like a telephoto lens until stepping back widens it. Sheri Huber's story in Trying to Be Human imagines saving the world only because we want to, with no blame and no one else involved. Kanho closes with gathas from the Avatamsaka Sutra, such as wishing, while washing the face, that all beings attain the pure teaching.

title: Prajna Paramita
speaker: Sokaku Kathie Fischer
summary: Sokaku Kathie Fischer takes up the sixth paramita, prajnaparamita, and translates it as understanding and love rather than wisdom, drawing on Norman's book The World Could Be Otherwise. Sokaku looks at how language traps us in a false narrative of subject and object, with each word a small container implying its opposite, even emptiness and boundlessness. Sojun Mel Weitsman's line that everyone is the center of the universe at the same time becomes a wheel with many centers, then the sky and the ocean, which have no center to find. Sokaku closes on the Heart Sutra, spoken by Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of love, and describes love as the ground we walk on, the air we breathe.

title: Faith and Our Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up faith as one of the three essentials of Zen practice, starting from Kyogen Carlson's paragraph on the "illusion of a key," the hope that one realization or book will make life make sense. Nomon then turns to Taigen Dan Leighton's essay "Zazen as Enactment Ritual" and the eighteenth-century Soto reformer Menzon Zuiho, who warns that sitting to rid oneself of delusion only creates the karma of acceptance and rejection. Faith in Buddha, Dharma, and sangha follows, including the confusion when a longtime member simply stops coming, along with Nomon's own agitated sit that evening. Nomon closes on Saint Patrick's Day with the prayer attributed to Saint Patrick that begins "I arise today through a mighty strength."

title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Zen teaching of great faith, great doubt, and great determination, reading Torei Zenji's Bodhisattva Vow and passages on faith from Kyogen Carlson. Nomon pauses after each paragraph of the vow and recalls a work day at Green Gulch when a man named Terry folded his jacket and called it Buddha's clothing. Kyogen's three levels of faith build toward the deepest, that it is okay no matter what happens, and Nomon adds Kyogen's advice that if zazen is in the middle of everything, it always works out. Great doubt gets a short gloss, "don't be so sure." Nomon ends with Chogyam Trungpa's line: "The bad news is we're all falling. The good news is there's no bottom."

title: How Does it All Fit Together?
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up a Doku-san question: how do the precepts, Four Noble Truths, koans, Dogen, and Brahma Viharas fit together? Kanho begins with the robes, a mix of Chinese koromo, Japanese kimono, and Indian okesa, and answers the cultural appropriation concern by noting that each culture borrowed from the one before. Next comes a tour of the books, from the Middle Length Discourses to the Book of Serenity and the Mumonkan, and of how India, China, and Japan each reshaped Buddhism. Kanho ends on the six perfections and the Eightfold Path, where wisdom comes last in one and right view comes first in the other, and finds it endearing that commentators insist on both orders.

title: Conversations With the Buddha and Our Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Diamond Sutra as one long conversation between the Buddha and Subhuti, and asks what it means that the Buddha's opening question is about how to control the thinking mind. Nomon tells of a friend, Janina Scarlett, who grew up near Chernobyl, took comfort in the X-Men character Storm, and now writes books on superhero therapy. Nomon joins her online practice session sending loving-kindness to Ukraine, then wonders aloud whether merit is real. Nomon reads Thich Nhat Hanh's comment on chapter 13 and closes with the sutra's last verse, "a star at dawn, a bubble in the stream."

title: The Diamond Sutra
speaker: Sokaku Kathie Fischer
summary: Sokaku Kathie Fischer takes up the Diamond Sutra, reading Chapters 11 and 13, where worlds filled with the seven jewels and given to the Tathagatas bring less merit than grasping a single four-line verse. Sokaku follows the emptiness teaching through Bodhidharma and Emperor Wu in Blue Cliff Record case 1, Zhaozhou's answer "non-Zhaozhou" and a visit to the redwoods with grandchildren, Huineng's mirror poem, and case 89's hands and eyes. Asked in the discussion how to hold the war in Ukraine, Sokaku answers with returning again and again to this moment. Sokaku also describes Tetsugen Glassman's practice of entering a hard situation with the heart of not knowing.

title: Zazen on the Road and in the Zendo
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan reflects on zazen as a practice that travels from hotel beds to the zendo, and on what sitting with the sangha has given Seiu during a practice period spent studying the Diamond Sutra. Seiu recalls Peter Levitt sneaking a look at his watch to find only seven minutes had passed, and Goenka's story about why retreatants stay silent rather than trade reports of "tingling." Seiu tells how sitting steadied Seiu through Seiu's husband Jerry's open heart surgery and Seiu's son-in-law's death from alcoholism, and how the wall between Seiu and a hard family member dissolved. Seiu closes with Joan Halifax's letter on Ukraine and Robert Aitken's vow to "speak of original peace."

title: Jizo Bodhisattva
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Jizo, or Kshitigarbha, the third bodhisattva in a practice period series drawn from Taigen's book Bodhisattva Archetypes, and traces how the name travels from Sanskrit to Dizang to Jizo. Nomon shows photos of weathered stone Jizos in bibs along Japanese roadsides, then reads from the Earth Store Bodhisattva Sutra, including the past life in which Jizo vows to free suffering beings in all six realms before becoming a Buddha. Nomon lists some of the sutra's benefits of honoring Jizo, along with two that show its misogyny. Nomon ends with the ceremony of sewing red bibs for Jizos, where a longtime practitioner spoke of grief from an abortion.

title: The Diamond Sutra, Part I
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan opens a practice period on the Diamond Sutra by reading its first verses, where Subhuti asks the Buddha how a bodhisattva should stand, walk, and control thoughts. Following Thich Nhat Hanh's advice to read the sutra before the commentaries, Seiu takes up the perception of a self through the examples of tying a shoe and being a doctor. Seiu then turns to gift giving and the meal chant on the emptiness of giver, receiver, and gift. Breakout rooms bring up chanting the sutra, Kerouac's reading of it, and both the freedom and the terror of no self. Seiu closes by assigning verses seven through 14, with a ten-minute sit and a writing exercise.

title: The Flower Ornament Scripture
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Flower Garland scripture, and its bodhisattva Samantabhadra, whom Kanho calls a longtime patron. Kanho recalls practice periods at Tassajara and Green Gulch, then turns to bodhicitta, using Patrul Rinpoche's king, boatman, and shepherd kinds and Pema Chodron's description of a love that drops the barriers between self and others. Samantabhadra, named in the meal chant between Manjushri and Avalokiteshvara, is where wisdom and compassion meet in action, and Vairochana explains why he cannot be seen. Kanho closes by reading the opening of Samantabhadra's vows.

title: Continuous Mistake
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells the story of a rough opening-retreat day, after two hours and 27 minutes of sleep, when a muted phone, a broken laptop, wrong Zoom settings and a lost Han pattern all piled up. Kanho opens with Norman Fischer's poem "Responsibility" and its line "it's not our fault," followed by Norman's addition, "And yet, it is our responsibility." From there Kanho describes "one continuous mistake," the inner judge who gets invited to tea on a park bench, and a short lesson in belly breathing from a karate teacher. Kanho closes with a wingless bumblebee rescued by a woman named Shay, and Mary Oliver's poem "Hum."

title: Way Seeking Mind
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan tells the story of Seiu's own path to Zen, opening with a childhood memory of imagining the world outward from Seiu's bed to the galaxy and a Methodist slideshow called Members One of Another. Seiu moves through a broken heart, the early death of Seiu's mother, and the drinking of Seiu's father. Seiu finds comfort in Wendell Berry's "The Peace of Wild Things," Gary Snyder's mountain poems, and the twelve steps. Meeting Seiu's husband Jerry, hearing Norman Fischer's talks at Samish Island in 2013, and studying with Peter Levitt and Kathy Fisher follow. Seiu closes by answering the girl staring at a candle who asked "is this it?" with "just this is it."

title: Diamond in the Rough
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona tells a story from Tania Aebi's Maiden Voyage, in which the 18-year-old sailor, lost and frightened on the way to the Galapagos, finally finds that the plastic sextant from her father's boat has warped, while an aluminum one sat unused in a locker. Heigaku reads the sextant as a metaphor for practice and gathers Zen stories of a treasure already possessed: the old woman who taps her heart when asked where Amitabha is, Dazhu told by Mazu that "what you are asking is your treasure house," and Yantou's family jewels that never came through the front gate. Heigaku then turns to the five hindrances and reads the Sangarava Sutta's images of a bowl of water clouded with dye, boiling over a fire, choked with algae, or churned by wind, so that no reflection shows.

title: Bodhidharma's Outline of Practice
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up Bodhidharma's Outline of Practice in Red Pine's translation, and tells the story of Bodhidharma's meeting with Emperor Wu, who hears "No merit" and "I don't know." Joden follows the text's four practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing, and practicing the Dharma. Each gets a short commentary, drawing on Ryokan's lines about meeting disaster, illness, and death, and on a Shodo Harada prayer that begins "I vow to choose what is." Joden offers a New England proverb for wanting less, "Use it up, wear it out, make it do, do without," and closes with Dogen's threefold mind from Instructions to the Tenzo.

title: Thoughts on Ego
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up Vasubandhu's Thirty Verses on Consciousness Only, reading the first six verses on store consciousness and manas, the consciousness of self, to look at how ego works. Scott compares karma to a needle wearing a groove in a record, and tells two stories: the Zen master who answers "Is that so?" when accused of fathering a child, and Shin-yu's own anger at drivers merging ahead, who turn out to be Shin-yu's best friend's family. Shin-yu lists bodily signs of ego, such as shallow breathing and muscle tension, and offers tools: counting to ten, slowing the breath, inviting ego in as Thich Nhat Hanh suggests, and consulting mentors. Shin-yu closes by asking the sangha for their own techniques.

title: Thoughts on Rohatsu and the Condition of the Nation's Welfare
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the opening of the Maha Parinibbana Sutta, where the Buddha names seven conditions for a nation's welfare. Kanho frames the reading with Rohatsu and the year ahead, then sets the scene: King Ajatasattu of Magadha vows to destroy the Vajjis, and his minister Vassakara goes to ask the Buddha about it. The Buddha puts one question after another to Ananda, asking whether the Vajjis meet often, honor their elders, and keep up their shrines, and each time answers that their growth is to be expected. Kanho closes with the war's outcome: Magadha wins after Vassakara spends three years sowing discord, until the Vajjis' seven conditions have fallen apart.

title: Climate and Spiritual Activism
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up how Zen practice informs spiritual activism on climate, working through Dogen's fascicle Valley Sounds and Mountain Colors and Layman Dong Po's verse about the valley's long, broad tongue. Reizan reads Daido Loori on understanding self and universe together, tells of a Maasai junior elder in a National Geographic story who says trees grow in families, and reads "The Tent," an old poem in which ravens and bulldozers blur into a waking dream. Dongshan's five ranks lead from separation toward a compassion that puts one's life on the line. Reizan ends with the Lorax, who speaks for the trees as one of them.

title: The Devotional and the Practical
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the pull between devotion to Zen's monastic forms and what works for actual people, starting from a debate among teachers over shrinking Japanese monasteries like Eiheiji. A Rohatsu schedule change from 6 to 7 a.m. and Nomon's memory of an all-night, full-moon hike in the Marin Hills show how a sangha might keep tradition with more room for choice. Nomon then returns to Zoketsu Norman Fischer's eight stages of monastic life, from the honeymoon through the dry place to gratitude, love, and letting go, with the story of a student who left, came back smiling, and left again. It closes with Norman's reminder that the stages are another finger pointing to the moon.

title: The Bodhisattva's Practice of Gratitude
speaker: Chiko Amie Diller
summary: Chiko Amie Diller takes up gratitude in the weeks after Thanksgiving, questioning how self-help claims of better sleep and a happier life shrink the practice, and reads David Whyte's poem "Everything Is Waiting for You." Chiko describes gratitude as a door to belonging, with gratitude as the in-breath and generosity as the out-breath. Chiko tells of Maureen Stuart Roshi, who answered every banging door and every new IV in her last days in the hospital with "Thank you," and of a walk by the American River, where an angry young man blocked the trail and the leaves and water suddenly shone. Chiko closes with Suzuki Roshi's line that zazen is sitting you.

title: The Peace of Wild Things
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Wendell Berry's poem "The Peace of Wild Things" and the opening of Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra, offered after the scheduled speaker cancels at short notice. Kanho pairs them with Thoreau's essay "Walking" and its line "in wildness is the preservation of the world," then admits to not understanding Dogen and to once translating his words into what Kanho calls "Mekong crap." Zazen becomes the way to lie down by still water, and breath counting, back to one at every lapse, is the practice Kanho trusts most. Shohaku Okumura's remark that only in zazen do we stop making karma leads to Berry's "Do Not Be Ashamed," which closes with the heron's evening flight.

title: Stages of Monastic Life
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Zoketsu Norman Fischer's essay "Stages of Monastic Practice," collected in When You Greet Me I Bow, and adds a personal sketch of its eight stages. Memories of Norman come first: a 1986 Rohatsu sesshin at Green Gulch, where Norman answered complaints about straining with "isn't breathing wonderful?", and the years Norman flew north to teach small groups in Bellingham and Vancouver. The stages run from the honeymoon, disappointment and betrayal, and exploration of commitment through commitment and flight, the dry place, gratitude, love, and letting go. Nomon illustrates commitment and flight with a sangha member who left for years, returned, and left again. The essay's passage on love closes at a graveside, where the person being buried is Buddha.

title: We Are Always Walking Each Other Home
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up a phrase that keeps visiting during sitting, "We are always walking each other home," and reads a passage from Norman Fischer's Sailing Home about leaving and returning. Kanho describes leaving home with firm ideas of the road ahead, finding there is no map, and discovering that the ground covered shaped a life more than the goal did. A candle made by a friend and by many bees, and a breakfast of oatmeal touched by farmers, truckers, and grocery clerks, show how hard it is to find the line between dependence and independence. Kanho closes with a Mary Oliver poem in which a new voice, slowly recognized as one's own, keeps company with someone determined to save the only life that can be saved.

title: Dukkha, Rollercoasters and Nonduality
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up dukkha through the image of the Giant Dipper, the wooden roller coaster on the Santa Cruz boardwalk, as a way to see how differently people ride out 2021. Kanho reads the Buddha's list of dukkha and a long modern list of its meanings, then describes friends whose views on masks and vaccines differ sharply, and quotes Shunryu Suzuki on watching people instead of controlling them. An Inuit song from South Baffin Island, about a kayaker drifting out on a shore wind, shows a conclusion that is not dualistic: only the dance remains. Kanho closes with Thich Nhat Hanh's poem "Please Call Me by My True Names."

title: Our Zen Ancestors and Koans
speaker: Chikyo Ewan Magie
summary: Chikyo Ewan Magie takes up the Zen ancestors and the koan tradition, starting with Bodhidharma's curt reply to Emperor Wu in the Blue Cliff Record and Huineng pounding rice for nine months after hearing the Diamond Sutra. Chikyo draws on Mazu's "Ordinary mind is the way" and on Thich Nhat Hanh, whose years of statelessness pushed him toward deeper practice. A central story is Deshan's encounter with the dumpling seller, who asks which mind is eating, followed by Case 28 of the Gateless Gate, where Longtan blows out the candle. Chikyo closes with Fayan Wenyi, who answers "I don't know" when asked why he is on pilgrimage and hears that not knowing is most intimate.

title: Zen Mind, Beginners Mind - Control
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the "Control" chapter of Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, beginning with the burnout signs Nomon recognizes in a busy life and teaches to doctors, such as escape fantasies and turning people into problems to solve. Nomon reads Suzuki Roshi's advice to give a sheep or cow a large meadow and just watch, then sets it beside Wanda's observation that the tidy, schedule-driven families were the ones who failed at taking in children from the state system. The malaria vaccine and the sangha's fundraising campaign passing its goal serve as examples of control and its limits. Nomon then turns to Dogen's remark that time goes from present to past, and to samadhi as being undivided. The closing word is Suzuki Roshi's: everything looks beautiful as it loses its balance against a background of perfect harmony.

title: Karma
speaker: Karen DeCotis
summary: Karen DeCotis takes up karma, drawing on Dale Wright's chapter on morality in his book on the six perfections, which Karen turned to after starting Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise. Karen defines karma as volitional action that ripens like a seed, then walks through Wright's areas of karmic justice, including cosmic and social justice. Karen tells of a woman who lost her two children in a car accident, and of after-school staff who ask "what happened to you?" rather than "what is wrong with you?" Karen argues that internal effects on character matter more than external rewards, and ends by admitting that interdependence leaves karma fuzzier than when Karen began.

title: Instant Dukkha, Suzuki Roshi Walk Like an Elephant
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Shunryu Suzuki's "Walk Like an Elephant," a 1970 talk collected in Not Always So, and reads two passages from it about practicing zazen step by step without a gaining idea. Kanho begins with instant suffering in the 21st century, from Kindle pre-orders to the damage Instagram bullying does to young people. A Russian doll set stands for the lineage running from Suzuki through Uchiyama, Dogen, and Bodhidharma back to the Buddha. Kanho then returns to last Sunday's "worry box," describing how opening it on the cushion becomes an invitation to the suffering to visit, and closes with Mary Oliver's poem "Heavy."

title: Trust, Worries and Self Improvement
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up worry and self-improvement through Ed McManus's short story "The Worry Box," in which a camper's eyelid cramps and a bear's snuffle crowd every other concern out of the box. Kanho describes carrying a large worry box, built from early parental and school expectations, to the cushion, the one place where it can be opened gently and each worry examined. Leonard Cohen's poem "Roshi" gives Kanho something to put in the box in place of a worry. Kanho then calls self-improvement an ego activity that misses the tender moments of practice, and closes by reading a Katagiri Roshi poem about living in vow.

title: Moments of Realization
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells two stories of acceptance from a single morning and then turns to the breathing chapter of Shunryu Suzuki's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind. The first story is a late board report for Mindfulness Northwest, where picturing each board member's face while addressing an email softens the agitation, and the sun breaks through the clouds. The second is NPR's report on the 2020 fire that killed at least 9,000 mature giant sequoias, which brings up Nomon's own part in the climate crisis, along with heat pumps. Suzuki's image of the throat as a swinging door leads Nomon to feel the diaphragm moving like a jellyfish, and to recall a two-hour sit in a Bellingham park pavilion.

title: Suzuki Roshi, Something Else, Zen Practice is Useless
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the posture chapter of Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, after announcements about ill sangha members and the $550,000 capital campaign for a building. Nomon recalls Zoketsu Norman Fischer saying Zen practice is useless, reads Holly Hughes's poem about the mind wanting more, and works through three points: the posture as a practice of "not two and not one," zazen as a chance to allow something to happen, and the close link between body and mind. Nomon also tells of visiting Jakusho Kwong Roshi on Sonoma Mountain, where an expansion permit triggered over a million dollars in code upgrades. Nomon closes by assigning homework: reread Suzuki Roshi's posture directions on page twenty-six.

title: Suzuki Roshi's Students, Katherine Thanas
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads two short chapters by Katherine Thanas, a direct student of Suzuki Roshi, from her book The Truth of This Life. In "Set Ourselves to Zero," Katherine judges a bemused young man at Suzuki Roshi's ashes ceremony at Tassajara, until a thought arises that the moment is already perfect. In "No Pressure to Improve," she urges stopping the veering off and moving toward fear in small steps, breathing with it inside the body. Nomon describes a cold, dark stone of fear in the gut and the practice of naming fear while turning down the story that someone must be upset. Nomon closes by asking listeners whether greed, hatred, or delusion most often grabs them.

title: The Women at the Beginning of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the story behind Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, tracing how weekly talks in Marion Derby's Los Altos living room became a book edited chiefly by Trudy Dixon. Nomon reads David Chadwick's account in Crooked Cucumber of Trudy's illness and her "breath struggle samadhi," then her own words praising Suzuki Roshi. Nomon reads the opening chapter on beginner's mind and describes noticing the release after constriction, planting wholesome seeds in the Yogacara sense. A plumber freeing a sheared bolt from Nomon's old faucet shows that expertise helps when the attitude is open. Nomon closes with Shosan Vicki Austin's memory of Suzuki Roshi's margin notes listing alternative translations of shoshin.

title: Suzuki Roshi's Life and Teachings, Creating a New Temple
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett begins a study of Shunryu Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, setting the Lotus Sutra aside for now as the sangha raises money for a new temple in Bellingham in Suzuki Roshi's lineage. Nomon reads a draft of the fundraising cover letter, then Huston Smith's preface, which includes Suzuki Roshi's reply when asked why satori never appears in the book. Richard Baker's funeral words follow, along with cautions about putting the great man on a pedestal and about Baker's claim that Suzuki Roshi came to a land without Buddhism. A short video of Bill Kwong closes the evening, recalling the glass of wine Suzuki Roshi suggested to loosen him up before dokusan.

title: The Power of Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Book of Serenity Case 16, where the traveling monk Xiushan meets Dizang and is asked, "What do you call the world?" Nomon starts from the shift between feeling pinched and feeling open, and finds that reading the novel Damnation Spring, set among 1970s California redwood loggers, melts the narrowness. From there stories become the subject: the ones people tell about climate change, about Red Cedar's $550,000 capital campaign, about the world itself. Announcements cover a planned return to in-person Wednesday sitting and a Lotus Sutra series drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's Peaceful Action, Open Heart. Case 27, Fayan pointing to a blind, closes with "One gain, one loss."

title: Continuous Practice
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up continuous practice, defining it as sangha practice year after year together with bringing attention into daily life, and then turns to Dogen's 1242 fascicle on the subject. With help from Norman Fischer's commentary, Seishu reads Dogen's "circle of the way," where aspiration, practice, enlightenment and nirvana have no gap, and compares the ancestors' work to switching on a light and activating Thomas Edison's labor. Seishu then reads Sojun Mel Weitsman's 1997 Rohatsu sesshin talk, in which Mel puts "how" ahead of "why," pictures a boat caught in a storm, and uses comic-book heroes to describe the battle between head and heart. Mel's talk ends with picking up a cup of tea with both hands.

title: Ummon's Medicine and Sickness Correspond to Each Other
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Case 87 of the Blue Cliff Record, Yunmen's line "Medicine and disease correspond with each other. The whole world is medicine. Where do you find yourself?" Reizan traces the saying to the Avatamsaka Sutra, where Manjushri sends Sudhana to find something that is not medicine, and Sudhana comes back holding a blade of grass. Reizan then describes yelling at Brian Kilmeade on television during a week of fires and floods, and asks whether Yantou's great roar, paired with "Although he's young, he's capable," offers a way to meet that anger. The pandemic becomes disease and medicine at once, and Reizan closes by opening the floor so each person can say where they find themselves.

title: Oops
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona tells a story from a summer at Shady Oaks Camp, where mocking a fellow counselor named Chuck in front of his friends becomes a regret carried for thirty years. Heigaku sets it beside the Fugai Ekun story of the cook who eats the snakehead found in the soup, and finds a second reading: the cook may be sincerely thanking the master for showing the mistake. From there Heigaku turns to confession in Shantideva's second chapter and sorts harmful errors into five kinds, from not seeing the harm to acting out of a wish to hurt. The last example is a bell struck at the wrong moment in a service when Norman was the priest, a mistake Heigaku is grateful for because it taught how much the bell ringer and priest depend on each other.

title: The Venerable Ananda
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Venerable Ananda, the Buddha's attendant and the memory behind the opening formula "thus have I heard," after announcements and news of a partner's breakthrough COVID-19 case. Kanho reads a long passage from the Vinaya Pitaka in which Ananda, refused three times, wins the Buddha's consent to ordain Maha Pajapati Gotami by asking whether women can realize stream entry and arhatship. Kanho then tells of the earthquake that signals the Buddha's relinquished will to live, when Ananda misses years of hints and asks too late to keep him in the world. Kanho closes with Mary Oliver's poem "The Buddha's Last Instruction" and the four bodhisattva vows.

title: Anathapindika
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Anathapindika, the Buddha's great donor, reading from a mashup of Pali sutras and Wikipedia just as a fundraising campaign approaches. Anathapindika meets the Buddha in the dark before dawn, buys Prince Jeta's park by covering it in coins, loses his fortune to a flood, and evicts a deva who urges him to stop giving. Near death, Anathapindika hears Shariputra and Ananda teach on impermanence and asks that such teachings be given to lay people too. Nomon then plays a Thich Nhat Hanh Q&A on the deathbed scene, where recollecting the Three Jewels waters seeds of happiness, and ends wondering about Visakha, the female patron the sources barely describe.

title: The Body
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the body on the eighth day of a seven-day sesshin, drawing on Zenju Earthlyn Manuel's writing about the Tokeiji mirror practice and on a poem by Robert Creeley. Norman opens with news of a wildfire threatening Tassajara and the first national Juneteenth, then reads a poem of Norman's own about being old and an essay asking where the body is. The Abhidharma finds no body, only momentary events, while the Buddha answers Mara's army by touching the earth and saying the earth is his body. Norman closes with the Creeley poem, which repeats the line "the plan is the body," and thanks the sangha for its chanting, bell ringing, and altars.

title: The Zen Mirror of Tokeiji
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up "The Zen Mirror of Tokeiji," a Hidden Lamp case about a 13th-century Japanese convent where nuns sat zazen before a great mirror, and Princess Yodo's verse, "Heart unclouded, heart clouded, standing or falling, it's still the same body." Norman tells how the mirror began in a nun's dream off Yue Beach, then ties it to Yogachara great mirror awareness and the sixth ancestor's poem. Ruth Ozeki's three hours watching her own face and Zenju Earthlyn Manuel's seven days of asking "what is old?" in the mirror make the koan concrete. Norman adds that wearing robes in sesshin is a practice, and closes with Manuel's passage on silence from The Deepest Peace.

title: The Seven Wise Women in the Charnel Ground
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer tells the story of the seven wise women in the charnel ground, from Florence Caplow and Susan Moon's collection The Hidden Lamp, and follows it to Case 14 of the Book of Serenity. The women go to a place of corpses in springtime, and one asks where the person has gone. Norman sets the story beside memories of cherry blossoms in Brooklyn and of sitting with the body of Norman's mother, who later asked what Buddhists say happens after death. Deshan's "What? What?" to Huo echoes the women's question, and Norman closes with Dogen's reply to Indra: the cypress in the garden is the rootless tree, and the charnel ground is land without north and south.

title: Reunion, Welcoming Trouble, Privilege
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the June Samish sesshin, held on Zoom, by recalling the reunion ground where the group usually gathers, then asks how to welcome agitation and worry as part of sesshin. Nomon reflects on white and economic privilege through a family story of New Deal home ownership and a Lummi totem pole gathering held in a gravel parking lot. Nomon then speaks up for kinhin and reads Thich Nhat Hanh's five-stanza verse on breathing and walking, which carries the whole Awareness of Breathing Sutra in miniature. Nomon ends on the question of how practice can just practice itself.

title: More About the Breath, Sutra on the Full Awareness of Breathing
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Sutra on the Full Awareness of Breathing, reading its sixteen steps aloud from Thich Nhat Hanh's book Breathe! You Are Alive after a quotation from Mel about impermanence. Norman first reminds listeners that practices without the breath are fine too, then walks through the steps: the whole breath and body, calm, the oasis difference between joy and happiness, and mind and its objects. Norman ties non-thinking in Dogen's Fukanzazengi to being aware of a thought without clinging. Norman notes that Thich Nhat Hanh sets aside the eight jhanas and that breath counting is a later addition. The final steps arrive at impermanence, where there is nothing to let go of, and Norman closes with trusting "the wreck that you are."

title: A Dharma Talk in Two Chapters
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart offers two chapters partway through the online Samish sesshin: a report on COVID, then poems by Dogen. The first chapter recalls Kanho's fear of the virus a year earlier and sets it beside World Health Organization figures, the situation in India and Brazil, and the deaths of more than 3,600 U.S. healthcare workers, two thirds of them people of color. Kanho places that suffering next to the comfort of sesshin, two facts that coexist without hindering each other. The second chapter offers homage to Sojun Mel Weitsman, sketches Dogen's life, and reads Dogen's poems on coming home and on the evening rain at Fukakusa. It ends with Dogen's verse on the colors of the mountains and the streams in the valleys.

title: Memorial Sesshin, Mel Weitsman on How to Sit Zazen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Sojun Mel Weitsman's short essay on how to sit zazen, a photocopied Berkeley Zen Center newsletter piece, as a memorial offering during sesshin. Mel describes zazen as a balance of gravity and spirit, passive and active, and ends with the line "your shoulders don't hold you up." Nomon then takes up Dogen's "think not thinking" in Fukanzazengi and the Yaoshan koan behind it, drawing on Koun Franz's explanation that the Japanese shiryu means measuring, evaluative thought. Along the way Nomon tells of catching a sudden urge to check a phone and coming back to the breath. Nomon closes by breathing with Mel and Buddha, with no gaps.

title: Sojun Mel Weitsman on Breathing
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads Sojun Mel Weitsman's words on breathing at the opening of a Zoom sesshin, after remembering two priests lost since the sangha last sat together: Jay Semino and Mel, who died in January. Mel's text calls breath the link between inside and outside, a friend to treat warm-heartedly, and something to keep low in the hara, even while reading the newspaper. Mel describes sitting beside the dying Maylee Scott, who lay breathing day after day, being breathed by the world. Norman adds a practice of counting exhales from one to ten, then asks everyone to bring that attention to meals, walking, and washing their faces during the week.

title: Zazen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up zazen through two paired qualities, the ordinary and the extraordinary, drawing on the two darts of the Sallatha Sutta, Hongzhi's poem "Silent Illumination," and the rival poems of Shenxiu and Huineng. Ordinary zazen settles a person into life, and Nomon shows it with an afternoon on the porch, when a neighbor asks for help with her husband's manic episode and the plan for writing gives way. A guided stretch covers posture, mudra, the soft belly, and breath counting. The extraordinary side points past concepts, as in Mazu's two contradictory answers to the question "What is Buddha?" Nomon closes with Blanche Hartman's story of telling Suzuki Roshi her mind was calming down and hearing him answer angrily that she does not do zazen.

title: Another Dharma Talk on Dharma Position
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dharma position, the translation of Dogen's term juhoi, following Chris's talk the week before on Shinshu Roberts' commentary on "Uji." Nomon reads Josho Pat Phelan's description of the horizontal and the vertical, and tells of a hot bike ride on which Raysla feels revived by eating a salad before any of it could be digested, an example of the brain's predictions shaping experience. Passages from Dogen's "Genjokoan" follow: its opening sentences, the boat and the shore, and firewood and ash. Nomon ends with Mayu, who answers a monk's question about the wind reaching everywhere by simply fanning himself, and with Dogen's line that the wind of the Buddha house ripens the cream of the long river.

title: Dharma Position
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the phrase "Dharma position" from Shinshu Roberts's Being Time, a commentary on Dogen's fascicle Uji, and opens with the passage from Yaoshan that begins that fascicle. Kanho retells the parable of the blind men and the elephant, then offers Kazuaki Tanahashi's definition of a Dharma position as the unique, non-repeatable stage of a thing's existence, which carries all of time. Uchiyama Roshi's poem ("though poor, never poor") and Indra's net, where each jewel reflects every other, show the particular and the boundless together. Kanho names the movement between those two poles as what makes practice come alive. Kanho closes with the last lines of Uji, on raising the eyebrows and blinking.

title: Diversity and the Way We Collectively Create a Social Reality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the last two chapters of Lisa Feldman Barrett's Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain, on diversity and the social reality people create together. Nomon describes the five-stage intercultural development model learned at Mindfulness Northwest, where an assessment landed Nomon in minimization, then turns to Barrett's example of Balinese people who relax and sleep when threatened. The 51 dharmas of Abhidharma raise the question of whether ancient Indian meditators had minds like ours, and a news story of a young man whose hand was amputated after too-tight handcuffs shows what rigid perception costs. Nomon closes by reading Joy Harjo's "Rabbit Is Up to Tricks," in which Rabbit makes a clay man with no ears.

title: What is it to Wake Up and Be Here Together?
speaker: Hoka Chris Fortin
summary: Hoka Chris Fortin takes up the question of what it is to wake up and be here together, working with Joy Harjo's poem "Rabbit Is Up to Some Tricks," in which a rabbit makes a clay man who wants more and more and has no ears. Hoka reads Zenju Earthling Manuel's "Darkness Is Asking to Be Loved," which invites the listener to fall down on the earth, and offers Suzuki Roshi's image of the breath as a swinging door. Duncan Williams on healing through ritual and the memorial for Asian American ancestors place the practice in a world of pandemic deaths and drought. Hoka closes with Li-Young Lee's "From Blossoms," read for a sangha member whose husband is in the ICU, and asks whether the peach can be tasted all the way through.

title: What am I? Awakening to the Question of Being
speaker: Anita Feng
summary: Anita Feng takes up the question "What am I?" as a hwado, a Korean Zen question kept alive by broad, spacious don't-know mind together with close attention to the fleeting present. Anita reads the Blue Cliff Record kongan in which Matsu, asked about his health, answers "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha," and walks through the five skandhas with a passage from the Anattalakkhana Sutta. Along the way come the story of the shared last breath in the room as Anita's father died, and the story of telling Zen Master Seung Sahn the question was boring and being handed a mantra instead. Anita closes with Weishan's vow to be reborn as a Kao in a neighbor's yard, a picture of service, and three sitting practices: relaxing the eyelashes, centering the air around the body, and balancing the cosmos at the crown of the head.

title: How Our Brains Influence Each Other
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the fifth lesson of Lisa Feldman Barrett's Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain, "Your Brain Secretly Works with Other Brains." Nomon describes co-regulation, where loved ones' breathing and heartbeats synchronize and a held hand lessens pain, and the cost when brains work harder around unfamiliar people. Nomon commits to attending a Lummi Nation blessing ceremony for a totem pole and to sharing an anti-racism curriculum with the sangha. The rest of the time plays excerpts from "May We Gather," the 49th-day Buddhist memorial for the Atlanta shooting victims, including two sons remembering their mother, Yong Ae Yue.

title: Case 29 of the Gateless Gate
speaker: Heather Shoren Larusso
summary: Heather Shoren Larusso takes up Case 29 of the Gateless Gate, in which two monks argue over whether the flag or the wind is moving until Huineng tells them it is the mind that moves. Heather sketches Huineng's life and the Diamond Sutra verse that woke him, then tells of the nun Miaoxin, whose shout awakens seventeen monks still arguing over the same koan 150 years later. Using the Buddha's teaching on papañca, Heather asks what the American flag stirs in a patriot and in an Indigenous person, and how views harden among people who gather with those who agree. Heather closes with Huineng's verse about the bright mirror and the question of where any dust could alight.

title: The Sallatha Sutta
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the Sallatha Sutta, an early Pali text in which painful feeling strikes like a dart and an untaught worldling takes a second one. Nomon tells of banging a toe on the bed frame at night and catching the self-scolding that followed, then reads on from the worldling's craving for pleasure to the well-taught disciple who feels only the first dart. A passage from the Nissaraniya Sutta on letting go of "I am" leads Nomon to hold two levels together: training in noticing second darts, and imagining a life not fettered at all. A closing exercise asks listeners to compare how they spoke to a suffering friend with how they spoke to themselves after a mistake.

title: How the Mind Generates Reality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dr. Barrett's neuroscience book on the brain, retelling its opening story of a Rhodesian soldier who aims at guerrilla fighters with AK-47s, then sees a boy with cows and a herding stick. Nomon presents the brain as predicting experience from the inside out, and shows a checkerboard shadow illusion in which two squares look different but are the same color. A personal example follows: freezing before difficult phone calls, then planting positive seeds, as Yogacara puts it, by savoring how good the call felt afterward. Nomon applies the same predicting brain to bias and to the shooting of Daunte Wright, then asks whether suffering comes from how minds construct reality.

title: Awakening, Mumonkan 19 and the Best Things I've Found
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up awakening through Mumonkan case 19, in which Nansen tells Joshu that ordinary mind is the way. Seishu gathers views from Susan Moon, Dale Wright, Joan Sutherland, Suzuki Roshi, and Norman Fischer's book What Is Zen?, then looks for enlightened activity in daily life. The examples are Norman handing his cup of tea to a coughing woman at a Bellingham retreat, the patient nurses who cared for Seishu's wife after knee surgery, and a friendly checker in a crowded Fred Meyer. Seishu closes with a passage on nirvana from Karen Armstrong's Buddha and the story of Seishu's father, who died in 2002 at 90, frail and cheerful, telling Seishu, "It's okay to die if you've had a good life."

title: How the Mind Generates Reality, a First Look
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the opening of lesson four in Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain, "Your brain predicts (almost) everything you do," after a vaccine appointment cuts into preparation time. A drafted Rhodesian soldier aims at a line of guerrillas carrying an AK-47 until a buddy whispers that it is just a boy leading cows with a herding stick. Nomon connects this constructed, predictive seeing to the Yogachara storehouse consciousness, where seeds of fear or patience wait to sprout, and promises a fuller treatment next week. The evening closes with congratulations to Corinne and Richard, who received jukai over Zoom, and an update on the campaign committee.

title: Zen Life, Enlightened Life, Sojun Mel Weitsman
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the teaching of Ryushin's late teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman, reading his view of enlightenment through Dogen's Genjokoan and Tozan's five ranks. Ryushin sketches Mel's life: cab driver, painter, a man who walked out of his first sesshin and came back from the Embarcadero knowing nothing else called him. Line by line, Ryushin pairs Genjokoan with his words and Ryushin's own memories: his secret love of sleeping in despite decades of rising at 4:15, Suzuki Roshi's "find something more difficult," and how he lifted a zabuton instead of nudging it with a foot. It closes on Mel's last lucid day, when he told visitors, "This has to be really hard for you."

title: Baby Brains - Nature vs. Nurture, Not So Simple
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the third of seven and a half lessons on the brain from Dr. Lisa Feldman Barrett's book, here on how baby brains develop and why nature versus nurture is too small a frame. Nomon describes infants starting with twice as many neurons as adults, then being tuned and pruned by caregivers who regulate the physical environment and share attention, as when a mother looks at a toy dog, then at the baby, then back. The Romanian orphanages under Ceaușescu show what happens without that care. A New York Times article on the Baby's First Years study, which gives poor mothers monthly cash cards, leads Nomon to a Family Promise exercise with Smarties candies standing in for a family's resources.

title: Finding Freedom Through Ethical Conduct - Liberty
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the difference between freedom and liberty, defining liberty as the responsible use of freedom without depriving anyone else, and cites Abraham Lincoln's line that the right to swing a fist ends where another person's nose begins. Kanho quotes Ibram X. Kendi's Stamped from the Beginning on racial discrimination and asks listeners to keep learning where their own liberty ends. Two Buddhist supports follow: the paramitas, and the precepts as read from the San Francisco Zen Center full moon ceremony, which Kanho frames as voluntary limits on freedom. The story of Siddhartha's four sights and great renunciation leads to Mary Oliver's poem on the Buddha's last instruction, "Make yourself a light."

title: The Brain as a Network
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the brain as one vast network in Dr. Lisa Feldman Barrett's second lesson, then questions whether "network" is itself still a model. Nomon walks through neurons, axons, dendrites and synapses, the airline-hub picture of brain clusters, and neuroplasticity, with relearning fingerstyle guitar as a living example. The Yogacara storehouse consciousness and its karmic seeds follow, with Ben Connolly's bike-messenger story and Nomon's own awkward exchange with a neighbor in the co-housing community. Nomon closes with Byakuren Judith Ragir's passage on freedom and Dogen's line about forgetting the self.

title: Continuous Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up continuous practice through Suzuki Roshi's line "one step at a time, one breath at a time, with no gaining idea" and the opening of Dogen's essay Gyoji. Nomon reads Dogen's claim that practice leaves no gap between aspiration and nirvana, and that the practice of ancestors and the practice of today's sitter actualize each other, even the sun, moon, and stars. Then Nomon reads Jean Giono's story "The Man Who Planted Trees," in which the shepherd Elzeard Bouffier plants a hundred acorns a day, through two wars, until a barren land has water and villages again. Nomon notes that Giono admitted Bouffier was invented, to make planting trees likeable, and closes on one acorn, one breath, one donation to the food bank at a time.

title: The Dharma of Neuroscience - The Triune Brain
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the second chapter of Lisa Feldman Barrett's Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain, which dismantles the triune brain theory of a lizard limbic system held in check by a rational neocortex. Nomon recalls being taught the theory with a hand gesture, hears Carl Sagan's voice from The Dragons of Eden, and admits to having taught it in mindfulness classes. Plato's charioteer and two winged horses, and Freud's id, ego, and superego, show the same inner-war picture. Nomon sets beside it Dogen's Genjokoan: the moon and the dewdrop, firewood and ash, and the monk who asks why fan yourself if the wind is everywhere.

title: Awakening on the Way of the Bodhisattva
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva, the eighth-century text Kanho has carried for years, and reads from three of its sections. Kanho opens with the Han inscription, "Do not waste your life," then reads Shantideva's prayer on taking hold of bodhicitta and tells of imagining retirement and grabbing at a moment of spacious peace that vanished. The Patience chapter's warning about anger meets Kanho's own family history and the book tucked in Kanho's purse at City Hall. Kanho closes with a taste of the wisdom chapter and the story that Shantideva levitated until only his voice remained above the clouds.

title: Neuroscience and Buddhism, Mind and Brain
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a series on neuroscience by reading Andrew Olendzki's short article on whether mind and brain are the same, then the first chapter of Lisa Feldman Barrett's Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain. Olendzki places the Buddha's middle way between eternalism and annihilationism and asks whether all consciousness is conditioned, using the lamp and its light and the fire that has gone out. Barrett's chapter follows the Amphioxus, a stomach on a stick, to the hunters of the Cambrian, whose brains evolved to budget the body's energy through prediction (allostasis). Nomon ends by sending the group into breakout conversations about how tired, hungry, or grouchy states change a person.

title: Awakening
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna takes up Dogen's instruction to turn the light inward and take the backward step, working with the twelve nidanas as Norman Fischer condenses them into four factors. Kate finds the pivot at vedana, the sensation of pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral that arises at contact, and ties it to the Heart Sutra's "no sensation." Ryushin's examples include a first love who stays the same while Ryushin's feelings change, and body scans and pain in zazen. Kate also takes likes and dislikes to Fred Meyer, where a recorded self-checkout voice keeps telling Ryushin to place Ryushin's item in the bag. Kate closes with Shantideva's cotton cloth swayed by a wafting wind.

title: Jungian Psychology and Buddhism
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Jungian psychology through Finding Meaning in the Second Half of Life by the analyst James Hollis, pairing it with the Diamond Sutra exchange between Subhuti and the Buddha about liberating countless beings while no being is liberated. Nomon sets the conditioned mind that Hollis describes against the unconditioned, then follows Hollis from the anxiety of birth and separation to the choice between anxiety and depression at every turning point. Nomon admits to almost scrapping the evening's talk out of that same anxiety. Six unconscious responses to feeling overwhelmed or insufficient follow, from retreat and control to accommodating, which Nomon names as a personal favorite, and then undeservingness, overcompensating, and reassurance seeking. The evening ends with breakout rooms where each person looks at which response is most their own.

title: Living the Awakened Life : Reflections on the Dhammapada
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first chapter of the Dhammapada in Gil Fronsdal's translation, then returns to its opening verses and comments on four themes. Nomon sets the verse "all experience is preceded by mind" beside a psychology study in which subjects recall a red car on an on-ramp that was never in the picture. Nomon then turns to the call to live ethically, to the verse that hatred never ends through hatred, and to the advice to focus on the unpleasant. A Tricycle interview with Bhante Piyananda, Miranda Shaw, Reggie Ray, and Sojun Mel Weitsman supplies different views on pleasure, and Mel's story of Suzuki Roshi taking one drink of champagne at a party closes that thread.

title: Building a Sanctuary, Coming Home to Continuous Practice
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose closes an eight-week study of Shitou's Song of the Grass Roof Hermitage by taking up Case 4 of the Book of Serenity, in which Indra plants a blade of grass and declares the sanctuary built. Joden pairs the koan with Manjushri asking Sudhana for one stalk of medicinal herb, and with the Zoom sangha, where pandemic limits turn scattered homes into knots in Indra's net. Dogen on practice without a monk's hall and Suzuki Roshi's sixteen-foot golden Buddha made from one blade of grass show how little a sanctuary needs. Joden recalls sitting on the edge of a bed in Barcelona, in the fo'c'sle of a purse seiner, and facing a stucco wall in Mexico.

title: The Meaning of Sesshin
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the word sesshin, reading its two characters as setsu, to touch or receive, and shin, heart and mind, during a sesshin on Shitou's "Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage." Nomon connects the poem's theme of being at home to leaving home, telling of the twenty years since ordination, Suzuki Roshi's departure from Rinsoin in Yaizu, and Nomon's own move last January into a home alone. A Rumi poem that repeats "Don't go back to sleep" and the calligraphy phrase "Mu So Jo," no resting place, pair ease with wakefulness. Nomon closes with the case in which Shitou tells a monk that being unsatisfied to be just human keeps awakened mind out of reach.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Conclusion
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose closes a seven-week class on Shitou's Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage with excerpts from Red Pine's Road to Heaven, a book about meeting Chinese hermits. Joden reads the Four Worthies poem, Tao Yuanming's hut beside a path, and abbots who speak of keeping the precepts and of asking who is chanting the Buddha's name. The readings end on the saying "The small hermit lives on a mountain. The great hermit lives in a town." Class members then name the lines that stayed with them, among them "Though the hut is small, it includes the entire world" and "Let go of hundreds of years and relax completely." Joden closes by reciting the whole poem.

title: Dropping Fear
speaker: Ninen Susan Elbe
summary: Ninen Susan Elbe takes up fear as a Zen topic, drawing on Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise and the Sandokai. Ninen begins with the imposter syndrome that rose when Chris asked for a talk, then describes the gift of fearlessness, which Norman names as the third kind of generosity, given by giving love. Lines from the Sandokai become images: a wooden blanket box with its lid, Mahakasyapa smiling back at the Buddha's flower, a driver lost in a city of new overpasses, and a coffee-break walk without a goal. Ninen closes with Norman's suggestion to wipe public restroom counters for the next person.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 27-32
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up the final six lines of Shitou's Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, starting with encounter dialogues that include the monk Huilang, told he lacks awakened mind because he is not satisfied to be just human. Joden links "open your hands and walk, innocent" to the Heart Sutra's no attainment and no fear, and to Kosho Uchiyama's "opening the hand of thought," illustrated by a bumper sticker reading "Don't believe everything you think." For the undying person in the hut, Joden turns to the Dhammapada on vigilance, Dogen on body-mind, and the Xinxinming. The evening closes with the five remembrances and a breakout question: how do you stay one with your skin and live your practice?

title: Spiritual Intention
speaker: Jeff Bickner
summary: Jeff Bickner takes up spiritual intention through stories of Jeff's first teacher Kobun Chino and readings from Tsoknyi Rinpoche's Fearless Simplicity and Norman Fischer's Training in Compassion. Kobun, asked to demonstrate Zen archery at Esalen, draws the bow with perfect form and shoots the arrow off the cliff into the ocean, calling "Bullseye!" Jeff describes taking the bodhisattva vows many times, and recalls a Green Gulch sesshin that ended with Norman playing Ella Fitzgerald over the zendo speakers. Tsoknyi's passage on correcting motivation and Norman's on the Lojong step of resolve lead to Suzuki Roshi's line about observing the precepts without trying to.
