Jeff closes by recalling Dogen's awakening at the sound of Rujing's voice.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 23-26
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up lines 23 to 26 of the Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, opening with Shitou stories of Changzhi Kuang and Ling Mo and the koan "Ask the post." Joden reads "turn around the light to shine within" alongside Dogen's Fukanzazengi and its backward step. On "meet the ancestral teachers," Joden offers five ways to meet them: through texts such as The Roaring Stream, the Lotus Sutra's sixteenth chapter, zazen, ritual, and being an ancestor oneself. On "don't give up," Joden turns to the I Ching's "perseverance furthers" and Huineng's Platform Sutra. Discussion and breakout rooms follow, with one participant describing a teacher who turned out to have done terrible things.

title: Jijuyu Zanmai, Isolation, Vulnerability, Suffering and Courage
speaker: Chikyo Ewan Magie
summary: Chikyo Ewan Magie takes up Dogen's Bendoa by stepping back to the isolation and vulnerability that come before practice, picturing Dogen alone in Fukakusa and Shohaku Okumura at 32, broke and sitting by himself. Chikyo recalls Dogen's early loss of his parents and the story of Sumeda, then considers modern secular life, the pandemic, and the silence that trauma can bring. A newspaper account of a skier in the French Alps, who finds the word COURAGE traced in the snow above a steep chute of moguls, becomes an image of ancestors leaving traces for those who follow. Chikyo ends with Gotama, starving, restored by a young girl's warm rice porridge.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 19-22
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up lines 19-22 of the Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage: "Just sitting with head covered, all things are at rest. Thus, this mountain monk doesn't understand at all. Living here, he no longer works to get free. Who would proudly arrange seats, trying to entice guests?" Joden opens with Shitou's move to a rock ledge and his exchange with Nanyue, then reads each line through Dogen's "think of not thinking," Norman Fischer's talk on Book of Serenity case 20, and a passage from Barry Lopez on watching a grizzly bear. Joden also cites Pascal's remark and a study in which students shocked themselves rather than sit alone. Participants then debate why the head is covered before breakout rooms on how to bring practice into life.

title: Enlightenment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the word "enlightenment," tracing it from the European Age of Enlightenment to awakening, the sense of bodhi. Drawing on Gil Fronsdal's introduction to the Dhammapada, Nomon sets out two goals, happiness and liberation, and two methods, systematic and trust, and asks what binds each of us. Nomon sets the Camp 220 eviction in Bellingham beside Suzuki Roshi's call in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind to build practice beyond enlightenment. Nomon closes with Chögyam Trungpa's story of a lay practitioner who says he has forgotten every teaching, then dies and leaves only nails and hair behind.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 13-18
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up lines 13 to 18 of the Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, beginning with "Will this hut perish or not?" and the original master who is present either way. Joden connects the original master to the Dharmakaya, reading Suzuki Roshi on just sitting, and to Huineng's commentary on the Diamond Sutra, where the bodhisattva dwells nowhere. Joden also notes that the Chinese character for steadiness shows a roof over a cow, a stable. The character for the shining window combines sun and moon, the same bright (Ming) found in Dharma names. Participants offer thoughts on the middling and lowly, on cows in a pasture, and on Yunmen's dried shit stick, and one describes a 10-foot-square room as a palace.

title: Jijuyu Zanmai, Escape This Crazy Life of Tears
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads the opening passage of Dogen's Jijuyu Zanmai, then takes up ritual through Escape This Crazy Life of Tears, a poetic diary of the 2010 pilgrimage to Japan to perform the Zuisei ceremony at Eiheiji and Sojiji. Norman reads entries about the Hokyoji abbot's advice to do at least three minutes of zazen a day, the red slippers, eel cookies, and children killing ants at Rinsoin. Japanese priests see the forms as preserving the past, while American practitioners look to the future, and Norman holds that each needs the other. Kathy says ritual is not a performance, and Norman answers that it is one, like an actor disappearing into the role of Buddha, which is what Dogen means by sitting zazen. The reading closes with the Sojiji instructions to thank the officials in a very loud voice and to leave the certificate on the cake uneaten.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 9-12
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up lines 9 to 12 of Shitou's Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, opening with Shitou's awakening and a dream of riding a tortoise with Huineng across the sea. Joden compares several translations and reads the Chinese characters, tracing "ten square feet" to the fangzhang, the size of Vimalakirti's room, where Manjushri and a crowd of guests find space while Shariputra worries about a chair. Participants read the hut as a practice, as the self, or as a park bench, and weigh the line "the middling or lowly can't help wondering" against the hierarchical societies the poem came from. Breakout rooms return with the idea that practice is portable and with the trouble of explaining practice to people who don't sit.

title: Reflections of Relentless Rain
speaker: Kukushin Kate McCandless
summary: Kukushin Kate McCandless takes up Blue Cliff Record case 46, where Qingjing asks a monk about the sound outside the gate and hears "Sound of raindrops." Kate starts from a winter of relentless rain, a hemlock fallen across the backyard, and haiku by Isa and Basho. Qingjing's "I almost don't lose myself" meets Dogen on delusion and realization, and Xuan Xia sends a new monk to enter the way through the sound of a stream. Sound becomes a way to watch the mind, and the raging mob at the gate raises the question of which parts of ourselves stay outside. Kate ends with Gary Snyder's story of a roshi's inaudible rainy-season talks, which a fellow student finally hears years later as raindrops on the roof.

title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose tells the story of how a life arrives at steady Zen practice, framed by a Lou Welch poem and Dogen's chapter on the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance. Joden traces the path from a Miami childhood and pre-med studies at Tufts through poetry in Buffalo, boatbuilding in Vancouver, and decades of land conservation in the Skagit Valley and Hawaii. A shipyard teaches giving as Dogen describes it. A Lonely Planet listing for Saturday tours at San Francisco Zen Center leads to a week's residency, a chair offered for aching knees, and Blanche Hartman's advice to visit the Bellingham sangha. Joden closes with the Tenzo's prayer offered to Nomon Tim when he became the sangha's guiding teacher.

title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 3-8
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose tells the story of Shitou's childhood from Richard McDaniel's Zen Masters of China, then takes up lines three through eight of the Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage. On the weeds that appear once the hut is finished, Joden offers a gardener's fable, Suzuki Roshi's teaching that weeds become nourishment, and Sojun Mel Weitsman's commentary on Dogen's line about blossoms and weeds. Participants then consider the shift from "I" to "the person in the hut," a Diamond Sutra line about dwelling nowhere, and Satchel Paige's remark that the social ramble ain't restful. Breakout rooms take up where we actually live, and the session closes with the four vows.

title: Self-Receiving
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up Dogen's essay Bendowa and its phrase Jijuyo Zanmai, the self-receiving concentration that Dogen names as the basis of transmission. Heigaku reads the self as empty of independent nature and therefore boundless, and recalls a classmate's remark that the grass hut builds us. A quantum physics experiment, in which two physicists named Alice and Bob get different results from the same coin toss, leads into paradox, dreams, and holding contradictory feelings at once. This is Heigaku's first Dharma teaching since the death of Heigaku's wife Diane in July, and it brings in tears of gratitude, karma, and the three wheels of giver, receiver, and gift. It closes on the open question of how to plan for the future while living in the present moment.

title: Dukkha and Waking Up
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens with Mary Oliver's poem "The Buddha's Last Instruction" and takes up dukkha, the first of the Four Noble Truths and one of the three marks of existence. Kanho tells of a barefoot, shivering stranger ringing the doorbell at 4:20 one freezing morning, then turns to the pandemic and the events at the Capitol as sources of background stress. Avoiding dukkha only teaches avoidance, so Kanho proposes turning toward it, drawing on Frank Herbert's Dune and Shohaku Okumura's line that only in zazen can we stop making karma. Kanho closes with Robert Bly's "Things to Think," where a ringing phone might carry a message vaster than anything yet heard.

title: In Gratitude to Keizan Jokin
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to Keizan Jokin and the 1324 opening of the dharma hall at Yokoji, after first telling of delivering the sangha's old zabutons to the homeless encampment around Bellingham City Hall. Nomon sets Dogen's narrow, deep vision beside Keizan's broad one, which offers lay precepts to farmers, listens to his mother, and gives transmission to a woman, Enzan. Nomon reads from the ceremony, including the four incense offerings and the monks' questions, then Keizan's two vows and his dream of shaking the filth from an old robe and wearing it anyway. Nomon closes with the opening of Keizan's Zazen Yojinki and its line that zazen transcends worldly and sacred, delusion and enlightenment.

title: Layman Pang
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Layman Pang, a householder who studies with Shitou and Mazu, through a short biography written by a wandering monk named Satya. Pang sinks his possessions in a lake, sells bamboo utensils, and asks each teacher who is not attached to the ten thousand things; Shitou answers by covering his mouth. Nomon lingers over Pang's daughter Lingzhao, who answers a question about the hundred grass tips by repeating her father's own words, and over Yaoshan, who calls dropping one thing and picking up another useful. Lingzhao dies sitting on her meditation bench, and Pang recites a verse before dying. Nomon closes with Pang's lines on past, present, and future, and Yaoshan's reminder that time is still in use.

title: Levels of Consciousness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Yogachara model of eight levels of consciousness and sets it beside Lisa Feldman Barrett's Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain. Nomon describes manas, the seventh level, as a shuttle diplomat carrying reports between the busy thinking mind and the storehouse where seeds of conditioning wait to sprout. Abraham Maslow's pyramid of needs, long a favorite, gets a second look, since the brain keeps tending food and safety all the time. Nomon then reads Barrett's first chapter, which follows the amphioxus, a "stomach on a stick," toward brains that run a body budget by prediction.

title: Keizan's Zazen Yojinki, Part 3: Practice with Stephen Levine
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the second half of Keizan's Zazen Yojinki in the closing talk of a seven-day online Rohatsu retreat, playing a guided soft-belly meditation from a 1988 Stephen Levine workshop. Keizan's advice on regulating the breath and choosing where to sit and whom to keep company with leads to the line about never forgetting the significance of impermanence. Nomon recalls the cremation of Anne Mikkelsen, with the oven audible as friends spoke, and Norman's story of a star swelling until it swallows the Earth. Nomon then describes a flash of comparing mind on seeing a Facebook photo of rose petals on a laptop, and explains the Rohatsu plans: sitting through the night, the morning star, and flower petals thrown for the Udumbara blossoms.

title: Mara and the Buddha
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells the story of Mara, setting the colorful later account of the night of awakening beside the plain telling in the Bhayabherava Sutta. Kanho describes Mara's ten legions defeated by the ten paramitas, the Buddha touching the earth to call it as his witness, and Mara's three daughters, Tanha, Arati, and Raga, who fail to draw the Buddha from his seat. Kanho proposes that Mara wakes, brushes teeth, and eats alongside the Buddha, and that Mara vanishes whenever recognized and named. The closing story, drawn from a book on the Buddha's life in the Pali Canon, has the Buddha hesitate to teach until Brahma Sahampati kneels and asks.

title: Keizan's Zazen Yojinki, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Keizan's Zazen Yojinki, beginning with William Bodiford's account in Soto Zen in Medieval Japan of the dreams and visions that guided Keizan's choice of temple sites. The manual's next paragraphs link ignorance to distraction, tranquility, wisdom, and clear seeing, and Nomon pictures the mind as the jar of muddy water from Moody Cow Meditates, which clears only when left to settle. Keizan's rules on clothing and food get a flexible reading, and a retreat participant who realized that cleaning house was just stirring the jar makes the point. Nomon ends with a passage from Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind and a plan to eat a yam with sesame seeds for dinner.

title: Keizan's Zazen Yojinki, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Keizan's Zazen Yojinki, reading the paragraphs where mind is ocean water and body is waves, after opening with a poem Katagiri Roshi left unpublished in his papers. Nomon adds context from William Bodiford's encyclopedia entry on Keizan, who lived from 1264 to 1325 and founded Yokoji. The wave image leads to a photograph of Diane's body after her death and to the cremation Nomon will attend that afternoon for Ann Mikkelsen, with chanting of the Heart Sutra. Nomon then reads the line "Listening and thinking are standing outside the gate. Zazen is sitting calmly in one's own home," and closes by inviting the sangha to let the belly soften.

title: Dogen on Enlightenment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens Rohatsu sesshin with Dogen's phrase "practice enlightenment" and the Genjokoan story of Master Baochu fanning himself, then turns to the first three paragraphs of Keizan's Zazen Yojinki. Nomon introduces Keizan as an organizer raised by his grandmother, who gave an early Dharma transmission to a woman and followed his dreams. A yoga therapist's posture exercise, turning the arms outward as if holding a platter, grounds the phrase "dropping off body and mind." Nagarjuna's mirror image of the self arrives with the third paragraph. Nomon recalls Katagiri Roshi saying "Full autumn moon" in a San Francisco Zen Center sesshin and closes with Ikkyu's poem about reading the love letters sent by wind, rain, snow, and moon.

title: Thoughts on zazen from Zoketsu Norman Fischer
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first third of the meditation chapter in Zoketsu Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise, part of Nomon's study of the six paramitas, and adds comments of Nomon's own. Norman traces the word meditation from Old French and Latin, describes the tripod of ethical conduct, meditation and understanding, and defines shamatha through Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga. Nomon lingers on the five hindrances: attachment, aversion, flurry and worry, laziness, and doubt. Norman's favorite practice is breathing in the lower belly, and he also offers the phrase "May all beings be happy." Nomon closes by sending everyone into groups of three to share what hindrances showed up in that evening's sitting.

title: 101 Zen Stories, Part 2: Japanese Zen Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a second batch of stories from Nyogen Senzaki's early English collection 101 Zen Stories, after announcements about Rohatsu sesshin and the Sunday schedule. Ryōnen burns her face with a hot iron to win acceptance as a disciple, which recalls the Zen sewing teacher Josu-san, who burned off a fingertip to change teachers. Hakuin goads a samurai into drawing his sword, and Ikkyu tells a dying man there is no coming or going. Nomon closes with Shuichi's silent temple, where a neighbor knows the master has died when she hears bells and sutras.

title: 101 Zen Stories, Part 1: Japanese Zen Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Nyogen Senzaki's 1919 collection 101 Zen Stories, reading from its first half to show how Zen stories look once they move from Chinese koans into Japan. Nomon tells the stories of Nanin's overflowing teacup, Hakuen's "Is that so?", Tanzan carrying the girl across the mud, and Chiyono's pail with no bottom. Nomon adds Soyen Shaku's daily rules ("the fearless attitude of a hero and the loving heart of a child") and Bankei keeping the thief in sesshin. A sidebar on Paul Reps and his line "Drinking a cup of tea, I stopped the war" opens the evening. Participants close by trading family stories, including one about a child who thinks the moon is following the car because it wants some of the chicken.

title: Shosai Myo Kichijyo Dharani
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Shosai Myo Kichijyo Dharani from the chant book, the last in a year of Sunday talks on that book. Nomon sorts its texts into sutras, Chan poems, essays by Dogen, and dharanis, then explains that dharanis work through sound, drawing on a Shingon temple visit in Seattle where the chanting seemed to shake the building. A Sanskrit source turns up for this one, an invocation of the goddess Lakshmi, and Nomon reads it line by line: adoration, blaze forth, stand firm, patience, svaha. Her four hands stand for Dharma, Kama, Artha, and Moksha. The questions afterward turn to transliteration and to a listener who chanted it every morning before breakfast at Rinzai-ji.

title: On Being Shuso in 2020
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the opening of the 2020 practice period and the installation of a new Shuso, held in a emptied zendo as the community leaves its building. Kanho reads Blue Cliff Record case 14, Yunmen's "An Appropriate Statement," with the start of its verse commentary, and closes with Dogen's "Practice Period" fascicle from the Shobogenzo. Along the way, Kanho describes the Shuso role as a rite of passage with Zoom as a "sub hub," and recalls treating early practice periods as a challenge event and signing up for everything. Kanho names the suffering of COVID-19, racial injustice, and long food bank lines, then ends by saying the community will take up the paramitas as bodhisattva practice.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 48: Kan-feng's One Road
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 48 of the Mumonkan, the last koan in the series, in which a monk asks Qianfeng where the one straight road to nirvana lies and Qianfeng draws a line in the air with his staff. Nomon connects the question to the six paramitas, recommending a morning practice of sitting on the edge of the bed and naming an intention, then asks how sangha members can help each other practice them wisely. A Jungian image of students handing their gold to a teacher, who must hold it and give it back, frames the question. After breakout groups, Nomon closes with Nyogen Senzaki's final talk of 1939, which asks for "no stink of Zen."

title: Basic Human Goodness - Buddha Nature
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up basic human goodness, which is Buddha nature, against the backdrop of the COVID-19 fall surge. Kanho opens with a prayer for essential workers by dharma sister Sean Evans, then turns to impermanence and the Western sense of original sin and shame, set beside the Zen view that problems are temporary defilements covering basic goodness. Generosity follows, with the emptiness of giver, receiver and gift and a short poem of Kanho's own. Kanho then thanks postal workers, grocery and farm workers, and hospital staff, and reads names of doctors and nurses who have died, ending with the four bodhisattva vows.

title: The Jewel Mirror Samadhi
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, the chant attributed to Dongshan, and its Five Ranks. Kanho recalls Abbot Steve Stuckey's laughter in dokusan over the line about Yi the archer, then reads Dogen's "Old Mirror" and Xuefeng's old mirror that shows a barbarian or a Chinese person. Dongshan's five stanzas follow, from the sleepy-eyed grandam who fails to recognize her face in the mirror to the one who returns to sit among coal and ashes. In the discussion, Kanho cautions against placing oneself in a rank and retells Jack Kornfield's story of grizzly paw prints to show that fear lives in the future.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 47: Tou-shuai's Three Barriers
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 47 of the Gateless Barrier, where Tou-shuai sets three barriers: see into your true nature, be free from life and death when your eyesight fails, and know where you go when the four elements separate. Nomon turns to Nyogen Senzaki's comment that true nature is "not confined in a thing" and so is found in everything. Nomon compares practice to the slow rising of light at dawn and describes turning over stones with interest and trust rather than a hunger for answers. Talus rolling Diane's body out of Whatcom Hospice House, with the staff gathered to thank them, shows the koan in life. Nomon closes by asking where each person is sending their light right now.

title: What are koans?
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Mumonkan, the thirteenth-century collection of 48 koans also called The Gateless Barrier, and reads four of its cases. Nomon sets aside the reputation of koans as merciless puzzles, pointing instead to two workers quietly smoothing wet concrete on a sidewalk and to the possibility that koans began as poetic drinking games. Case 5 (the man hanging from a branch by his teeth) becomes a question about everyday choices, case 16 (Yunmen's robe and bell) about intention, and case 37 (Zhaozhou's oak tree) about really seeing a tree. Case 42 follows Manjushri, a woman in samadhi, and the bodhisattva Ensnared Light, whose name can also be read as "diluted wisdom."

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 46: Proceed From the Top of the Pole
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Mumonkan case 46, "Proceed From the Top of the Pole," and traces it to its longer source, Book of Serenity case 79, where Changsha sends a monk to ask his Dharma brother Hui about life before and after meeting Nanquan. Hui's answer, "There couldn't be anything else," becomes a phrase Nomon invites listeners to feel in body and heart. Nomon imagines the pole as a comfortable platform and links stepping off it to the sangha leaving its building on Saturday, with Dogen's backward step as another way to picture the leap. Nomon closes with Wumen's verse against drawing another's bow, riding another's horse, or discussing another's faults, and the memory of forty-something people walking slowly up Laurel Street.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 45: Wu-tsu: "Who Is That Other?"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 45 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Wu-tsu asks who the "other" is that Shakyamuni and Maitreya serve. Nomon reads the question as an urging to look past even Buddhahood, and applies it to the pull of zendo positions and to the ordinary generosity that the paramitas call not yet enough. Mumon's four "don'ts" about another's bow, horse, faults, and affairs lead into a story from a noon mindfulness class, where a chat message about a Nalanda Bodhi retreat exposes a fear of rejection behind Nomon's habit of not mentioning upcoming events. Nomon closes with Kabir's poem of a thousand-petaled flower inside the body that serves as a seat.

title: Modern Love - A Glance and a Rooster That Changed Everything
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads "A Glance and a Rooster That Changed Everything," a Modern Love column by Naomi Brynvillis, after announcing the September 19th closing ceremony for the dharma hall. Nomon frames the story with the six realms, the Manjushri koan, and Dogen's literal belief in rebirth, and asks how to engage strange material without flattening it into myth or psychology. The column follows a Haitian woman after the 2010 earthquake, when a Vaudoux priest prescribes a green onion, a wooden spoon, and a young rooster. A month later she meets Xander, a white aid worker, at a cholera treatment center. Nomon closes by asking how to hold all of it as stories, and opens the floor.

title: The Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom, which the sangha chants after the Heart Sutra, and traces it to the opening of chapter seven of the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita Sutra, the Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom. Nomon sets the hymn beside the six paramitas and the rise of Mahayana, then reads the passage where Shariputra praises wisdom as a source of light and the mother of bodhisattvas, and asks the Buddha how a bodhisattva should stand in her. When Sakra asks why, Shariputra's answer turns on practicing from "no basis," and Subhuti's teaching that a bodhisattva stands nowhere, as the Tathagata does. Nomon closes by reciting the hymn and noting that the original last line reads "the Buddhas, the Lords."

title: Autumn Light
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton reads from Shuko's book Autumn Light: My 50 Years in Zen, beginning with the Red Cedar zendo in Bellingham and a first class with Kobun Chino Sensei in the early 1970s. Most of the readings come from the three-month practice period at Tassajara, entered at age 78. They include Tangaryo hallucinations of handwriting on the wall, the abbess's teaching on the "karma body," a Shosan question about fear followed by a dream of a leopard, and the final month when body and mind give out. In the discussion, Shuko describes reaching the limit of effort and finding relief in learning that doing more is unnecessary. Shuko closes by saying the experience loosened a long habit of obedience.

title: Gateless Barrier, Cases 43–44: Zen Sticks
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Mumonkan cases 43 and 44, in which Shoushan holds up a Zen stick and asks what to call it, and Bajiao gives a stick to those who have one and takes it from those who have none. Nomon reads the stick through flattening, the habit of boxing complex things into single words, and sets John Muir's invisible cords and Mary Oliver's grasshopper beside it. A recent step in the divorce process, when the urge to gather hugs from everyone gave way to a quiet day alone, shows a freedom no one else can hand over. Two early nuns' poems from the Therigatha lead to the phrase "Take it seriously, but don't take it personally," and small groups then share times of not getting what they wanted.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 42: Manjusri and the Young Woman in Samadhi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 42 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Manjusri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, cannot rouse a woman sitting in samadhi near the Buddha's throne, and the earthy Ensnared Light wakes her with one finger snap. Nomon recalls a Samish sesshin evening when a woman stayed motionless in zazen after everyone left, until Norman Fischer softly touched her shoulder. Suzuki Roshi's words on practice and enlightenment and the image of snow sliding off a roof or melting slowly shape a look at stages versus gradual waking. Nomon reads the case as a reminder to seek wise friends who can snap us out of our trances, friends who are a bit of a mess themselves. A poem by the early nun Muta, about her first bite of food as a free woman, closes the evening.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 41: Bodhidharma Pacifies the Mind, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 41 of the Gateless Barrier, where Bodhidharma answers the second ancestor's plea to pacify his mind by asking him to bring it. Poems by early Buddhist nuns from the Therigatha, read from Maddy Weingast's translation The First Free Woman, frame the case, including Mittakali's thoughts building a house and then a city. Nomon imagines the second ancestor waiting outside the cave and blurting out his agitation after years of chores and sitting, then finding no mind to show. Nomon links this backward step to the forward step of anti-racism work, reading Naomi Shihab Nye's "Kindness" and its line about seeing the size of the cloth.

title: Prajna Paramita
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up the sixth paramita, prajna or wisdom, using Dale Wright's The Six Perfections for Cultivating Character and Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise. Wright describes wisdom as a way of being in the world: facing the truth without being unnerved, and being disillusioned but not disheartened. Shuko connects emptiness, impermanence, and co-arising to the teaching of no self, then reads Norman on the irony of taking things too seriously and on the bodhisattva's humility. Alan Senauke's practice of limiting his news and recalling daily joys, and Shuko's memory of the Vietnam years with Milton's line "They also serve who only stand and wait," bring the teaching into the pandemic. Small groups close the evening with a conversation about anxiety and panic.

title: The Meal Chant, The Three Wheels
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the meal chant line "May we, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver, and gift," beginning with Dogen's 1246 Fushuku Hanpo passage on being intimate with food. Kanho moves from thoughts arising and falling away in zazen to the oxygen cycle, where eight trees supply one person's breath and the trees receive exhaled carbon dioxide in return. Norman Fischer's words on giving as life itself and Mary Oliver's poem "When Death Comes" sit beside a list of gifts: listening, a poem, a cooked meal, a bridge. Kanho ends with a plea during COVID-19 to share with a neighbor in need and to give to the food bank.

title: Virya Paramita
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna takes up virya, the paramita of energy and joyful enthusiasm, in an evening offered in memory of Diane, who met her cancer and her death with directness and courage. Drawing on Dogen's line about using the ground to get back up, Ryushin describes second arrows, the emotional energy released by George Floyd's killing, and Ringu Tulku's teaching on relaxing within anger. Ryushin shares Norman Fischer's practice of patient endurance for insomnia, Shantideva's call to cultivate desire for the wholesome, and Louis Richmond's list of five great fears, which includes public speaking. The evening closes with Joseph Goldstein's words on vulnerability and a Zoom breakout question about energy for practice.

title: Kshanti Paramita
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Kshanti Paramita, the perfection of patience, beginning with an evening when a loud outburst at Carolyn over driving directions ruined a dinner out. Meditation becomes the training ground for patience, starting with a sore knee, and Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise is quoted on how facing pain with tolerance beats avoiding it. Seishu sorts patience into personal hardship, relationships, and the reality of impermanence, with Suzuki Roshi's "Accept what is as it is and help it to become its best" and Joko Beck stopping two fighting men on a San Diego beach as examples. Martha Postlewaite's poem "Clearing" closes the evening, read twice.

title: Sila Paramita
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up sila, the paramita of ethics, as the second in a series on the six paramitas, tracing it to right speech, right action, and right livelihood in the Eightfold Noble Path. Reizan describes the path as a wheel, notes that Theravada students begin with ethics before meditation, and favors guidelines as touchstones over moral absolutism, always imagining oneself slightly off the mark and working toward it. Reizan then opens a discussion on living ethically in a turbulent time, where participants offer listening, Suzuki Roshi's shining one corner of the world, and a friend's daughter who answers her angry brother by asking, "What would happen then?"

title: The Five Contemplations
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the five contemplations of the meal chant, reading them at the start and again after a passage from the Huayan teacher Dushun on Indra's net. Kanho thanks teachers with verses from Shantideva, then recalls the online Samish session of July 2020 and misses the sesshin food and the herons along the walk. Indra's net becomes a way to see a morning cup of coffee and a bowl of oats with yogurt, which call up cows, rain, bees, trucks, and the iron in our blood from exploding stars. Kanho closes with Blue Cliff Record Case 14, where Yunmen answers a monk's question about the teaching of a lifetime with "An appropriate response."

title: Dana Paramita
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens a series on the six paramitas with dana paramita, the perfection of generosity, drawing on books by Dale Wright, Norman Fischer, and Tenshin Reb Anderson. Kanho traces the word paramita to meanings like "highest" and "gone beyond," then sorts giving into material gifts, fearlessness, and the Dharma. A grizzly on a Yellowstone trail shows fear living in the future, and readings include Shantideva on giving up the body and Luopu's death scene in case 41 of the Book of Serenity. Kanho closes with Norman's instructions for sitting in the spaciousness around thoughts, then hands listeners the question of generosity amid Black Lives Matter, COVID-19, and climate change.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 41: Bodhidharma Pacifies the Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 41 of the Gateless Gate, "Bodhidharma Pacifies the Mind," in which the second ancestor Huike (Weike in the transcript) stands in the snow, cuts off his arm, and asks to have his mind put to rest. Nomon sets it beside Bodhidharma's exchange with Emperor Wu ("no merit," "vast emptiness, nothing holy," "I don't know") and the four disciples who answer with skin, flesh, bones, and marrow. A story of Nomon nearly mistaking a visiting Japanese teacher for the sangha's own teacher, until Norman Fischer set Nomon straight, shows how readily we look outside ourselves. Dogen's line on forgetting the self leads to the practice of "I don't know," and Nomon closes with July plans, including six practice leaders taking over the Wednesday talks.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 40: Kuei-shan Kicks Over the Water Bottle
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 40 of the Mumonkan, in which Baizhang sets a water bucket on the floor and asks what to call it, and Guishan kicks it over and walks out. Nomon adds the backstory of the geomancer friend who had already sized up the shuso and the tenzo, and wonders whether the contest is a rigged game. The shuso's answer, "a wooden clog," stays in the realm of objects, which leads Nomon to the concept of resisting arrest, a Ta-Nehisi Coates article on housing, and East Palo Alto across the creek from the Palo Alto of Nomon's childhood. Bodhidharma's skin, flesh, bones, and marrow become a measure of how deeply racism is understood, and Nomon ends on the bucket whose bottom finally falls out.

title: Ecclesiastes
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Ecclesiastes, called Kohelet in Hebrew, and reads its opening verses alongside Robert Alter's translation, which renders "vanity" as "mere breath." Norman links that breath to the week of sesshin, hearing the inhale as living spirit and the exhale as letting go. The sun going round, the forgotten dead in Thomas Hardy's graveyard poem, and Dogen's bird flying through a traceless sky show how forgetting and legacy look from Zen practice. "A time to be born and a time to die" becomes Genjokoan, each moment given as it is. Norman closes by thanking the sangha for the first Zoom sesshin and standing in awe before the verse "whatever God does is forever."

title: Matsu's Meaning of the Ancestor's Coming From India
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up case 108 of Dogen's Three Hundred Koans, in which a monastic asks Matsu the meaning of the ancestor's coming from India and is sent on to Zhitang and then Baizhang, none of whom answers. Norman reads the monastic's question as the human urge to seek truth, then turns to Anam Thubten's Choosing Compassion and its "mind of disenchantment." Norman retells Anam's fear that his gentle teacher would see through him, and the story of two wolves, where the one fed most wins. A line from James Baldwin about hatred shielding people from pain leads Norman to racism. Matsu's "white head, black head" becomes each person's moment as the whole truth, and Norman closes on the last full day of sesshin.

title: Shilou's Shortcomings
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up case 50 of Dogen's Three Hundred Cases, in which a monastic asks Shilou for skillful means, Shilou answers "I don't have earlobes," and the monastic's bow earns a blow. Norman recalls the late-1960s evening Lyndon Johnson stopped the bombing and an old settler in Israel who insisted everything is always going toward peace, arguing for modest hope now and faith over the long run. Norman then turns to Ibram Kendi's second kind of racist idea and to teaching in Marin City, where Norman received far more than was given. Shilou's "My faults lie in your shortcomings" becomes shortcomings held in common, and Tiantong's poem closes it: when clouds gather on the mountain, thunder fills the sky.

title: Tianhuang's Essential Dharma Gate
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up story 106 from Dogen's collection, "Tianhuang's Essential Dharma Gate," in which the rice-cake seller Long Tan becomes Tianhuang's attendant and learns that the teaching has been in the bowing, standing, and tea all along. Norman opens by grieving the police killing of Rayshard Brooks, then argues that practice is mostly hanging around together, since any moment of encounter can change us. Norman tells of missing Norman's own enlightenment when a bowl fell in the room Norman had just left, and of the Hasidic rabbi who only wanted to watch his teacher tie his shoes. Norman closes by dedicating the sesshin to racial justice.

title: Guishan's Do Not Betray Others
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up case 47 of Dogen's Chinese Shobogenzo, "Guishan's Do Not Betray Others," in which Guishan points at straw sandals and tells Yangshan that all day long we receive people's support. Opening a sesshin during the pandemic and the protests after George Floyd's death, Norman argues that the whole world is the body, so sitting cannot be a retreat from politics. Norman draws on the historian Ibram X. Kendi, who says there are no racists, only racist ideas, and who survived stage four cancer by first digesting the truth of it. Yangshan's reply that wearing socks for others is not prohibited brings Norman to a closing image: when it's cold, I put on my socks for you, and when it's warm, you take off your jacket for me.

title: Black Lives Matter
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first sections of Ta-Nehisi Coates's Atlantic article "The Case for Reparations" as part of a personal study of the koan of whiteness. The reading follows Clyde Ross from Mississippi, where his family's land and boyhood horse are taken, to a contract-sale house in North Lawndale, Chicago, and the Contract Buyers League's 1968 push for reparations. Nomon then describes how the article moves past "I know I'm privileged," recalling a grandmother's owned trailer home and a great-aunt and great-uncle's chicken farm as footholds in a wealth engine closed to Black Americans. Silence follows, and Nomon asks what words there are for this.

title: Self-Receiving and Employing Samadhi
speaker: Kanshin Allison Tait
summary: Kanshin Allison Tait takes up "Self-Receiving and Employing Samadhi," the section of Dogen's Bendowa that the sangha chants, and first sketches Dogen's life from his ordination at age 13 through his years in China with Rujing. Kanshin explains the Japanese title jiji u zanmai and reads through the text line by line, with Kosho Uchiyama's commentary alongside. Along the way come the Buddha holding up a flower for Mahakasyapa, the claim that earth, grass, and roof tiles awaken along with the sitter, and the image of zazen as a hammer striking emptiness like a bell. Kanshin closes with Uchiyama's verse on meeting oneself in heaven or hell.

title: Paramitas, Tonglen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett steps away from koan study for a week to introduce the six paramitas, which six senior students will each take up in July talks while Nomon is on sabbatical. Nomon reads the opening of Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise, where the poet Robert Desnos reads palms in a line of prisoners headed for the gas chambers, predicting long lives and joy until the guards cannot carry out the executions. Nomon connects this story of imagination to the bodhisattva path, then leads a tonglen meditation: breathing in suffering as dark smoke, first one's own, then a friend's, then a whole group's, and breathing out light.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 39: Yun-men: "You Have Misspoken"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 39 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Yunmen interrupts a monk quoting Zhang Zhuo's enlightenment poem and says, "You have misspoken." Nomon tells how Zhang Zhuo, whose name can be read as "awkwardness," wrote the poem after his teacher asked who he was, then asks where the monk went wrong: borrowed words, showing off, or a teacher's misused authority. Interruption becomes the subject, tied to the pandemic's sudden stop on the whole world. Nomon ends with the Japanese saying nanakorobi yaoki, fall down seven times, get up eight, and sends the sangha into small groups to discuss being thwarted.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 38: Wu-tsu's Buffalo Passes Through the Window
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier case 38, in which Wu-tsu describes a buffalo whose head, horns, and four legs pass through a window, then asks why the tail cannot. Nomon treats the visible parts of Zen practice (zazen, chanting, study, robes) as the buffalo's body and the quieter essence as the tail. Wumen's comment about getting "upside down" leads Nomon to look at an odd personal path: starting the Bellingham sitting group, the 2007 offer of a $100,000 donation that pulled attention away from family, and becoming a Dharma teacher on Zoom. Nomon closes by asking what it would be to spend years sitting with the single phrase "upside down."

title: The Eko, Dedication of Merit
speaker: Kakumyo Lowe-Charde
summary: Kakumyo Lowe-Charde takes up the eko, the dedication of merit chanted at the end of service, as the focus of Kakumyo's spring ango term vow. Kakumyo describes small "offertories" through the day, such as a dedication while washing dishes for people without clean water, or while checking email for all beings' interconnection. Kakumyo sets Soto Zen's view of practice as realization against the Western wish for predictable cause and effect, and cites the Pali Canon's fetters of skeptical doubt and attachment to rites. Kakumyo also describes telling imagination from discovery: imagining is fast and high in the body, while investigating is slow and low. Kakumyo closes by inviting comments and questions.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 37: Chao-chou: The Oak Tree in the Courtyard
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 37 of the Mumonkan, in which a monk asks Zhaozhou about the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West and hears "The oak tree in the courtyard." Nomon turns to bird watching: the lack stirred by an expert birder's warbler photos online, then a neighborhood walk with binoculars that turns up about forty yellow-rumped warblers a few blocks from home. The monk's follow-up, "Please don't teach me with reference to outside things," brings in the mind that creates inside and outside and keeps looking elsewhere. Nomon closes with Dogen on leaping beyond abundance and lack, and a photo of the warbler shared on screen.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 36: Wu-tsu: Meeting Someone Attained in the Way
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Mumonkan case 36, where Wuzu asks what to do when meeting a Zen master on the road, unable to speak and unable to stay silent. Nomon recalls meeting Robert Aitken, whose translation the series follows, at a Dharma transmission ceremony in the mid-1990s, where a polite "Good to meet you" was the only answer on offer. Nomon then tells of Nyogen Senzaki, whose teacher Soyen Shaku set down a suitcase in Golden Gate Park fog and told him to stay in America. Nyogen kept a zendo going at the Heart Mountain internment camp and wrote of opening his empty fist on a Los Angeles street corner. Nomon ends with the way Norman Fischer walked to the dokusan room.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 35: Wu-tsu: "Which Is the True Ch''ien?"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 35 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Wuzu asks his monks which was the real Qian after the woman and her spirit separated, and reads the Chinese folktale behind it. Torn between a man of rank and her betrothed cousin Chou, Qian splits: one half sails off with Chou and raises two children over six years, while the other half lies silent and ill at home. Nomon dwells on the reunion, where each half turns toward the other and the sick one rises, and on Wumen's poem of moon and clouds, mountains and valleys, "Is this one? Is this two?" Nomon closes with the softer, younger-looking faces at the end of a long retreat.

title: The Merging of Difference and Unity
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the Sandokai, "The Merging of Difference and Unity," the poem by the eighth-century Chinese master Shitou that the sangha has just chanted. Seishu explains the title's three characters, including the merchants who break a wooden board in half and rejoin it to confirm an agreement, and ties the poem to the Heart Sutra's "form is emptiness" and to a passage from Karen Armstrong's book on the Buddha. Four sections of the poem follow, with the body as an orchestra and light and dark as the front and back foot in walking. Seishu then tells of a sleepless night when an ordinary cup of tea tasted like the best of Seishu's life, and closes with Dogen's instructions to the cook.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 32: The Buddha Responds to an Outsider
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier Case 32, in which an outsider tells the Buddha he asks for neither the spoken nor the unspoken, and the Buddha sits still. Nomon connects the case to Nagarjuna's line that emptiness is a departure from all views, then follows Ananda's question to the fine horse who runs at the shadow of the whip. Reading the Patoda Sutta, Nomon applies its stages to the coronavirus moving from another village to the body. A passage from Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind says the worst horse may be the most valuable. Nomon closes with Thich Nhat Hanh's boat people, where one calm person made each boat safer, and sends everyone into breakout rooms.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 31: Chao-chou Investigates the Old Woman
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier case 31, in which a monk asks a roadside tea seller the way to Mount Wutai and hears "Go straight ahead," then "a good, respectable monk, but he too goes that way." Nomon describes the mountain where Manjushri is said to live, and imagines Zhaozhou, known for his humility, going to investigate the old woman and perhaps being seen through in return. Nomon turns the question of going straight ahead to the pandemic, reading Lama Willa Miller's essay about a drug store with bare shelves, fear as an invitation, and quarantine as retreat. Nomon plans a device-free Sabbath day in the woods and closes with Wendell Berry's "The Peace of Wild Things."

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 30: Ma-tsu: "This Very Mind is Buddha"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 30 of the Gateless Barrier, Mazu's "This very mind is Buddha," reading Robert Aitken's essay on the case during a sesshin day when Nomon admits to grumbling at the 5 a.m. jolt alarm. Aitken tells how Nanyue rubs a roofing tile to make a mirror and asks whether to beat the ox or the cart. Then Damei, who hears Mazu's answer and settles in a forest hut, still says "this very mind is Buddha" after a visiting monk reports that Mazu now teaches "not mind, not Buddha." The reading ends with Yajnadatta, who panics at finding no head until a friend knocks him on it. Nomon calls the tradition ridiculous and finds that this mind includes the voice asking whether sesshin could start at 6:30.

title: Why we chant
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the question of why Red Cedar Zen Community chants, opening with a Mary Oliver poem and the memory of Kanho's first visit, when the Heart Sutra and the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo arrived as bewildering sounds before Kanho was sent to clean the toilets. Kanho recalls lying sick at Tassajara and hearing the sangha chant the names of the ancestors across the valley, like the pulse of the world. Kanho offers a loose list of reasons: chanting teaches, honors ancestors, links Zen centers, builds sangha, serves devotion, and occupies the mind. Kanho ends with chanting the ancestors' names when cookies and computer games have failed, then closes with Oliver's "When Death Comes."

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 29: "Not the Wind; Not the Flag"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 29 of the Gateless Barrier, in which two monks argue over whether the flag or the wind is moving until Huineng says it is the mind that moves. Speaking during the first weeks of the coronavirus outbreak in Washington State, Nomon describes the fear that stirs the mind, from the Kirkland class closures to the five remembrances. The sesshin instruction turns to the Buddha's teaching on mindfulness of breath and body, with breath counting framed as returning to one. A story of Suzuki Roshi nearly drowning at Tassajara, then resolving to take up counting again, anchors that practice. Nomon ends with Martha Postlethwaite's poem "Like a Clearing."

title: The Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo
speaker: Shinmon Michael Newton
summary: Shinmon Michael Newton takes up the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, the short chant the sangha has just recited, and goes through it line by line. Shinmon tells of chanting it beside Shinmon's dying mother in the hospital and of the 108 fast repetitions at a Rinzai temple's 4 a.m. sesshin. Kanzeon is read as the compassionate heart within, with Dogen calling out during a storm at sea as an example. The phrases "in" and "en" become a seed and its soil and rain, or the hilltop vista and the climb that earns it. Shinmon ends by calling the chant a "Cliff notes" of practice and handing out sheets for writing personal translations.

title: Practice Period 5 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the closing lines of Shitou's Sandokai, recapping the poem in sets of eight lines before reading lines 33 to 42. The recap runs from the opening reassurance through the senses, the four elements, and the fish who cannot see water. Nomon notes that "principle" and "sameness" translate the same character, and the group wrestles with the image of two arrow points meeting midair. On "don't set up standards of your own," Nomon recalls a Zurich head student correcting the way a zafu was turned, and reads Suzuki Roshi on Tassajara's rules as the finger pointing at the moon. The session ends with the group's poems, including Nomon's about crows and a sidewalk.

title: Practice Period 4 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up lines 27 through 32 of Shitou's Sandokai, the passage on light and darkness, after a small-group discussion of Norman Fischer's essay on teaching Zen. Nomon reads light as what can be described and darkness as mystery, and compares the circle of knowledge to a lamp whose circle of darkness grows as the light widens. Looking at the Chinese characters, Nomon finds light and dark fitting together and accepting each other. The "oppose one another" line becomes the front and back foot in walking, which a participant extends to a binary star system. A closing group explores light and dark in personal relationships.

title: Practice Period 3 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the third eight-line section of the Sandokai, lines 17 to 24, which turns from feeling tone to the first skandha, form, through the four elements and the six senses. Nomon suggests noticing what is seen, heard, and smelled without the "I," and reads the trunk and branches that "share the essence" as a way to question the line between revered and common. A neighbor's blankets spread to dry in the back parking lot, which Bob Penny folds into a shopping cart, serve as one example. The story of the two monks and the woman at the river, with its sexism noted, closes the teaching on the question of what we carry. Participants add comments on speech, acorns, and language fixing things into nouns.

title: Practice Period 2 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up lines 9 through 17 of the Sandokai, Shitou's eighth-century poem on the interplay of Ji, the things of the world, and Ri, emptiness or unity. After zazen and a chant of the full text, Nomon looks at how the mind sorts the senses into pleasant and unpleasant, tracing the repeated Chinese character for "interact" to pieces meaning walk and turn around. A Dogen poem about waterbirds that leave no traces leads into a reading from Mingyur Rinpoche's In Love with the World, where the lama, newly vanished from his monastery, is squeezed onto the lowest-class Indian train, sits on the floor for the first time, and catches himself judging the passengers' smell and dirty feet.

title: Fukanzazengi - Why Sit?
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Dogen's Fukanzazengi, written in 1233, and asks what it means to sit when political upheaval has shaken many people's sense of what is solid. Kanho traces Dogen's own question from Tendai original enlightenment to China and back, then reads the line "Think of not thinking... Non-thinking" through a plain-English paraphrase: we are perfect and sacred, and also messed up by grasping and aversion. The non-hippo that turns out to be a red-tailed hawk shows how hard it is to define by negation. Kanho closes on Dogen's dragon gaining the water and the tiger entering the mountain, with effort as showing up for life.

title: 'Ritual, "Just" Do It, Ji and Ri'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up sesshin as one big ritual, in which sitting, eating, and even chanting are done "just" to do them, and then turns to Case 28 of the Mumonkan, "Longtan Blows Out the Candle." Nomon connects the "just" of ritual to the Sandokai's ji (things) and ri (sameness), which need each other, and to light and dark as ways of seeing and not seeing. In the case, Deshan, who arrives with a cart of Diamond Sutra commentaries and is stumped by a tea seller, receives a candle from Longtan that is blown out. He then burns his notes. Nomon closes by asking whether we can apologize for pride and listen to the darkness.

title: Suffering Humans Practice Here, The Heart Sutra
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra at the first Sunday-morning meeting of Red Cedar Zen's new monthly schedule, after announcing Chris Burkhart's new post as Tanto, the head of practice. Nomon asks what it means to commit to practice, then answers with the phrase "suffering humans practice here" and the idea of taking life seriously while holding it lightly. Reading Suzuki Roshi on emptiness, Nomon describes the frame story of Avalokiteshvara speaking to Shariputra and Thich Nhat Hanh's added phrase "not separate self-entities." Nomon then offers a prayer in that spirit, "May we someday be free," and closes by moving the room into a circle for tea.

title: Teachings I've Appreciated
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley shares teachings drawn from recorded talks online, starting with Gil Fransdell's daily question, "If this was the last day of my life, how would I like to spend it?", and Shodo Hirata Roshi's poem "In This Passing Moment." Seishu recalls a month of post-surgery rest that went better once the complaining stopped, and reads Karen Armstrong's description of nirvana as an inner haven in the midst of pain. Two more teachings follow: the path is always a step away, and Zen forms introduce us to limits. Seishu then turns to Gloria Steinem's evening at the Mount Baker Theatre, where "linked, not ranked" and small daily kindnesses echo sangha, Dogen, and Suzuki Roshi's "shining one corner of the world." Seishu ends with the three pieces of advice Norman Fischer gives new priests: be humble, see everyone as Buddha, try to be helpful.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 26: Fa-yen: Two Monks Roll Up the Blinds
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 26 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Fayan points at the bamboo blinds, two monks roll them up, and Fayan says, "One has got it, one has lost it." Nomon reads the line as a question about gain and loss, tied to the Eight Winds of the World, and recalls Fayan as a young pilgrim who answers "I don't know" and hears that not knowing is most intimate. A reading from Venerable Thubten Chodron on happiness sits beside the Heart Sutra's "neither increase nor decrease" and the shared happiness at the end of Rohatsu sesshin, which no one can name as a gain. Nomon closes with Mumon's verse about throwing away the sky so that not a breath of wind comes through.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 24: Feng-hsueh: Equality and Differentiation
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 24 of the Gateless Barrier, in which a monk asks Feng-hsueh how to escape the faults of speech and silence, and Feng-hsueh answers by remembering spring, with partridges singing and countless flowers fragrant. Nomon starts with stories of waiting for late lecturers, then reads Dogen's line in the Genjokoan about finding your place where you are, along with Wendell Berry's lines on being baffled. Several translations of the monk's question show how tangled the case is, and Nomon sets Feng-hsueh's answer beside Suzuki Roshi walking to the kitchen for breakfast. Rumi's poem "Bird Wings" offers the image of a hand opening and closing, with words and silence balanced like two wings and grief named as part of the practice. Nomon closes by hoping to have baffled the room, since the impeded stream is the one that sings.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 27: Nansen''s "Not Mind, Not Buddha, Not Things"'
speaker: Kanshin Allison Tait
summary: Kanshin Allison Tait takes up Gateless Barrier case 27, in which a monk asks Nansen whether any dharma remains untaught and Nansen answers, "Not mind, not Buddha, not things." Kanshin reads the answer as Nansen giving away the last of his treasure because the monk asked, then sets it beside "ordinary mind is the way" with a friend's expired bus pass that has become a bookmark and a workplace quarrel over whether leggings are pants. Sheng Yen's teaching of a path that widens until the whole field is the path leads to Rumi's poem about a field beyond right and wrong, and to living with "no" the way a student lives with Joshu's Mu, inviting it to tea. Mumon's verse ends the case, and his "no comment" is itself a comment.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 46: Shih-shuang: "Step from the Top of the Pole"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 46 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Shih-shuang asks how to take the next step from the top of a hundred-foot pole, and Changsha answers that those who sit there have entered the way but are not yet genuine. After opening with appreciation for the joint sesshin with Seattle Soto Zen and for Jeff Kelly, who proposed it, Nomon reads the pole first as a picture of rising above a messy life, then as the wobble of a mind facing a hard decision and wanting certainty. Nomon closes with Suzuki Roshi's comment from Not Always So, that the pole has no top, and the practice is to say yes and walk into the kitchen for breakfast.

title: Meditation in the Trees, Metta Practice
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny retells the origin of the Metta Sutta, in which monks flee a forest that seems full of menacing spirits until the Buddha sends them back to practice for the suffering trees. Reizan turns to Peter Wohlleben's The Hidden Life of Trees, where roots keep a 500-year-old stump alive, and to John Welwood's Perfect Love, Imperfect Relationships and its "wound of the heart," the habit of numbing ourselves against unlove. Metta practice starts with kindness toward ourselves and extends outward to all beings, and Reizan recommends Sharon Salzberg's Loving Kindness. Reizan ends by reading an essay about a hike around the Three Sisters in Oregon, closing on a Sangha day when the group chants the Metta Sutta on an escarpment above eastern Oregon.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 25: Yang-shan's Sermon from the Third Seat
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier case 25, in which Yangshan dreams of Maitreya's palace, is seated in the third seat, and is called on to speak. Nomon asks how different dreaming is from waking, then tells a vivid dream of switching off a Dzogchen Ponlop Rinpoche recording, meeting Robert Thurman's smiling gaze, and leading metta phrases that kept coming out loud after waking. Nomon explains the weight of the third seat through the Shuso and monastic seniority, reads Zhuangzi on dreams, and tells how Wangyal Rinpoche met his teacher in a dream. Yangshan's sermon, that the truth of Mahayana is beyond proposition and denial, leads to holding views with an open hand and to the closing instruction to listen carefully.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 23: Hui-neng: "Neither Good Nor Evil"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier case 23, in which the sixth ancestor Huineng meets the head monk Ming on Da Yu Peak, after first reading Aitken Roshi's telling of Huineng's youth as a firewood seller, the Diamond Sutra, and the rival mirror poems. When Ming cannot lift the robe and bowl from the rock, Huineng's question about his original face stops the chase. Nomon reads the case through form and essence, comparing it to the morning service, and imagines an email from the board announcing a new guiding teacher. The case ends with "maintain your realization carefully," and Nomon turns to the lay ordination of five sangha members, reading Hozen Alan Senauke's description of home-dweller ordination.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 22: Mahakasyapa's Flagpole
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 22 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Mahakasyapa calls out "Ananda," hears "Yes," and answers, "Knock down the flagpole at the gate." Nomon tells of Ananda's perfect memory and his near-awakening, the night before the First Buddhist Council when practice finally breaks through, and the flags raised over ancient Indian debating grounds. A sesshin at Samish, where Nomon sits with that "yes" until Norman says no more study is needed, leads into a practice of silently saying "Yes" at the end of each exhale. Mary Oliver's "Wild Geese" follows, and Nomon closes by asking how listeners have answered when a teacher calls their name.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 21: Yun-men's Dried Shitstick
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up case 21 of the Mumonkan, in which a monk asks Yunmen "What is Buddha?" and Yunmen answers, "A dried shit stick." Nomon reads Robert Aitken's note linking the stick to the corn cob in his grandparents' outhouse, then tells of wheelbarrowing barrels of feces on an undergraduate biology expedition until the load felt like ordinary stuff. Nomon then turns to Suzuki Roshi, whose special power, as Nomon's teacher put it, was seeing the extraordinary in the ordinary, and reads many short stories from David Chadwick's To Shine One Corner, among them the forgotten shovel, the jelly beans, and the student who begs for enlightenment while Suzuki Roshi sleeps in the car. Nomon closes by returning to Yunmen's answer: a dried shit stick, and everything else.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 20: Sung-Yuan's Person of Great Strength
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier Case 20, in which Master Sungyuan asks why a person of great strength can't lift a leg. Nomon reads the Wikipedia entry on Jiriki (self-power) and Tairiki (other power), then asks who directs the mind in zazen, recalling a philosopher and a neuroscientist debating whether anyone can notice wandering and bring the mind back, and an Eddie Murphy movie where a tiny alien drives a human robot. Nomon then reads Sandy Boucher's Tricycle essay about her partner Martha's painful recovery from knee surgery, when a wrong turn in Oakland leads Sandy to a lit shrine of Guan Yin, and a Vietnamese woman there greets Sandy with a hug.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 19: Nan-ch''uan: "Everyday Mind is the Way"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Mumonkan case 19, in which Zhaozhou asks Nanquan "What is the way?" and hears "Everyday mind is the way." Nomon sets the case beside the Eightfold Path, a list the Zen stories never quote, and reads Nanquan's reply to "How should I direct myself?" as a warning that directing yourself betrays practice. Knowing is delusion and not knowing is confusion, so Nomon asks what we think we know, and notes that the "Oh" moments usually come after the plan is abandoned. Right view serves as the example: once there is a right view, a wrong one appears. Mumon's verse closes the case with spring flowers, autumn moon, summer breezes, winter snow, and no urgent matters hanging in the mind.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 38: Wu-tsu's Buffalo Passes Through the Window
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Case 38 of the Mumonkan, in which an ox passes through a window screen but its tail cannot, using Thomas Cleary's translation. Kanho places koans as beloved family stories, as Norman Fischer describes them, and as a finger pointing at the moon, which means doing the work rather than reading about it, like an exercise routine followed only on paper. Dogen's lines from Genjokoan on the dharma that fills or does not fill body and mind lead Kanho to ask what is missing, and the ox herding pictures show the buffalo as the heart. If the buffalo goes all the way through, it falls into the pit of non-duality; if it comes back, it is spoiled. Kanho closes by wishing the sangha to stay stuck in the window joyfully, with a little piece of tail hanging out the other side.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 18: Tung-shan's Three Pounds of Flax
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 18 of the Gateless Barrier, where Dongshan answers a monk's "What is Buddha?" with "Three pounds of flax." Nomon sets beside it other abrupt answers, including Zhaozhou's cypress tree in the garden, and describes hitting a barrier while preparing, right after a productive morning of shrinking an inbox. Mary Oliver's poem "Mysteries, Yes" and Nyogen Senzaki's story of Pestalozzi's pupil pointing at a real window speak to living with what can't be explained. Nomon then leads a pairs exercise in which a student asks "What is Buddha?" again and again, and the room's answers range from a cushion to a dead deer and an old banana.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 17: Kuo-shih's Three Calls
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier Case 17, in which the national teacher calls his attendant three times and then says "I was about to say that I was ungrateful to you, but the fact is that you are ungrateful to me." Nomon opens with a rock tumbler, where rough stones need both each other and an abrasive slurry to become smooth, and treats the teachings, and faith in the process, as that slurry. Calling and responding becomes the heart of ordination, since the sangha calls a priest forth, and Nomon recalls Norman Fischer's three points: be humble, see everyone as Buddha, try to help. The "ungrateful" of the koan points to a life wider than gratitude or its opposite, and Nomon closes by saying "I'm ungrateful. And I hope you are too."

title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 4
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart completes the Eightfold Path in part four of the Four Noble Truths series, taking up Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. Kanho describes the four foundations of mindfulness from the Satipatthana Sutta (body, feelings, mind, phenomena), notes that "feelings" there means likes and dislikes, and contrasts right concentration with the one-pointed focus of a thief breaking into a house. Along the way, Kanho tells of searching Amazon for a book on Buddhist meditation and finding Dirty Cowboys ranked second, then names the misogyny in the ancient texts and in monastic institutions for women today. Kanho closes with the Dalai Lama's line, "My religion is kindness."

title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 3
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Noble Eightfold Path in part three of a series on the Four Noble Truths, drawing on Thanissaro Bhikkhu's booklet The Noble Eightfold Path. Kanho describes the path as a wheel with eight spokes around a common center, where working through them one at a time risks getting stuck at right view. Kanho then covers the wisdom category of right view and right intention, asking when life is on the freeway, on the frontage road, or in the blackberry brambles. Right speech gets the longest treatment, including the five conditions from the Patimokkha for admonishing another: right time, facts, gentleness, profitable words, and a kindly heart. The evening ends with a paired listening exercise on discernment.

title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Second and Third Noble Truths, the cause and the end of suffering, drawing on Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche's book The Truth of Suffering. Craving and the mistaken belief in a separate, solid self make up the cause. Kanho's own example is a 25-year dream of hiking the Torres in Chile, now complicated by a knee that cannot carry a loaded pack, and the suffering that comes from insisting on the original plan. The eightfold path and zazen appear as the way out of the rut, giving enough space to review actions instead of reacting. The evening closes with dyads of five minutes each, where listeners give full attention and sit with the silence if the other person stops early.

title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart opens a series on the Four Noble Truths by reading the Buddha's account of his awakening and first teaching at Deer Park, drawn from the Pali Canon. Kanho then turns to dukkha, setting the Buddha's list of birth, aging, illness, and death beside Norman Fischer's essay "Suffering Opens the Real Path" and Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche's eight categories. One person wants rain for the fields while another plans a picnic, and seven point seven billion such wishes collide. Kanho cautions against using the teaching to fix others or to beat ourselves up, like drowning someone dying of thirst, and closes by saying practice has no Deus ex Machina, only one step at a time.

title: What is Zen, Part 4
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Reizan Bob Penny take up the chapter on everyday life and relationships in Norman Fischer's book What Is Zen?, turning to conflict in institutions, sanghas, and personal life. Ryushin recalls the imprimatur on Catholic school textbooks and the brokenhearted, excuse-free way Norman spoke of ethical breaches among Zen teachers, then describes Red Cedar's conflict-resolution document and trained mediators. Reizan reads Norman on the precept against speaking ill of others. The two then demonstrate a role play with "dance cards" running from Anchor through Negotiation, and two participants try a zendo-setup scenario in which a newer sitter zigzags the cushions. The session closes with the remark that the steps could just as easily form a circle or a zigzag as a line.

title: What is Zen, Part 3
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona and Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona and Nyogen Connie Martin take up Sangha, the third of the three treasures, through Norman Fischer and Susan Moon's book What is Zen. Heigaku reads Norman on practicing together, and Nyogen tells of the young monk Meghiya, who asks three times to meditate in a cool mango grove and is overrun there by unskillful thoughts. The Buddha's answer begins with admirable friends. Nyogen then reads Ananda calling friendship half of the holy life and the Buddha correcting that it is the whole, and listeners pair up for active listening on Susan's question about someone who likes sangha potlucks more than zazen.

title: What is Zen, Part 2
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton and Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shuko Edie Norton and Shin-yu Scott Allen take up the chapter on teachers in What Is Zen? by Norman Fischer and Susan Moon, answering its questions about whether a teacher is needed, whether more than one is allowed, and what training means. Shuko recalls Kobun, who answered questions about emptiness by handing over a book of Nagarjuna, and later Reb Anderson, and calls sangha life a rock polisher. Shin-yu tells of meditating on the Chain of Rocks Bridge in St. Louis, picking grass beside a Japanese abbot who wanted a moss lawn, and Kaylin McAllister's bakery run by inmates. Shin-yu closes with a stained glass window, where one teacher shows only a single red shard.

title: What is Zen, Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seishu John Wiley
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seishu John Wiley take up form and ritual, opening a month of talks based on Zoketsu Norman Fischer's book What is Zen?, a conversation with Susan Moon. Kanho contrasts an autopilot shower with a shower at Tassajara, where a bow, incense, and unchangeable water temperature keep attention on the moment, and reads Norman's comparison of Zen forms to musical scales. Seishu turns to Paula Arai's Bringing Zen Home, telling of a woman who copies the Heart Sutra to ease chronic pain and of Honda-san, who greets her parents' photos on a home altar. A participant adds a story of six months in the Saudi desert, where routine carried everyone along until they got home and chose nothing.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 16: Yun-men: The Sound of the Bell
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up case 16 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Yunmen asks why a monk puts on the seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell when the world is vast and wide. Nomon sorts it as a one-sentence teaching phrase, recalls Katagiri Roshi's "Great autumn moon, high in sky" at a City Center sesshin, and traces the robe to the Buddha's rice-field story. Koun Yamada's comment on the "why" and Wumen's question of whether sound comes to the ear or the ear goes to the sound lead to Wumen's verse, whose second couplet reverses the first. Nomon closes by sparing the sixty blows.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 15: Tung-shan's Sixty Blows
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 15 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Dongshan asks Yunmen about the sixty blows spared him, and reads Wumen's comment about a night spent in an ocean of yes and no. Nomon recalls turning a zafu tag around at a Zen center in Zurich, and a visiting teacher asking in a restaurant lobby, "How will you train?", as tough encounters of Nomon's own. Reading Dogen's Genjokoan, Nomon asks what enlightenment is, describing a student troubled by constant meditation visions and noting that "got enlightenment" condenses years of practice. Nomon closes by singing Cat Stevens's "Father and Son" as a picture of the sudden and gradual voices within us.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 14: Nan-ch'uan Kills the Cat
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 14 of the Gateless Barrier, Nan-ch'uan kills the cat, at a Samish sesshin, first setting it beside Mary Oliver's poem "The Summer Day" and the title's "barrier that has no gate." Most of the hour reads Norman Fischer's commentary, which compares the case to Solomon and the baby, gives Dogen's alternate replies, and reads Zhaozhou's sandals on his head as mourning for a cat already dead. Norman also pictures the quarreling East Hall and West Hall monks as meditators and workers. Nomon adds Ryokan weeping over a wayward teenager, then a friend who answers a rude son with "that hurts my feelings," and the son apologizes.

title: Save the World by Saving Your Own Mind
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Zen claim that meditation is really wisdom, starting from Huineng, who becomes the sixth ancestor while pounding rice in the pantry and never entering the zendo.
