Norman describes practice as a whole life of ritual, community, study, and gradual change of mind, and offers a rabbi's teaching: use the morning glance at the phone as a cue to say Modeh Ani, the Jewish prayer of gratitude. Norman reads Grace Schireson's account of meeting Suzuki Roshi, then her commentary on Blue Cliff Record case 86, where Yunmen says everyone has a light. Norman closes by calling Norman doomed, yet happy and careful, and calls practice an offering to a troubled world.

title: The Reappearance by Aspiration Sutta
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Sankharupapatti Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 120), opening with a joke about Niels Bohr's good-luck horseshoe, which works whether or not anyone believes in it. In the sutta, a bhikkhu fixes the mind on rebirth among nobles and then among ever higher gods, until the last paragraph drops any future and enters deliverance here and now. Norman connects this to the Buddha's one more miracle, a thought arising and passing away, and to Dogen's death poem. Norman recalls doing Ayya Khema's funeral with Ajahn Amaro, one celebrating her freedom from rebirth, the other her return again and again. Norman closes with the practice of showing up when the bell rings, sitting, bowing, and answering yes when the Buddha calls.

title: Practicing at Samish, The Six Subtle Gates to the Sublime
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer returns to the six subtle gates to the sublime (counting, following, vivifying, discriminating, questioning, leaping off) and then reads Suzuki Roshi's 1964 talk on Blue Cliff Record case 51, about Xuefeng and Yantou. Norman opens with listening to silence at Samish, starting from feeling the body and the earth pulling it toward its center. Suzuki Roshi tells of the two friends stranded in a snowstorm, where Yantou tells Xuefeng that insights from outside are not the family treasure. Two monks later ask Yantou for his last word, and Yantou answers "This is it" before bandits kill him as he sits in zazen.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 13: Te-Shan : Bowls in Hand
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 13 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Deshan carries his bowls toward the dining hall before the bell and drum, and Yantou later says the old master "does not understand the last word." Nomon first describes the pleasures and irritations of a week of sesshin, including the insider knowledge of oryoki that can embarrass newcomers, and Paul Haller's saying that nothing is happening that shouldn't be. Dogen's Fukanzazengi and a definition of mindfulness from Linda Carlson and Shauna Shapiro lead into emptiness and the gift of silence toward one another. The case follows, with Xuefeng and Yantou snowed in at an inn and Yantou whispering in Deshan's ear. Nomon closes with sangha news and the blue heron rookery here that once held 800 nests.

title: The Meal Chant
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the meal chant used in oryoki, going through it line by line at the first oryoki meal at Samish. Norman begins with the verse naming the four events of Buddha's life, then the prayer to realize the emptiness of giver, receiver, and gift, drawn from the Diamond Sutra. The ten names of Buddha are an invocation that summons Vairocana, Locana, Shakyamuni, and Maitreya, along with Manjushri, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteshvara. The five reflections ask whether we deserve the food, and a thank-you goes to the government for keeping armies off Samish Island. Norman closes with the translation committee's arguments, including Griff Falk's refusal to change the lotus line.

title: Working With Upset
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva as a source of practical help for working with anger, fear, and despair, offered at Samish as the "how" to follow Tim's talk on why we practice. Kanho tells how Shantideva, according to the stories, answered a hostile Nalanda assembly with a teaching so deep that his seat rose into the sky. Verses on the rope of mindfulness tethering the elephant of the mind, on wrapping leather around the feet instead of covering the earth, and on a single flash of anger shattering a thousand ages of good works anchor suggestions to feel the body, work on the mind rather than the world, and remember anger as the enemy. The last suggestion, dis-identification, means stepping back from conditioned thinking, such as Kanho's own habit of working harder when going the wrong way.

title: Master! Yes! Stability and Clarity
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a Samish Sesshin by welcoming the sangha and reading the Buddha's words on repaying one's parents, which Nomon takes to mean confidence in practice. Nomon then turns to the precepts on stealing and sexuality as lenses for seeing the mind's habits, and takes up Mumonkan case 12, in which Zhiyin calls "Master!" to himself each morning and answers "Yes!" Nomon reads the exchange as zazen instruction, pairing stability and clarity, and warns that a flash of insight can knock a sitter off the seat. Nomon closes with a page from Katagiri Roshi on shikantaza and suggests watching the mudra.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 12: Jui-yen Calls "Master"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Gateless Barrier Case 12, in which Jui-yen calls "Master" to himself each day, answers "Yes," and tells himself to be aware and not to be deceived by others. Before the case, Nomon explains the evening's chants: the Heart Sutra in Sino-Japanese as translated by Xuanzang, a female personification of the Prajnaparamita, and a dharani of sounds said to prevent disaster. Nomon suggests calling the roll with your own name on waking, on entering a new room, and on sitting down in zazen, then doubts the word "others," since the chief deceiver is already here. Stability and clarity in meditation come next, with a seven-and-a-half-day sesshin approaching, and Nomon stays curious about whether Jui-yen should have said "others" at all.

title: Faxiang's Created World
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona retells a fifth-century story from The Hidden Lamp in which the nun Faxiang gives her best food and clothing to Huisu, whom the other nuns call an idiot, until Huisu sits in deep meditation through a seven-day retreat. Heigaku connects the story to the defense of self, an Australian nurse's refusal to be "just a nurse," and Dogen's line that dull and sharp-witted are no different. Linji's "true person of no rank" in Book of Serenity case 38 and Norman Fischer's reminder that practice is something lived lead to the laywoman Yu Daopo, who throws down her tray of donuts on hearing a beggar sing and answers with a verse about a person who splits Mount Hua.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 11: Chao-chou and the Hermits
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 11 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Zhaozhou asks two hermits "Do you have it?" and answers the same raised fist with scorn from one and a deep bow for the other. Nomon sketches Zhaozhou's long life, including his pilgrimage at age 80, and retells the story of his stone bridge that "lets horses cross," then recalls crossing a humble log bridge on a snowy hike near Mount Baker. From there Nomon questions what approval and comparison do to us, reading Wumen's verse and Seung Sahn's commentary, which quotes the Tao Te Ching on seeking the approval of others. Nomon closes by observing that whatever work we do, someone is looking to us.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 10: Ch'ing-shui: Solitary and Destitute
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 10 of the Mumonkan, in which the monk Qingshui tells his teacher Caoshan that he is alone and poor and asks for help. Nomon weighs two readings, a cry of loneliness and a quiet claim of freedom, drawing on Thomas Cleary's comment and on Ryokan's poems, including the one about the moon a thief leaves behind. Nomon then reads the parable of the rich man and his son from chapter four of the Lotus Sutra, where a son gone for fifty years clears away excrement for twenty more before he is named heir. Caoshan's answer, that Qingshui has already drunk the finest wine in China, ends with Nomon's hope that we notice before we are ninety.

title: The Center of All Existence
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the question of what keeps green grass growing through cracks in concrete, using it to frame Ryushin's farewell to the sangha and five factors for living a life from its center. Ryushin tells of a friend whose every hardship made him who he is, and of Suzuki Roshi planting a garden during the war to test whether the Dharma works. Ryushin works with Dongshan's "The vast sky does not hinder the white clouds from flying" and with Dizang and Fayan's "Not knowing is most intimate." In the discussion, a participant asks how anyone trusts life after war or loss. Ryushin answers that people without privilege must find that inner core for themselves.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 9: Ch'ing-jang's Nonattained Buddha
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 9 of the Gateless Barrier, in which a monk asks why a Buddha who sat zazen for ten kalpas never attained Buddhahood, and Ch'ing-jang answers that he is a "non-attained Buddha." Nomon sets the case beside the poems of the Fifth Ancestor's head student and Huineng, the tile-polishing exchange between Nanyue and Mazu, and the Lotus Sutra's longer version, where flowers rain down for ten small kalpas before the Buddha awakens. Along the way come a kalpa measured in sesame seeds and a few stories from Tassajara returnees. Nomon ends on Mazu's laughter, like a man who has drunk ghee, after Nanyue tells him to neither grasp nor forsake the non-abiding Dharma.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 8: Hsi-chang Builds Carts
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 8 of the Mumonkan, in Nyogen Senzaki's translation, where a teacher asks whether Hsi-chang is still a master wheelmaker if the hub is removed from his fifty-spoke wheels. Nomon removes parts one at a time to find where a wheel stops being a wheel, and ties the question to emptiness, svabhava, and the Metta Sutta's line about the wise holding no fixed views. Old photographs of Nomon at 22 and at 10, and of this room as an empty shell, show how each person sees a different room. Chapter 11 of the Dao De Jing, in Red Pine's translation, praises the empty space in the hub, and Nomon compares it to a shuso, terrified at first to be the hub, who finds the wheel turns itself.

title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 7: Chao-chou: "Wash Your Bowl"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 7 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Zhaozhou answers a new monk's request for teaching by asking if he has eaten his morning gruel, then telling him to wash his bowl. Nomon compares translations of the monk's final realization, reads the exchange literally as full attention to eating and washing in the oryoki meal, and notes that "just" begins the word "justice." Two recent deaths follow: Nancy Welch, whose cremation ceremony Nomon describes, and seventeen-year-old Butch Mullins, struck on I-5, which raises the mind's hunger for the full story. Nomon ends with news of a lay entrustment and a jukai cohort, and the hope that you have washed your bowl.

title: Sharing Our Maturity
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up maturity through Norman Fischer's book Taking Our Places, which records Norman's conversations with four adolescents, and asks what its principles mean for adults. Shin-yu argues that continued growth means facing challenges, revisiting issues skipped in youth, and then passing that learning to others. Stories carry the point: a rough rock thrown into a clear river, smooth on top and rough underneath; a flight to Frankfurt with an overheating engine, where a younger commander handled the repair as well as Shin-yu would have; and a five-year-old who mowed his lawn beside his elderly neighbor. Shin-yu ends with Norman's answer to the question of how practice should change over the years: show more kindness and love.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 12: Juiyen Calls Master
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Case 12 of the Gateless Barrier, Zuigan Calls Master, in which Zuigan calls out to himself each day, answers "Yes," and warns himself never to be deceived. Ryushin tells of Zuigan's early interview, where a proud, clever answer is only seen as foolish years later. A friend's story of a successful man in his sixties who rolls his car, curses his mother, and then asks someone to tell him how to grow up shows the wish for a master outside oneself. Ryushin links the case to the harmony of sesshin, Uchiyama's call to grow up, and Dogen's Gyoji. The sequel closes it: Gensha asks whether the dead Zuigan would answer if called, and the reply is mountains answering a temple bell in the moonlight.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 5: Hsiang-yen: Up a Tree
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 5 of the Mumonkan, Xiang Yan's story of a man hanging from a tree by his teeth, who must answer a question about Bodhidharma or lose his life. Opening with a Gary Snyder poem about log truck drivers and a Wendell Berry poem, "The Real Work," Nomon links the koan to the practice period's study of maturity and to the upcoming shuso ceremony. Yamada Kuan's commentary calls for a response that is "factual," and Nyogen Senzaki calls the story a "kindness of unkind action." Nomon closes with Norman's advice to be humble, see everyone as Buddha, and try to help, then sings a Cat Stevens song.

title: Winter Practice Period Shuso's Class - Continuing Our Maturity Part 5
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up Chapter 8 and the afterword of the book the class has been reading, on conduct and the precepts. Shin-yu recalls a military review of a reckless young lieutenant, where no ethical guidance could be found, then asks the room why people delay resolving their mistakes, comparing rumination to a record played with a bad needle. A walk through the triple treasure, the three pure precepts, and the ten grave precepts follows, with examples such as a lie that grows longer with each excuse and a wife who yells at the evening news. The class closes with a passage on the mature self and Shin-yu's joy in passing lessons on to others.

title: Winter Practice Period Shuso's Class - Continuing Our Maturity Part 4
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen closes a chapter on maturity from Norman's book by looking at what meditation does with fear and delusion, then takes up the difference between a goal and a vow. A hypothetical fear of kumquats that shrinks with each return, and a man who fights the phone company without ever paying his bill, show how people cause their own pain. The class offers examples of vows, including military oaths, marriage, and court testimony, and concludes that a vow is spoken publicly and points beyond the self. Shin-yu brings in Uchiyama Roshi's How to Cook Your Life, where a vow becomes the middle way between cause and effect and impermanence, and ends on Suzuki Roshi's "inmost request" and a teacher's calling.

title: Winter Practice Period Shuso's Class - Continuing Our Maturity Part 3
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up persistence and connection from Norman Fischer's chapter on maturity, the third of Shin-yu's shuso classes. Shin-yu separates persistence from stubbornness and tells of a pickup truck Shin-yu has worked on for 28 years, then of a Delaware construction zone where Shin-yu plotted nails and tank-track jacks against merging drivers until Shin-yu's best friend's family waved from a station wagon. Turning to connection, Shin-yu urges calling living parents and asks them questions without accusation. Shin-yu recalls a week of backpacking with Shin-yu's mother in Yosemite and Shin-yu's father's answer: "I'm still pissed off and I'm afraid to die."

title: Winter Practice Period Shuso's Class - Continuing Our Maturity Part 2
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up listening as a part of maturity, working from a chapter in the class's book by Zoketsu Norman Fischer. Shin-yu lists habits that block hearing: rehearsing a snappy reply, interrupting, and dismissing a speaker after one opening statement. Two stories illustrate them. One is of two Air Force officers going chest to chest like chimpanzees, and the other is of a conservative coworker, a climate change disagreement, and the fifteen good minutes that followed once the labeling stopped. Class members discuss why people avoid listening to themselves, and pairs practice "looping," repeating back what they heard. Shin-yu closes with Norman's lines on isolation and prejudice, then a prayer to Avalokiteshvara about listening so attentively that the unsaid is heard too.

title: Winter Practice Period Shuso's Class - Continuing Our Maturity Part 1
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Shin-yu Scott Allen takes up the introduction to Zoketsu Norman Fischer's book on growing up, starting from the point that age is not maturity. Shin-yu asks the room what keeps people in their 30s and 40s from looking at maturity, and the answers include fear, ego, and being too busy being a grownup. Stories from the military's mentoring, retirement rules like putting on pants, and 28 years in recovery, where writing out every resentment revealed patterns of ego, lead to three marks of maturity: self-awareness, flexibility, and reliance on others. The session closes with a participant describing how the repentance verse frees an old regret.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 4: Bodhidharma Has No Beard
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 4 of the Gateless Barrier, Huoan's question "Why has the Western Barbarian no beard?", a koan with almost no story around it. Nomon reads Huoan's death poem about the iron tree in bloom and the rooster laying an egg, along with Master Guojun's passage comparing Chan to learning to float. Nomon then tells of an eight-day rohatsu sesshin at Palolo Zen Center in Hawaii, where Michael Kieran assigned the koan "Basui asked, who is the one who hears?" Lying in the valley listening to birds, Nomon arrives at an answer: the one who hears is the one who isn't trying to be someone. Nomon closes by suggesting the beardless Barbarian can be worked with in the same way.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 3: Juzhi Raises a Finger
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 3 of the Gateless Barrier, "Juzhi Raises a Finger," in which a master cuts off his attendant's finger after the boy imitates the teaching. Nomon starts with the slap in Case 2 and Robert Aitken's advice to hear Zen violence the way we hear fairy tales, then reads the case as a call to commit to one practice, citing Suzuki Roshi on remembering the most important thing. Three of the Eight Verses for Training the Mind, on cherishing those who give hard lessons, follow. Wumen's verse leads Nomon to Aitken's telling of the nun True World, who circles young Juzhi three times in his hut while he sits speechless.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 2: Baizhang's Fox
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 2 of the Gateless Gate, Baizhang's Fox, in which an old man reborn as a fox for 500 lifetimes asks whether an enlightened person falls under cause and effect. Nomon compares English renderings of Baizhang's answer ("does not evade," "is one with") and reads the Chinese characters as "dividing obscures cause and effect." Nomon links the case to the Buddha's words to the Kalamas, to Gandhi's chain from belief to destiny, and to teachers who treat sexual misconduct as beyond karma, then reads from Dogen's "Great Practice." A Kenyan story of a hummingbird carrying beakfuls of water to a forest fire leads to climate change, and Nomon closes by hoping our children get 500 lives to figure it out, as the fox kept coming to talks through all of his.

title: Gateless Barrier, Case 1: Zhaozhou's Mu
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 1 of the Gateless Barrier, in which a monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha nature and Zhaozhou answers "Mu." Nomon reads that answer as a "no" meaning "don't be so sure," and offers two zazen practices: breathing out the sound Mu, or breathing into the question "What is it?" Wu Men's commentary follows, with its red-hot iron ball and eyebrows entangled with the ancestors, and Nomon points to the love and joy running through its gnarly language. Nomon also weighs the value of intensity against the extra tension that comes from trying too hard. Nomon closes by holding up calligraphy of the character mu in block, semi-cursive, and grass script styles, including copies of versions by Kaz Tanahashi and Akiba Roshi.

title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination, Part 4: River Obstacles
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
series: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley offers a river as a metaphor for great faith, great doubt, and great determination on the third day of sesshin. Faith is a rumor of a river, doubt is a holy dissatisfaction with the obstacles in its way, and determination is patience paired with skill. Eko recalls a chalk poem from Eko's college sidewalk, "It's a fresh wind that blows across the empire," and describes returning to faith through freshness and loving awareness. Rocks can be blasted out or left to erosion, yet wanting turns out to be part of the river already flowing. Eko closes by inviting sitters to try a night sitting with the clock turned off.

title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination, Part 3: Without Your Knowledge
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Rohatsu with Dogen's account in Kesa Kudoku of weeping for joy at hearing the robe verse in Sung China, then Dogen's image of walking through mist and dew. Nomon sets gradual and sudden practice side by side, names great doubt as the fulcrum between faith and determination, and separates heavy little-d doubt, one of the Five Hindrances, from the alive uncertainty of "don't be so sure." Nomon closes with Soyen Shaku's 1895 Rohatsu story, translated by his student Nyogen Senzaki, of sitting naked on a ship's deck near Bangkok, offering his body to the mosquitoes, and finding after a dawn storm that they were stuffed with his blood like berries.

title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination, Part 2: Coming Together
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
series: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up great faith, great doubt, and great determination through a passage from Koun Yamada and Suzuki Roshi's "Jumping Off the Hundred-Foot Pole" in Not Always So. Eko sets the heroic Bodhi tree story beside a second telling in which the earth bears witness to interconnection, then reads a Rumi fragment about crying out so milk might come. A deer missing a hoof, crossing the road that morning in frosty headlights, leaves Eko wordless. Working with Suzuki's line that the Buddha nature you think you have within yourself is not Buddha nature, Eko finds a wanting for continuation that will not let go, and surrenders to it. The pole disappears, and Eko is held.

title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination, Part 1: Stepping Forward Quietly
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Zen phrase "great faith, great doubt, great determination" at the start of a sesshin, opening with the invitation to trust one's role and keep attention within a two-and-a-half-foot circle of concern. Nomon reads Koun Yamada Roshi's tripod image and Master Wuman's red-hot iron ball of mu, then sets Soto and Rinzai styles side by side with a knot-untangling comparison. The Buddha's years of fasting and his memory of resting under a rose apple tree lead to Nyogen Senzaki, who stays in America, teaches in Los Angeles, and writes poems from the Heart Mountain camp. Nomon ends with Senzaki's funeral wish: "Silence is the best offering to me."

title: Integrating Thankfulness
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny expands on a short statement prepared for the Bellingham Unitarian Fellowship's interfaith Thanksgiving service, asking how thankfulness can become part of everyday life. Reizan links the breath, which is both willed and involuntary, to the Formal Meal chant's line about the emptiness of the three wheels: giver, receiver, and gift. Reizan proposes bringing an inner smile to sitting, going a step past Thich Nhat Hanh's half smile, and welcoming each breath as a surprise gift that leaves without grasping. In the discussion, a listener describes respiration as gas exchange, and Reizan adds that a breath might hold a molecule once breathed by a dinosaur.

title: Moving from Form to Formlessness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Rodney Smith's book Touching the Infinite, which recasts the Buddha's mindfulness sutra as a movement from form to formlessness. Nomon connects it to last week's pairing of limited and unlimited life. Smith describes form as everything with edges that rub and cause friction, and Nomon invites a practice: soften the gaze, sense the space in which objects appear, and feel the formless. Nomon then takes up the Heart Sutra's "no eyes, no ears" as pointing to the same thing, and warns that chasing a big experience of formlessness turns it into another form. Nomon ends on the invitation to practice "non-getting" alongside getting.

title: Fundamentals of Zen Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the two sides of meditation, stability and insight, drawing on a five-day session held with Seattle Soto Zen at a former Methodist camp. Nomon teaches "go back to one" breath counting as a place to stand in awareness, then loosens it toward open attention and the question "What is it?" A story of getting reactive with a student during the retreat shows how mental patterns become visible and lose some of their hold. Nomon then turns to limited and unlimited life, from Vizzini's "Inconceivable!" in The Princess Bride to Dogen's mist that leaves a robe damp.

title: The Stranger Who Loves You
speaker: Edward Espe Brown
summary: Edward Espe Brown opens with Derek Walcott's poem "Love After Love" and returns to its line about greeting yourself arriving at your own door. Edward tells of the young Suzuki Roshi and the rotten pickles his teacher Gyokujun So-on kept serving, then of Joseph Goldstein's reply at a Vipassana retreat: "It may not be the dessert you ordered. But it's the dessert that's being served." Edward describes a Karme Choling kitchen where "klesha attacks" excused people from work, and a grieving student, Marie, who decides to take herself in hand. The evening closes with William Stafford's poem and Zhaozhou's refusal to point the way to the summit of Mystic Peak.

title: Suzuki Roshi's Compassion
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach returns from a week at Tassajara and takes up Shunryu Suzuki Roshi's teaching on compassion and emptiness, reading his 1968 exchange with a student who asks where compassion is in emptiness. Ryushin tells of the stones at Tassajara, dry creek beds, and Suzuki Roshi's own hard path through wartime Japan and the death of his first wife's successor in his family's tragedy. Two stories show him moving stones: he finds the spot where a rock splits, and when asked what he is doing replies, "We don't know!" Ryushin ends with a young woman in the dry creek bed who watched fish die as the water vanished.

title: Lojong - Smoke in the Air
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the lojong slogans in the section "transform bad circumstances into the path," reading from the introduction to Norman Fischer's Training in Compassion. Nomon begins with a silent day hike in the mountains, then describes a smoky trip to Darrington with a friend, where headaches, a pair of barred owls at a small lake, and a sad Monday on the couch bring climate change home. Norman's slogans, from "turn all mishaps into the path" to "whatever you meet is the path," become touchstones, joined by a Rumi poem about the guest who clears out the house. Nomon closes with Dogen's image of walking with a good companion as walking through mist and dew, where the robes gradually become damp.

title: The Compassion of No-self and Emptiness
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Ken McLeod's An Arrow to the Heart, a commentary on the Heart Sutra, to point toward no-self and emptiness, which Kanho says words can only gesture at. Kanho pictures meeting life as standing on a beach and asking an incoming wave set to wait while emails get answered. Biting a ripe strawberry and jumping into a cold river show what living without the "me filter" feels like. Kanho also chants the Heart Sutra in its long form, naming each of the five aggregates in turn. Kanho closes with Bodhidharma's meeting with Emperor Wu, where "No merit" and "I don't know" leave the Emperor baffled, and Master Chi says that even the whole country could not bring Bodhidharma back.

title: The Compassionate One Who's Not Busy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns from a sabbatical month to Norman Fischer's Training in Compassion, the book the senior students studied while Nomon was away, and takes up its Tibetan slogans, such as "turn all mishaps into the path." Wildfire smoke in the air and a Kenyan farming family the sangha supports make suffering concrete: a pump bought for a dry farm beside a creek, and Mercy's account of running at fifteen from a village policeman's offer of marriage. Nomon then turns to the story of Yunyan sweeping the ground, Daowu saying "Too busy," and Yunyan's reply, "You should know there's one who's not busy." The evening closes with tonglen, breathing in sticky black smoke and breathing out light.

title: The One Who's Not Busy, Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces Yunyan and Daowu, the brothers of the "one who's not busy" case, through their teacher Yaoshan and his phrase "think not thinking," which Dogen condenses in Fukanzazengi. Nomon reads Yunyan's enlightenment story, twenty years with Baizhang before Yaoshan's questions open it, then Daowu's coffin koan ("I won't say alive, I won't say dead") and Daowu's answer about the Bodhisattva's many hands and eyes: "like somebody reaching back for a pillow at night." Nomon also explains the closing Shosan ceremony for the Samish Island sesshin and thanks the cooks and crew. Zhaozhou's reply to a monk with nothing to throw away, "Well then, go on carrying it," comes last.

title: The One Who's Not Busy, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Shurangama Sutra and Yunyan's "You should know there's one who's not busy" during a small sesshin, offering breath counting and a lighter open awareness of breathing as companion practices. Nomon reads the sutra's opening, where Ananda, who has memorized every teaching, falls in love on his begging rounds and then asks the Buddha for basics. The Buddha answers by questioning where Ananda's mind and eyes are located, and each answer gets taken apart. Nomon recalls telling Norman Fischer a flurry of worries at the first sesshin and hearing back only, "You know what's great, Tim? Breathing." Nomon closes with a variant of the Yunyan story, "one with nothing to prove."

title: The One Who's Not Busy, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the koan of Yunyan and Daowu from the Book of Serenity, in which Daowu tells the sweeping Yunyan he is too busy, and Yunyan answers that one is not busy. Nomon opens with painting the camp cabins, where a single brush stroke depends on chemists, trees, sunlight, and loggers. Then Nomon tells the three phases of Western views on Zen stories: devotion, debunking, and a third view that holds both. A short experiment of silently repeating "too busy" shows the constriction in the body. Nomon closes by holding up the question Yunyan asks of the broom, "which moon is this?", with the second moon left for tomorrow.

title: Bodhisattva Vows of Compassion
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the four Bodhisattva vows, beginning with the verse that jumped out from a book on a California bookstore's remainders table when Nomon was fifteen or sixteen. Drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Nomon treats the impossibility of vowing to save all beings as the energy of the practice, then turns to Dogen's poems about bringing others across first and to the joyful, parental, and magnanimous minds from Dogen's essay on monastery cooking. The second vow brings in the kleshas and four pairs of opposites, such as praise and blame, and gain and loss. Nomon closes by reading Dainin Katagiri's poem "Peaceful Life" twice, then reminds listeners that "free all beings" includes themselves.

title: Mahaparinirvana Sutra, Part 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads the closing chapters of the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, from the twin sal trees blooming at Kusinara to the Buddha's last words, the cremation, and the divided ashes. Norman lingers over the devas crowding the air so thickly that Upavana is asked to stop fanning, and over the Buddha's reply to Ananda's fear of losing a teacher. Norman describes how the sangha sits with the dead and says goodbye four times, and recalls taking up compassion work after Rabbi Alan Lew died. A long passage from the Mahayana Nirvana Sutra on the Tathagata's body follows, and the week closes with three sayings: be humble, see everyone as Buddha, try to help.

title: Mahaparinirvana Sutra, Part 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Mahaparinirvana Sutra where the Buddha hints three times that he could live on, Ananda misses each hint, and Mara announces that the time has come. Norman reads Ananda's cluelessness as something the Buddha needs, and tells how Ananda woke up just before the first council and how his pleading won ordination for women. The sutra becomes a lesson in dying: we go on living because others need us, until they no longer do. Norman ends with Kunda's last meal for the Buddha and the Zen Hospice Project advice to enter a dying person's room as if visiting a teacher.

title: Mahaparinirvana Sutra, Part 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Pali Mahaparinirvana Sutra, number sixteen in the Long Discourses, and sets it beside the far longer Mahayana Nirvana Sutra, in which the Buddha never dies. Norman follows the Buddha's last tour, where the same short teaching on morality, concentration, and wisdom is repeated in every town, and describes how shabby conduct makes a person jittery, like the jewel thief in a Dustin Hoffman movie. The courtesan Ambapali crashes her chariot into the Licchavis to keep the Buddha's meal invitation, and Ananda receives the mirror of Dharma in place of more answers about the dead. Norman ends with the Buddha's instruction to Ananda to be islands unto yourselves.

title: Dogen's Refrain From Evil Part 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer returns to Dogen's "Refrain From Evil" fascicle, starting with practical instructions for sesshin: holding the teacup with two hands, walking back and forth in the robe, and entering the zendo as Buddha. Norman then reads the second half of the text, which treats the three pure precepts as one thing and says wholesome action is stronger than a vairambhaka storm. Dao Lin's reply to the governor Zhu Yi, that even an eighty-year-old can't practice what a three-year-old can say, anchors the close. Norman ends on the child of three, who is perfect even when screeching.

title: Dogen's Refrain From Evil Part 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Dogen's fascicle "Refrain from Unwholesome Action" on Juneteenth, reading selected passages on the three pure precepts: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Norman explains that the seven original Buddhas stand for infinite Buddhas, so the precepts have no first moment, and that transmitting, receiving, and practicing them is one shared activity. Examples of changing customs, from radio profanity to summer clothing, show how good and bad shift with conditions. Anger in the name of compassion becomes its own unwholesome action, and bodhisattvas turn anger into energy as wrathful protectors of the Dharma. Norman closes with Dogen's claim that refraining from evil is actualized across the whole universe, and with a physicist's book about time that a brother sent.

title: Taking In The Whole Landscape - Treatment of Immigrants to the US
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a sesshin by describing a converted Walmart in Texas that holds 1,500 immigrant boys, then recounts a radio interview with a director at the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project and the thank-you note that follows a donation. The note tells of lawyers promising to represent detained parents at no charge. Nomon then turns to time, the top source of stress among the doctors in the mindfulness classes Nomon teaches, and reads Dogen's "Uji" through Shinshu Roberts's commentary: doubts about time are themselves time, and the bodhisattva of the chanted Prajnaparamita hymn is unstained and removes fear. Nomon closes with Zen Master Sung-san's words "Hurry up. Hurry," and an invitation to be time completely.

title: Compassion Stories
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley tells compassion stories, first from reading and then from the family of origin. Bankei keeps a monk who steals three times, Diane Rynerson's boss answers her lie about typing skills by asking where she wants her life in five years, and Joanne Cacciatore sits with a beaten horse on a desert trail and ties grief to love. Seishu then recalls parents who hold back judgment after a 1967 flunk-out and during an unplanned pregnancy that brings daughter Gillian. Seishu closes with the letter Gillian's mother writes after the gathering for Seishu's mother's 100th birthday, thanking her for kindness that still lasts.

title: Because Something Has to be Said
speaker: Marc Anderson
summary: Marc Anderson opens by explaining that Iroquois elders began gatherings with a Thanksgiving prayer so hearts start as one before disagreement arrives. Marc then traces the region's geological and human ancestors, from the Pacific Ring of Fire to the Salish Sea. Poems by Leonard Cohen and Nanao Sakaki alternate with Marc's own, and Marc plays the berimbau, which turns out to be tuned wrong after a bow switch. A fox woman story anchors the middle: a lonely hunter loses her when he complains of her belt's scent, and he mourns every season. Marc reads Sakaki's "Love Letter," whose widening circles end with sitting, praying, and singing.

title: Everything Is Hidden
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, the Dongshan poem the group chanted at morning service, during a retreat at Hidden Mountain, a place named because water runs off its high ground in every direction. Nomon reads passages on thusness, the silver bowl of snow, and the heron hidden in moonlight, and links them to our habit of taking a small visible fraction for the whole world. Stories along the way include a two-year practice of sitting with the question "what is it?" and Norman Fischer's offhand remark that the poem is Cliff Notes for Zen teachers. Nomon dwells on the line about a hair's breadth deviation, then reads the whole poem aloud, ending with the birds that keep practicing.

title: Buddhist Practice on Western Ground
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton gives a book report on Harvey Aronson's Buddhist Practice on Western Ground, which sets Asian and Western cultural assumptions side by side. Shuko recalls teaching English at a Japanese women's university, where a student who skipped all the homework was kept in the course by a program director who put belonging to the group ahead of fairness to individuals. From there Shuko follows Aronson through self and ego, anger, attachment, and emptiness. Along the way Shuko quotes Jack Kornfield's admission in A Path with Heart that years of meditation in Thailand had done little for his relationships. In the Q&A, a participant finds the book simplistic, and Shuko answers that Asian cultures and Buddhist traditions are not monoliths.

title: Blossoming of Spiritual Path
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny reads from Pilgrims and Sacred Sites in China, taking up the pilgrimage to Miaofeng Shan, the "mountain of the marvelous peak" northwest of Beijing. The story starts with a jade statue of a goddess, daughter of the god of Mount Tai, and grows into temples around the city and a small stone stele left by 700 devotees in 1689. By the 1800s, associations of shoemakers, tea sellers, and jugglers staff rest houses along three routes during a two-week season around Buddha's birthday, until a freak snowstorm in 1900 freezes many pilgrims. Reizan also gives an update on the Wilderness Dharma hikes, which carry a glass of seawater up toward the Nooksack headwaters and back to the ocean.

title: The Making of Me - Caring for self without elevating self
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with Shantideva's line that cherishing others is the source of all happiness and cherishing ourselves over others is the source of all suffering. Nomon separates self-cherishing from wise self-care, names suffering as the reliable guide, and turns to the three poisons: raga (wanting), dvesha (aversion), and moha (ignorance). Along the way come Dogen's "In aversion, weeds spread; in desire, flowers fall," the image of the self as film frames, and the claim that strong emotions fade in about forty seconds until the self regenerates them. Nomon closes with a boy in a video who asks what we practice, and proposes practicing joy.

title: The Heart of Zen
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up an untitled poem by Jane Hirshfield, "You must try, the voice said, to become colder," which Ryushin first heard in a talk by dharma sister Mary Mocine. Colder comes to mean receiving pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral feeling equally, as when Ryushin sat in sesshin between a dear friend and a disliked man and let the body be both hot and cold. A man who leaps onto the subway tracks to shield a stranger from an oncoming train and says only "I just did it" shows what the poem's heartlessness looks like. In the closing questions, a participant asks about people who lack that automatic kindness, and Ryushin answers that the seeds of wholeness are present in everyone.

title: Compsassion Bodhisattvas
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, as part of the sangha's 2018 theme of compassion. Kanho reads Blue Cliff Record case 89, where Yun Yang and Dao Wu discuss the thousand hands and eyes as a person reaching for a pillow in the night. Kanho then tells the story of Kuan Yin's head splitting in grief, and Amida Buddha giving her new heads. Four present-day bodhisattvas follow: Joan Halifax and her GRACE model, Shane Claiborne on peacemaking, Marshall Rosenberg's nonviolent communication, and Daniel Dennett's rules for answering an opponent. Kanho closes by asking listeners to try one week without snide remarks or one-upmanship.

title: Compassion for Self
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up self-compassion, starting from the fears of compassion that came up the week before and then turning to psychology research on those fears, such as the worry that kindness to oneself breeds weakness, self-pity, or lost motivation. Two guided reflections compare how Nomon treats a friend in need with how Nomon treats the self after a mistake, and participants share what they found, including a harsh inner voice and early defensiveness. Nomon then offers three practices from the Mindful Self-Compassion class: mindfulness, common humanity ("just like me"), and self-kindness. Suzuki Roshi's image of giving the cow a big meadow illustrates the second. The evening closes with the question "What do I need right now?" and the breath phrase "may I be kind."

title: Compassion Kickoff
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the year's study theme of compassion by asking small groups to finish the sentence "compassion is," then sets out Stanford's four-step definition and the near enemy of pity. Paul Gilbert's list of fears about giving compassion, receiving it, and turning it toward oneself is read aloud so listeners can notice which ones catch. Nomon also takes up the koan of Yunyan and Daowu on the Bodhisattva of great compassion's many hands and eyes, and dwells on Daowu's image of reaching for a pillow in the dark. The evening ends with Alan Sinaki's letter about a trip to a Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh, and a donation box set out in the room.

title: Quietism and Activism - Difficult and Easy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the story of Layman Pong, his wife, and their daughter Lingzhao, who answer "difficult," "easy," and "neither" to the same question, and applies it to Connie's time as Shuso. Nomon then turns to activism and quietism, recounting the Parkland students, a Bellingham high school rally, and a Southern Poverty Law Center email about who receives empathy. Four gifts of sitting practice follow: holding opposites, holding suffering, slowing down (illustrated by the Princeton Good Samaritan study), and curiosity about perception. Nomon closes with Naomi Shihab Nye's story "Museum," in which two teenagers wander through a stranger's home believing it is the McNay, and the woman who lived there thanks Nye thirty years later.

title: Moral Suffering
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads from Katherine Thanas's The Truth of This Life, opening with the story of a farmer who brings the Buddha his problems and learns that wanting no problems is the 84th. Norman then takes up Joan Halifax's Standing at the Edge and her four kinds of moral suffering: moral distress, moral injury, moral outrage, and moral apathy. The Parkland school shooting brings all four close to home for Norman, who weighs the push for gun regulation against Billy Graham's choice to change hearts one by one. Katherine's passage on loving the world as it is, with all our thoughts and regrets, closes the morning.

title: Shuso's Insights on Anger
speaker: Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Nyogen Connie Martin takes up anger as the theme of Nyogen's shuso practice period, opening with the verses from Shantideva's Bodhicharyavatara ("hate is not conquered by hate") that Nyogen keeps on the refrigerator. Nyogen traces anger from Nyogen's son's disability and divorce to school shootings, climate change, and the genocide in Myanmar, asking whether righteous anger can exist and answering that it must. Nyogen turns to Norman's teaching that we are not at fault for the world's condition but are responsible for what comes next, then walks through the ninth precept on literal, compassionate, and ultimate levels. Nyogen closes with the rocks Nyogen's class carried, Nyogen's dog Angus running loose in the snow, and Wendell Berry's "The Peace of Wild Things."

title: Layman Pang and the Obvious Case
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up two stories from the sayings of Layman Pang, in James Green's translation, after sharing a scholar's finding that "Genjokoan" began as Yunmen's phrase for an "obvious case." In story 27, Pang grabs a monk who says he isn't acquainted with him, and Changsha and Pang then argue over the awl and the chisel as ways of teaching. In story 30, Pang asks Sung Shan whether the old man still has vitality, and Sung Shan whacks him with his staff, then shouts. Norman closes on Pang's line "from out of the clear blue sky suffering arises."

title: Way Seeking Mind
speaker: Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Nyogen Connie Martin tells the story of Nyogen's path to Zen as a shuso, offered as a series of chapters framed by the verse "hate is not conquered by hate." Nyogen describes turning away from church at thirteen after two Black classmates invited were made unwelcome, then turning toward practice through anger at the loss felt in raising Nyogen's son Nathaniel, who hears but cannot speak. Along the way come a first retreat at Samish Island, where about 80 great blue herons stop Nyogen's mind, and Nathaniel driving a John Deere tractor. Nyogen closes by reading Norman Fischer on the sacredness of everything within and without.

title: Working With Defilements and Hinderances
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up the three defilements and five hindrances through the political turmoil after the 2016 election, reading from Ajahn Tejaniya's Don't Look Down on the Defilements. They Will Laugh at You and Gil Fronsdal's Unhindered. Shuko describes a vow to stay politically active through the 2018 election and a three-step practice: perceive what is happening, fully feel the reaction until it subsides, then decide what to do. Calling members of Congress stirs up fear, so Shuko writes out scripts, practices them aloud, and logs every call as "C" and every email as "E" in a notebook. When overwhelmed, Shuko steps away with a novel or a movie, or drinks from a cup that says "Talk to strangers."

title: The Appearance of Light - Encouragement for the New Year
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Dogen's Bendoa and its jijuyu samadhi, the self-fulfilling and receiving samadhi, as light returns after the solstice. Christmas lights scattered across Lake Whatcom, churned by wind, become Ryushin's image for letting every thought and aching knee into zazen. Kobun Chino's last talk, where zazen means being a candle in the dark, leads to Ryushin's teacher telling students to "dig deeper," and Ryushin answers with kindness and with a fearlessness that comes from seeing that everything ends. Participants then name their own candles: calm in action, eye contact at the checkout counter, slowing down, and trust.

title: Gratitude and Desire
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett explores how gratitude and desire share the same ground, reading Naomi Shihab Nye's poem "Famous" and passages from Brother David Steindl-Rast's gratefulness.org. Nomon recalls a wave of gratitude at Tassajara that attached itself to a yoga teacher, and offers the monk's phrase "What you practice grows stronger" as a way to face political anger without feeding it. Desire gets a close look too, especially the wish that everyone likes us, which sitting down in the middle of a churning mind gradually softens. Nomon closes with the first letters of Brother David's gratitude alphabet, ending on the fireflies Nomon noticed when a hill blocked Nomon's view of the fireworks.

title: Hongzhi, Part 4: Wonder
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley returns to Hongzhi's guidepost for silent illumination and its line "Inner illumination restores wonder," closing a sesshin series on that teaching. Eko reads images like dew in the moonlight as a river of stars and weaving gold on a jade loom, then offers examples: sesame seeds from gamasio scattered across the breakfast floor, and the courtroom exchange between a police officer and the mother of the man he shot. Boredom and a self-serving agenda cover wonder, while brief flashes of curiosity, like a single seed that is an uncultivated field, let it appear. Washing the bowl, emptying the self, leads to the Bodhisattva's wonder at one being helping another, and Eko ends with the invitation to stay for the night sit.

title: Hongzhi, Part 3: Guidepost For The Hall Of Pure Bliss
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Hongzhi's "Guidepost to Silent Illumination" on Rohatsu morning of a sesshin, reading the opening poem and a practice instruction from Taigen Dan Leighton's Cultivating the Empty Field. Nomon asks what silence and illumination might mean, tells of a car in a white Subaru barely brushing Nomon's own, with both drivers apologizing, and adds a line to Dogen's "forget the self": to love the self. Hongzhi's "upright cauldron" and Zhaozhou's "wash your bowl" and "have a cup of tea" lead to the news of Walter Scott's mother forgiving Michael Slager in court, with her quiet "I know" following his "I'm sorry."

title: Hongzhi, Part 2: Guidepost For The House Of Silent Illumination
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up Hongzhi's poems "Guidepost for the House of Silent Illumination" and "Guidepost for the Hall of Pure Bliss," reading them alongside Taigen's commentary. Starting from the question of what would actually help in a given situation, Eko turns to Hongzhi's image of the empty field, a rich field of non-separation that sesshin brings to life. Silence and illumination work together, and Vimalakirti's thunderous silence stays fully engaged in the world. Eko closes on the line "beings do not obstruct each other," and invites listeners to discover how that already holds in sesshin, even when another person seems to be in the way.

title: Hongzhi, Part 1: Introduction
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces Hongzhi, Dogen's great-grandfather in the Dharma, by reading Taigen Dan Leighton's retelling of the traditional biography in Cultivating the Empty Field. A rock dropped from a ferry onto a windshield, remembered by Nomon and not by Nomon's mother, frames three truths: historical, devotional, and practical. The biography moves from Hongzhi's awakening at Incense Mountain to the 1,500 monks at Mount Tiantong and a death in full lotus. Nomon then reads two short teachings, "The Bright Boundless Field" among them, and ends with Dogen's question of why practice is needed when wind is everywhere.

title: Hakuin's Song of Zazen
speaker: Koshin Chris Cain
summary: Koshin Chris Cain takes up Hakuin's Song of Zazen, reading it in full after a sketch of Hakuin's life. Koshin tells of the eleven-year-old terrified by a preacher's eight hot hells, who turns to Tenjin and Kannon for protection, later becomes a monk, suffers Zen sickness, and wakes at 42 while reading the Lotus Sutra. Koshin then works through the song's images of ice and water, the young fish who asks "What is water?", and the line "Is anything missing now?" Questions close the evening, covering Hakuin's death, his love of sweets and tobacco, and the nights he sat bound in a mattress.

title: Inclusive Thinking
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a newsletter piece Nomon wrote on holding opposites, after announcing the Jukai ceremony, the new Dharma names, and Dale Withers' accident. The piece sets the mind's habit of dividing things into good or bad against an inclusive mind, using a truck attack on cyclists in New York that killed five Argentine friends on a reunion trip. In the conversation afterward, sangha members question the word "evil," and Nomon names three limits of mind: time travel, flattening, and reification. Nomon shows a model pelvis for sitting posture and closes with Mary Oliver's "The Summer Day," where one grasshopper is more than a nine-letter word.

title: Trying On Zen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett recites Mary Oliver's "Wild Geese," then tells how arriving at Green Gulch Farm at 21 felt like trying on a new suit of clothes that might not fit. Norman Fischer taps Nomon's shoulder in a lunch line to ask about staying, and later mentions that he is about to start teaching near Vancouver, just as Nomon heads to Washington State. A note in a Bellingham bookstore leads to a small sitting group, and then to Jukai in a garden in 1993, where Nomon receives a name taken from a seal made in China for Norman. Nomon ends by describing how Norman simplified the ceremony forms and suggests calling the ceremony a "precepts remembering ceremony."

title: Caring for Hungry Ghosts
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Segaki ceremony for feeding hungry ghosts and reads an essay on it by Kyogen Carlson. Nomon describes the hungry ghost realm, where beings with huge bellies and pencil-thin necks cannot swallow food, and says they respond to sound. Kyogen's essay tells of Moggallana's dreams of his mother, whose food turned to fire in her mouth, and explains why the offering table stands apart from the Buddha. Nomon then walks through the ceremony: calling the ghosts with noise, chanting the Gate of Sweet Dew and the Daihishin Dharani, and making a dedication in which each person can name someone who has died or a clinging of their own. A song by Krishna Das, requested by Bernie Glassman, closes the evening.

title: Ash
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the firewood and ash passage from Dogen's Genjokoan, beginning with a memorial service Heigaku attends by mistake at the wrong church. Wenjue's koan of dying upside down, until his sister Wenjie topples the stiff body, is read through Melissa Myozen Blacker's commentary on getting stuck in emptiness. Heigaku then tells of a heated argument over programming radio stations and compares oak, cedar, and cottonwood in a windstorm. Cottonwoods survive by shedding huge limbs, an invitation to loosen fixed ideas like "I am always on time." Heigaku closes by calling this very hour a condition complete in this moment.

title: Genjokoan
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Dogen's Genjokoan, a fascicle of the Shobogenzo, and reads its passage about sailing out to sea where the ocean looks circular. Kanho describes coming to see the Buddha through love and then reading Dogen as speaking to practice as it is now. After Kanho asks whether seeing the single round ocean is enlightenment, the group breaks into paired, confidential discussion. Participants return to the ocean image, the limits of subjective view, and the shuso's apology as a chance for humility. Kanho closes with a passage from Shohaku Okumura's Realizing Genjokoan: seeing the limit of what we can see is wisdom.

title: Sesshin
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up sesshin, starting from the Japanese word, which joins Setsu, "to touch," with Shin, the heart-mind character from the Heart Sutra. Nomon describes stopping as a practice, since nothing needs deciding at sesshin, and then watches preferences show up in a peanut butter cookie at afternoon tea. Other examples follow: projections on a neighbor, bell-ringing and shame, a sleep-and-energy theory that fails at 2 a.m., and a spider phobia. Nomon calls the practice a non-method that heals anyway. Participants add stillness that lingers after sesshin, companionable silence, the gassho on the path, and a sesshin that ends in joy after a sleepless night.

title: Towards a Participatory Buddhism, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first part of Carl Bielefeldt's essay on participatory Buddhism, which names five trends in American Buddhism: secularism, individualism, eclecticism, egalitarianism, and activism. Before reading, Nomon sits with news of the shooting at Freeman High School near Spokane, where a student who confronted the shooter was killed, and offers a minute of silence. Nomon then gives each trend a local example. A student in a mindfulness class asks to "have joy" instead of studying suffering, and white and black slippers at a Japanese training monastery show how rank works there. The essay's answer, Dogen's participatory Buddhism, waits for next week.

title: Jizo's Vow
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach introduces Jizo Bodhisattva and Jizo's vow, following Red Cedar's first Jizo ceremony earlier this month. Ryushin describes Jizo as a childlike monk who carries a six-ring staff and the cintamani jewel and travels all six realms, and retells the story of Sacred Girl, a Brahmin maiden who goes through the hell realms to rescue her mother and becomes Kshitigarbha. Ryushin connects that fearlessness to present uncertainty, citing a man who comes to the office unable to sleep after Houston and Charlottesville. Participants share stories of buried grief, a kind stranger, and a German shepherd on a beach. Ryushin closes by noting that Jizo allows creativity, even a ceremony for good-tasting miso.

title: Three Poisons and Seventy Farmworkers
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the Fire Sermon, in which the Buddha tells a thousand monks that the eye, forms, and every pleasure or pain are burning with passion, aversion, and delusion. Nomon then describes seventy H-2A farmworkers stranded near Sumas after a 28-year-old coworker died and the crew was fired for striking over heat, smoke, and poor food. A neighboring farm family takes the men in, and Community to Community organizes donations and flights home. A short report on exercise and brain growth follows, along with a collection for the workers. Nomon closes with Al Gore's line in a new film that the Paris accord withdrawal is "just a setback."

title: Franma and the Mustard Seed
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the early Buddhist story of Kisa Gotami, who carries her dead child through town until the Buddha sends her to find a mustard seed from a household untouched by death. Nomon pairs it with the memorial weekend for grandmother Fran in San Diego, where her ashes and those of her husband Frank, who died by suicide in 1956, are held together. Fran's last poem, written on the 47th anniversary of his death and found clipped to a talk Nomon had mailed her, sits beside Mary Oliver's "When Death Comes," read on a boat at sea. Rose petals form a circle around the boat, and the captain rings the ship's bell.

title: Uji - Time Being
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona and Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona and Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna take up Dogen's fascicle Uji, "Time Being," with Ryushin reading Kaz Tanahashi's translation and Heigaku reading Brad Warner's paraphrase, which Warner calls "psychedelic Dogen." Heigaku opens with boundlessness applied to time and compares intellectual effort to rubbing a finger across greasy glasses. Ryushin tells of washing windows beside a weevil-infested rhododendron, climbing the ladder again and again until stuck in Tanglefoot. There the questions pour out: can time be saved, is a short moment six feet tall, who watches zazen? Ryushin gives up the windows and sits under the tree. A stream-of-consciousness writing exercise follows, then small groups, counted off in fives, taking turns on what surprised them about time.

title: Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seishu John Wiley
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seishu John Wiley take up Dogen's four methods of guidance (giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action), building on a talk Andrea gave two weeks earlier. Giving gets a close reading through the phrase "free giving," with the image of offering patience as dana from inside a traffic jam. Beneficial action brings in the burning house parable from the Lotus Sutra, where a father promises his children toy carts to coax them out of the fire. Identity action rests on a passage from the Guanzi, where the ocean does not exclude water and so is large. Kanho and Seishu close by asking what this practice looks like in the marketplace and open the floor to discussion.

title: Mountains and Waters Sutra
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra (Sansuikyo), placing it in the Kamakura period and in 1240, when Dogen gave it as a midnight talk. Reizan then leads the sangha through the sutra the way the Red Cedar group has walked it for 17 years, stopping at set places on a trail below Mount Baker to recite a section at each. A sweat lodge opens the trip, and a tree top crashes down while the group walks in silence. Rain runs across the paper as they read, and a stone is carried to a log hut for an altar. The last stop ends with "mountains are mountains" and a dedication of gratitude to nature.

title: Shishobo - A Bodhisattva's Embracing Method of Guidance
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Dogen's Shishobo, the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance, in an evening Ryushin runs as a study hour in the style of Ryushin's teacher Shohaku Okumura. Ryushin sets the fascicle in Dogen's last months at Koshoji before the sudden move to Echizen, and in the history of the precepts. Ryushin then works with its opening lines on dana, where not being greedy means not coveting and not flattering. Ryokan's poem about picking violets instead of begging, the Tibetan lama who gives a coin to a beggar in Bodhgaya, and Ryushin's father's story of the man who dropped his cigarette case in Nazi-occupied Greece show how a gift keeps moving. The evening closes with a participant discussion that includes a question about what we give back to birdsong in the woods.

title: Shikantaza
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up shikantaza through Hongzhi's poem "The Guidepost of Silent Illumination," read from the collection The Art of Just Sitting. Nomon explains the word as shamatha and vipassana sitting, silence and illumination woven together, and passes on five posture points from sesshin: seat, belly, mudra, sternum, and the lengthening back of the neck. Yasutani Roshi's call for sitting so hard that sweat pours out meets Sojun Mel Weitsman's memory of Suzuki Roshi, who taught shikantaza as day-to-day selflessness. Nomon ends on the countless people who made it possible to go to sesshin or even to the grocery store, and on seeing one's own selfishness as the path to selflessness.

title: Paramitas
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the six paramitas on the seventh day of sesshin, reading one verse for each from Thokme Zongpo's 37 Practices of a Bodhisattva, in Ken MacLeod's translation Reflections on Silver River, alongside stanzas from the Prajnaparamita Eight Thousand Line Sutra. Norman opens with Ken's account of a miserable retreat, where a prayer to accept illness, recovery, or death led him to lean against a tree beneath blooming acacias and find peace in the pain. Generosity draws on the Jataka tales of the Buddha giving his body to a tigress and leaping into a fire as a rabbit, and on the fiction of owning land. Patience turns on the idea that a person who hurts you is a treasure. Norman closes with Emily Dickinson's lines about easing one life the aching.

title: Desire
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads Thomas Traherne's poem "Desire," a seventeenth-century clergyman's thanks to God for a longing that burns, empties the world of its beauty, and proves sacred. Norman goes stanza by stanza, setting the poem's despair beside the bodhisattva's listening to the cries of the world, and admits to being puzzled by one stanza. The Song of Songs and the troubadours show where romantic longing in Western culture comes from, and Shantideva's verses on being addicted to the task describe bodhisattvas as holy failures, satisfied only by endless practice. Norman closes with a passage from Traherne's Centuries of Meditations and asks the sangha to add a spirit of reaching out for the beloved to their sitting.

title: Vasubandhu's Yogacara Text
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Vasubandhu's Thirty Verses, a Yogacara text studied in recent months with Ben Connolly's commentary, Inside Vasubandhu's Yogacara: A Practitioner's Guide. Norman sets mind-only teaching against the droning of the emptiness teachings: because the world appears through our minds, training the mind matters. Norman explains the eighth consciousness, the storehouse of seeds, and the seventh, self-consciousness, which gives us exactly the suffering needed to see that I am you. Four practices from Ben's epilogue follow: awe, mindfulness as remembering, awareness of interdependence through breakfast, roads, and washing machines, and zazen. Norman closes with Dogen's Fukanzazengi, where zazen is a tiger roaming the mountains.

title: What Do You Preserve?
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up case 2 of the Blue Cliff Record, in which Zhaozhou quotes the opening of the Xinxin Ming ("avoid picking and choosing") and answers a monk's challenge, "What do you preserve?", with "I don't know." Norman begins with Freud's essay on Carl Abel's finding that the oldest words held opposite meanings, such as strong and weak, which suggests that language grows out of an older wholeness. Zhaozhou puts picking and choosing and clarity into the same basket, so preferring and letting go happen together. Norman connects this to the dharma name Rin Sho, "turning toward the light," and closes with a sangha member's solo performance as an old woman, who says "fall down, get up" as one word.

title: Waiting for What?
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads William Carlos Williams's poem about a sparrow, prompted by a walk across Brooklyn while visiting grandchildren, and then turns to teachings on nothingness from Jewish mysticism that came out of a retreat with Daniel Matt. Williams's flattened sparrow ends with "This was I, a sparrow. I did my best. Farewell." Moses de Leon splits the Hebrew word for wisdom into "wait" and "what," which Norman links to prajnaparamita as waiting with life. A Yom Kippur joke about the synagogue caretaker who calls himself nobody leads into humility as being a channel, and Norman closes by urging soft eyes in sesshin, even toward a squashed sparrow on the sidewalk.

title: Prajna Paramita in Eight Thousand Lines
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads the opening verse of the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 Lines at the start of a Samish sesshin, and wishes the room a happy Father's Day along the way. Norman works through the lines that say there is no wisdom, no bodhisattva, and no bodhicitta, and tells of the wanderer Shrenika, who sees emptiness without retiring into nirvana. A koan about an old tea lady on Mount Taishan, who answers every monk with "Right straight ahead," shows how to live that. Norman closes with five points of sitting posture, the last a gossamer thread from a heaven gently lifting the top of the head.

title: Befriend Everyone
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up a New York Times article by British novelist Rachel Cusk, "The Age of Rudeness," to ask how to speak respectfully with people who differ and to regard everyone as a friend. Shuko reads two airport scenes: a passport official who answers "You're rude," and a security officer who berates a woman over her bags of cosmetics until Cusk's painter friend meets her with a long, silent, steady gaze. Shantideva's verses on the sameness of self and others, an older painter friend in Portland who simply looks at things, and Lincoln mourning his son Willie in George Saunders's Lincoln in the Bardo follow. Shuko closes by inviting the room to chant the Merging of Difference and Unity together.

title: Tenzo Kyokun - Dogen's Instructions to the Cook
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's Tenzo Kyokun, the Instructions to the Cook, at the start of a spring study retreat, reading a sectioned translation aloud and stopping at the story of Xuefeng sifting rice for Dongshan. Dongshan asks whether he is removing the sand or the rice. Xuefeng answers that both go at once, then overturns the bowl when asked what the assembly will eat. Nomon connects the story to the old Zen warning against picking and choosing, and to Dogen's instruction to guard the monastery's ingredients like one's own eyes. A guided contemplation follows, asking listeners to name what they appreciate in themselves and then their rough edges, before groups of three talk about how the mind handled each question.

title: Bendōwa 4 - Zen Practice as Expressing Enlightenment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's early essay Bendōwa and the burning question the main biography attributes to him: if everyone is born with Buddha nature, why did the buddhas practice at all? Nomon reads Uchiyama Roshi's commentary from The Whole-Hearted Way, where zazen is described as the deep sleep of enlightenment, and nobody sleeping well thinks "I'm sleeping well." Nomon then describes a Facebook debate in which James Ford argues that Zen must not drop awakening, and offers the north star as an image for enlightenment. Nomon closes on Dogen's lines about entering and leaving realization without disturbing a single mote of dust.

title: It's All Over
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Suzuki Roshi's last words, "It's all over," together with Master Ma's reply to an attendant who asks how he is: "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha." Drawing on thirty years as a physician, Ryushin argues that the last moment is nothing special because people prepare for it by how they live, and that life has an edge only because death gives it one. Katagiri's three aspects of existence (suffering, separation, oneness) come alive through Maurice Sendak's late interview, a friend watching crows and maggots take apart a dead mole, and the moment Ryushin's 20-year-old dog stopped breathing, when everything changed and nothing happened. The close returns to Dogen's moon in dew drops shaken from a heron's bill, with lives shaken free as Kate and Connie and Anne and Bob.

title: Bendōwa 3 - Transmission of the Dharma
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the lineage passage of Dogen's Bendowa, where Dogen traces the Dharma from Shakyamuni through Mahakasyapa and Bodhidharma to Huineng and the five Chinese houses. Nomon offers three ways to read the lineage, as historical, devotional, and practical truth, and reads the offering made to Norman Fischer at Sunday's ceremony. Stories follow of the Buddha's raised flower and Mahakasyapa's grin, and of Lee de Barros telling Nomon over lunch to find a disciple. Uchiyama Roshi's comment on living through concepts leads to an imagined strawberry and Mary Oliver's "The Summer Day," which ends on her question about one wild and precious life.

title: Bendōwa 2 - For Authentic Seekers
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the opening paragraphs of Dōgen's Bendōwa and the Jijuyu Samadhi they name, sketching Dōgen's early life: a mother's death at seven, ordination at thirteen on Mount Hiei, and nine years at Kenninji with Myōzen, who dies in China. Nomon reads Teijo Munnich on losing herself in dance until the dancer is danced by the dance, then a Suzuki Roshi passage about establishing practice where there is no practice or enlightenment. Dōgen's return from China as a solitary voyager with something precious earns a comparison to coming home from retreat and being handed the baby. The evening ends on a take-home question: where does the mind separate me from something I think I'm supposed to be, and can I notice that without beating myself up?

title: Bendōwa 1 - Holding to Fixed Views
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a five-week series on Dogen's essay Bendōwa, using the Waddell and Abe translation, and begins with a cold that kept Nomon from sleeping until trying Janet's advice to sleep propped up, which exposes Nomon's fixed views about what is needed for sleep. Nomon connects this to the line "not holding to fixed views" in the Metta Sutta and to Thich Nhat Hanh on suffering well. Then Nomon sketches Dogen's life and three kinds of truth: historical, mythic, and practical. The first two paragraphs of Bendōwa follow, with the Jijuyo Samadhi ("self-fulfilling enjoyment") and the line that the Dharma "is amply present in every person."

title: Possibility
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Jane Hirshfield's unpublished poem "On the Fifth Day," in which silenced scientists give way to rivers, wind, and fruit-tree buds that keep speaking, and Ryushin borrows from a conversation between Hosen Alan Senauke and Rebecca Solnit on hope and hopelessness. Ryushin separates ordinary hope, a wish for a particular outcome, from the trust Suzuki Roshi calls inner power, where vow grows like an acorn into a tree. Ryushin tells of Ryushin's first teacher sitting zazen by the Livermore tracks as nuclear waste passed, answering "I don't know, but it's most important that I do it." The Tibetan farmer's "Maybe" and the Clamshell Alliance's arrests ask whether any act succeeds or fails. In the discussion, Bernadette describes putting out fresh hummingbird feeders every morning.

title: Awareness of Diversity
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Dogen's line that "you see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach," and works it through birds. A poetry professor's desert exercise sharpens what students can see once the plants are named, while a Lummi woman who knows only bald eagle, raven, and robin sees every bird as one of those three. Reizan's son, before the son can talk, puts his hands on his head to name the great horned owl in the field guide. A passage from Gary Snyder's The Real Work on "still hunting" in meditation leads to the northern goshawk, which Reizan glimpses for years before a pair chases each other in cartwheels over the pump house.

title: Three Aspects of Consciousness
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up a framework of three kinds of consciousness drawn from Dale Wright's book on the six paramitas: immediate, reflective, and self-consciousness. Norman traces how meditation touches each level, from the wonder of sun, rain, and snowflakes, to the slow revision of old stories and emotions through the teachings, to the puzzle that a fingertip cannot touch itself and an eye cannot see itself. A senior student once scolded Norman for failing to notice an acquaintance across the street, and Norman tells it to show that presence is no contest. Norman ends with the Buddha under the Bodhi tree, where Dogen's words "mysterious existence, non-existence, empty and unknowable, marvelous and eternal" mark the recognition that self cannot be an object.

title: Appreciating Tathata
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
