summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with a slim book of poems by the Tibetan refugee Tenzin Tsundue, found in the retreat library, and reads "Space Bar of Proposal," whose narrator offers to sleep under the bed and asks, "Call me when you are awake." From there Nomon takes up tathata, thusness or suchness, as a language of appreciation in which "not good enough" makes no sense. Two stories carry the teaching: Norman Fischer tapping Nomon on the shoulder in a Green Gulch lunch line in 1988 to ask about working in the kitchen, and the characters setsu and shin, "touch heart-mind," that give sesshin its name. Nomon ends with tomorrow's shuso ceremony and a reply to any request: "I have a breath to breathe."

title: Reflections on Intimacy in the Heart of Conflict
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna takes up case five of the Mumonkan, the man hanging from a tree by his teeth, as a picture of uncertain political times. Along the way Ryushin draws on Blanche Hartman's advice that a Shuso be completely authentic, and on Brené Brown's definition of vulnerability. Ryushin describes practicing conflict with Jeff, a husband of 37 years, at the "balcony" moment when tension rises. From the branch, Ryushin asks how to meet a neighbor who backs armed militias without clenching onto a position. The closing image is a squirrel at the bird feeder who falls from a cedar limb, lands, and returns to ordinary life, leading to the sangha's hands and eyes.

title: Caring for the Heart of the Human Family
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer tells the story of Nakagawa Soen Roshi bowing to prisoners and weeping, asking their forgiveness because priests had not done their job well enough. Norman describes the human family as one dysfunctional household and follows the Buddha, who meditated intensely first so that his care for suffering would rest on wisdom. Suzuki Roshi's instruction to practice dying on the exhale leads into a seven-step breathing practice drawn from the mindfulness of breathing sutra. Norman closes with Mazu asking Nanquan about the way, and Nanquan's reply that everyday mind is the way and that aiming for it points in the wrong direction.

title: Ritual and Home Practice
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Paula Arai's book Bringing Zen Home: The Healing Heart of Japanese Women's Rituals, which follows a dozen Japanese lay women through their daily ritual practice. Seishu describes Honda-san, who calls "I'm home" to her late parents' photos each time she enters her apartment, and reads Arai's account of setting up a mortuary altar by phone, guided by a Zen nun, after her mother's death. Seishu then tells of placing photos of Seishu's father, Aunt Marie, Uncle John, and brother-in-law Butch on the home altar, where reflecting on their lives has deepened gratitude. Seishu closes with Naikan, a Japanese reflection practice of asking what has been received, what has been given, and what trouble has been caused.

title: Buddhist Practice for Climate Change
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton reports on EcoSatva, an online course from One Earth Sangha that four sangha members took, and treats climate change as a contemporary koan, with invented questions like whether a category five hurricane has Buddha nature. Shuko lays out Buddhist guidance for action: abstain from evil, cultivate good, and benefit all beings. Joanna Macy's advice to take refuge in sangha when helplessness sets in follows, along with the course's eight reflection questions. Shuko urges small steps, such as asking a coworker what they think about climate change, and describes finally calling the Department of Justice and speaking into a recorder. Wendell Berry's line "Be joyful even though you have considered the facts" ends the prepared remarks, and questions about local groups follow.

title: When Truth Moves
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up Book of Serenity case 75, in which a monk asks Yantou about the original and everlasting truth and is told, "It moved." Heigaku starts with Laywoman Yu Daopo, a donut seller who is awakened by a beggar's song and throws her tray to the ground. Heigaku then turns to Dogen's Genjokoan and to three habits that surface while sitting with the koan: confidence that blocks listening, turning a difficulty into a crisis (hands crushing the steering wheel), and grasping. After comparing Robert Aitken's translation with Thomas Cleary's, Heigaku reads the monk's second question as asking what this truth means in everyday life. Heigaku ends with a list of ordinary moments, from toasted almonds downstairs to a street lamp reflected on wet asphalt, and asks whether that is the original and everlasting truth, dancing.

title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 1: Observation of Body (3)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Buddha's instruction on mindfulness of the body, beginning with the story of an old woman who asks Zhaozhou how to be free while living in a body full of obstacles. Nomon follows the sutra through every posture, including going to the toilet, and through the body's impermanence and its billions of bacteria. A reading from Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind on practice with no gaining idea leads to the koan of Zhaozhou and Nanquan, "Everyday mind is the way." Nomon closes by inviting everyone to sit the Rohatsu night sitting for as long or as little as body and mind choose.

title: Avowal and Repentance
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up the verse of "ancient twisted karma" that the sangha recites in sesshin, drawing on Shohaku Okumura's commentary in Living by Vow and a Samantabhadra Sutra verse about sitting upright. Eko tells two small stories: dropping a kutsu with a clatter during zazen and choosing to confess it aloud, and mistaking dripping water for a person making noise across the zendo. Both show how an imagined "them" gets created, and how attachment to outcome keeps the habit going. Atonement becomes a platform for acting, and zazen is where effort without figuring can show itself. Eko ends with Zhaozhou's answer to the old woman and her five obstacles in The Hidden Lamp, "Pray that all beings are born in heaven and that you yourself suffer forever," and names karmic conditioning as the site of liberation.

title: David Loy's Response
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a talk that David Loy gave in Boulder two weeks after the election, sent around by Norman Fischer. Nomon first praises the discomfort of sesshin, where a crowded room and a picky mind become practice inside a supportive container. Loy then pictures a bus speeding toward a precipice while two parties fight over the wheel, and describes the Bellingham bubble of comfort that will pop. He turns to the bodhisattva path, using the marathon, the first bodhisattva vow, and don't-know mind to describe acting without knowing whether anything will matter. Nomon adds a few words on dualistic thinking and closes by thanking the sangha for the "together part."

title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 2: Observation of Actions
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with Naomi Shihab Nye's poem "Famous," then takes up the Four Foundations of Mindfulness Sutra's instruction to bring full awareness to walking, eating, and every other bodily activity. Nomon reads from Blanche Hartman's Seeds for a Boundless Life: Dogen's line that one person's zazen resonates through all time, Blanche's daily verses for waking, bathing, and sleeping, and Suzuki Roshi's "intimate as milk and water." Her husband's potato-and-rock-tumbler image leads to the winter practice period and Kate Ryushin as shuso. Nomon asks whether each of us will be famous like a buttonhole or like a marcher, and closes with Nye's "Shoulders."

title: Loving My Country
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Claude Anshin Thomas's memoir At Hell's Gate, a Soviet-free Vietnam veteran's account, in the week after the presidential vote. Nomon opens with a supermoon lost behind rain clouds, then seen at 5:30 one morning glowing through clouds and trees, and asks whether the dark days are really new. Nomon wonders what it would mean to learn to love our country without sorting everyone into liberal or conservative. Thomas's passages describe rain that returns him to the monsoon fighting, and a father who beats his young son and says it is because of love. Nomon ends by asking everyone not to be too quick to think they know what is going on, since finding out may only happen together.

title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 1: Observation of Body (2)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues the Sutra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness with its first section, observation of the body, and the instructions on mindfulness of breathing. Nomon reads Thich Nhat Hanh on returning to ourselves through conscious breath, Suzuki Roshi's image of the throat as a swinging door, and Blanche Hartman's story of being told "Zazen sits zazen" after counting every breath in a full period. Larry Rosenberg's account of a ninety-day Korean retreat, including a week without sleep, carries Ajahn Chah's advice to keep it simple and stick to the present moment. Nomon closes with Norman Fischer's suggestion to drop the word "observation," then leads a short practice of repeating "There is a body here" on each exhalation.

title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 1: Observation of Body (1)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first section of the Sutra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, the observation of the body, and opens with a passage from Blanche Hartman's Seeds for a Boundless Life, where she meets a riot policeman's eyes and feels a shared identity. Nomon reads the sutra's phrase "the body in the body" as an invitation to feel the body from the inside, then leads a few minutes of breathing in and out, long and short, with a wood turner at the lathe as the image. Gil Fronsdal's argument that sati is a noun closer to faith than to an activity complicates the idea of mindfulness as something a person does. Nomon closes with the cooks talking too loudly in the kitchen, which the breathing can include.

title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 0: Introduction
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a new series on the Sutra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipatthana), reading its first section from Thich Nhat Hanh's Transformation and Healing. Nomon starts with a mindfulness retreat at Samish Island, where participants read John O'Donoghue's poem "Beannacht" in place of the evening chant and practiced Sharon Salzberg's stealth metta in place of bowing. Drawing on Yogachara seeds in the storehouse consciousness, Nomon recalls a flash of aversion at a one-year-old's Korean-American features, and offers the four foundations as a way to notice such moments before a story forms. Nomon then explains sati, the word ekayana ("one direction"), and the body, feelings, mind, and patterns, closing with the Pali Tisarana refuge chant.

title: To Forgive and Forget
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the phrase "I forgive you but I haven't forgotten," prompted by an email from a longtime member of a group Ryushin belongs to, who also unfriended Ryushin. Ryushin looks at the definitions of forgive (to stop resenting, to cancel a debt) and notes that Pali and Sanskrit have no word for it, only patience or forbearance. Ryushin reads Nagiri Roshi's line that all beings are already forgiven for living, and tells of a Tibetan monk who weeps for the karma of those who burned a temple. Ryushin then turns to forgetting, tied to watering seeds in the Alaya consciousness and to the precept against harboring ill will, and ends with meeting someone in friendly open-heartedness without going out for coffee.

title: Yogachara Love Seeds
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Yogachara model of mind from a recent weekend study, asking what blocks the wise love that Andrea Thatch's talk and the interfaith project Let Love Be Our Legacy point toward. Nomon describes the storehouse consciousness, Alaya Vijnana, as a dark underground farm of seeds that sprout when conditions allow. Before leading the weekend, Nomon felt anxiety and inadequacy, then recognized seeds sprouting and planted mindfulness and hope instead. Nomon reads Thich Nhat Hanh's verses on the store consciousness and closes with Gateless Gate case 7, where Zhaozhou tells a new monk to wash his bowl, so that washing a bowl becomes washing the world.

title: Understanding Consciousness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Yogachara model of eight consciousnesses, working from Thich Nhat Hanh's Understanding Our Mind and Vasubandhu's verse summaries. Nomon sets the ground with the three marks and the story of the man who wants to study the arrow before it is pulled out, then tells how the monk Xuanzang walked out of China to bring the Yogachara texts home. The center is the alaya vijnana, a storehouse of seeds that sprout under conditions, and manas, the shuttle that ties them to a sense of self. Nomon's own example is the stream of insecurity that rose while preparing the weekend, and Pema Chödrön's advice to hang in there while the biggest seeds of anger use themselves up.

title: Deb's Wayfinding Talk
speaker: Manja Deb Wibe
summary: Manja Deb Wibe tells a wayfinding story, prompted by Tim in dokusan, about finding the way to practice. Raised on the North Dakota prairie with a childhood belief that the world depends on bedtime prayers, Manja moves through nursing, divorce, and graduate philosophy until Stan Lombardo introduces the Southwind Zen Center. Zen Master Seung Sahn's image of field potatoes in a potato washer describes living there, and Manja's daughter Anna urges a return to the cushion because Manja seems different after sitting. After thirteen years of sitting alone in a farmhouse, hunger for sangha brings Manja to Bellingham, and a Thich Nhat Hanh quote on Anna's poster, "I have arrived. I am home," closes the evening.

title: Everything We Do Is About Love
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up the phrase "everything we do is about love," which Ryushin's teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman offers when a student asks why Zen never talks about love. Ryushin begins with the September 11 response in Manhattan, then describes love as grandmotherly mind from Dogen's Tenzo Kyokun, using a friend's story of a grandmother who would make tea after a murder. Ryushin finds that love in forms and rituals: fluffing the cushion, Suzuki Roshi's scolding about moving chairs, Katagiri Roshi's glass of water, bowing, and zazen as making the self transparent. Ryushin closes on the Buddha's line that only love can change hate.

title: Revival
speaker: Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Nyogen Connie Martin tells the story of how a girl from Wilmington, Ohio ended up as Eno at a Zen sangha in the Pacific Northwest, and what Nyogen loves in the Zen forms. Nyogen follows a pattern of turning away and turning toward: a revival tent preacher and the unwelcome treatment of two classmates at church, then a son, Nathaniel, born with severe disabilities. Anger brings Nyogen to practice and to Norman Fischer. At Nyogen's first retreat, eighty Great Blue Herons crossing a lagoon stop Nyogen's mind. Nyogen calls ritual alive, citing a Zhaozhou exchange on zazen, and ends with Nathaniel driving a John Deere tractor and playing in a rock band.

title: Breathing and Healing in Africa, Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shows photographs and short videos from the July trip to Kenya to meet Marcy Okumu, the young woman Nomon and Janet have sponsored through school for ten years. The pictures move from Nairobi, with its motorcycle taxis, crowded train, and Marcy's small apartment, to a safari in the Masai Mara, where park guards ask for a bribe, and on to her home village near Lake Victoria. At Ombogo Girls Academy, Nomon invents a call and response, "Please take care of each other" and "We will," and Marcy speaks for half an hour about being orphaned at twelve. Time runs out before the slides of the largest slum in East Africa, which Nomon visited at the end.

title: Breathing and Healing in Africa, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett describes a two-week trip to Kenya to meet Mercy, an AIDS orphan whose schooling Nomon and Nomon's wife Janet have sponsored for nine years. Mercy's brother Wellington shows the fields where a poor rain season means no school fees for their sister Sonia, and a five-hundred-dollar irrigation pump stays out of reach. Back home, a stranger named Dennis lends Nomon a ladder at Home Depot, saving three hundred dollars. From there Nomon turns to breath counting, the Buddha's story of the two arrows, and a Tassajara teacher's advice to count backward from ten when counting goes stale. Nomon closes with Samantabhadra's seven-legged elephant, awkward yet stately.

title: Japan Pilgrimage
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan, Joden Bob Rose and Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan, Joden Bob Rose and Seishu John Wiley describe a May pilgrimage to Japan through a slide show, moving from a Kyoto inn to Rinso-in, Suzuki Roshi's home temple, and Eiheiji, the monastery Dogen founded. At Rinso-in the group sits morning and evening, cooks tempura with the family, and hears Suzuki Roshi's son say, "Practice with joy." At Eiheiji, 160 monks chant the Heart Sutra at 4:30 a.m. to a mokugyo as big as a small Volkswagen. The slides go on to the 200,000 memorial stones among huge trees at Mount Koya, the favorite place of many in the group, and end on Kyoto streets without a single cigarette butt.

title: Our Embodied Life, Part 4: Resiliancy and Chiyono's No Moon, No Water
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach closes the Our Embodied Life series by reading the story of Chiyono, a servant whose patched bucket gives way under a full moon, and her poem "Where water does not collect, the moon does not dwell." Ryushin names resiliency as the thread through the month's stories, pairing effort with pliancy alongside Mahapajapati's fearlessness and Kisa Gotami's compassion. Examples include a student who sat a whole sesshin with an abscessed tooth and Alan Senauke's teacher telling him, as a young jikido fussing over cushions, "Just let it fall apart." Sangha members then share their own patched buckets, including a memory of women in Africa carrying water on their heads.

title: Our Embodied Life, Part 3: Who is Senjo?
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach tells the Chinese folk tale of Senjo, case 35 of the Mumonkan, in which a young woman lies silent in her bed for five years while another Senjo lives with her husband Ochu and their two children. Ryushin follows the story through the family expectations, roles, and bodies that shape who anyone takes themselves to be, and connects it to Dogen's Genjokoan and the line about studying the self. Ryushin recalls a retired teacher who went back to what delighted him at ten. Goso's verse, "Not two, not one," frames the discussion, in which a geriatrician, a nurse, and a woman who gave up working with horses describe their own shifting roles. Terry closes by hearing everything as himself.

title: Our Embodied Life, Part 2: Kisagotami and the Tender Heart
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach reads the story of Kisagotami from the children's book Siddhartha and the Swan, passing it around the room, then returns to the mustard seeds Kisa gathers house by house while looking for medicine for her dead son. Ryushin sets the story beside Siddhartha's first sight of old age, sickness and death, and beside the first abbess of San Francisco Zen Center, who started over after her heart attack and ended every conversation with "I love you." Ryushin draws on Christina Feldman's phrase "a state of argument with our lives," Stephen Batchelor's rendering of dukkha as life, and Issa's line "The dew drop world is the dew drop world." Participants answer with a mother's lost sense of special protection, a family member's mental illness, and the police shootings in the news that week.

title: Knock Down the Banner
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Case 22 of the Mumonkan, in which Mahakashyapa answers Ananda's question about what else the Buddha transmitted by calling "Ananda" and then telling him to knock down the flagpole. Ryushin pairs the case with Sengcan's poem Faith in Mind and its opening line that the great way is difficult only for those with preferences. Ryushin brings both to the fear and polarization that followed the Orlando shootings and to an interfaith group in Whatcom County. Preferences are neutral until mistaken for truth, and love and hate make trouble as a pair. In the discussion, Ryushin tells of a temple board meeting about giving up incense, where dropping a fixed idea shifted the whole conversation.

title: Evaluating Doctrines
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Kalama Sutta, in which the Buddha, camped outside Kesaputta, tells villagers confused by rival teachers not to rely on tradition, scripture, logic, or a speaker's charisma. Norman reads the sutra through, including the four assurances of a mind free of ill will, and notes that people citing it for self-verification often skip its call to check with community and the wise. The reason is plain: we may be unreliable judges, enjoying a teaching because it matches our preconceptions. Norman closes on loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, which family members would confirm by saying "you're such a much nicer person now."

title: When Mountains are Mountains
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Qingyuan's story of seeing mountains as mountains, then as not mountains, then as mountains again, and pairs it with Case 11 of the Wumenguan, where Zhaozhou asks two hermits "Have you got it?" and judges their identical raised fists differently. Norman finds the joke in right and wrong, from worry over which stage of practice we are in to the corrections people receive in sesshin about bowing and cushions, forms the community collectively made up. Dogen's story of Magu fanning himself answers why anyone practices when the wind already reaches everywhere. Norman ends with Rebbe Nachman's king, who eats the maddening grain with everyone else and has a blue dot painted on each forehead to remember being crazy.

title: Self
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Buddha's teaching on self, tracing the five skandhas and reading the early sutta in which the Buddha tells the five ascetics that body, feelings, perceptions, impulses, and consciousness are not "mine." Norman recounts Vacchagotta's questions about self and no self, which the Buddha answers with silence. Norman then turns to Case 251 in Dogen's collection, where Daowu asks the ailing Yunyan where the two will meet, and reads the exchange as love's meeting beyond meeting. Norman ends with Shantideva's verse on compassion for anyone projected through delusion, and with Fayan's reply to Huichao: "You are Huichao."

title: About Nothing
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up nothing, a title borrowed from Seinfeld's show about nothing, and follows it through Christian and Jewish mystics, including Meister Eckhart, who prays that God will rid him of God, and the Hasidic teacher Dov Baer. Norman then turns to emptiness in Buddhism, comparing it to a balloon whose inner nothing makes it a balloon, and tells case 248 from Dogen's collection, where Shigong yanks Zhigong's nose to show how to grasp emptiness. Norman closes by remembering Zenkei Blanche Hartman, who died days after turning ninety, and reads from her book Seeds for a Boundless Life, ending with her passage on finding home wherever you are.

title: Mumonkan 7 - Clean Your Bowl
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up Mumonkan case 7, in which Chao Chou answers a new monk's request for teaching with "Have you eaten your rice gruel?" and then "Wash your bowl." After a sketch of Chao Chou and Wu Men, Shuko reads the koan as "do what is needed" and names two ways of learning what that is: being instructed, and taking responsibility, as with a volunteer role in the zendo or brushing off a zabuton before leaving. Zazen widens awareness until, like Avalokiteshvara, we hear the cries of the world, which leads Shuko to the Orlando shooting and an open discussion of gun culture, education, and compassion. One participant describes asking gun-owning friends in southern Illinois, "What do you think we should do about it?"

title: Perception
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up perception as the first step in a process of compassion, noticing that someone is suffering, and tells three stories about it. A woman at a cafe eats cookies from a stranger's bag, believing they are hers. Nomon gets an email ending "I hope this teaches you" that turns out to be a typo for "reaches you." Naomi Shihab Nye's short story "Museum" follows two teenagers who wander through a family's living room, mistaking it for the McNay Art Museum. In the open conversation, participants share their own mistaken perceptions, including a first aid volunteer who offers help to a man sighting along a curb, and a hiker pointing out bear scat who misses the bear.

title: Zenkei Blanche Hartman
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from a 1995 interview in which Zenkei Blanche Hartman tells David Chadwick about her early years with Suzuki Roshi at San Francisco Zen Center. Her stories include hearing "You're perfect just as you are," sending cookies to Tassajara and wanting thanks, bowing at Dokusan and finding Suzuki Roshi bowing back, and carrying an offering tray and a cigarette until his waggling finger stopped her. Nomon adds memories of Blanche bowing deeply to passersby at Green Gulch and teaching Nomon's Tassajara training period. Nomon ends on her habit of spending half a talk describing how hard it was to prepare, and on Suzuki Roshi's word that stumbling is part of being yourself.

title: Mumonkan 5 - Up a Tree
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up Mumonkan case 5, in which Xiangyan describes a person hanging from a branch by the teeth while someone below asks about Bodhidharma's coming from the West. Heigaku opens by asking the room to take that posture, then connects the dilemma to the five remembrances, to Xiangyan's awakening when gravel struck bamboo, and to Aitken's old Indian tale of a man dangling between two tigers who stops to taste a strawberry. Wumen's verse and the Buddha's two arrows lead to the thought that the tree may be a stick held in the mouth on a lawn. A participant's question about renunciation and a special needs child at home closes the session, and Heigaku answers by suggesting the renunciation of addictions, or of the wish to run off to a monastery.

title: Compassion, Part 3: To Hell and Back Again
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues the series on compassion by describing the traditional Buddhist practice of contemplating the six realms, from the hell realms up through the heavens. Nomon starts with a phone call to a friend whose mother has stage four cancer, a call that stays on logistics because Nomon never felt into her suffering. Nomon then tells of the table-and-saw hell and the cheese-grater hill, where a figure at the top keeps vanishing, and names the hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas. Nomon closes with the four remembrances, and a participant's reflection on Norman Fischer's word "obligation."

title: Taking Up the Way of Letting Go of Anger
speaker: Charlie-Anne Mikkelsen
summary: Charlie-Anne Mikkelsen reads from Charlie-Anne's book Love's Last Measure, Lessons Found at Death's Door and takes up the precept of letting go of anger from Diane Rizzetto's Waking Up to What You Do, applying Stephen Levine's "taking tea by the fire" to death and dying. Charlie-Anne tells the story of Charlie-Anne's husband Mike, an artist with Parkinson's, who answers a question about his illness with "Parkinson's tenderized me," meets his father in a hallucination, and leaves notes in tiny script that Charlie-Anne reads with a magnifying glass. On his last morning he rallies to stop the lorazepam, and a neighbor who is a chaplain blesses him on Valentine's Day. Charlie-Anne closes by asking what happens to inner gold after the person who received it dies, and answers: love is.

title: Nothing is ever out of place.
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up Ummon's remark in case 86 of the Blue Cliff Record that everyone has a light, dark and dim when sought, which Ummon answers with "The kitchen pantry and the main gate." Ryushin then tells of a koan from The Hidden Lamp, in which Ryushin's first teacher, Seisho Maylie Scott, answers a lonely student with "Don't think anything is ever out of place." That student was Ryushin, who recalls a crack in the world during a thirty-day silent Vipassana retreat, the pain of being adopted, and finding the same difficult traits in photographs of a birth mother. In questions, Connie asks about people in refugee camps and under bombs, and Ryushin answers with sitting with them and trusting the impulse to be of use.

title: Compassion, Part 2: Contemplation of Death
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the contemplation of death as the second step in Tibetan compassion training, following Jeffrey Hopkins's book, and begins with news that Joan Casey, a longtime friend of the Bellingham sanghas, died the day before. Nomon reads Thich Nhat Hanh's version of the five remembrances and offers Yun Men's koan answer, "Body exposed in the golden wind." Joan's husband says on the phone that her spirit is flying, and Nomon recalls Gyokuko of Dharma Rain Zen Community telling her grieving sangha, three weeks after Kyogen's sudden death, not to hurry to be remade. Nomon closes with a poem about ten feet of grass.

title: Compassion, Part 1: All Beings Want Happiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Tibetan contemplation that all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering, then turns to Gateless Gate case 16, where Yunmen asks why monastics put on the seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell when the world is so vast and wide. Nomon tells of the family cat Luca dying, of a head full of platitudes giving way to shared sorrow with Janet, and of Janet then objecting that Nomon and Janet's son had planned the weekend as if she didn't exist. Muman's verse, in which all things are one family and disconnected both with and without realization, leads Nomon to ask how to answer the bell after the bombings in Belgium. Nomon closes with the Dhammapada lines on hate being conquered by love.

title: Inner Gold, Part 2: Handling Inner Gold
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to Robert A. Johnson's idea of inner gold, the worth we project onto other people, and reads Johnson's rules for getting it back: never pester the person carrying it, and don't mix levels. Nomon tells of a co-leader on a retreat whose gold went unnoticed, ending in anger over the retreat's closing, and of a Bellingham woman whose emailed updates turned out to be a way of checking that her gold was safe. Johnson's night in Calcutta follows, when a stranger in a park, a Roman Catholic priest, agrees to be the incarnation of God for him. Nomon closes with Wendell Berry's poem about sitting among the trees and singing with fear.

title: Inner Gold, Part 1: Why did Zen take root in the West?
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the question of why Zen took root in the West, opening a sesshin talk with Wendell Berry's poem "The Real Work." Nomon weighs suffering, charismatic teachers, and reverse Orientalism as answers, then turns to Robert A. Johnson's book Inner Gold, which describes projecting our own gold onto another person to carry for a while. Nomon tells of a physician who says Nomon "has the glow," and reads Johnson's story of hero-worshiping a cousin's husband, Thor, on a boyhood squirrel hunt. Nomon ends by wondering whether students and teachers in the lineage have been exchanging gold all along.

title: Devadatta - Trouble in the First Sangha
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer tells the story of Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin, who opposes the aging Buddha, draws hundreds of disciples away, helps Prince Ajatasattu starve King Bimbisara, and makes three attempts on the Buddha's life, the last with a royal elephant that the Buddha stops with an elephant cry. Norman asks why the Buddha does not retire, then turns to Anathapindaka's death, where Shariputra guides a contemplation of "not me," and to Hoitsu Suzuki's poem about failing ears and eyes becoming more truly his own. Ajatasattu, shown mercy after losing a war, comes to the Buddha in remorse, and Devadatta, dying on a stretcher, takes refuge with the Buddha's hand on his forehead.

title: Anapanasati Sutra On Breath Mindfulness
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer teaches the Anapanasati Sutra, the Buddha's instruction on full awareness of breathing, as Thich Nhat Hanh renders it in Old Path, White Clouds. Norman opens with the recent death of Ted Marshall, a Tassajara comrade who took the precepts in a Jukai ceremony only a week earlier, and the urgency that brings. Then Norman walks through the sixteen breaths, from the body to feelings, the mind, and impermanence. Along the way Norman describes the mind as an ocean with waves above and still depths below, and suggests three conscious breaths in a crisis. Norman closes by describing impermanence as everything arising and passing away together, and calls the breath Norman's best friend.

title: Essence
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up form and essence on a sesshin day, reading Suzuki Roshi's "kind enough with yourself" passage from Not Always So and Dainin Katagiri's comments on faith as tranquility. Katagiri's teaching leads to the story of Saganandi and Gayashata asking whether the wind or the bell is ringing, and to Dogen's answer in the "Immo" chapter of the Shobogenzo that the ringing rings. Nomon applies this to the day's silence and looks up "serious" in the dictionary, finding "sincere" and "wholehearted" among its meanings. Nomon ends by asking where each person's breath is right now, and whether it is the wind, the bell, or the mind ringing.

title: Western Ancestors, Part 5: Henry David Thoreau
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny reads from Henry David Thoreau's Walden, starting with a passage from "Sounds" about sitting in a sunny doorway from sunrise till noon. Reizan sketches Thoreau's life in Concord: the schoolteaching, the surveying work, the night in jail over a poll tax, and the unsold copies of A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers that left Thoreau with a library of nearly 900 volumes, 700 of them self-written. Reizan follows Emerson's influence, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Lotus Sutra excerpts printed in The Dial, then turns to the essay "Walking," where "saunterer" as "holy lander" becomes a way to see kinhin. Reizan closes with Thoreau's image of time as a stream to fish in, with a sky whose bottom is pebbly with stars.

title: Understanding Conflict
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Seishu John Wiley
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Seishu John Wiley report on a Whatcom Dispute Center workshop that seven sangha members attended, and they connect its interest and needs based model to the sangha's own ethical guidelines document. Ryushin and Seishu describe the cycle of trigger, escalation, crisis, recovery, and depression, with an early "window" for assessing a situation the way firefighters size up a fire. An iceberg of positions above the water and needs below it is illustrated with two neighbors and a fallen tree, and with two men who settle a dispute over shade and apples. The group reads ten tips and weighs avoiding, competing, compromising, and collaborating, with Congress offered as an example of avoiding. A participant closes by proposing that the quarterly sangha conversations use pre-structured questions to build trust.

title: Western Ancestors, Part 4: Suzuki Roshi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from the Suzuki Roshi chapter of Rick Fields' How the Swans Came to the Lake, after first describing the sense of "okay" that zazen touches. Nomon tells how Nyogen Senzaki was left by his teacher Soyen Shaku in Golden Gate Park to meet America on his own, then follows Shunryu Suzuki from his arrival at Sokoji in San Francisco in 1959. The reading covers the 5:30 sitting open to anyone, the increase from three bows to nine, and students who wait for the green light on an empty Bush Street. Nomon closes with Norman Fischer's teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman, who wrote "all I can give you is my Zen spirit" on Norman's rakusu.

title: The Self and the Listener
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Lew Welch's poem "Small Sentence to Drive Yourself Sane" and Barry Magid's passage comparing just sitting to looking in a mirror. Nomon then turns to the fourteenth-century teacher Basui and his question "Who hears?", found in Nelson Foster's The Roaring Stream. In Basui's recorded exchange, skeptical listeners ask where the practice comes from, and Basui points to the Shurangama Sutra, where Manjushri tells Ananda to listen to the listener. Nomon sets this beside a personal story: five years of counting breaths, then counting backward at a teacher's suggestion, then the question "What is it?" from Norman. The evening closes on Welch's line "So, it's all come to this," offered for moments of tangling up in self-improvement.

title: Dongshan's Companion
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up the case of Dongshan at Nanquan's assembly, where Nanquan asks whether the late Mazu will come to tomorrow's memorial feast and young Dongshan answers, "If he has a companion, he'll come." Eko reads the companion as a resolute presence and also as the gentle one Thich Nhat Hanh describes, an older sister looking after an angry younger sibling. Sesshin itself invites Mara, so Eko asks what each person has invited and how each has met it. The invitation to true nature resembles a campfire in dark woods, where the animals draw near.

title: Western Ancestors, Part 3: Nyogen Senzaki
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Nyogen Senzaki, the Zen priest who arrived in San Francisco in 1905 with his teacher Soyen Shaku, drawing on Rick Fields' How the Swans Came to the Lake. Following the theme of effort, Nomon traces Senzaki from the Russell household, where Soyen Shaku leaves him in Golden Gate Park to face the city, through hotel work and a "floating zendo" of rented halls and borrowed chairs, to internment at Heart Mountain and a monthly bow across the ocean to Nakagawa Soen. Nomon asks what could sustain such steady, long-haul effort and leaves the question open. Nomon closes with Senzaki's recorded voice playing at his funeral and the first traditional seven-day sesshin in America, held in his memory.

title: Western Ancestors, Part 2: Katagiri Roshi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues a series on Zen's Western ancestors by turning to Jiyu Kennett and then Dainin Katagiri. Nomon reads from James Ford's memoir If You're Lucky, Your Heart Will Break, where Ford recalls kyosaku-driven training in Kennett's small San Francisco zendo, and dates the golden age of American Zen from 1966 to 1984. Katagiri's story runs from wartime Japan, where as a teenager he serviced kamikaze planes, to Minnesota and the 14 priests he trained. Nomon remembers meeting Katagiri in 1987 and hearing "Whoa, maybe some small enlightenment," then closes with Katagiri's passage on returning to silence.

title: Compassionate Communication
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up compassionate communication, drawing on Marshall Rosenberg's nonviolent communication and Gregory Kramer's insight dialogue, which Eko's sangha is studying in an eight-week class. Eko tells of a sangha member whose fight over a bowl of Halloween candy led down to a fear of being invisible, and of a canceled prison visit in Monroe that Eko answered with a carefully worded email. Kramer's three desires, for sense pleasure, for being seen, and for not being seen, raise the question of how a bodhisattva keeps a human heart. Eko answers that a bodhisattva works to create conditions in which all beings flourish, and offers the image of momentary waves of self-centeredness rising on the ocean of the bodhisattva heart.

title: Western Ancestors, Part 1: Jiyu Kennet
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona opens a series on Western ancestors, running through the end of practice period in March, with Roshi Jiyu Kennett, founder of Shasta Abbey. Heigaku describes her years at Sojiji, her question about why cruelty and death exist, and her Anglican-flavored wording for Zen. Heigaku then follows the line of women from Myochi and Ekan to Keizan, reading Sallie Tisdale's account of Keizan's dream of his grandmother and the young nun Sonin's answer in Dharma combat: "In the branches of the tree without shadow, is there any kind of time?" The evening closes on Ananda's koan of "yes," which Heigaku sat with for several months under Tim's guidance.

title: Compassion Seminar
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett leads a seminar on compassion, opening with a flip-chart brainstorm of what compassion is and is not. Nomon then lays out compassion as a process: noticing suffering, feeling something, deciding to care, being willing to stay, and taking skillful action, with ways of dropping out at each step, such as denial, overwhelm, and self-protection. A Venn diagram of overlapping circles shows how much closeness is too little or too much, and compassion is split into three directions: for others, from others, and for oneself. A writing exercise follows, in which each person records a self-critical voice, thanks it for any helpful intent, and writes a kind letter to themselves as a best friend, before breaking into groups of three.

title: Mara, Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart returns to Mara, continuing a conversation from some weeks earlier, and takes up the Pali Canon stories in which Mara visits the Buddha and the bhikkhunis. Kanho cites the scholar G.P. Malalasekera's definition of Mara as death and tempter, then tells of Soma, whom Mara taunts for her "two-fingered wisdom," and Upacala, whose verse about a burning world leaves Mara no place. In each story the nun recognizes Mara, and Mara disappears sad and disappointed. To learn that recognition, Kanho offers metta meditation and mindfulness of the mind, befriending thoughts and turning away from nothing, and closes by repeating Upacala's verse.

title: Mara, Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Mara, the personification of the kleshas, starting with the old story of Mara's attack on Gautama under the Bodhi tree and then reading the short sutra The Splinter, where Mara questions the Buddha for lying down to rest with an injured foot. Kanho points out that Mara speaks the language of practice, urging effort and equanimity, and offers impermanence, suffering, and non-self as the test for telling him from the Buddha. Kanho then proposes, as a tentative view, that Mara sat under the tree with Gautama the whole time, two sides of one coin. Kanho closes with Thich Nhat Hanh's image of flowers and garbage, in which the gardener turns garbage into compost for lettuce, tomatoes, and flowers.

title: Paramitas - Patience Beyond Patience (Kshanti)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up kshanti paramita, the practice of patience on the bodhisattva's list of six, and reads the Sanskrit as "unaffected by, or able to be with" and paramita as "patience beyond patience." Nomon contrasts the Western picture of patience as putting up with an idiot and as a fixed trait with a practice of merging, where impatience becomes information and a seed that can sprout. Mary Oliver's poem "I Worried" shows how many times "I" appears in a worrying narrative. A Prajnaparamita passage about giving away even one's life to robbers meets Aristotle's idea that one should be neither irascible nor non-irascible. Nomon closes with Seisho Maylie Scott's reply to a lonely student, "Please do not ever think anything is out of place," and a reflection on the moment the hook came out.

title: Paramitas - Perfection of Conduct (Sīla)
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up sila, the perfection of conduct, and opens with a nephew who asks why he didn't get cowboy boots, then says no when asked if he wants them. Heigaku traces conduct from the eightfold path through the 250 monastic rules and Dogen's 16 precepts, then turns to Subhuti's question in the Diamond Sutra about how a bodhisattva should stand, walk, and control thoughts. A Thai nun who took 311 precepts says she keeps only one: watching her mind. Heigaku closes with the slave Punika, who asks a shivering Brahmin at the river what he is afraid of.

title: Gratitude
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 93 of the Blue Cliff Record, where a monk asks about giving thanks at lunch and Daguang answers by dancing, along with the earlier Case 74 on Jinniu's rice pail. Before that, Nomon sets a rain-soaked Zen backpacking trip on Mount Baker beside a day at a Volkswagen dealership, where desire for a flood-damaged 2012 Golf TDI meets bad news. Drawing on Kate's talk about fearful doubt, Nomon asks whether gratitude can reach difficult states of mind, then turns to play, recalling Kate's story of a two-year-old bouncing a ball. The monk who copies Daguang's dance is called a stupid fox, so each person must find a dance of their own.

title: Doubt
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna takes up doubt, the fifth of the Buddha's five hindrances, and describes how it shows up in daily life and on the cushion as overgeneralizing stories, social comparison, and the sense of not doing zazen right. Ryushin turns to the dark night of the soul, with Mother Teresa, Jack Kornfield, and Joan Halifax's Sonicare toothbrush story, and then to great doubt, where Hakuin finds great awakening. A toddler named Quinn, absorbed for two hours in a rolling basketball, becomes "the koan of the basketball." Ryushin closes by reading Norman's quote about tearing down today's truth, and invites a go-around of the circle.

title: Paramitas – #4 Effort
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up effort, the fourth of the six paramitas, after a quick review of how the perfections grew from sila, samadhi, and prajna. Shuko recalls monthly seven-day sesshins at Sogenji, where the roshi urged "effort, effort, effort," and the abbess at Tassajara pressing everyone to keep the full schedule. Observations follow on why American practice takes effort: sore knees, just sitting, discipline, the forms, and the bodhisattva vow, with Shantideva's image of a warrior. A tea ceremony rehearsal that steamed up the car windows shows how much energy zazen gathers. Shuko ends with the new effort of learning to honor an aging body's limits.

title: Two Ways of Knowing
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells of a fall during a sesshin on Salt Spring Island, when a dog chasing a ball hit the back of Kanho's legs and left Kanho briefly paralyzed after landing on head and neck. Kanho recalls the night spent holding a mala, breathing "this moment, this breath," and quotes Shantideva on whom to blame for pain. At an interfaith panel days later, a pastor's plea to choose Jesus before the second coming leads Kanho to vow to stay behind with those left behind, like Jizo, the Bodhisattva of hell beings. Kanho sets the knowing that has lost street names and the Heart Sutra beside a knowing that holds the Metta Sutra without the words, and closes with three questions: Did I love enough? Did I live fully? Did I learn how to let go?

title: The Bodhisattvas Four Methods
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Eihei Dogen's "Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance": giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action. A morning ferry mix-up, in which men in vests shout at Nomon over a trivial mistake, shows how easily the narrow mind finds ammunition, and the Dalai Lama's puzzled "Why would you not be compassionate towards yourself?" shows the separation Dogen's methods work against. The woman who admires the image on Nomon's credit card at the ticket booth illustrates kind speech. For identity action, Nomon retells Norman Fischer's story of the poet Robert Desnos, who reads palms in a line of prisoners outside a gas chamber and changes the mood of prisoners and guards alike. The Q&A closes on asking permission before offering a kindness.

title: Bodhisattva Methods, Part 4: Identity Action
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to Dogen's essay on the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance and finishes it, moving from giving, kind speech, and beneficial action to the fourth method, identity action. Nomon opens with forms recalled from Tassajara, such as the mudra and which foot crosses the threshold, and with two recent stretches of intensive practice, including a guest who felt judged in the kitchen one morning and welcomed the next. Dogen's image of the ocean that does not refuse to be water frames the practice of stepping into and out of roles. Nomon closes with Norman Fischer's story of the poet Robert Desnos, who takes up the role of an exuberant palm reader on a truck bound for the gas chamber.

title: Compassion For Charleston
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett sets aside a prepared talk on sacred time, built on Mircea Eliade's The Sacred and the Profane, to speak about the shooting at Emmanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston. Nomon traces the church from its founding in 1816 by enslaved people through its burning, thirty years of secret worship, and reopening in 1865, then describes the victims' relatives telling the shooter "I forgive you." Naomi Shihab Nye's poem "Shoulders" and a Stanford process of noticing, feeling, and willingness frame wisdom and compassion as two wings. Nomon ends by offering the sesshin's merit to the healing of suffering, with a rewording of Dogen's "Being Time" verse.

title: Bodhisattva Methods, Part 1: Giving continued
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues Nomon's series on Dogen's four bodhisattva methods with the second half of the section on giving, opening with Naomi Shihab Nye's poem "Shoulders." Nomon reads Dogen's stories of Emperor Tai of the Tang dynasty giving his beard as medicine and of a child offering sand to the Buddha and becoming King Ashoka, then tells of Ashoka's turn from conquest to Buddhism. Andy Goldsworthy's impermanent leaf chains and his ten-foot snowball left on a London sidewalk show giving as delight and surprise. Nomon asks what it would be to walk into work as an act of giving, and the discussion that follows closes on a participant's "Thanks mom" for a gift of curiosity about what lies down the trail.

title: Bodhisattva Methods, Part 1: Giving
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first of the four methods in Dogen's "Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance," giving, and reads the passage that opens with "giving means non-greed." Nomon slows the text down phrase by phrase, studying greed and the urge to curry favor, such as needing a smile from a quiet audience. Next comes "give yourself to yourself and others to others," which Nomon links to Katagiri Roshi's "settle the self on the self." A gratitude-journal research list follows, then listeners share recent gifts: broccoli from a garden, a stranger's grocery bill, a dead brother's generator sent to Haiti. Nomon closes with a bow to the dying Blanche Hartman.

title: Gratitude
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up gratitude after setting aside his planned talk on the paramitas, and describes a personal experiment sparked by a quote at the Y: "Any amount of gratitude changes the present." When his mind drifts toward complaint, Seishu stops and asks what he can genuinely feel grateful for. In a noisy tent camp at Yosemite, he thinks of people who lost their homes in the Nepal earthquake and lets the irritation go. Seishu draws on Brother David Steindl-Rast, Dogen's Fukanzazengi, and Norman Fischer, and closes by reading Norman's One Heart Grace before inviting everyone to name something they are grateful for.

title: Paramitas – #1 Dana – Generosity
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up dana, the first of the six paramitas, starting with a Snickers bar tossed around a high school Spanish class and the Oryoki chant on the emptiness of giver, receiver, and gift. Heigaku reads Hidden Lamp stories of Lingzhao dropping to the ground beside her fallen father, Layman Pang, and of the nun Fa Zhang sharing her best food with Hui Su, then Hui Hai's answer that dana means relinquishing dualism. Heigaku admits to mid-afternoon exhaustion from giving every person full attention. A closing exercise adapted from Jan Chozen Bays has listeners imagine the energy of rain, freight trains, and volcanoes passing through them, give it away, and add a smile as a gift of no fear.

title: Bodhisattva at the Gas Station: Studying the Ways of the Bodhisattva
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the bodhisattva path as the theme for the rest of the year and lays out the traditional six practices: generosity, ethical living, patience, energy, meditative concentration, and wisdom, recommending Dale Wright's book The Six Perfections. Nomon tells a story on Nomon's own part: after teaching multitasking in Seattle, Nomon leaves late for a 2:30 meeting, starts the pump, buys a coupon latte, and drives off with the gas hose still attached. The station manager pats Nomon's shoulder, says "Perhaps you are a little stressed," and trusts Nomon with just a name on a pad. Nomon connects the manager to the Chinese ancestor Joshu, who vowed to learn from a seven-year-old girl, then asks the room where they have met bodhisattvas lately, drawing answers about a band called Out of the Ashes and a Brian Doyle reading.

title: Dharma Talk 1 – Way of the Bodhisattva
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up psychologist Paul Gilbert's work on the fears that block compassion, which runs in three directions: toward others, from others, and toward oneself. Nomon reads a passage from a book by Ram Dass and Paul Gorman, in which an unnamed voice wavers over when and whom to help, then reads items from Gilbert's fear-of-compassion scale one at a time. Partners then try a structured exercise of speaking, listening, and sharing appreciation. In the closing conversation, Chris separates compassion from pity and indulgence, and Nomon retells the story of the Dalai Lama asking, puzzled, whether people really lack compassion for themselves.

title: Study Group 1 - Way of the Bodhisattva
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a six-week study group on Shantideva's Bodhicharyavatara by explaining the format: a selection of verses drawn from the Dalai Lama's commentary, read aloud in turn around the circle. Nomon sets out the pattern of intention, practice, and dedication of merit, then the group reads chapters one through three and stops to talk. They puzzle over Shantideva's line that he has no thought of benefiting others, admire the offering of everything in nature "without the tiller's work," and stay with "we cannot stay" and the verse about taking pleasure in sin, which brings up anger. The homework is to ask for help sometime in the coming week.

title: Entangled
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's essay "Twining Binds," which a study group of former shusos has been reading, and its retelling of Bodhidharma asking four students for their understanding and answering them with skin, flesh, bones, and marrow. Nomon first lays out the stages of training in the sangha: showing up, taking roles in the zendo, receiving the precepts at jukai, and serving as shuso, whose final ceremony brings quick questions and answers the shuso often cannot remember giving. Dogen rejects the usual ranking of the four answers and says all of them express attainment. Dogen also treats the entangled teacher-student bond as something to study and enjoy, "more as a hug than a rope."

title: Bodhisattva Path
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton closes the evening with housekeeping and no teaching. Shuko calls the sangha to page three of the chant book, notes that it is after nine, and says the refuges will be skipped tonight. The remaining instructions are to pass the chant books back, straighten the cushions and leave them in a neat row, and gather in the lobby. The transcript holds nothing of the Bodhisattva Path talk itself.

title: Temple Pillars
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up the practice of "following the body" and Dogen's Eihei Koroku passage "Jumping and Stumbling in a Fragrant World," in which temple pillars and lanterns expound the Dharma. Eko draws on Suzuki Roshi's reading of Dogen on teachers and sincere practice, then describes offering incense behind a teacher, folding a robe in the dokusan room, and the intimacy of eating oryoki together. Bowing to a teacher becomes a freedom from needing to be equal, better, or less, and the roles of teacher and student can be switched. Eko recalls four wooden pillars in the St. Paul zendo and ends with sixteen people coming to dokusan the day before.

title: Precious Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett leads a guided reflection on how rare and precious it is to practice together, using a Tibetan-style visualization of people who cannot practice because of illness, disability, poverty, or war, and of the founding teachers Suzuki Roshi and Katagiri Roshi in 1950s America. Nomon then reads from Suzuki Roshi's 1961 remarks, later titled "Teacher and Disciple," on emptiness, the unbroken effort between practice and enlightenment, and the Yakusan story of the Zen master who asks to be acknowledged. Along the way, Nomon recalls a quiet day with Norman Fischer making calligraphy on a rakusu, after which a sister-in-law says "you really seem different." Nomon closes with Dogen's line that everyone is your teacher, and the habit of hurry.

title: Every Day is a Good Day
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Blue Cliff Record case 6, in which Yunmen asks for a phrase about after the fifteenth of the month and answers himself, "Every day is a good day." Nomon reads the saying as gratitude with no "because," tells the story of Yunmen's leg broken in a monastery gate, and describes a hard conversation with colleagues in a Seattle Starbucks, after which a weight settles for a day and then lifts. John Tarrant's comment on gratitude as a path follows. Nomon then walks through the winter practice period on Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara and ends with Thomas's list of volunteer options for a service day on Saturday, February 28th.

title: Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart continues with Dongshan's Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, reading the lines on the illumination hexagram as a riff on the five ranks. Kanho describes each rank as a circle of black and white, from vexations covering most of the circle to the all-black fifth rank, where vexations become the means of helping sentient beings. Other images follow: a tethered colt and a frightened mouse as false enlightenment, the archer Yi whose skill cannot make two arrows meet in mid-air, and a wooden man singing while a stone woman dances. Kanho closes with Dongshan's five-ranks poem, ending on the one who returns to sit among the coal and ashes.

title: Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, a poem attributed to Dongshan that Dogen brought home from China along with the teaching of the Five Ranks. Kanho admits to having missed the poem's connection to Zen at first, then reads the opening lines slowly, setting them beside the Buddha's instruction to Bahiya, the heron hidden in moonlight and snow in a silver bowl, and Mumonkan case 19, where Zhaozhou asks Nanquan about the way. Sheng Yen's commentary supplies the image of enlightened people becoming the fire. Kanho closes with Dongshan seeing his reflection while crossing a river, where body and reflection depend on each other like mirror and image.

title: Metta Sutta, Part 4: The Teachings on Loving Kindness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the Metta Sutta, the fourth talk in a cycle, after a trip to teach a Heart Sutra retreat in San Miguel de Allende. Nomon names the companion practices that travel with metta (generosity, mudita, compassion, and equanimity), then reads verses four through nine against two translations, one reflecting early Buddhism's sense that something is broken and one reflecting later Buddhism's view that we are already whole. A rebirth passage and the wave and ocean image lead into Bhikkhu Bodhi's story of a law graduate who failed job interviews until she pictured herself as a teacher welcoming her students. Nomon closes on the line about doing nothing the wise would reprove, with a joke about taking scotch tape back to work.

title: Heart Sutra 7 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra at the Meditation Center of San Miguel de Allende, starting from the sounds in the room: birds, running water, a passing truck, and the mind's quick conclusions about each. After reciting the sutra in English, Nomon describes prajnaparamita, wisdom beyond wisdom, through a Zen master who pours tea until the cup overflows and a hydrogen atom whose nucleus would be a 200-meter block inside a planet-sized space. A five-minute listening practice follows. In the conversation, a participant names the bird as a canyon wren, and Nomon tells of a longtime homeowner for whom the barking of roof dogs means the house is guarded.

title: Heart Sutra 5 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues through the Heart Sutra at a retreat in San Miguel de Allende, taking up the Four Noble Truths, "no attainment," the six paramitas, and the sutra's turn toward a mind without hindrance. Early on, Nomon offers emptiness metaphors: a right hand pulling a splinter from the left without asking for thanks, and three lines on the board that become the letter A, then lose that meaning when one line is removed. Nomon reads Thich Nhat Hanh's "Call Me by My True Names" in Spanish and English, along with the letter about a girl who drowned herself after being raped by pirates, which led to the poem. The session closes with a writing exercise in which each person chooses a word for nirvana and keeps the pen moving.

title: Heart Sutra 6 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the sixth Heart Sutra session in San Miguel de Allende with Portia Nelson's poem "Autobiography in Five Chapters," about walking past the same hole in the sidewalk until finally taking another street. Nomon then turns to prajnaparamita and the final mantra, setting the two commentary schools against each other: one calls the mantra a later addition, the other reads the whole sutra as a mantra. Nomon reads Thich Nhat Hanh on chanting with full attention and parses "gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha" word by word, then listens as two participants offer the translation as past description or present command. Questions about a death-contemplation exercise follow, and Nomon closes with Bruce Cockburn's song about being stuck in a cage.

title: Heart Sutra 3 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra in San Miguel de Allende, opening with a poem about waking one day to find the walls between people forgotten. Nomon then works through svabhava, the assumed separateness of things, using a piece of paper, a car that won't start, and the mariachi music from the neighbors' construction. Each of the five skandhas gets a plain description, with a friend who is always late as the example for thoughts that grow into stories. A blind-spot card exercise shows the mind filling in what the eye cannot see, and the group reads line three on form and emptiness. Questions on whether emptiness is form's opposite lead to Nomon's closing advice to study one's own suffering.

title: Heart Sutra 4 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up lines 5 through 10 of the Heart Sutra during a bilingual retreat in San Miguel de Allende, opening with a science article showing that bacterial cells outnumber human cells in the body ten to one. Nomon offers two definitions of emptiness, "empty of inherent existence" and Suzuki Roshi's answer "not always so," then uses waves and ocean, and the hiker and the mountain, to show form and emptiness arising together. A man who tells Nomon he now loves his daughter no more than a flower or a nail shows what happens when emptiness is held without love. The session ends with a partner exercise in which each person imagines the other at every age, from baby to deathbed.

title: Heart Sutra 1 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra at a retreat in San Miguel de Allende, starting with the text's path from India to China to Mexico. Nomon tells of the monk Xuanzang, who chants the sutra while lost in a desert and carries a pack of sutras home after sixteen years. Then Nomon reads the prologue from the longer version, where Shariputra asks Avalokiteshvara how to practice, and considers how asking a question opens space for both people. The session ends with a paired exercise: one person asks "What do you want to offer the world?" again and again, and the other answers from the heart.

title: Heart Sutra 2 San Miguel de Allende
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra in San Miguel de Allende, opening with a partner exercise in which pairs ask each other what they want to offer the world. Participants report in Spanish: one hears only "love" and doubts she can believe in her own capacity, another finds her eyes watering, and another settles on silence and listening. Nomon then turns to Avalokiteshvara, "the one who hears the cries of the world," pictured with hundreds of arms, at least one hand empty. Nomon explains emptiness as a Sanskrit term close to zero, then has the group look at a sheet of paper and name what is inside it: a tree, human sweat, a town, ambition. Nomon ends on a cliffhanger, promising the answer next week.

title: Metta Sutta, Part 3: The Teachings on Loving Kindness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the Metta Sutta through a commentary story in which 500 monks settle into a Himalayan forest for the rains retreat and are driven out by displaced tree spirits, until the Buddha sends them back with the sutra as their protection. Nomon frames the story with a Home Depot parking lot, where a truck assumed to be blocking handicapped spaces turns out to be in trailer parking, an example of how readily the mind invents conditions. Participants report on practicing contentment, being less busy, and being easy to instruct, and Nomon then studies the Pali of "May all beings be happy," including its two words for happiness and its word for physical safety. Nomon ends back at Home Depot, liking the lumber clerk who helped get the 2x6s down.

title: Metta Sutta, Part 2: The Teachings on Loving Kindness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the first verses of the Metta Sutta, reading Thanissaro Bhikkhu's literal translation from the Pali beside the version the sangha chants. Thanissaro's wording addresses one who wants to break through to peace, the chanted version one who has already found it, and Nomon hears early Buddhism and Mahayana in that difference. Nomon recounts a study in which seminary students told to hurry mostly walked past a person in pain on the way to give a sermon on the Good Samaritan, a case for having few duties. Nomon closes by reading the list of virtues aloud and asking everyone to pick one, such as being easy to correct, and wonder about it for two weeks.

title: Metta Sutta, Part 1: The Teachings on Loving Kindness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Metta Sutta on page 12 of the chant book, starting with a story of Nancy Welch thanking people at noon zazen for supporting her practice. Nomon leads a guided loving-kindness meditation with four people in turn: a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person, and oneself, each offered the wishes "May you be happy, may you be safe, may you be able to meet life's challenges." Students then share what they noticed, including one who finds the practice quieter than regular sitting. Nomon closes with background on Pali, the 500 years of oral transmission, and the Pali Canon, and notes that Norman Fischer added the sutta to San Francisco Zen Center's liturgy in the mid-1990s.

title: On Hongshi
speaker: Shinmon Michael Newton
summary: Shinmon Michael Newton introduces Hongzhi Zhengjue, the Chinese ancestor who compiled the koans of the Shoyoroku (Book of Serenity), as a warm-up for Norman's coming sesshin talks on that collection. Shinmon opens with a stick found on the beach that turns out to be a kotsu, then speaks of gratitude to ancestors, and tells how Hongzhi, handed new straw sandals on arriving at a monastery, asks, "What, did I come here for shoes?" Passages from Taigen Dan Leighton's Cultivating the Empty Field, including "Today is not your first arrival here," lead to dropping off everything and sparkling in response to the world, pictured through a young sangha member's glitter. Shinmon closes by asking listeners to hear the eagles, the heron, the robins, and the swallows, all saying the same thing.

title: No Distractions
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens sesshin by reading a poem by Rosemerry Wahtola Trommer about forgetting to build the wall between us, then takes up Dongshan's answer when a monk asks what Yunyan meant by "just this is it." Nomon recalls sitting with a dying stepmother and asks whether sesshin aims at complete stillness. A ten-part list of states, from contact and expansion to distraction, numbness, and intention, serves as a map, and each state gets the phrase "just this is it." One example is a Tassajara neighbor who wrote plays in his head during a retreat. Nomon closes by asking the room to hold the question "What's my intention?" without an answer.

title: No Aims
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett rehearses the opening teaching for Samish Sesshin by taking up Book of Serenity case 49, where Dongshan is asked what his teacher Yunyan meant by "just this is it," alongside Thich Nhat Hanh's three doors of liberation. Nomon begins with the image of a pilgrim walking a path, then asks what it means when meditation turns out scattered, numb, or painful. Emptiness arrives through Thich Nhat Hanh's wind with no blower, signlessness through a swallow too rich for the word "swallow," and aimlessness through the raft that gets put down. In the Q&A, Nomon places this Mahayana list, the vimoksha mukha, against the early three marks of reality.

title: Sandokai Part 4
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona returns to the Sandokai, "The Merging of Difference and Unity," for a fourth talk, opening with the inscriptions in the wedding bands, "Spirits Shine in the Dark" and "Branching Streams Merge in Light," and with Diane's habit of loading silverware out of alphabetical order. The poem's two incompatible truths, phenomenal and noumenal, are set out through Kant's terms and the plain fact that the fork still has to reach the mouth. Suzuki Roshi's three teachers pointing at the moon and Alan Watts's image of sucking on the finger lead to the line about mountains and rivers blocking the confused, and to Dogen's walking green mountains. Heigaku closes on Suzuki Roshi's translation, "Do not expend your sunbeams and shadows in vain," and on spirits shining in the deepest darkness.

title: Sandokai Part 3
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up the third part of the Sandokai, "Merging of Difference and Unity," reading the chant alongside Shohaku Okumura's translation and commentary in Living by Vow. Shuko works through the lines on light and dark as front and back foot in walking, where light stands for relative, discriminating truth and dark for absolute unity. Shuko recalls Kobun Chino saying that if all the electricity left the world, people would still shine, and tells of making pottery lids that rarely fit, which gives the box and lid image its weight. The arrow points meeting in midair comes from a Chinese story of a master archer and his best student, and Shuko ends on the practice of being both "me and us" within the sangha.

title: Sandokai Part 2
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the second section of the Sandokai, the "Merging of Difference and Unity," drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Shunryu Suzuki's Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness, and Norman Fischer's talks on the poem. Seishu reads the lines on light and dark, the four elements, and roots and leaves, and borrows Okumura's image of the hand, with five fingers that each have a name and a function yet belong to one body. A 3 a.m. cup of tea, whose warmth, steam, smell, and taste felt unusually vivid, serves as a small example of the relative and the absolute together. Seishu closes by describing the habit of pausing once or twice a day to notice who made the park or the road under the bike, and assigns it as the week's homework.

title: Joan Memorial
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett remembers Joan Burnett, Nomon's stepmother, who has just died of stage four lung cancer and pneumonia, and reads Thich Nhat Hanh's Five Remembrances. Nomon tells how two couples in San Diego traded partners in the 1970s, then describes the family standing around Joan's hospital bed as the respiratory therapist Enrico gently removes the breathing tube. Joan's life comes into focus through her social work, her years of supporting Nomon's father's physics career, and the sick shelter cats she nursed until they died. Nomon admits that Joan could seem fussy. The memorial closes with thanks to Joan and the news that Nomon's father, sobbing and laughing, is staying open and looks forward to a larger part in the lives of his children and grandchildren.

title: Sandokai Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Sandokai, Shitou's poem on the merging of difference and unity, after reading Shitou's Song of the Grass Shack aloud. Nomon goes through the opening lines: the northern and southern schools of Chan, Dogen's word that sharp or dull makes no difference, and the warning that grasping at things is delusion while according with sameness is still not enlightenment. The Buddha's instruction to Bahiya, that in the seen there is only the seen, shows how the senses can bind or free. Nomon closes by suggesting a week of pausing and silently asking "What is this?" on each exhalation in zazen.

title: Dai Hi Shin Dharani
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the Daihishin Dharani, also called the Nilakantha Dharani, a long mantra whose sounds passed from Sanskrit through Chinese and Japanese into the chant book. Heigaku reads the Soto Shu translation and connects the blue-necked one to Shiva drinking the world's poison, a match for Avalokiteshvara hearing the cries of the world. A story from Heigaku's work at a hospital follows, in which a small elderly housekeeper untangles a jam of hospital bed and x-ray equipment in an elevator with a few pointed words. Heigaku closes with Yu Daopo, the doughnut seller who awakens when a beggar sings "happiness in the lotus land" and throws her tray to the ground.

title: Heart Sutra Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra a second time, following Avalokiteshvara's answer to Shariputra's question about how to practice deep wisdom, and the claim that seeing the five aggregates as empty relieves suffering. Nomon pairs emptiness with dependent origination, reading the Dalai Lama on the flowers carried past him to a Japanese altar and on a clay pot made from many conditions. Nagarjuna's verses and Mipham's moon reflected in water show how a perceived image differs from what is there. Nomon closes with the boy Huineng overhearing the sutra and saying "I have eyes," then glosses the mantra "gate gate para gate."

title: Heart Sutra Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra, starting with the story of Xuanzang, the seventh-century Chinese monk who snuck out of China after a dream and walked India for 16 years before bringing the sutra back. Nomon reads the longer preface that sets the scene, with Shariputra asking Avalokiteshvara how to practice prajnaparamita, and then goes through the five skandhas one at a time: form, sensations, perception, formations, and consciousness. The lectern becomes an image for emptiness, as oak, then wood, then cells and atoms that are mostly space. Nomon closes on things going sideways and later turning out to be exactly what needed to happen.

title: Communication
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton describes a fall practice period at Tassajara Monastery and takes up the koan in which Dizang tells Fayan, "Not knowing is most intimate." Shuko relays how the Tassajara director Linda Galijan and the practice leader Christina Lehnherr taught that fixed stories about other people limit both sides, and tells of dropping those stories while living among 46 near-strangers and finding new freedom. Christina's examples include fantasizing about others, acting as a self-appointed boss, and asking someone to keep a secret.
