Christina also quotes David Wagoner's line to treat everyone as a powerful stranger to be respected. Shuko closes with the meal chant's opening words, "In trusting ourselves to the Sangha."

title: Zen Marketplace
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva of enlightening activity in the Avatamsaka Sutra, whose ten vows were the theme of a winter 2014 practice period that began with a question to Zoketsu Norman Fischer. Kanho sets those vows against advertising, from an expensive French perfume called Samsara to a Bali comfort shape bought at Fred Meyer, whose hang tag promises to shape your destiny. Alan Watts's web of dewdrops, Katagiri Roshi's poem "Peaceful Life," and Suzuki Roshi's reply to a woman slipping down a ladder lead to Dogen's "Continuous Practice," where no moment's gap separates aspiration from nirvana. Kanho closes by asking the sangha to keep practicing together after the practice period ends.

title: No Teachers of Zen
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Huangbo's line that China has Zen but no teachers of Zen, the subject of an essay written for Buddhadharma magazine. Norman recalls arriving at San Francisco Zen Center in 1970 with no wish to meet Suzuki Roshi, then being ordained in 1980 and startled by the offer of Shiho in 1988. Zen practice works like a machine whose parts all have to turn together, and Norman names faith grounded in lived experience and willingness to share life with others as the capacities a Zen teacher needs. Thich Nhat Hanh answers an early crisis of doubt with "we're all just helping each other." Norman closes with students who return decades later, including a troubled young woman who arrives with her three children, grateful for the practice.

title: Two Sides of Zen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the many voices that arrive during sesshin, starting with Rumi's "The Guest House" and Amy Newell's response poem, which builds a bare Greek temple instead of a welcoming parlor. Nomon notices a habit of arriving late to the zendo, then draws on self-compassion research, including a Berkeley study where students who got a self-compassion message after a failed math test did better on the next one. Nomon sets the Heart Sutra's "nothing to attain" beside the chant to Prajnaparamita and a passage from the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines, holding effort and non-doing together. Nomon closes by reading Dan Nussbaum's "In Meditation You Have Permission."

title: On Zazen
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up zazen at the start of a weekend sitting, after thanking Shuso Chris and her teacher for the Shuso ceremony. Norman retells the Buddha leaving home as told in Ashvaghosha's Buddhacarita, then recalls growing up just after World War II, sensing the grief the adults never mentioned. A study of people over eighty-five who talk mostly about their parents shows how the past never goes away. Zazen is compared to tuning an instrument by feel and careful listening, plucking a string and adjusting again. Norman closes by answering the Tibetan saying that everyone wants happiness: the path to happiness runs right through suffering.

title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells a way-seeking mind story as a snapshot, opening with Dogen's line in Genjokoan that you see only what your eye of practice can reach. Kanho sets a German childhood of domestic violence and abuse beside parents who loved and cared for their children, and asks which story is the self. A Catholic upbringing gives way to Zen books, Thomas Cleary's Mumonkan, and a Bellingham sitting group where the hoped-for koan work turns out to be Soto zazen. Norman Fischer tells Kanho that crying at lay ordination would give others permission to cry, then challenges Kanho to bring sangha work style into a code enforcement job. The story closes on Sri Nisargadatta Maharaj: "Love says I am everything. Wisdom says I am nothing. And between the two my life flows."

title: Enlightening Activity Class 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva of great activity, by asking how practice looks once the sitting stops. After a round of introductions, Kanho describes a default pattern of urgency and narrowing focus, like a hamster on a wheel, and reads Cheri Huber's "A Project for Saving the World." The class offers its own images of transformation, and Kanho adds horse manure turned into compost. Kanho places Samantabhadra as Manjushri's wisdom and Avalokiteshvara's compassion expressed in action, then hands out gathas from the Avatamsaka Sutra and Robert Aitken's The Dragon Who Never Sleeps. The week's assignment is to cut the gathas out, post them around the house, and journal on body sensation and self-talk.

title: Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, the chant to Kanzeon, the one who perceives and responds to suffering. Heigaku opens with a week of illness after a trip to Colorado, when a migraine aura, a stuffed nose and an ear infection leave one thought while picking up manure: "Poor me." From there Heigaku goes through the chant line by line in Robert Aitken's translation, alongside chapter 25 of the Lotus Sutra and the koan of Yunyan and Daowu on the hands and eyes of the Bodhisattva of great compassion. Heigaku closes with Merle Kodo Boyd's words on facing the wall and being okay with who we find there.

title: Bodhisattva Vows 2
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch takes up the last two bodhisattva vows, entering boundless dharma gates and becoming Buddha's unsurpassable way, with help from Reb Anderson's Being Upright and Shohaku Okumura's Realizing the Genjokoan. Yuzan recalls reciting the vows by rote, like the Catholic Masses of childhood, until one evening at a Samish sesshin the words landed and sobbing followed, rooted in perfectionism and self-pity. Reb reads every meeting as a gate, and Okumura describes Dogen's practice as returning to awakening again and again. Yuzan ends with three desert travelers who find a walled paradise, where the third turns back to help others find the way.

title: Bodhisattva Vows 1
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the chant that closes the evening, looking at its opening line on intentions and the first two bodhisattva vows, to save numberless beings and end inexhaustible delusions. Drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Seishu describes vow as a compass toward Buddha and recalls Norman Fischer saying the vows can never be completed, so the work goes on at a sustainable pace. Everyday examples include greeting a homeless person and listening fully to someone whose views differ. Seishu ends with a personal practice: noticing opinions about how things ought to be, finding that things often turn out fine or better, and turning down the volume on those opinions.

title: Rohatsu 2013
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up the sense of being a particular person through Deshan and the old tea lady from The Hidden Lamp, after opening with the nun's advice to Chiyono. Eko describes a photo of a six-year-old son hiding behind a tiny Lego action figure, an image for the identities we assert, even "Zen teacher," that need constant reassurance. Deshan, carrying his Diamond Sutra commentaries in a bag, cannot answer the tea lady and burns them; as an old abbot, he turns back when told the bell hasn't rung. Eko reads the Lotus Sutra passage on Avalokiteshvara, who becomes whatever person is needed, and ends by asking whether we can set the action figure down and dance.

title: Rohatsu 2013
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Chiyono, an illiterate servant in a Zen convent, from the book The Hidden Lamp, as a way to ask how to honor Buddha at Rohatsu sesshin. An elderly nun meets Chiyono's doubts about her lack of skill with warm encouragement, and on a full moon night the bottom of her water bucket gives way and the moon's reflection vanishes. Nomon describes a crowded Trader Joe's in Bellingham, where looking closely at the shoppers shows young people turning old and each person woven into a larger family, and recalls Maud's answer in Harold and Maud: "They're my species!" Nomon urges the retreatants to let the bucket's bottom drop out in its own time, and closes by saying each of them, like Chiyono and the nun, creates Buddha's enlightenment over and over.

title: Three Treasures 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Pali and Sanskrit refuge chants on page two of the chant book, the Tisarana and the Jukai version of the three refuges, and adds the word meanings that Bob's talk the week before left out. Nomon explains that "saranam gacchami" means "I go for refuge," that "dutiyampi" and "tatiyampi" mark the second and third times, and that a Dhammapada verse names the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha as the secure refuge. The body, the ocean of Buddha's way, and harmony in community each get a turn, along with the five hindrances and the difference between little doubt and great doubt. Nomon closes with Subhuti's question in the Prajnaparamita teachings, where bodhisattvas stand in perfect wisdom by seeing there is nowhere to stand.

title: Three Treasures 1
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up the Pali chant of the three refuges, sung at the end of the day in the Soto Zen tradition, along with the tenth precept, not defaming the three treasures. Starting from the astronaut's view of the whole Earth and 23 years of remodeling a farmhouse, Reizan describes refuge as home: all things are Buddha, life unfolds in a moral universe, and everything is connected and supported. A two-week hike around the Three Sisters, whose peaks climbers nickname Faith, Hope, and Charity, gives each word a meaning. Reizan closes with a donor's plan for an Earth meditation room, built around a poster of the whole world, which lacked a practice to sustain it, and names the chant as that practice of going home.

title: Repentance Verse
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Repentance Verse at the bottom of page one of the chant book, beginning by chanting it three times with the sangha. Nomon leads a guided forgiveness meditation borrowed from Jack Kornfield: forgiving someone who harmed you, asking forgiveness of someone you harmed, and forgiving yourself. Then Nomon goes through the verse line by line, from "ancient twisted karma" to "avow," noting that responsibility is not the same as fault. Nomon reads a passage from Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow on starting over from silence, and closes with Thich Nhat Hanh's poem "Call Me By My True Names," which holds the arms merchant and the child in Uganda in one heart.

title: Jukai Retreat
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Jukai ceremony for Jeffrey, Bob, and Georgia, opening with a Rilke poem about receiving flowers from the wind. Nomon explains that the afternoon combines Jukai, the receiving of the 16 bodhisattva precepts, with Zaikei Tokudo, which gives a new name, a rakusu, and lineage documents. Nomon traces the rakusu to eighth-century China and to the rice-field pattern of the Buddha's robe, and describes sewing it stitch by stitch while saying "Namu Kie Butsu," with perfectionism the first thing to fall. Nomon also compares how teachers in Seattle and on Salt Spring Island understand the bond after Jukai, and closes with Mary Oliver's "Wild Geese."

title: Dedication of Merit
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the dedication of merit on page one of the chant book, beginning with the old idea of merit and the story of Punika in The Hidden Lamp, who tells a Brahman that a cold river bath cannot wash away evil acts. Heigaku reads Bodhidharma on karma as cause and effect passing from one state of mind to the next, then Shantideva's verses of offering and dedication. Heigaku goes through the echo line by line, including the ten directions and the Lotus Sutra scene where Buddhas from every direction crowd in around the treasure stupa. The evening closes with the Prajnaparamita in three words: "Love this story."

title: Robe Chant
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the robe chant on page one of the chant book, the first text in a plan to work through the book's chants in turn. After a handshake story from a French train station, Nomon goes through the chant line by line with Shohaku Okumura's commentary, finding that the English translation strays from the three names for the robe: liberating, signless, and field. Nomon asks how sewing and wearing a robe could answer suffering, recalling a hungry man whose food went untouched. Nomon closes with Dogen weeping as monks in a Chinese monastery put their robes on their heads, and with the official Soto Zen translation that Okumura never adopted.

title: Zen Work
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Zen approach to work through stories of Bai Zhang, who goes on a hunger strike when the monks hide his tools, and a passage from a 1997 talk by Norman Fischer. Nomon describes the training of starting and stopping work at the bell, with attention on the effort of the task itself instead of its completion. Nomon tells of the horsetails coming up in the new back garden, where anger and disappointment turn around when Matt asks to come weed on his own. Practical pointers for work leaders follow: assign tasks around the circle, speak only about what is in front of you, and keep working until the clackers sound.

title: Prajna Paramita Retreat 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to a passage from Ayya Khema ("On the spiritual path there's nothing to get, and everything to get rid of") and introduces Edward Conze's translations of the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines. Nomon tells of catching a sulky thought about a sangha friend who skipped the retreat, then turning it into an offer of love instead of a fish hook. Conze's life gets a sketch, from a boy reading Diamond Sutra quotations in Lafcadio Hearn to decades of translating, before three groups read Conze beside a contemporary illustrated selection. A closing Ayya Khema passage names a love that arises without any cause, simply because love is the heart's quality.

title: Prajna Paramita Retreat 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines, starting with passages on Mara as the confusion that arises whenever people study the sutra, and on the Tathagatas who send help. Small groups then report on the Goddess of the Ganges, whose sex change appears in the Conze translation but not the Jamieson, and on the ten bodhisattva precepts and irreversibility, which a participant compares to someone who gets sober and then drinks again. Story hour follows with Sadaprarudita, who searches east for the teaching, tries to sell his body as an offering to Dharmodgata, and is tested by Sakra while Mara blocks the townspeople's hearing. The story stops as the merchant's daughter and her five hundred maidens vow to become Tathagatas.

title: Prajna Paramita Retreat 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a weekend study retreat on the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines by reading Naomi Shehab Nye's poem "Kindness," in which loss and sorrow come before kindness makes sense. Nomon then sends the room into small groups to talk through terms on a flip chart, including wisdom beyond wisdom, vedana, the three marks, the unconditioned, and the six perfections. Back together, Nomon tells the story of the scholar whose teacup overflows at the Zen master's table. The session ends with the sutra's opening scene on Vulture Peak, where Subhuti is asked to teach and Shariputra wonders whose power speaks through him.

title: Prajna Paramita Retreat 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the six paramitas, correcting Nomon's earlier mix-up on the fifth, Jhana, and adding the four later ones, then reads from the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 Lines. A quote from Ayya Khema, "there's nothing to get and everything to get rid of," opens a discussion about giving love without turning it into self-blame. In the sutra, Subhuti tells Shariputra that no Bodhisattva or perfect wisdom can be found, and Sakra hears that a Bodhisattva should stand nowhere, as the Tathagata does. Nomon compares beginning snowboarders sitting on their butts to practicing perfect wisdom, then introduces the one-letter sutra, "Ah," and leads the group downstairs to write the letter.

title: Prajna Paramita Retreat Mantra
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett chants the Prajna Paramita mantra in this recording, which contains only the closing line of the Heart Sutra: "Gate, gate, paragate, parasamgate, bodhi svaha." The transcript is a few words long, and the Sanskrit is rendered phonetically and unevenly. Nomon sings the lines, repeating the syllables of "gate" several times, and no spoken teaching, story, or commentary appears.

title: Touching Earth Sangha
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett and Satya
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett and Satya take up the Mahayana teaching on wisdom with no basis, drawn from the prajna paramita sutras the sangha has been studying. Nomon names ways Zen practice removes the usual footing: ritual roles filled by people who are not experts, private interview without a prepared question, and multi-day retreats where the schedule makes the choices. Nomon then invites Satya, a guest from Touching Earth Sangha, to describe a life with almost no money, no fossil fuels, and no plastic packaging. Satya tells of alms rounds in Japan, a friend named Suelo who must spend any money by midnight, and a bicycle trip through western Washington in search of land. The evening closes with thanks for the sangha's openness.

title: Prajna Paramita 5 Friendship
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Prajna Paramita Sutra in Eight Thousand Lines, reading Edward Conze's translation of the passage on good friends, after sharing Gillian Welch's song "Hard Times" and news of sangha members in the wilderness and at Tassajara's five-day waiting period. Nomon recalls Ananda telling the Buddha that good friendship is half the Buddha way, and the Buddha answering that it is all of it. The six perfections are the good friends, and the sangha brainstorms what friendliness means: trust, kindness, mutuality. Nomon asks what it would be to greet one's own stinginess or resentment as a friend. Asking questions about the sutra turns out to be practicing it.

title: Prajna Paramita 4 Hymn to Prajna Paramita
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads two passages from the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 Lines, the source of the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom the sangha chants, a dialogue between the Buddha and his disciples Shariputra and Subhuti. Nomon goes through the hymn line by line: Prajnaparamita as light for the blind, unstained though she lives in the messy world, and doing nothing about dharmas. Along the way come glossary digressions on the triple world, the six realms, the five eyes, and the Buddha's ten powers. Nomon suggests reading such texts impressionistically and for the feeling, and recalls a colleague who learned only last year that one can make a plan, put in full effort, and let go of the result.

title: Prajna Paramita 3 Emptiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up emptiness (shunyata) in the third of a series on prajnaparamita, opening with Maezumi Roshi's description of wisdom as concrete and real, found in the floor, the lectern, and your own hair. Nomon traces the move from the Three Marks to the later teaching that all dharmas lack svabhava, or intrinsic nature, and uses a blue plastic box lid to show how any label gets slippery. Everyone then holds, studies, and imagines being a small plastic toy, and checks the experience against six wrong views from Mahamudra. Nomon closes with Edward Conze's two-sentence summary of the Prajnaparamita and a week of practice: look at a tree until the labels run out.

title: Prajna Paramita 2 Vedana
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 Lines, beginning with Nomon's own night of waking twice: the first time with an instant "oh no" feeling, the second time, after seeing 5:40 a.m. on the clock, with "oh, perfect." Nomon uses the story to introduce vedana, the early Buddhist feeling tone that sorts experience into good and bad before thought arrives. From there Nomon turns to the Diamond Sutra's single verse comparing conditioned things to a dream, a dewdrop, and lightning. Nomon reads an adapted passage in which Subhuti finds no reality in the word "bodhisattva," and explains negation as a softening of grasping. The evening closes with a quote from Leigh Brassington on ethical conduct and an obituary for Toni Packer.

title: Prajna Paramita 1 Three Marks
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a series on prajna paramita, the "wisdom beyond wisdom" named in the Universal Dedication, the Heart Sutra, and the evening's hymn. Nomon reads Donald Lopez on the two etymologies of paramita, "perfection" and "gone to the other side," and says wisdom of this kind rests on something other than cleverness and comparison. Nomon offers the three marks (anicca, dukkha, anatta) as one basis, with Bodhidharma telling a distressed disciple to find the mind and show it. Nomon then lists the other five paramitas, asking of each what its basis is, and ends on the 8,000-line sutra and the October study weekend.

title: Dongshan Suchness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up suchness, the Buddhist idea of things being just as they are, starting with Mary Oliver's poem "The Summer Day" and its grasshopper. Nomon then tells three stories about the Chinese teacher Dongshan: his teacher Yunyan answering "Just this is it," the verse Dongshan composes after seeing his reflection in a river, and the students asked to go where "there's not an inch of grass for 10,000 miles." Dongshan's answer about cold and heat leads Nomon to a dentist visit without anesthetic, then Dogen's comment on the story. Nomon closes with Ryokan's poem about the moon and flowers inside the brushwood gate.

title: Precepts as Inner Work
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Zen precepts as inner work, closing a series of talks by the sangha's speakers, and draws on Norman's three suggestions for priests: be humble, try to help, see everyone as Buddha. Nomon describes precepts as mirrors held up to speech, generosity, and sexuality, and offers the three pure precepts as "do what increases awareness, refrain from what increases suffering, live for and with all beings." The weather, sunny and rainy at once during sitting, becomes an image of anger holding spaciousness. Nomon reads the story of Master Zuigan calling to himself "Master!" and answering "Yes!", then hands out a short morning practice to recite.

title: Three Treasures
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up the tenth precept, not defaming the three treasures, as the last in a months-long series of precept talks. Reizan reads Reb Anderson's account of how Suzuki Roshi protected the Triple Treasure through upright sitting, wholehearted practice with no gaining idea, and group practice, and recommends books by Aitken, Katagiri, and Thich Nhat Hanh. Defaming the treasures means making them less than they are, as when Buddha becomes someone outside oneself, which Reizan links to Linji's "if you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him." Reizan then reads Dogen's passage on accepting life with respect and gratitude, and names the inner cynicism that narrows things, since noticing it shows where to open to the three treasures.

title: Intoxicants
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the fifth precept, reading Robert Aitken's The Mind of Clover and Reb Anderson's Being Upright alongside three written wordings of the precept, one of them Norman Fischer's poetic version. Seishu looks up "intoxicate" and finds it covers doctrines, beliefs, and possessions as well as drugs and alcohol. Anderson's story of a Minnesota visit, when rain brought the thought "it would be better if the sun was shining," shows how wanting things different drives addictive habits. Seishu draws on Pema Chödrön's words about staying with rawness, tells of quitting drinking and of patience at work as a psychotherapist, and closes with a personal view on prescribed medication through wisdom, compassion, and the middle road.

title: Not Anger
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up the ninth precept, against anger and ill will, and reads Aitken Roshi's advice not to indulge in anger alongside Thich Nhat Hanh's counsel to treat it with respect and tenderness. Shuko sorts anger into righteous anger, ill will, and sudden emotional rage, and studies the last by asking what feeling sits underneath. A carton of milk thrown across the kitchen, and a sprained toe from kicking a door after a divorce lawyer laughed at a word Shuko did not know, lead to shame as the hidden driver. The lojong slogan "drive all blames into one" points to the self being defended, and seeing that lets the air out of the anger. The lawyer becomes a clever man who got a rise out of someone, nothing more.

title: Not Misusing Sex
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the precept on not misusing sex, opening with Allen Ginsberg's poem "Song" and its line "The weight of the world is love." Nomon traces the Buddha's monastic rules, where sexual intercourse is the first offense bringing permanent expulsion, then names the destructive side of sexual power through wartime rape, including the Bosnian rape camps. Nomon turns to Robert Aitken's Mind of Clover, which finds only one koan on sexuality, and reads the old woman who burns the hermitage of a monk "a withered tree on a cold boulder," and Miao Zong's interview with the monk Wanan. Nomon closes by rereading the Ginsberg poem and inviting a conversation the next Wednesday at six.

title: Right Speech Precepts
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch takes up the precepts on not lying, not slandering, and not praising oneself while disparaging others, beginning with her poem "Right Speech, Right Words." Yuzan describes children discovering they can lie, a small fib about her age at a movie ticket counter, and a story from Diane Eshin Rizzetto's Waking Up to What You Do in which Mara chuckles that people turn a little truth into a belief. A friend's gentle question, "Should I really be hearing this?", anchors the discussion of gossip, and Yuzan recalls casting herself as the worst Buddhist in the world. Yuzan closes with three questions to ask before speaking (is it true, is it necessary, is it kind) and a pause in the quiet "dead spot."

title: Precepts Generosity
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up precepts two and eight, not stealing and not being stingy with Dharma and money, working from a handout that sets five versions of each precept side by side. The evening begins with the green funeral of Kevin Bartlett earlier that day, where guests carried the shrouded body and filled the grave themselves. Nomon then tells of feeling greed rise while searching a University of Washington lost-and-found closet for a laptop part, and treats the precepts as tools for noticing such seeds sprouting. A Moth podcast story of nuns lying to protect children in wartime Marseille illustrates the literal, relative, and absolute levels of the precepts, and locking a door becomes a kindness that spares others temptation.

title: The Practice of Generosity
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the first two grave precepts, not killing and not stealing, with help from Robert Aitken's The Mind of Clover and the Heart Sutra. Heigaku stretches the scope of killing to reckless driving, investments, and dismissing a spouse's idea, and tells of watching a store employee dragged out by a man while the crowd froze, until a friend named Tanya knocked on the car window and startled him into letting go. Aitken's image of harmful thoughts as roughnecks at the door, to be greeted like neighbors, leads to apology as a way of honoring life. Heigaku then turns to stealing, including stealing from ourselves, and to giving, from money and time to attention, a smile, and patience with a rude clerk.

title: Precepts Intro
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the series on the ethical precepts of Zen by tracing where the sixteen Bodhisattva precepts came from. Nomon follows them from the Buddha's long monastic Pratimoksha rules, which grew out of particular problems such as monks who visited only the rich or only the poor neighborhoods on the alms round, to the Brahma's Net Sutra in China and Saicho's Tendai school in Japan. Dogen's claim that Rujing gave him the shorter list of sixteen, which historians doubt, leads to Soto Zen giving the precepts to lay people, some of whom first saw their names written on the papers they received. Nomon closes by recommending Robert Aitken's The Mind of Clover and noting that it sells for five dollars.

title: Equanimity
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett finishes the series on the seven factors of awakening with the seventh, equanimity, after correcting a handout that wrongly listed wisdom there. Nomon walks back through mindfulness, investigation, diligence, joy, calm, and concentration, then offers three steps of building a foundation, inclining the mind, and accepting results. The eight worldly concerns, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and dishonor, gain and loss, mark where equanimity gets tested. Nomon tells of Ruth Ozeki likening her book tour to sesshin, and of going home buzzed after a warm word of thanks at a NAMI presentation, then puttering in the kitchen until the feeling settled.

title: 7 Factors 6 Samadhi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up samadhi, the sixth of the seven factors of awakening, through the Gateless Gate koan of Huineng and the two monks arguing over whether the flag or the wind moves. Nomon offers a balance beam in place of a linear list, with mindfulness at the pivot, warm energetic factors on one side and cooler ones on the other, and describes samadhi as a stability of mind that can include movement. Mumon's comment, a passage on samadhi from the Platform Sutra, and Robert Aitken's reflections on polishing wisdom and compassion carry the koan further. Nomon closes with neuroscientist Kelly McGonigal opening a lecture by saying that ending suffering has to be the most important thing.

title: Calm and Permission
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the seven factors of awakening, focusing on calm, which Master Sheng Yan translates as lightness and ease. Nomon sets karmic beings beside vow beings, as in Shohaku Okumura's book, and recalls Paul Warwick's late-life practice of neither accepting nor rejecting, which echoes Tilopa's Song of Mahamudra. Blind spots come through rice spilled during oryoki and the Harvard experiments with the gorilla and the swapped stranger carrying a door. Nomon closes by reading Dan Nussbaum's litany of permissions, from permission to be bored to permission to sleep, and adds an announcement about tomorrow's Shuso Hossen Shiki.

title: Living in Vow 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the verse of the Kesa through Shohaku's chapter in Living by Vow, starting with Dogen weeping in China at the sight of monks chanting it with robes on their heads. Norman sets that feeling beside a recent visit to Google, where a brain-wave headband and a former Marine turned keynote speaker are among the plans to save the world with mindfulness. Norman then moves through the verse line by line, taking in the terraced rice-field pattern of the robe and the Buddha telling a skeptical farmer that faith is his seed. Norman closes with Dongshan's question about the most painful thing in the world, wearing Buddha's robe without having clarified the great matter, and the forty years of living with that pain.

title: Courage and Blind Spots
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up blind spots and courage, starting with the physical blind spot where the optic nerve meets the retina and the brain fills in what is missing. Heigaku then turns to a story from The Hidden Lamp, in which a tea-shop woman offers tea to the monks with miraculous powers and the three monks look at one another. Bodhicitta, emptiness, and Guanyin in the Heart Sutra follow, along with a new puppy that needs calling back again and again. Two disputes, a board member's departure and a colleague's retirement party, show how each side fails to imagine the other's view. Heigaku closes by returning to posture and the question "what is this really?"

title: Living in Vow 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Shohaku Okumura's book Living by Vow, after first reading aloud a Sweeping Zen post on Zen teachers' sexual misconduct and the community collusion that lets it happen. Norman then works through the book's contrast between ordinary people pulled by karma and bodhisattvas who live by vow, quoting Katagiri Roshi on swimming in Buddha nature during zazen. Suzuki Roshi's joke that he was not smart enough to realize he could quit appears, along with Shohaku's reading of the four vows against the four noble truths. Norman ends with the distinction between formal repentance (Jisange) and formless repentance (Risange), describing how shame that comes up in zazen is let go to return to emptiness.

title: Courage 4 Zongchi
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the story of Bodhidharma's four disciples and the nun Zongchi, drawing on Andy Ferguson's Zen's Chinese Heritage, Dogen's "Katto" chapter of the Shobogenzo, and Sallie Tisdale's Women of the Way. Heigaku opens with last week's koan of the old woman and Hakuen, then reads Bodhidharma's "skin, flesh, bones, marrow" exchange, where Dogen insists the four answers are not ranked. Tisdale imagines Zongchi walking with Bodhidharma beside the Great Wall, free of her palace life. Heigaku then explores Akshobhya Buddha through his association with water, and reads Zongchi's line, "felt at the first glance, but not at the second," as a caution against grasping any arising experience.

title: Blindspots 3 Vimalakirti
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the Vimalakirti Sutra and its teaching of non-duality as a way back into the tea lady koan, where decrepit and miraculous are both fully present. Joan Tollifson's description of opposites as inseparable points toward the dissolving of subject and object. Heigaku reads Burton Watson's translation of the scene in which a goddess scatters flowers that fall from the bodhisattvas but stick to Shariputra and the other major disciples, then answers his questions about emancipation by claiming to have seized on nothing. Heigaku closes with Kiku Christina Lerner's image of practice as Vimalakirti's living room, a heart large enough to be a meeting place for all the angels and demons.

title: Courage 3 Heart Sutra
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the Heart Sutra, opening with a koan about sand in the eye that shows pain and feeling remain after clear view. Heigaku asks who practices Prajnaparamita in the story and finds the answer in Avalokiteshvara, the embodiment of compassion, rather than Shakyamuni, Manjushri, or Beyonce. Anna Thorn's account of nuns chanting the sutra at a women's conference in Vietnam leads into a reading of the five skandhas and emptiness as boundlessness, empty of separateness. Heigaku closes by handing out index cards and envelopes for a meditation that asks "What is it?" of each thought and of the space between breaths.

title: Blindspots 2 Bodhicitta
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona returns to the story of Naropa and Vajrayogini, in which Naropa assures her that he knows the inner meaning of the teachings and is deluded, as a way into blind spots. Heigaku tells of a heart-attack patient who revives amid a full code team and asks his nurse, "Where the hell is my glass of water?" Bodhicitta, the simple wish for all beings to be happy, becomes the tool, like a pinprick of light through black paper, with Pema Chödrön's fresh looking and Thanissara's practice of the vow as next steps. Everyone then opens an envelope holding an object from nature and writes a conversation with it on an index card about the happiness of all beings.

title: Courage Week 2 Equanimity
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona returns to the story of Mahapajapati asking the Buddha to ordain women, and the Buddha's reply "don't set your heart on this," then takes up equanimity as a tool for courage. Heigaku describes equanimity as balance in the storm, like a surfer riding waves that keep changing, with room for grief and no squeezing of emotion down inside. The Buddha's story of the two arrows shows how a second arrow of self-made stress can be left unshot. Equanimity appears last among the four Brahma Viharas, and Heigaku closes with Sylvia Boorstein's view that loving-kindness is natural to us, and with the finding that newborns show distress at the distress of others.

title: Courage Week 1 Part 1
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona opens a course built around a new book of stories by and about female Zen teachers, asking how teachings from women and men might differ. Heigaku reviews brain research, then sets out five caveats: the findings are statistical, non-causal, and blurry at the edges of sex and gender, and the surviving record comes through a male-dominated structure, as census data showing 15% women among Buddhist practitioners in 10th-century China suggests. A hiking example contrasts Diane remembering the red-berried bush and the flat-faced rock with Heigaku tracking valleys and washes. The evening turns to samadhi, the sixth factor of awakening, through Christina Feldman's "collected mind," Sharon Salzberg's "a lot of moments in a row," and Huineng on being unattached to characteristics.

title: Courage Week 1 Part 2
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona leads a guided sitting in Week 1 of a class on courage, using a worksheet of arcs drawn like the layers of an onion. With eyes closed, participants write the name of a fear in the top layer, such as fear of talking on the telephone or fear of conflict, greet it with "Hello, fear. I recognize you," and then peel back to what lies beneath. Toward the end, Heigaku offers Sharon Salzberg's teaching that the antidote to fear is kindness or gentle friendship, and invites everyone to treat their fears as friends who were invited over. The session closes with a round of sharing on three topics: gender, courage and fear, and where the class is headed.

title: Blindspots Week 1 Wisdom
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up wisdom, the seventh factor of awakening, as the discernment of what is skillful, and treats karma as plain causation. A story about Heigaku's hat, left on a car roof and later found hanging from a tree branch by neighbors, ends with one neighbor going out at ten at night and finding a stray tomcat locked in her car. It shows how little of the causal web anyone can see. Heigaku separates judgment, which sorts things into good and bad, from discernment, using the walk to the co-op as an example. Readings from Judy Leaf's "The Sharp Sword of Prajna" bring in the double-edged sword and the never-setting sun, and Heigaku closes with Prajnaparamita's four arms and the three aspects of prajna to bring to a koan: academic knowledge, cutting through deception, and direct perception of emptiness.

title: Way Seeking Mind
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona gives a shuso's way seeking mind talk that starts from the present and works backward to see how it came about. Heigaku describes life with wife Diane at Joy Heart Farm, a hospital maintenance crew of seven, and service as Eno. That service includes a Samish ceremony honoring women ancestors, planned entirely by men, that went badly and shaped this practice period's study of the Record of the Hidden Lamp. The telling reaches back to martial arts practice in a marina restroom, a first marriage that ended as mental illness took hold, and Peace Corps years in Uganda, where Heigaku's father died. In a Ugandan market, a merchant answers Heigaku's search for the exit with "we don't have that here."

title: On Practice Period
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Eihei Dogen's writing on the ninety-day practice period as the winter practice period begins next week. Nomon reads Dogen's lines on the lineage of practice periods running from the Buddha through Bodhidharma to America, and on how joining one means seeing and practicing Buddha. Nomon suggests showing up as Buddha from the first clack of the clackers, not to get something, and offers the hub and rim of a wheel for Talus as shuso. Nomon then lays out the schedule, the seven factors of awakening, a memorial for the musician Majnuun, and a request to practice the room from the inside of the body.

title: 7 Factors 5 Joy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up joy, the fifth of the seven factors of awakening, beginning with Buddhaghosa's passage in the Visuddhimagga that separates pīti (joy) from sukha (happiness) through the image of an exhausted traveler in the desert who hears about a pond. Nomon offers three ways to cultivate joy: loosening identification with thinking, engaging fully with relationships and the senses, and working directly with desire by staying in it or doing the opposite of what it demands. Thich Nhat Hanh's Google talk, whose whole message is "you have to be here," and a recent quarrel on vacation serve as examples. Nomon closes by dedicating the evening to Paul Warwick, who has severe leukemia, advises trusting emptiness and preparing for death, and keeps a Trungpa Rinpoche calligraphy on his wall that means courage.

title: Steer the Ship
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up the moment when awareness interrupts a habit pattern such as complaining, hurrying, or self-criticism. Eko pictures the pattern as a giant container ship in a sea of molasses and reads Juan Ramón Jiménez's poem "Oceans," in which a boat strikes something in the depths. Eko calls that tremor a glimpse of true nature and describes Manjushri's sword as one that cuts delusion with love. Two stories follow: Changsha's poem about stepping off the top of a hundred-foot pole, and the spy monk in the Platform Sutra who switches loyalty to Huineng. Eko closes by suggesting that complaining can simply be left alone.

title: Great Effort
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Soko Morinaga's autobiography Novice to Master, which describes life at Daitokuji monastery: rising at 3 a.m., barley gruel, about three hours of sleep, and koan interviews on "original face." Nomon then turns to the Buddha's six years of ascetic practice, when the Buddha crushes his mind with his awareness until a bowl of rice pudding and a childhood memory of sitting peacefully under a tree point another way. Nomon asks whether hard training is needed or was a mistake, admits to having no answer, and invites each person to find steady effort for the Rohatsu retreat. Nomon closes by wondering whether ease and even joy can sit in the middle of strong effort, pain in the knee included.

title: Drumming Interdependence
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells of returning to an informal West African drum class in the basement of Keith's small house after six months away. When Nomon offers ten dollars toward Keith's broken ski bindings, Keith answers, "I could not play the drums without you." That leads to the five hindrances, with doubt as the disco ball above two pairs of dancing partners: desire with aversion, restlessness with dullness. Nomon recalls teaching meditation to University of Washington medical residents, where thin Sunday attendance stirs a self-concern that blocks noticing the five people actually in the room. Kleshas, understood as coverings to study and clear away, take the place of adding more skills. Nomon ends on a second rhythm played fast, with the part half-remembered and the playing simply happening.

title: 7 Factors 4 Energy Cont
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the third of the seven factors of awakening, energy, and questions the image of personal energy as a tank of gas that only drains. Exercise is the example: pushing past tiredness often leaves a person with more energy, not less. Small groups of three or four reflect on the actual days just past, asking what helped or hindered getting to the cushion, with the five hindrances as a guide. Nomon then reads a list of ten early Buddhist suggestions for keeping energy up, including remembering the noble ones, avoiding lazy people, and spending time with energetic friends, plus a shorter list of four for mindfulness. Nomon closes with Czesław Milosz's "A Poem for the End of the Century," read twice.

title: 7 Factors 3 Energy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up energy, the third factor of awakening (virya), after a check-in on how the first two factors and the five hindrances have shown up in people's weeks. Stories of strong aversion passing overnight and of dullness arriving after a robbery lead into exercise, where showing up often brings more energy, a fact that breaks the gas-tank model. Nomon sets Wumen's red-hot iron ball in the throat from the Gateless Gate beside a Dzogchen teaching to forget effort, and adds Norman's sesshin instruction to stop working on one's faults. Nomon's own avoided errand to a body shop becomes an energy practice, and the week's assignment is to investigate the causes and conditions behind daily home sitting.

title: 7 Factors 2 Discernment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up discernment, the second of the Seven Factors of Awakening, and its Sanskrit name dharmavichaya, "analysis of experience." Nomon links it to mindfulness and to later teachers' translation of the factor as interest, illustrated by James Baraz's story of a college friend who earned top grades by getting curious about why professors loved their subjects. Nomon leads a standing mindful check-in on body, emotion, and thinking, then reads the Buddha's two-arrows and poisoned-arrow passages, where a wounded man refuses a surgeon until he learns the archer's clan and the bowstring's material. Nomon's homework is to notice which of the five hindrances is strongest and meet it with mindfulness.

title: 7 Factors 1 Intro
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces a series on the Seven Factors of Awakening, taught in the weeks before Rohatsu, and begins with mindfulness as the center of the list. Nomon sets the factors beside the 52 mental factors of the Abhidharma, then reads them as both a stepwise progression and a balance with mindfulness as the fulcrum. Bhikkhu Bodhi's reading of the Satipatthana Sutta's praise of mindfulness as that which leads forward without turning back leads into the four frames of reference: body, sensations and reactions, thinking and emotion, and lists such as the five hindrances. The week's practice is to notice which hindrance is most present and feel the body in that moment.

title: Dale Wright Challenges of Zen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reports on Florence Caplow's Shuso ceremony at the Bay Area Everyday Zen Sangha, where Florence answers Nomon's question "Is this enough?" with "Yes. Right now, it is." Nomon then returns to Professor Dale Wright's address to Soto Zen priests in Oregon and lists the challenges Wright named: Zen's distance from politics and the environment, its dismissal of intellect, its tough-guy streak, and its limited attention to suffering. Nomon closes with poems by Hafiz and Rumi, and a discussion follows about whether practice itself is a form of service. Nomon answers with the sandwich question: can a small sangha also make sandwiches for the homeless?

title: Three Noble Truths
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Buddha's Four Noble Truths and re-translates each as a verb: suffering is to be known, its cause is to be comprehended or examined, its ending is to be practiced, and the path is to be lived. A flip chart opens the evening with the Dalai Lama's line "If you want to be happy, practice compassion," which Nomon first used on a room of therapists. Nomon then turns to the Heart Sutra chanted earlier, where "nothing to attain" sits beside the work of knowing and practicing, and to Prajnaparamita, who does not turn away from anything. The evening closes on a question: when everything goes wrong and life is at its wit's end, will these phrases come to mind?

title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Retreat 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the Four Ennobling Truths and the Three Marks of impermanence, not-self, and dukkha, then reads Sheng Yen's chapter on the five roots and five powers from Things Pertaining to Bodhi. Nomon illustrates not-self with a story from student teaching a sixth grade class, where a gruff mentor's advice to get new clothes turns out to point at trusting the activity itself, with no solid identity to stand on. Sheng Yen's account of two flooded Taiwanese towns, one that evacuated and one that did not, anchors the discussion of faith. Writing prompts and small-group listening about faith and diligence follow, and Nomon ends by singing Bob Dylan's "You Ain't Goin' Nowhere."

title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Retreat 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Bodhi Pakshika Dharma, a set of Buddhist lists of practices for being free in the middle of whatever is happening, and gives a quick tour of the whole chart. Nomon explains concentration through a darkened theater, where awareness is a spotlight and mindfulness is remembering that hands rest on the controls. Next comes the Buddha's formula "When this is, that is," set beside Jain, Brahmin, and caste-based views of causality. Nomon then reads from Thanissaro Bhikkhu's The Wings of Awakening about six animals tied together and dragged around until they are tethered to a post, which stands for mindfulness of the body. The Q&A ends with a participant asking how to be of help to Jim, a bitter, ranting brother-in-law.

title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Retreat 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with Mary Oliver's poem about death, "When Death Comes," then takes up the Four Foundations of Mindfulness as four frames of reference, using a retreat break that seemed too long and turned out to be perfect. Nomon reads Thanissaro Bhikkhu on skillful effort and tells the story of Sona, whose strained persistence the Buddha compares to a vina strung too tight or too loose. Partner conversations on magical thinking and on the four proper exertions follow. Nomon then describes the four bases of freedom, with Sheng Yen's sign of a warm and soft mind, and leads a paired exercise in which one partner keeps asking, "Do you want to be peaceful and happy?"

title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Retreat 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the weekend retreat by reading a passage from Florence Caplow's research on the great women of the Zen lineage, which says the dharma cannot arise without the mountains, magpies, and flowing water. Nomon then tells of a shower knob that won't turn off, with its screwdrivers, a small crowbar, failing eyesight, and rising agitation, until a hidden cap over a screw comes to mind. The story becomes a way to retranslate the three poisons as desire and aversion, annoyance, and ignorance, and to describe freedom in the middle of illness, aging, and death. Nomon closes by reading the Buddha's last exhortation to monks and nuns, whose stated purpose reaches past the students to compassion for the whole world.

title: The Strengths of Zen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reports on the Soto Zen Buddhist Association meeting at Great Vow Zen Monastery in Clatskanie, Oregon, and takes up the strengths of Soto Zen in America as the scholar Dale Wright lays them out. Nomon describes the ceremony welcoming twenty-seven newer priests among ninety ordained people, then moves through Dale's list: serious practice, groundedness, no required beliefs, friendliness with science, freedom, playfulness, going beyond the master, the arts, and the literary tradition. Nomon adds a twelfth strength, that Zen trains people to stay with suffering without rushing to fix it. Nomon closes with greetings from Taigen Leighton, who still remembers salmon running wall-to-wall in Whatcom Creek.

title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma 2 Foundations of Mindfulness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a passage from the Parinirvana Sutra in which the dying Buddha returns to the seven lists of teachings later called the Bodhi Pakshika Dharma, 37 items in all. Nomon takes up the first list, the four foundations of mindfulness from the Satipatthana Sutta, and describes mindfulness as remembering, using the image of a theater spotlight that the person sitting on the stool can move, narrow, or widen. Mindfulness of the body comes first, including the desire, anger, and confusion that show up in how people regard their own bodies. A short look at the four proper exertions follows, and Nomon closes with news of six people who completed a silent hundred-mile hike around Mount Rainier.

title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Practice 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett recites the Bodhi Paksika Dharma, the 37 Aids to Awakening, as a chanted practice. The recitation opens by venerating the three treasures and vowing to practice the aids with whole hearts, bodies, and minds, day and night. Nomon then names each group in turn: the four foundations of mindfulness (body, sensations and reactions, thoughts and emotions), the four proper exertions, the four bases of freedom, the five wholesome roots, the five strengths, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble path of right action, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samadhi. It closes with a dedication of the benefit to all beings in all directions and a wish to enter the fullness of Buddha's way.

title: On Duality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Bodhipakshika Dharma, a list of seven lists that makes up thirty-seven aids to awakening, and asks how to hold steps to take alongside a wholeness already present. Nomon reads the opening of Dogen's Fukanzazengi with its "and yet," then Diana Winston's Wide Awake, where Ajahn Buddhadasa's "little nirvana" and Hakuin's line on awakening to one's own nature sit beside the slow weeding of greed, hatred, and delusion. Nomon also pictures the Buddha as a doctor and describes how language divides the world into this or that. The evening closes with standing chants and prostrations that recite the thirty-seven aids.

title: Letting in the Darkness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett remembers Catherine Tanis, a senior woman teacher who died the morning after the Samish sesshin, and reads Jane Hirshfield's poem "Rebus," sent in her memory. Nomon recalls watching Catherine at a 1987 San Francisco sesshin and calls each person a time capsule, as with Dorothy Hoskins, who loves the altar flowers because her Oklahoma farm family could not afford any. The poem's bitter honey leads to the darkness everyone carries, including a hurtful remark Nomon made late in sesshin, and to Catherine's newsletter piece on the Ryoanji garden, where one of fifteen rocks is always hidden. Nomon closes by playing a video of the Baika song "Namu Honshi Shaka Nyorai," sung at Rinsoin temple in Japan.

title: Buddhas Zen Brain
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch takes up what happens in the brain during meditation, drawing on the book Buddha's Brain, interviews with the Dalai Lama, and Dogen's instruction in Fukanzazengi to think of not thinking. Yuzan describes the sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response and the Buddha's two darts, where unavoidable pain is the first dart and the reaction added on top, like anger at a stubbed toe, is the second. Sitting practice lets thoughts pass, so the parasympathetic system can become the brain's default. In the questions, Yuzan tells of a twelve-year-old client who got the magic cards he wanted and immediately wanted something else, and of the grinding self-hate that meditation let go of around juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Nothing Holy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett begins a series on Zen's family stories with Case 1 of The Blue Cliff Record, Bodhidharma's meeting with Emperor Wu of Liang and his answer "Empty, without holiness." Nomon traces the word "holy" back to an Old English root meaning whole, and wonders whether "I don't know" is a humble, honest reply rather than a show of strength. Master Qi's praise of Bodhidharma as Avalokiteshvara joins wisdom with compassion. Nomon tells of Bodhidharma's nine years facing the wall, his eyelids thrown from the cave and becoming tea plants, and Huike cutting off an arm in the snow. A "don't know" breath practice, a review of breath-counting, and David Budbill's poem "Bugs in a Bowl" follow.

title: Zhaozhou's Bridge
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Zhaozhou's Bridge, a koan from the Blue Cliff Record, which Nomon first gave as a short talk at a Zen temple in Worcester, Massachusetts. A monk arrives expecting a famous stone bridge and sees only a log bridge, and Zhaozhou answers, "You just see the log bridge," without correcting him. Nomon pictures a visitor someday finding only a dandelion at Red Cedar, then follows the stone bridge and log bridge through feeling hurt, being judged, judging institutions, and measuring ourselves. A student's question about what happens when both bridges fail gets the reply, "Is there really a river that we need to get across?"

title: Buddhas Birthday
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the legend of baby Buddha's birth for the Buddha's birthday celebration: Queen Maya's dream of a white elephant, the birth in Lumbini Grove, and the infant's seven steps. Nomon offers an image of every moment as a birth, with each of us a midwife, and describes a grumpy, tired day when resisting a moment made it feel like a breach birth, while letting it be born let it pass. Birth-and-death, the great matter in Zen, belongs together, so Nomon reads Japanese Jisei death poems, turns the cherry-blossom poem into a wish to be born, and shares Mary Oliver's lines about not wanting to end up "simply having visited this world." A short discussion leads into the ceremony of bathing the baby Buddha under the flowered pagoda.

title: Women in Buddhism
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a chapter from Susan Murcott's First Buddhist Woman about Maha Prajapati, who asks three times to ordain women, is refused, and then walks 150 miles barefoot with other women to Vaishali. Nomon then turns to Dogen's fascicle "Raihai Tokuzui" and the nun Miao Xin, a guest house director who overhears seventeen monks misreading the wind and the banner and wakes them with a few words. Along the way come the eight special rules, Ananda's change of question to the Buddha, and the yearly ceremony in which Japanese nuns thank Ananda. In discussion, Nomon wonders whether the Buddha was skillful or bound by his time, and ends on Eiheiji, where, as far as Nomon knows, no such ceremony is held.

title: Lotus Sutra Intro
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton introduces the Lotus Sutra study group, which meets eight times into June, and gives a background lecture using Gene Reeves's translation. Shuko sketches the sutra's place in Mahayana development, Indian cosmology, and its claims: one vehicle, enlightenment open to all including women, and a Buddha present in every world. Shuko then reads the sutra's description of the Buddha's body, sixteen feet tall and shining purple gold, and the group wonders why it is so extravagant. Shuko suggests not getting hung up on it and assigns pages 82 and 85-102 on skillful means for next week.

title: Practical Work with the Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads essays from David Rynick's book This Truth Never Fails, opening with "First Day Back," where an anxious morning mind is a young dog sniffing every bush and a memory of a kayak on Maine's Medomak River brings comfort. Nomon adds five suggestions from a Seattle mindfulness class for young doctors: be friendly with the crazy mind, attend to posture, slow down a little, see thoughts as thoughts, and practice formally each day. More essays follow, including "Reluctant Adventurer" and an Ango breakdown that ends with asking others for help. After conversations in pairs, the room turns to doctors dreading the pager on call, and one who left residency over stubborn bodily tension.

title: Impermanence
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads an essay written for the Shambhala Sun on impermanence, beginning with the death scene in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, where the Buddha's last words are "all conditioned things have the nature of vanishing." Norman tells of a dream in which an ailing mother-in-law, nearly ninety, and Norman squeeze past each other in a Paris cafe doorway and trade sides, then argues that vanishing happens right now rather than later. Dogen's line "impermanence itself is Buddha nature" leads Norman to approve both the weeping monks and the calm monks in the sutra, since every grief Norman has known has deepened love. The essay closes on the Buddha's message that everything vanishes and practice continues.

title: Heart of the Matter 5
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Donna Jo Napoli's children's retelling of the Greek creation myth, in which Gaia pulls sea, earth, and sky out of chaos, and offers it as a picture of how each person builds a myth of the self. Nomon then reads from the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines, where Subhuti tells the Buddha he can find no bodhisattva and no perfect wisdom, and Shariputra asks about the thought that is no thought. Along the way, Nomon recalls chanting the Heart Sutra in a converted Santa Cruz garage around 1985, and reports Kate McCandless's discovery that sesshin means "touch the mind," an open hand, where Nomon had first been taught "gather the mind." The closing example is a painful knee that the mind predicts will worsen for 72 hours.

title: Heart of the Matter 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens with the sperm whale, a deep-diving creature whose oil-filled head helped power the Industrial Revolution and lets it "see" a squid a mile away by sound, then turns to the Heart Sutra and the Prajnaparamita literature behind it. Nomon reads from the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines, where Subhuti and Shariputra argue over a thought that is no thought. The story of translator Edward Conze, who learned Sanskrit to reach the original text, and the Tibetan teacher who delayed the medicine Buddha mantra with his life story, show how teachings pass from person to person. Nomon then takes up the line "all dharmas are marked by emptiness," the three marks of impermanence, not-self and dukkha, and closes with Freeman Dyson's advice and the Japanese chant.

title: Heart of the Matter 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Dalai Lama's Essence of the Heart Sutra and the sutra's line "form does not differ from emptiness," then rewrites it with other words, such as "thought itself is boundless." Nomon links the Dalai Lama's account of grasping and the three poisons to the skandhas, especially Vedanā, which Nomon renders as "leanings." A participant, Nancy, tells a dream about a stranger who rides the same kind of bike, and traces the Chinese character nen, affinity, through the Kannon chant. Rumi's "The Guest House" and section 51 of Whitman's "Song of Myself" widen the picture. Nomon ends with two home practices: chanting the mantra "gate gate" aloud, and asking how a particular trouble could be Buddha.

title: Extraordinary in the Ordinary
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the ordinary and the extraordinary, starting from a William Carlos Williams poem ("So much depends upon a red wheeled barrow") painted on a mural along High Street in Bellingham. Nomon reads from the poet's biography as a family doctor who wrote on prescription pads between patients, then turns to Blue Cliff Record case 52, in which a monk finds only a log bridge at Zhaozhou's place and Zhaozhou answers that the stone bridge lets donkeys and horses cross. Two more Zhaozhou stories follow: the dust that is "another bit," and "wash your bowl." Nomon closes with Norman's remark that Suzuki Roshi's supernatural power was seeing the extraordinary in the ordinary, then opens a discussion that gathers gratitude, curiosity, and full engagement.

title: Heart of the Matter 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra in the second week of the six-week seminar The Heart of the Matter, opening with housekeeping about practice period partners and upcoming events. Nomon introduces Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion with a thousand arms, and Manjushri, who holds a sword and a flower, then reads the sutra's first line. Nomon walks through the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, thoughts, consciousness), explaining emptiness with a wooden lectern and a Harvard study in which students failed to notice the person asking directions had been swapped. Nomon closes by singing a Tracy Chapman love song.

title: Heart of the Matter 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a six-week practice period seminar on the Heart Sutra by reading it aloud slowly, then asks what people think they know about wisdom and knowledge, sending the room into groups of three for a turn-taking conversation. Nomon tells the story of the pilgrim Xuanzang, who crossed the Gobi Desert chanting the sutra against evil spirits and returned to China after eighteen years. Nomon then breaks prajnaparamita into its Sanskrit parts, "deeply knowing" and "going beyond," and chants the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom. Four home practices follow, and Nomon closes with the "emptiness poem number one."

title: The Sun Wont Come Out
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the first talk of the Heart Sutra practice period with two Derek Walcott poems, "So Much Rain" and "Love After Love," and reads the longer Sanskrit version of the Heart Sutra, whose frame story has Avalokiteshvara answering Shariputra's question about how to practice. Nomon explains prajnaparamita through Thich Nhat Hanh's image of understanding as flowing water and Thanissaro Bhikkhu's "tactical wisdom," then offers "boundlessness" as another way to hear emptiness. Sesshin softens the edges of the self by having everyone sit, walk, and eat in the same way. The poem "Love After Love" closes with an invitation to a joyful reunion with oneself.

title: Being Seen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up an email newsletter on the responding gate and the work of letting ourselves be seen, as preparation for small group discussion. Nomon describes the persona we hold between ourselves and the world as a "human shield," and asks listeners to notice how the jaw, cheeks, and expression of the face are held. The Buddha's three kinds of suffering (dukkha-dukkha, suffering from change, and suffering from how the mind understands existence) lead to a sense of separation from others and from ourselves. Katagiri Roshi's line about settling the self on the self belongs here. Nomon closes by naming awareness and attention as the reliable tools for working with hiding.

title: Rohatsu Two Stories
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley sets two stories side by side during Rohatsu sesshin: the Buddha's enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and Wuzu's account of a puppet show. Eko tells how Mara attacks with fear, desire, and unworthiness, and how the Buddha touches the earth so that the arrows turn to flowers. Then Eko reads Wuzu's tale of calling out to the puppeteer behind the blue curtain and hearing, "Just watch the show. Why ask for names?" Eko follows the shifts from delight to the urge to explain to ideas overturned, and offers a bowl of oatmeal as a puppet show to stay loyal to.

title: Rohatsu Praise and Blame
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Suzuki Roshi's teachings and the Pali Canon story of the Buddha leaving his first teacher, Alara Kalama. Nomon asks what Buddha and awakening are, then has the sitters check in with body, emotions, and thinking. Suzuki Roshi's pigs, which won't eat while watched, and his "Letters from Emptiness" chapter turn awakening into a matter of listening. When Alara Kalama praises the young Buddha as an equal and invites him to co-lead, Nomon asks how anyone works with praise and blame in sesshin. Nomon ends with the cheap concrete garden Buddha on the altar, which has grown radiant over the years just by sitting patiently.

title: Buddhism and the Brain
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up neuroscience as a way into the Buddhist teaching of no self, drawing on Iain McGilchrist's The Master and His Emissary and Antonio Damasio's Self Comes to Mind. Shuko describes the left hemisphere as a certainty-seeking tyrant that has undercut years of Zen insight, while the right hemisphere knows connection and can live with uncertainty. Damasio's idea that the self is a process, not a thing, meets the Buddhist teaching of change and contingency, with the slow supermarket line as an everyday example of how clinging to preferences causes suffering. Shuko turns to Dogen's backward step as a way to pause in right-brain awareness, and reports that easing off the left brain's hold has brought some liberation.

title: Genjokoan 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a weekend study retreat on Dogen's essay Genjokoan, admitting nerves about leading what was Norman Fischer's retreat before. Nomon reads passages on seeing and hearing with body and mind, the ocean that only looks circular from a small boat, and the self that carries itself forward versus myriad things that illuminate the self. Viktor Frankl's account of a fellow prisoner who dreams of liberation on March 30th and dies on March 31st illustrates how thinking shapes a world. Nomon then traces Dogen's life of many deaths, from his mother's funeral incense to the poem about evening rain in the deep grass of Fukakusa.

title: Fukanzazengi Part 6
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett completes a series of talks on Dogen's Fukanzazengi, reading the final section line by line, from "intelligence or lack of it does not matter" to the blind men and the elephant and the true dragon. Nomon tells of seeing the apple tree outside the shop as beautiful one week and as a chore the next, an example of how much the mind interprets what the senses bring. Nomon then describes Carl Bielefeldt's finding that the familiar text is a late revision of a version from 1233, itself borrowed from a Chinese manual by Changlu Zongze. That earlier version tells the sitter to notice each thought until it vanishes, advice Dogen later replaced with an open instruction to let go of thinking.

title: Practice Beyond Preferences
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens an all-day sitting with David Whyte's poem beginning "Enough" and closes with a story of the Chinese master Zhaozhou and a persistent monk. Between them, Nomon names the three questions the mind keeps asking (what happens next, what just happened, how am I doing) and offers breath counting as a way back to "what is this?" Nomon recalls counting down 84 meditation periods on a first seven-day retreat, a strategy that lands hard on a bad sit. When Zhaozhou answers "I don't know" and the monk presses, the reply is "Just to ask is enough."

title: Fukanzazengi Part 5
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to Dogen's Fukanzazengi for a fifth session, reading from the bottom of page 16 to the top of page 18, where Dogen gives exact instructions for sitting and then says very little about how to meditate. Nomon brings in Taigen Dan Leighton's description of zazen as an enactment ritual, and describes how a still body retrains reactivity even while the mind races. Nomon reads Dogen's lines on practice-realization, the dragon gaining water, the shouts and whisks of Zen stories, and the claim that dull and sharp-witted students stand equal. The evening ends with paired listening on one question: how do I divide myself?

title: Taking A Step
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett describes the Dharma transmission ceremony completed with Nomon's teacher Norman Fischer, drawing on writings from Dogen about honoring the Buddha ancestors. Nomon tells of arriving at Norman's seaside home, of Norman's wife Kathy joining the ceremonies after a fellow diver died of a heart attack on her scuba trip, and of rising at 4:30 to chant the ancestors' names with prostrations. Nomon recalls copying the lineage documents in ink on silk, wanting praise for Nomon's calligraphy, then folding the page away and joining the conversation. Nomon reads Dogen's passage on the document of heritage and reads it as an invitation open to everyone, then closes with plans for the community and a request that people take their own next step.

title: Fukanzazengi Part 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the fourth part of Eihei Dogen's Fukanzazengi, beginning with its detailed instructions for lotus posture, hands, and spine, and offering a gravity check for anyone leaning forward. Nomon tells the story of Argya Rinpoche, a Tibetan lama born to a nomadic family in 1950, who kept studying with his tutors while hauling manure on a Great Leap Forward farm, as a case that conditions for practice are always right. Nomon then sets the line "think of not thinking" beside a more literal rendering: "When a thought arises, bring it into spacious awareness... The self will naturally become whole." Nomon closes with Juan Ramón Jiménez's poem "I am not I."

title: Your Best Season
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley reads case 19 of the Mumonkan, "Ordinary mind is the way," in Robert Aitken's translation, along with Wumen's verse that ends "that is your best season." Seishu describes how the koan study group has led to a new appreciation of the poems that accompany the cases, and how idle concerns narrow the world. A cold, rainy bike ride turns around when Seishu remembers a friend crippled by illness who would gladly be riding. A walk through the cemetery where Seishu's father is buried brings reflections on the equanimity of Seishu's father and on life's seasons. Seishu closes with Suzuki Roshi's saying "Life is its own magic."

title: Fukanzazengi Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues the series on Dogen's Fukanzazengi, opening with a talk by Michael Wenger of San Francisco Zen Center on transformation as small change, courage, and trust. Nomon recaps the first two parts, then reads the "backward step" passage and the line "for sanzen, a quiet room is suitable." Nomon traces sanzen to a character meaning "coming to Zen" and shows the character for sitting, which pictures sitting bones on the earth. Nomon relates "Eat and drink moderately" to the five strengths of practice and to staying up too late installing a new computer. The evening ends with paired speaking and listening on how each person sets up their life for practice.

title: Fukanzazengi Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the picture book Moody Cow Meditates, in which a grandfather settles a jar of sparkles to quiet a boy's angry day, and then returns to the opening of Dogen's Fukanzazengi. Nomon dwells on the turn of "and yet," where a slight discrepancy, a hundredth of a fine hair, lets liking and disliking arise. Nomon sets Norman Fischer's objection to the phrase "pride of understanding" beside the Tanahashi and Levitt translation, which sends practice back to the body. Nomon tells of Master Ruiyan calling "Master!" to himself and answering "Yes?" each day, then closes with the backward step that turns the light inward.

title: Fukanzazengi Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the opening of Dogen's Fukanzazengi (chant book, page 13), written in 1227 when Dogen was 27, after tracing a Gary Snyder story about not understanding a word of his Kyoto teacher's rain-soaked talks until decades later. The opening line, "The way is basically perfect and all pervading," leads Nomon to the story of Huineng the illiterate woodcutter and head monk Shenxiu, whose poems about a polished mirror and a mirror with no dust frame the text's question of why practice is needed at all. Nomon also offers "circulates" as a reading of the character translated as "perfect." Elizabeth answers that dust has nowhere to land if the mirror is upright, and the evening closes on chanting a text for years until one word breaks open.

title: Dogens Intimate Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up three passages from Dogen's Genjokoan, the best-known essay in the Shobogenzo, after reporting on leading a full moon ceremony in Spanish for a Zen group in Jalapa, Mexico. The passages on carrying the self forward, forgetting the self, and seeking Dharma from afar speak to the sense of separation, which Nomon pictures as a wave that cannot say where the ocean begins. Harold and Maud and Rumi's poem "Bird Wings" accompany the reading. In the discussion, a participant describes watching the hills on the commute, and Nomon recalls the Harvard study where a person giving directions fails to notice the asker swapped out behind a carried door.

title: Dogens Intimate Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up passages from Dogen's "Genjokoan," read in the Peter Levitt and Kazuaki Tanahashi translation, to ask about the sense of separation that brings people to practice.
