Nomon opens with a scene from the film Harold and Maud, where Maud calls people "my species," then offers the image of a wave that forgets it is the ocean. Along the way come Dogen's phrase "dropping away body and mind," the communal life of cleaning and eating at Eiheiji, and Thanissaro Bhikkhu's reminder of the Buddha's shock at sickness, age, and death. Nomon closes with Rumi's poem "Birdwings," in which a hand opens and closes like a pair of wings.

title: Hossenshiki Ceremony
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton answers questions as Shuso in a Hossenshiki ceremony that opens with the case of Zhaozhou asking Nanquan "What is the way?" and Nanquan replying "Everyday mind." Members of the sangha ask about loneliness, a mother's pain, despair at the world, and the monkey hanging from Hakuin's branch, and Shuko replies in a word or a few: "Enjoy it," "Nothing," "Look in the mirror." When one questioner mixes up renunciation with resignation, Shuko corrects the word and adds that discernment matters. Visiting Shusos and friends offer congratulations, and several say this is a beginning. Shuko dedicates the ceremony to deceased parents, a sister, two sons, and four grandchildren, then asks everyone to wash out their ears in the Dharma's harmonious silence.

title: Renunciation
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up renunciation, a word Shuko has puzzled over since Reb Anderson's retreat in the 1990s, and works through it using Norman Fischer's Sailing Home, Suzuki Roshi, and the Latin root of the word. Shuko sets it beside Fra Angelico's Annunciation in Florence and Shuko's own joy at learning of being pregnant. Shuko concludes that renunciation means giving up the belief in a separate self, and tells of a second cat who learns to beat the first into her lap each morning, as a picture of catching the mind quickly. Shuko returns to zazen mind and to Dogen's phrase "letting go of self-centered life," found in arriving on time, entering the zendo quietly, and volunteering for a job.

title: On Gender
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the story of Miaozong and the head monk Wanan at Dahui's monastery, a case about gender that follows news of sexual misconduct by two male Zen teachers. Miaozong lies naked on a bed for a "Dharma interview," tells Wanan that all the Buddhas come from this place, and answers his request to enter with "Horses cross, asses cannot cross," a line Norman connects to Zhaozhou's stone bridge. Norman reads her body as the Tathagatagarbha, the womb of all Buddhas, and her reply as the power of consent. Norman then turns to the small, unintended hurts between men and women in the sangha, and closes with Chris Fortin's words on "ferocious vulnerability" after she enacted the koan in a body stocking.

title: Opening and Closing
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the story Dogen returned to again and again, in which Nanyue arrives at Huineng's monastery and is asked, "What is it that thus comes?" Nomon follows Nanyue through eight years of living with that question, then brings in Rumi's poem "Bird Wings" on the hand opening and closing, Brené Brown's research on vulnerability and gratitude, and a visit to a campus meditation club where a student asks how Zen differs from Theravada. Remembrances of departed sangha members include Mark Livingston, who quietly built the concrete ramp at the Dharma Hall. Nomon closes with the twelve hundred new planets found by the Kepler telescope, and the question once more.

title: Resting in the Six Senses
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Zen story of Guishan, Yangshan, and Xiangyan sharing miracles, along with the Zen teaching that a Buddha's six miraculous powers are the six senses, thinking and feeling included. Norman begins with remembrances of four Zen Center priests who died in recent months, among them Jerome Peterson, who read the Avatamsaka Sutra weekly for 18 years and then started over on page one. Guishan turning to the wall, Yangshan bringing a basin of water, and Xiangyan making a bowl of tea become miracles of calling and responding. Norman then turns to Dongshan leaving when Yunyan asks what miracles are, and closes with the sorcerer who has five powers and answers "Yes" when the Buddha calls to him.

title: Zen and Creativity Class 2 Part 1
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton leads a writing session in which the class composes short descriptive poems in the manner of haiku, loosening the five-seven-five form and the rhyme. Shuko describes the qualities of haiku, such as image words over abstract ones and a quick turn after the first two lines, and reads the poem The Laws of Japanese Painting. Shuko recalls listening to Japanese literature on the radio in Japan without understanding the words, then reads poems by Basho and Issa, including the old pond and the frog. Shuko plays shakuhachi music and sets out photographs, paintings, and objects in the room to prompt the writing.

title: Zen and Creativity Class 2 Part 2
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton looks at how haiku are put together, reading through a list of poems by Basho and Issa, including the wind from Mount Fuji painted on a fan, a sleeping rider with the far moon in a continuing dream, and a line about steam from roasting tea. Shuko points out that the third line can seem unrelated or arrive as an unexpected sound, and that a poem can run two, three, or four lines. The group wonders whether the originals keep the 5-7-5 syllable count and why Issa's translations read lighter and more efficient than Basho's. Shuko then suggests choosing an ordinary object such as a chair or pillow and looking at it closely, and describes trying to see where a shadow would fall when painting.

title: Zen and Creativity Class 2 Part 3
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton leads a haiku-writing session in the Zen and Creativity class, with participants working from a table of photographs, including an aspen grove, a Kansas prairie, and Castle Rock. Members read their poems aloud, such as "Pinned by the sun, timeless hours, no place better than here" and "Can you see a warm breeze? Can you hear the blue sky?" Shuko asks what lies beyond what the eye sees, and the group describes their process: one person lies back and riffs on a train whistle, another struggles to find words for the dusty smell of a summer wood. Someone says the practice feels relational, with the tree and the poet writing each other. The session closes with scheduling for the next meeting and an assignment to bring a favorite Zen saying, typed out, to share.

title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton tells the story of 37 years of Zen practice, from reading Alan Watts and meeting Kobun Chino Otogawa to the question of home leaving that keeps returning in Shuko's life. Rodney Smith's Stepping Out of Self-Deception supplies the phrase "a partial heart," which names the hesitation running through that history. When Shuko's two grown sons decline to reconnect, months of cognitive therapy and Zazen reveal a hope that they would confirm Shuko was a good mother. Shuko concludes that a worthwhile life is lived wholeheartedly where one is, and that love travels in a wide circle from parent to child to grandchildren.

title: Zen and Creativity Class 1
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton opens a class called Zen and Creativity by explaining that zazen mind can shape how people make things, with attention on the process and not the product. Shuko describes plein air watercolor and poetry as practice, then guides a visualization and has everyone shape clay inside a bag without looking. Participants share the scenes they modeled: a hayloft ladder at Uncle Frank's farm, turtles in a rainy park beside the Yangtze, a motorcycle ride through the Tucson desert, humpback whales bubble net fishing. The second half turns to therapeutic touch, where partners feel the energy between their hands, then work with an intention the receiver names, and the class ends with plans to meet at Shuko's house on the 12th and bring photographs.

title: Awakening in A Female Form
speaker: Zenshin Florence Caplow and Jean LaValley
summary: Zenshin Florence Caplow and Jean LaValley tell the stories of awakened women from the Therigatha and from Chinese, Japanese, and Theravada traditions, opening a weekend on women's koans. Zenshin recounts Mahapajapati leading shaven-headed women to ask the Buddha for ordination, Soma sending Mara away, and Rionan burning her face to be accepted as a student. Jean describes arriving at koans from Vipassana, asks why gender goes unmentioned in the Dharma hall, and reads the story of Chiyono, a servant whose bucket loses its bottom. The evening closes with Dipa Ma taking a frightened student's hand on a turbulent flight and saying, "The daughters of Buddha are fearless."

title: Buddhas Enlightenment
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch tells the story of the Buddha's awakening on Rohatsu, beginning with the familiar Pali Canon account of Siddhartha's glimpses of suffering outside the palace walls and Mara's challenge under the Bodhi tree. A Mulasarvastivada version, translated by John Strong, follows. In it Yashodhara takes up every practice from home, is pregnant for six years, and gives birth to Rahula at the moment of awakening. Yuzan favors this telling because it keeps love beside the search, and recalls Zoketsu Norman Fischer's remark that leaving and returning home can stand for spiritual change. Norman's point that Asian languages have no word for "enlightenment," and that Suzuki Roshi chose it as skillful means, leads to a closing quote from Wittgenstein on language bewitching intelligence.

title: The Stories of Awakening
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Keizan Zenji's picture of Buddha sitting six years until reeds grow through the mat, and sets beside it case 41, Bodhidharma's nine years facing a wall. A poem about falling into the same hole in the sidewalk leads Nomon to ask whether the habitual "me" can appreciate such heroic stories at all. Bodhidharma answers the emperor with "no merit" and "vast emptiness," then Huike and Sengcan each search for a mind or a wrongdoing and cannot find it. Nomon closes with verses from Sengcan's Faith in Mind and describes the night's yaza, a bell-free sitting where people drift in, walk, or sleep.

title: Rohatsu 2010
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley opens the Rohatsu sesshin by welcoming the two sanghas to a two-and-a-half-day sesshin they are sitting together for the first time, then takes up why sesshin can be so difficult. Eko describes the identity each person carries, an idea of the self that gets built up or torn down by every experience and every evaluation of it. This morning's oryoki supplies the examples: a newcomer wonders what the awkwardness says about them, someone fluent starts to think things are going well, and others worry about having the right clothes. Eko traces the identity to a strategy for gaining affirmation, one that splits off whatever doesn't fit, and says it thrives on comparison, even in a room where no one looks around, as people notice how everything is going for everyone else.

title: Finding A Balance
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up two central Zen teachings, radical acceptance and acting for the benefit of all beings, through the opening lines of the third patriarch's poem Trust in Mind and Yunmen's answer that the teaching of a lifetime is "an appropriate response." Eko tells of a student who called "Bullseye" when a zabuton knocked over a cup of tea, and of Sue Ann Big Crow, a Pine Ridge freshman who answered a jeering gymnasium in Lead, South Dakota, by dancing a shawl dance at center court. Peter Hershock's virtuosity and Bernie Glassman's three treasures help join the two teachings. In the discussion, Eko takes questions on voting and attachment to outcome, and closes with a Zen teacher who admits to liking spring better than autumn.

title: Wilderness Basketball
speaker: Kusho Terry Thompson
summary: Kusho Terry Thompson tells the story of Kusho's 24-hour solo during the 2010 Mountains and Rivers hiking retreat on Mount Baker, which Kusho reads from notes written right after coming down, after a detour through basketball in Indiana, Kansas, and North Carolina. Alone in a meadow, Kusho sits with insects, bites from mosquitoes, and a line from the Heart Sutra about having no fear, then watches mites gang up on one and kill it. The sight leaves Kusho doubting that cruelty in nature can change. Rain on Kusho's tent settles Kusho, and a dream that ends on a basketball court leaves Kusho thinking Kusho should enjoy the game.

title: Koan Practice
speaker: Burai Rick Spencer
summary: Burai Rick Spencer takes up Blue Cliff Record case 53, in which Mazu twists Baizhang's nose after wild ducks fly past and asks, "When have they ever flown away?" Burai first recalls a Rinzai teacher who asked how to realize yourself when hearing a sound, and the day Burai snatched his stick, struck the floor, and heard "Not that sound, this sound." Next come nights in South Dakota when migrating geese could be measured only in hours, and the image of "here" as a prison whose door opens when the illusion of me against the world is released. The paragraph closes on Baizhang's crying and laughing, and the question of whether a doorway is an entrance or an exit.

title: Colliding Worlds
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells three stories from a week of colliding worlds, starting with the national meeting of the Soto Zen Buddhist Association in Oregon, where priests voted after about a decade to add women to the ancestor list and where a former elementary school now houses a training monastery with a marimba band. Nomon asks whether Red Cedar should stay a sitting group or become a Zen center. Next comes a tense VA badge appointment, where a form marked conscientious objector sends Nomon breathing through an hour of worry, tied to Dogen's "circle of the way." Nomon then reads Bhanteji Gunaratana on mindfulness and on treating distractions as temporary objects of meditation, closes with David Whyte's poem "Working Together," and sends the room into small groups.

title: Honoring our Ancestors
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett remembers Robert Aitken Roshi, who died at 93, and reads two of Aitken's late blog posts, "Our Tendency" and "Count Your Breaths," on the eve of a hiking retreat built around Dogen's Mountains and Rivers Sutra. Memorial services in Japan, at Rinso-in for Suzuki Roshi and at Eihei-ji for Rujing, lead Nomon to ask what it means to honor ancestors never met, including a son who chants wholeheartedly for a father he calls a poor parent. Nomon offers breath counting as a way to follow Aitken and sets out a three-part frame of establishing, releasing, and inquiring. Nomon closes with Dogen's line that the green mountains are always walking.

title: Our Practice Affects Others
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley describes a stubborn resistance to practice and the question "Where is the joy?", which Michael Newton offered in a practice discussion at Samish. Seishu recalls Thanissaro Bhikkhu's advice that the mind is like a committee, and Norman Fischer's counsel to make a best effort and let the worry go. Seishu then reads a letter from daughter Gillian in New Orleans, who passed the question along to friends, including a note left on a sun visor before a road trip to Montana. The letter shows practice reaching people in ways no one plans. Seishu closes by comparing the return to "Where's the joy?" with returning to the breath.

title: Wilderness Dharma Practice
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny describes the wilderness dharma practice Reizan's sangha has kept for ten years, tracing it from Reizan's own solo sitting on backpacking trips to the group's yearly retreat on the back side of the Twin Sisters near Mount Baker. Reizan places the practice beside Shakyamuni's departure from the palace, Thoreau's Walden, Gary Snyder's circumambulation of Mount Tamalpais, and the marathon monks of Mount Hiei. Reizan walks through the retreat's form: a cedar grove blessing, a sweat lodge, silent hiking behind a tanken, chanting the Mountains and Rivers Sutra at ritual stops, and a "sleeping bag okesa" for cold morning zazen. Reizan closes by inviting everyone to the old growth at mile post 43 on August 7th and reciting Reizan's poem "Because It's Always There," written after climbing Mount Hood.

title: Awakening Joy
speaker: James Baraz and Shoshana Alexander
summary: James Baraz and Shoshana Alexander speak about well-being and ease under the title Awakening Joy, though the transcript is only a handful of fragments. The passages include an admission that sometimes a person prefers being grumpy to being happy, a mention of a place in us that longs to develop something, and a study saying the average American is exposed to about three thousand messages a day unless on retreat. The text ends on the line "Just imagine if." Too much is missing to tell how these pieces connect.

title: Mindfulness Seminar 6
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the fourth foundation of mindfulness, mindfulness of phenomena or dharmas, in the final week of a six-week seminar on the Buddha's Four Foundations of Mindfulness Sutra. Passing over the sutra's lists of hindrances and factors of enlightenment, Nomon turns to the three marks of impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, and not-self, and offers softness as a way to meet the tension that self-clinging brings. One example is a friendly encounter with an acquaintance while riding the bike home from dropping off Walker at school. Nomon reads from Larry Rosenberg on anatta, closes with Rumi's "The Guest House," and then hears from participants about anger surfacing in practice and the phrase "Life is short, nobody said it was going to be easy, and don't take it personally."

title: Mindfulness Seminar 5
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the second and third foundations of mindfulness, feelings and mind, in the fifth week of the seminar. Nomon tells a story from a weekend retreat with Norman Fischer, where a forgotten breakfast sets off a swing between unpleasant and pleasant feelings, and a lunch delayed by an interview that Norman pauses for a break. Participants then report on practice, among them a cemetery visit and a night spent sitting with a dying father. Nomon closes with chitta, picturing thoughts as a river and the still mind as its bank, and offers two practices: noting, with labels like judgment, impatience, and peacefulness, and a quieter non-thinking.

title: Mindfulness Seminar 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the clear comprehension passage in the Foundations of Mindfulness Sutra, then turns to the second foundation, vedana, or feeling tone. Two commentary stories frame the opening: an elder who restarts his walk to the village whenever mindfulness lapses, and a monk who puts his limb back where it was after gesturing mid-conversation. Nomon offers two practices, asking "what is the feeling tone?" and listening to sounds for pleasant and unpleasant, and places vedana as a weak link in the chain of dependent origination. The homework is to notice habits that create internal noise, such as Nomon's own habit of working for hours without a break.

title: Mindfulness Seminar 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the breathing section of the Buddha's mindfulness sutra in the third week of a six-week seminar, along with a passage from Larry Rosenberg's book on mindfulness of breathing. Nomon reads "he understands, I breathe out short" as an invitation to investigate the endless variety of each breath, and offers a practice for the week: noticing the beginning of the inhalation and exhalation, then the middle, then the end. Rosenberg's passage, which opens with the Hasidic belief that everyone is given a corner of the universe to tend, treats attention to breathing as respect for every moment of life. Nomon leads a short standing and moving practice, then a sit, asking everyone to keep the same awareness of breath through the bell, the bows, the refuges, and the announcements.

title: Mindfulness Seminar 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a six-week seminar on mindfulness with a raisin-eating exercise, then asks participants to report on what they noticed. Reports include drifting into thoughts of cookies, a second raisin worked on deliberately, and the tongue's skill. Nomon gives three reasons for the seminar: mindfulness as foundation for Zen, studies with John Kabat-Zinn on mindfulness-based stress reduction, and brain-scan research. The psoriasis study, where skin cleared four times faster under meditation, is one example. Nomon defines sati, places it in the Eightfold Path and the Satipatthana Sutta, and leads a lying-down body scan, with walking awareness as the week's home practice.

title: Mindfulness Seminar 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the second week of a six-week mindfulness seminar by hearing participants report on the body scan, then reads from the Satipatthana Sutta in Bhikkhu Bodhi's translation. Nomon outlines the sutra's four foundations of mindfulness and the six groups of body practices Thich Nhat Hanh finds in it, and offers three qualities from its repeated formula: ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful. After a lying-down movement practice, Nomon suggests home work with a yoga recording and the five daily recollections of decay, disease, and death. One option is to recite them quietly in a graveyard, including at a child's grave.

title: The Second Arrow
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads a short sutta from the Pali Canon in which the Buddha contrasts an uninstructed run-of-the-mill person, shot by two arrows, with a well-instructed disciple who feels only one. Nomon walks through the sutta's sequence of resistance, reaching for pleasure, and identification with the experience, then offers recent examples. At a scientific conference on mindfulness, the conditioned thought "I don't belong here" was the first arrow, and the second arrow was the search for evidence of it. At Newark Airport, a spat with Janet over a pasta salad brought a strong urge to defend. Listeners then pair up to share examples of their own. Nomon ends on the idea that healing may lie in moving between figuring things out and letting go into silence.

title: Tasting the Flavor
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch begins with a little girl in a doctor's office who takes the gum from her mouth, says it has lost its flavor, and throws it away. From there Yuzan asks what to do when a marriage, a job, or Zen practice goes flat, and reads from Norman Fischer's article "Lost Love in Anxious Times," where the mind is a museum of negativity and a person can pick up a coat and walk out into the sunlight. Yuzan calls boredom a patina painted over feelings, and shares a friend's letter of gratitude after her four-year-old, fitted with a halo brace for a broken neck, rides a trike. Participants answer with jelly beans of every flavor, and with the reminder that sometimes it is time to let go, like the girl with her gum.

title: Jukai and Susho Rituals
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett describes the jukai and shuso ceremonies the community held over the weekend, after marking Tibetan National Uprising Day with a moment of silence. Nomon explains jukai, the receiving of the precepts, which four members took with Norman Fischer officiating, and names its benefits: a project to work on, a close group of Dharma siblings, and the ceremony's own magic. The problems get equal time, since special insignia can leave others feeling ranked or left out. Nomon then turns to the shuso ceremony, in which Bob answered questions on the spot from a high seat, and ends on Wikipedia's guess that the robe began as a garment Chinese monks could hide under their clothes during repression.

title: Non Abiding
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from a book of retreat talks by Ajahn Amaro, taking up the chapter "The Place of Non-Abiding." Nomon starts with the short letter Ajahn Chah dictated to Ajahn Sumedho weeks before a stroke ended his teaching, which says the Dharma is found neither in moving forward, nor backward, nor in standing still. From there Nomon turns to a passage from the Udana and the story of Bahiya, who hears "in the seen, only the seen" from the Buddha, awakens, and is killed by a runaway cow moments later. Nomon closes with a practice for the week: letting a passing car or a garbage truck be only the heard.

title: Master Ma is Unwell
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up the case "Master Ma Is Unwell" from the Book of Serenity, in which a monastery superintendent asks the ailing teacher how he is and hears "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha." Reizan reads the exchange as shared concern between two people, and ties it to the grief class held during the practice period, as nine deaths touched the sangha since October. Reizan recalls a hospital stay at fifteen, when a mother's daily question mattered though she could do nothing, and tells of an I Ching line about a deceased father, followed by a vision on a log in the snowy Vermont woods. Reizan ends on the case's own instruction, "Please try to bring it up," and the advice to find one person who will listen.

title: Bridge to Mindfulness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the story of a young monk who tells Zhaozhou he sees only a plain log bridge, not the famous stone bridge, and hears that it lets donkeys and horses cross. Nomon recalls starting this sangha nineteen years ago as a log bridge, then describes a week at a mindfulness-based stress reduction training, where Jon Kabat-Zinn and others ease a hall of medical professionals into silence while teaching straight from the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. Nomon reads the sutra's opening and the first foundation, the body in the body, and describes the body scan, which sends many participants to sleep. Nomon closes with the Buddha's breathing instructions and the observation that no one can remember yesterday's breath.

title: Grief Class 4
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny closes the grief class by widening the circle from personal loss to the world's, drawing on Miriam Greenspan's book and her distinction between the "carrier" who feels for a whole system and the "bystander" who stays numb. Reizan reads popular culture as the modern stand-in for myth, tracing how movies and books from the 1970s to now treat the near future, with Kubrick's 2001 and Dr. Strangelove, Star Trek, the vague "by the year 2000," and Y2K as markers. Reizan sees September 11th and climate change as further wounds in a collective psyche. The class ends with paired exercise: each person speaks about what they feel, rather than think, when looking at the future of the planet and of younger generations.

title: Grief Class 3
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Susan Berman's book The Five Ways We Grieve and walks through its five grieving styles: nomad, memorialist, normalizer, activist, and seeker. Each style comes with its gifts and its pitfalls, such as the widow who stays in a black dress for years, or the activist who burns out chasing a cure for cancer. Reizan shows how subtle the styles can be by describing a response to a father's death that looks like a seeker's but was really a memorialist's gesture of honoring him. After small-group sharing, Reizan names the nomad as the predominant style, recalls setting off on a bicycle trip with no plans, and wonders whether the normalizer's approach could bring some stability to finances.

title: Wayseeking Mind Part 1
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny tells the story of how Reizan came to Buddhist practice, given as the traditional Shuso way-seeking mind talk, first of two parts. Growing up in Eugene, Oregon, Reizan runs for South Eugene High under coach Harry Johnson, in the town of Steve Prefontaine, and sits among 7,000 people for a silent memorial in which the stadium clock runs out and the crowd applauds an imaginary final lap. Reizan's father's death follows, and Reizan decides at the hospital bed to seek out what life and death are. In college, a roommate's Bible, the I Ching, and Alan Watts tapes lead to Shunryu Suzuki's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind and a first sitting that ends with Reizan on the floor, hyperventilating.

title: Wayseeking Mind Part 2
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny tells the story of the road from the South Eugene running track to Zen practice in Bellingham. Reizan recalls running with Billy, watching Billy break from the pack with a mile to go in the 1980 Olympic trials 5,000 meters and finish third, and cycling to Jemez Bodhi Mandala in New Mexico. Years in Vermont and on the Audubon school buses bring Reizan to Green Gulch, where Norman and Tim first appear, and then to Bellingham, where Tim's front-porch sitting group begins. The deaths of Billy, Jim, and Paul run through the telling, which ends at a South Eugene track reunion where Billy's brother Steve asks, "Who are all those little kids up there?"

title: Grief Class 2
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up grief in the second of Reizan's short classes, working from an essay and guided meditation by Stephen Levine, whose line "When we are in grief, we are no longer blind to our blindness" frames the session. Reizan tells of losing a long-term relationship and waking in tears each morning for about four months, until the feeling shifted like cumulus thinning into cirrus. Grief, Reizan says, shows our same old fear, anger, and despair in a stark light, and surrender becomes the only option left. The class closes with Levine's meditation, pressing a fingertip to the sternum and breathing the pain into the heart.

title: Grief Class 1
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny opens the first session of a grief class by describing how the topic found Reizan, including a list Reizan once wrote of sixteen parents, grandparents, friends, and relatives who had died before Reizan turned forty. Reizan describes grief as an ongoing current in life, with ripples that reach the lost role and a "shadow self" of the life that might have been, and compares working with it to a trail maintenance crew keeping a path clear. Reizan says zazen has helped most, and that real shifts often arrive in quiet moments rather than in sharing groups. The session closes with a few minutes of settling on one loss, then pairs completing "I think of grief as" and "What my grief says about me is."

title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny tells the story of how Zen practice came into a life that begins in Eugene, Oregon, among runners at Hayward Field and the legend of Steve Prefontaine. Reizan describes the memorial for Pre, where 7,000 people sit through a running clock and applaud an imaginary final half mile. In a hospital room, Reizan's father says "there's a time when you have to let go" and mouths the Lord's Prayer during last rites, and that sight sets the search in motion. Alan Watts tapes and the line "We die and we do not die" in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind follow, then a bicycle trip, Vermont, and a Bodhidharma sticker on the dashboard of Tim's van in Bellingham.

title: Preparing for Practice Period
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the early Zen stories of Bodhidharma and his student Huike as the six-week winter practice period approaches. Nomon tells of Huike standing in the snow outside Shaolin until buried to the waist, then reads three exchanges, including the advice to have "no coughing or sighing in the mind." Stories from a mindfulness class for veterans at a Seattle VA hospital, where some find relief only on their motorcycles, sit alongside a visit to the Seattle Soto Zen group. Nomon closes by sending the room into groups of three to ask when adding effort to practice helps and when it becomes another failed resolution.

title: Life is Not A Featurette
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the question of whether lay practice without a monastery is complete practice, drawing on nearly twenty years with the Bellingham sangha. Nomon contrasts the movie Julia and Julia and its DVD featurette, where nobody has problems, with the wish to trade in a troublesome life for a better one. Stories of Bodhidharma and Huike follow: Huike standing in the snow, the teaching "outwardly cease all involvements, inwardly have no coughing or sighing in the mind," and the question "Where are we going?" Nomon adds faith in practice, a fisherman's advice to keep your gear in the water through the storm, and closes with Derek Walcott's poem "Love After Love."

title: Continuous Practice
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley reads "Continuous Practice, How and Why," a talk Sojun Mel Weitsman gave on the sixth day of a Rohatsu sesshin, and comments on it. Mel holds that how to live this moment matters more than why, and that practice means keeping the mind in harmony with the heart. Seishu responds with stories: sunlit dust at Samish Island that felt like an accomplishment, impatience while waiting for a private interview, and a 2 a.m. cup of tea with no separation from the cup. The last story, from a book about people taking on big barriers, tells of a woman standing in the rain at an antinuclear demonstration, unaware that Dr. Benjamin Spock had driven past and decided to join.

title: The Geometry of Self
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Buddhist teaching of non-self, anatta, one of the three marks of reality alongside dukkha and anicca. A seven-day retreat in Canada supplies the central story: Nomon sees the head organizer's name on the practice discussion sheet, panics, and then glimpses personality as a geometric shape with pokey corners that can be carried without fear. Nomon then tells of Shenxiu and Huineng and their two poems, ending on "where does the dust alight?" The evening closes with a reading from Ajahn Amaro's Small Boat, Great Mountain, where a young seeker leaves England, wanders the beaches of Thailand, and finds the cheerful monks of Ajahn Chah's forest monastery, learning that freedom was already within.

title: Rohatsu 2009
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Rohatsu through the word sesshin, which Kate Lun Lake's orientation reveals means "to touch" the mind rather than "to gather" it, and through the story of Shakyamuni Buddha's awakening. Nomon retells the ascetic years of breath-stopping and near-starvation, then the remembered childhood moment under the rose apple tree that turns Buddha toward the middle way. Nomon also names the story's troubles, including the abandoned family and the reluctance to ordain women, and the all-male ancestor list chanted that morning. Case 3 of the Book of Serenity, where Prajñātāra reads scripture by breathing, leads into six breath practices, beginning with counting and following.

title: All is Burning
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Buddha's Fire Sermon, reading the passage where the eye, the intellect, and all contact and feeling are burning, and the monks grow disenchanted and are released. Nomon starts with the news of deaths from swine flu and a school fire, then the chemistry of oxidation, where wood burns and a 2,000-year-old building turns out to have burned down in 1623 and been rebuilt. Nomon asks what is wrong with being enchanted, and answers that long-term students of the Buddha way stay engaged, building the building and appreciating that it burns. Nomon closes with a devata asking the Buddha how he crossed the flood without pushing forward and without staying in one place.

title: All Things Are our Teacher
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up "all things are our teacher," a phrase adapted from the Zen ethics ceremony, where the precepts are given with the words "Do not put another head on top of your own." Nomon asks listeners to recall something recent they disliked and to notice the experience beneath the story, then argues that the phrase only works when there is space in life, and leads a short sitting. Dogen's line "In attachment flowers fall, in aversion weeds spread" meets the droopy altar flowers, and a friend's $1,100 clutch repair sits beside $500 sent to a Kenyan orphan for college. Nomon ends on trust, and on saying "our" teacher rather than "my."

title: Zen and Conflict
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch takes up conflict in the sangha, ahead of an open meeting about recent changes in forms, and traces its root to fear. Drawing on Joko Beck's Everyday Zen, Yuzan retells the empty rowboat that bumps into ours in the fog and the woman who cannot show where her quarrel with her husband is. Yuzan then reads "The Case of Teasable Tim" from Destructive Emotions, where a man's anger at teasing traces back to a cruel father. Yuzan asks how each person copes with disagreement and ends by reading lines from the Dhammapada about thoughts and the cart that follows the beast that pulls it.

title: Rethinking Joy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett begins with the feeling of faking it, then retells John Wiley's story of Milarepa, who comes home to a cave full of demons. Milarepa teaches them from a high seat, runs at them screaming, and finally sits on the floor to practice beside them. All but one leave, and that last demon goes only when he puts his head in its mouth. Nomon then reads Chozen Roshi's list of the joys of practice from the Great Vow Zen Monastery newsletter, from discovering that you are not your mind to spiritual friendship, humility, and renunciation. Along the way Nomon describes getting reactive over small changes to the form, then letting go. Nomon closes by asking what the joy is right here, right now.

title: The Fruits of Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Umbrella Man, a book of appreciations by Sojun Mel Weitsman's Dharma heirs for his 80th birthday, sorting the quotations under themes such as steadiness, humility, ordinariness, and deep listening. After an opening story about Zazen loosening a tense, overworked afternoon before vacation, Nomon retells the koan of the teacher polishing a roof tile to make a mirror. One quoted student asks Mel when to hit the clackers and gets the answer "Hit them when it feels right." Another student describes Mel nodding off during dokusan until the student's voice turned fresh. Nomon then notes what the book leaves out, since nobody praises Mel for being right or brilliant, and closes with an offer to officiate anyone's funeral and a request that sangha members say what should happen to their belongings.

title: Metta Sutta 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett closes Nomon's line-by-line study of the Metta Sutta with verses nine and ten, reading the Pali alongside the chant-book and Thanissaro Bhikkhu translations. Nomon explains the Brahma Viharas and the sutta's final line about never lying in the womb again, then walks through the four stages from stream-enterer to arhat. The ending is reread as being freed from the duality of birth and death, and Nomon brings in the Buddha's "cultivate the good" and a Dalai Lama passage on warm-heartedness. Questions from the group take up rebirth and Jehovah's Witness ideas of a creator. Nomon ends by asking what class to offer after Friday sitting.

title: Steadfast and Patient
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Umbrella Man, a book of tributes from Sojun Mel Weitsman's Dharma heirs, and reads unattributed quotations grouped by theme. Nomon opens with the image of life as a mile-long ocean tanker that turns slowly after the rudder moves. The quotes gather around steadiness, humility, ordinariness, and deep listening, along with the polishing-a-tile koan and the story of Mel dozing off during dokusan while a student talked about problems. Nomon notes that nobody calls Mel always right, then invites the day's practice to be one breath, with contentment in whatever arises.

title: Metta Sutta 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the commentary's story of where the Metta Sutta comes from: 500 monks who go north to the Himalayan foothills for the rains retreat and are driven out by tree spirits with frightening sights, sounds, and smells. The Buddha sends them back chanting the sutta, and the spirits welcome them. Partners then discuss the sutta's fifteen virtues, including whether "unburdened with duties" means having none or not carrying them as a burden. Nomon returns to the text with the Pali words for well-being, safety, and happiness in the third verse. The list of beings in verse four ends with the five realms, read both literally and as states of mind.

title: Metta Sutta 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues through the Metta Sutta, the Pali poem on loving-kindness, taking up verses five through eight and setting a literal translation beside the more interpretive one in the sutra book. Nomon describes the seen and unseen beings of verse five through the Buddhist realms, from the hell with the broken-glass hill to the hungry ghosts with pencil-thin necks, and retells Bhikkhu Bodhi's story of a young lawyer who pictures her interview committee as her teacher's students. Verse seven's mother of an only child leads to the method in Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification: wish health, safety, and happiness for oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, and a hostile one. Nomon closes by assigning that practice as homework.

title: Metta Sutta 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a four-week study of the Metta Sutta by setting the chanted English translation beside Thanissaro Bhikkhu's more literal one. Nomon describes the monks and nuns who first heard the text, living on alms with a bowl and robes, and the centuries of recitation before it was written down in Sri Lanka. In verse one, the chanted version says the wise one "has obtained peace," while the literal reading says one "wants to break through" to it. Going word by word, Nomon finds "easy to instruct" missing from the chanted version and shows how "no greed for supporters" became "great possessions even for one's family." The final test from verse three is to avoid anything a wise person would disapprove of, even a small embarrassing act done in private.

title: Metta Sutta 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Metta Sutta, the loving-kindness text chanted at the Monday, Wednesday, and Friday noon services, as the first session of a four-week class. Nomon traces how the sutta reached the sangha through the Pali canon and Norman Fischer, then compares the chanted English with Thanissaro Bhikkhu's more literal translation. The comparison turns on the step-by-step early teachings versus Zen's "already complete" view, and on words like "easy to correct" and "having few duties" that the chanted version drops. Nomon plays a Sri Lankan chanting of the verses, then closes with the sutta's test of doing nothing the wise would reprove, a news story of four monks arrested in Yangon for reciting the sutta, and small-group sharing in threes.

title: Towards Wholeness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs alongside the Buddha's three levels of dukkha, then turns to the Tathagata Garbha Sutra. Along the way Nomon tells a story from Jon Kabat-Zinn's Full Catastrophe Living, in which cardiologist Bernard Lown's patient hears "T.S." as "terminal situation" and dies of heart failure that day. Nomon then reads three of the sutra's similes: honey guarded by bees, gold lost in a pit of waste, and treasure buried beneath a poor household's hearth, each picturing wholeness hidden under the kleshas. The evening ends with partners taking turns speaking on whether they feel whole and complete.

title: Teachers and Students 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Norman Fischer's reflections on his teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman, written for Mel's 80th birthday. Norman recalls the old Berkeley house on Dwight Way, with its attic zendo, Mel sitting at the head of the stairs every morning at five, and the plum tree and vegetable garden out back. Nomon adds comments on reading such stories without regret, keeping the seat warm for those who come later, and teachers being no different species from students. In discussion, Mary notes how few women appear in these early stories, and Nomon recalls Norman's wife Kathy taking her moldy okesa off the shelf at a Samish sesshin.

title: Teachers and Students 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Norman Fischer's written portrait of Fischer's own teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman, and adds remarks on teachers and students. After announcing a new schedule for fourth and second Wednesdays and thanking the weekend workers, Nomon shares Norman's memories of the Dwight Way attic zendo in Berkeley: Mel sitting motionless at the head of the stairs each morning, the plum tree in the backyard, and lunches under it in near silence. Nomon then notes that the story leaves out the wives, and recalls Jeff McKenna's saying that the sangha is "keeping the seat warm" for those before and after.

title: This is Us
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of the past seven years through "This Is Us," a song by Mark Knopfler and Emmylou Harris about contentment. Nomon traces the stress that builds after Walker's birth, Janet's chronic illness, the start of a new Dharma center, and a miserable day job, and names the fears of disappointing others and of not making sense that keep a change at bay. An old client's call comes just as Nomon reaches for the office phone to give notice. The Diamond Sutra's teaching on the separate self, studied for 21 years, finally sinks in, and Nomon ends by leading a guided mindfulness session like the one offered to the Community of Christ at Samish Island.

title: Lojong Teaching 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Lojong mind training slogans in the last of three talks, run more like a class with partner discussions. After reading Pema Chödrön's foreword, in which she draws a slogan card each morning, Nomon reviews the first five points and works through slogans from points six and seven. Blanche Hartman's story shows how Baker Roshi told her to do nothing for anyone else for a day, and she found every act was for someone. "Don't act with a twist" and "Don't expect applause" get close attention. The evening closes with a student's question about blame at work, and Nomon suggests using a position to lead in non-blame.

title: Lojong Teaching 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to the Lojong mind-training slogans, recapping tonglen, "regard all dharmas as dreams," and "drive all blames into one" with a reading from Pema Chödrön, then takes up the fourth point, the five powers, and the fifth, the yardsticks. Nomon shares the vow said each morning as aspiration practice and tells of Blanche Hartman, whose teacher told her not to do anything that day for somebody else. Atisha's difficult servant and Zorba's "full catastrophe" illustrate keeping a joyful mind. Nomon then describes stewing for miles over a dharma hall phone call on a Los Angeles freeway, the test case for "If you can practice when distracted, you are well trained."

title: Lojong Teaching 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett introduces the Lojong mind-training slogans, starting with a story of Atisha, who leaves his wedding night at age eleven after a vision of Tara and later brings an ill-tempered Bengali servant boy to Tibet to give him something to practice with. Nomon then walks through the first three of the seven points: "Regard all dharmas as dreams," with an account of holding a hard work situation more lightly, and "Drive all blames into one," with a long reading from Chögyam Trungpa on taking the blame. A participant questions that slogan, and Nomon asks the group to try it and report back. "Be grateful to everyone" follows, and Nomon closes by singing a Kenyan lullaby once sung to a young son.

title: Pacing the Cage
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Bruce Cockburn's song "Pacing the Cage" after setting aside the overview of the precepts class Nomon was asked to give. Nomon describes feeling off during that class and noticing instant suffering when Connie came in late. Playing the song, Nomon reads its lines as teaching: the sunset angel with a bloody sword becomes Manjushri's sword, the worn magnetic stripe becomes the burden of identity, and the "powers" in high places point to the lojong on making all blame one. Studying the bars shows the space between them, and Nomon closes by saying two things can be counted on: it is possible to feel what we feel, and there is more not yet felt.

title: Ambition
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Nomon's career and ambition, starting with the boxes of teaching materials Nomon finally sorts through after eight years in the garage. Nomon recounts a failed first attempt at student teaching, a hard year on Lopez Island, and twenty job interviews that never led to a hire. Nomon borrows the programming idea of technical debt to describe the burdens people shelve, then reads the eleven-point plan for Nomon's Dharma work that prompts Nomon's wife Janet to say, "Wow, that's really ambitious." Nomon redefines renunciation as no longer following ambition, and ends by renouncing ambition in front of the sangha, then admitting Nomon has already blown it.

title: Vimalakirti Nonduality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 48 of the Book of Serenity (Case 84 of the Blue Cliff Record), taken from chapter nine of the Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra, in which Vimalakirti answers Manjushri's question about entering non-duality with silence. Nomon marks the 25th and last talk in the koan series Norman Fischer selected, and reads several of the bodhisattvas' short answers before Manjushri's reply. Daido Loori's commentary supplies the sacred tortoise wiping away its tracks with its tail, and the cabbage and weeds in the garden. Nomon closes with a man who spent two weeks sitting and staring at the raw wooden beams of the old Bellingham Dharma Hall floor while newly sober.

title: Heart Sutra
speaker: Red Pine
summary: Red Pine takes up the Heart Sutra in a question-and-answer session, reading it line by line as an attack on the Sarvastivadin Abhidharma. Red Pine explains emptiness as the negation of a negation: to give a table self-existence draws a line around it and denies everything else. Avalokiteshvara answers Shariputra, the great logician, with set theory, as form and emptiness intersect and then prove identical. Red Pine reads the mantra's "gate" as "into the gone," a motion into the womb of Prajnaparamita, and jokes that the closing "svaha" echoes the self the Sarvastivadins sought. The session ends with translation as dancing with Avalokiteshvara, neither on the feet nor across the room.

title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: John Bailes
summary: John Bailes tells the story of John's own path to Zen in the shuso talk on way-seeking mind. John begins with a sunset on the family boat in the Great South Bay, shortly before the father dies of cancer at age ten. A car wreck on a Hudson River bridge, and an out-of-body moment in the hospital afterward, lead John to leave college in 1972 for the San Francisco Zen Center. Later chapters include study with Richard Baker and Nancy Wilson Ross, a round-the-world yacht race with southern lights over the Southern Ocean, and a 30-day seminary in France. John closes by thanking the sangha and Norman for making the shuso seat possible.

title: Ritual 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up ritual during a retreat, working with several of Zhaozhou's exchanges and the mindfulness sutra's four foundations of body, feelings, thoughts and emotions, and phenomena. Norman begins with silence as something strong that springs up in the middle of sound, and offers Zhaozhou's "It's just like this" as a phrase to use when the mind chases. Bowing, chanting, and offering incense, repeated over years, bring the Buddha alive, and ceremonies like Hossen Shiki and Jukai give grief and commitment a form. Zhaozhou's "Welcome" to difficulties leads Norman to the sutra's practice of staying with body and breath and letting what arises pass through awareness. Norman closes with a monk who asks what zazen is and hears "It's non-zazen," then "It's alive."

title: Ritual 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up ritual on the first day of a sesshin, asking why Zen needs its chanting, bowing, and formal walking at all. A evening crossing a street in Larkspur, California, with Norman's wife Kathy gives Norman an image: the pavement is a thin skin over the earth, and most of our ideas, including our dislike of ritual, are "news from Larkspur." Norman then walks through the morning service, from the verse of repentance and taking refuge to incense, prostrations, and sutra chanting. Norman closes with a Zhaozhou exchange about transmission and practical suggestions for sitting, including breathing out "Buddha, Dharma, Sangha."

title: Dongshan's Hot and Cold
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Blue Cliff Record case 43, in which a monk asks Dongshan how to avoid cold and heat and hears, "When it's cold, the cold kills you. When it's hot, the heat kills you." Nomon reads the case as a study of preferences, using a retreat memory of anger at a neighbor's stiff way of passing condiments and lines from the Xinxin Ming. Norman Fischer's Samish Island comments on the same case bring in a party story and his wife's saying, "If you can't be with the one you love, love the one you're with." Nomon closes with Dongshan's death, where the dying teacher comforts wailing monks and calls for a delusion banquet.

title: Land of the Dead
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer tells Tolstoy's "Master and Man," then reads the chapter "The Land of the Dead" from Norman's book Sailing Home, which uses Homer's Odyssey as its text. In Tolstoy's story, the greedy Vasili drives a sledge into a blizzard, abandons his servant Nikita, then comes back and lies on top of the freezing man, weeping and joyful. In the Odyssey chapter, Odysseus meets Tiresias, his mother Anticlea, and Achilles, who tells him death is no picnic. Norman adds a Zen story of a monk knocking on a coffin, asking "Alive or dead?", and three friends who met old grief at a graveside. Last-day sesshin plans close the session: Florence's priest ordination that evening, followed by a toasting feast.

title: Mind in Zazen
speaker: Shinmon Michael Newton
summary: Shinmon Michael Newton takes up a poem by Tiantong Rujing, quoted in the Maka Hannya Haramitsu fascicle of Dogen's Shobogenzo, in which a wind bell hangs in empty space and sounds prajna to every wind. Shinmon recalls austere Uchiyama-style sesshin under Shohaku Okumura, where the mind's broken-record chatter proved boring, and tells of Deshan and the old tea lady who quotes the Diamond Sutra. A sesshin beside a woman who snorted every few minutes shows how misery gets made, and Jan Chozen Bays answers with "enjoy the spaces in between." Shinmon closes with a Dogen poem about river sounds and moonlight, then invites everyone outside to listen.

title: Sense Perceptions
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the line from the morning service chant, "Eye and sight, ear and sound, nose and smell, tongue and taste," to open a sesshin with the six senses, their six objects, and the twelve ayatanas as doors through which the world arises. Norman points to awakening stories in which a pebble strikes bamboo, a flower is seen, or a light goes out, and to the Buddha seeing a star and saying "How marvelous." Early on, Norman also asks the sangha to support its newly developing priests and teachers as the fruit of its own practice. Norman closes with Dogen's poem about herding an ox in the spring rain.

title: Buddhisms Two Truths Q&A
speaker: Jason Ruvelson
summary: Jason Ruvelson answers questions on the two truths, starting with ultimate reality and how understanding of it keeps coming into question the further study goes. Emptiness and dharmakaya, which Jason calls the fabric of space, cannot be separated from form or relative reality, since arising and the people sitting in the room are part of what is there. Jason then describes the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, including the historical Buddha, Buddha nature, and the tea and study shared in the Bellingham Dharma hall. When a participant says Sangha means the community of the enlightened, Jason answers that it can include the lineage, the local group, all humans, and all beings seen and unseen. Indra's net comes up as the exchange closes.

title: Buddhisms Two Truths
speaker: Jason Ruvelson
summary: Jason Ruvelson takes up the two truths, relative and ultimate reality, beginning with the question of why people come to meditate. Relative truth is ordinary life, where sitting practice builds stability and leaves room around worries, such as co-workers' speculation about raises during budget season at Jason's job. Ultimate truth comes through a memory of a sunset on a Garden Street lawn in Bellingham after a breakup, when a pained, small self and a vivid sky were present together. From there Jason moves to emptiness, the four extremes of Madhyamaka, and the union of form and emptiness, then answers questions about the three jewels and who Sangha includes.

title: The Root of the Matter
speaker: Eileen Kiera
summary: Eileen Kiera takes up the image of roots, offering four for Buddhist practice: the intention of bodhicitta, practice, karma, and an essential rootedness. After leading a short breathing meditation with counted breaths, Eileen describes stopping at the kitchen tap to feel the water as glacier and cloud, and tracing a carved wooden chair back to the tree, the truck, and the hands that made it. The story of Shido Munan, whose room looks to a would-be thief like a giant oak, illustrates the fourth root. Eileen closes with slides of Mountain Lamp, a 114-acre practice center on a mountain lake that needs funds to build its meditation hall.

title: Wash your Bowl
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Zhaozhou koan in which a new monk asks for guidance and hears, "Have you eaten breakfast? Then go wash your bowl." Nomon sets the story beside John Robinson's talk on the Four Noble Truths from the week before and leads a short meditation on the breath rising and falling in the belly. From there Nomon describes the mind as a sixth sense, compares moods to weather, and tells of the resentful stories that arise at a kitchen full of dirty dishes. Washing one dish at a time, feeling its weight in the hand, becomes the practice, and Nomon names an early-morning sit, done whether or not it feels like it, as the touchstone that supports it.

title: Who Suffers When There is No Self Q&A
speaker: John Robinson
summary: John Robinson takes up questions from the sangha, starting with the three defilements of greed, aversion, and delusion and how the five precepts work against them. A shoplifter can't sit in calm meditation, John says, so the practice is to see the result of each action without judging yourself. Other answers separate calmness from passivity, compare the forms of Zen and Vipassana, and describe engaged Buddhism, with Thich Nhat Hanh's refusal to take sides in Vietnam as an example. John also explains that the "I" is a convention to see through rather than remove, and closes with the Buddha's silence on whether a god exists.

title: Who Suffers When There is No Self
speaker: John Robinson
summary: John Robinson leads a five-minute Metta meditation, then takes up the Four Noble Truths and the Buddha's refusal to say whether a self exists. John describes three stages of practice over 32 years: renouncing sense objects, catching the moment of grasping, and finally facing the attachment to "I, me, mine." The Big Dipper serves as the example of a concept, since everyone sees the shape and knows no dipper hangs in the sky, just as the conventional self lets people find their own house and car. John sketches the Eightfold Path and the young Buddha's contentment under a rose apple tree, and ends on the "us" that the opening Metta practice points toward.

title: Zen and Two Worlds Q&A
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer answers audience questions after a public lecture on Zen and the two worlds, a lecture Norman wrote as an essay for the Sun. Asked how to talk to a suicide bomber, Norman says prevention and investigation are necessary, then compares the response to 9-11 with a parent who answers a teenager's tantrum by declaring war instead of asking what is going on. Norman argues that everyone needs a religious life that turns the soul inside out, and that Buddhism, as a non-theistic practice, can join interreligious dialogue, citing Jewish and Christian meditation groups and the Episcopalians in Norman's home sangha. Norman closes by thanking Tim for the Bellingham lecture series.

title: Zen and Two Worlds
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads aloud a draft of his article "Zen and Two Worlds" for The Sun, a travelogue of a summer trip to Japan with his wife Cathy. A mossy temple garden in Fuji-Kawaguchiko, a Japanese tourist office in San Francisco, and a nun giving an old woman a back massage at Toji soften his long-held antipathy toward Japanese Zen. A morning service at Eiheiji, with acolytes passing out sutra books like ballet dancers, shows him priests trained to mediate between the ordinary and liminal worlds. Norman then contrasts Japan's Buddhist roots with America's lack of an established religion, and wonders whether fundamentalism is a cry to return to the liminal world. He ends by asking how people of different faiths might talk peacefully about what matters most.

title: Lotus Sutra 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer introduces the Lotus Sutra by tracing its rise within Mahayana Buddhism, then reads chapter 1 and the start of chapter 2 ("Expedient Means"). Norman describes Kumarajiva's 406 translation and the Tiantai school's ordering of the teachings. In chapter 1, a beam of light from the Buddha's forehead prompts Maitreya's question, and Manjushri answers with the story of the Buddha Sun Moon Bright, in which Maitreya was once the slacker Seeker of Fame. In chapter 2, five thousand listeners walk out as the Buddha says only a Buddha and a Buddha can understand the one great causal condition. Norman ends on the little boys piling sand into Buddha towers.

title: Lotus Sutra 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer opens with Edward O. Wilson's account of weaver ants, whose larvae serve as living silk shuttles, and then takes up chapters three through five of the Lotus Sutra. Norman retells the parable of the burning house, where a father coaxes distracted sons through the single gate with promises of goat, deer, and ox carts, and recalls reading it in Norman's early twenties at Norman's parents' home and sensing the house was on fire. In discussion, participants ask about intention and karma and about the meaning of the one gate. Norman then tells the parable of the prodigal son, whose father disguises himself to work beside him shoveling dung for twenty years, and closes with the medicinal herbs that drink the same rain and each grow differently.

title: Lotus Sutra 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Lotus Sutra's recurring contrast between the arhats and practitioners who see the world as already awakened and unlimited. Norman describes practice beginning in one's own suffering and widening into compassion, then points to the mind's endless capacity for desire and imagination, which the Sutra turns toward Dharma. A review of chapters five and six follows: the medicinal herbs watered by one rain, and Buddhahood predicted for Mahakasyapa, Subhuti, Katyayana, and Maudgalyayana. Norman then reads the start of chapter seven, the Phantom City, where the age of the Buddha Great Universal Wisdom Excellence is measured by grinding the earth of countless lands into dust, one speck per kalpa.

title: Lotus Sutra 4
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Chapter 12 of the Lotus Sutra, the Devadatta Chapter, after recalling the stupa that emerged in Chapter 11 and still hovers in the sky with the Buddhas around it. Norman reads the Buddha's account of a past life as a king who sought the Lotus Sutra for many kalpas and served a seer for a thousand years in exchange for the teaching. The revelation comes that the king was the Buddha himself and the seer was Devadatta, who gave him the sutra and made him a good friend on the path to the six paramitas and the four immeasurables. Norman then explains why this matters: Devadatta is the Buddha's cousin and nemesis, who tried to overthrow him and take over the Sangha.

title: Lotus Sutra 5
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer finishes the Lotus Sutra by taking up chapter 20 and the story of the bodhisattva Never Disparaging, which the Buddha tells to the mahasattva Gainer of Great Authority. The story is set in the time of Awesome Sound King, the first of 20,000 million Buddhas who all bear that name, during an age when arrogant monks wield great authority. Never Disparaging does no study or recitation. He bows to everyone he meets and tells them they are certain to attain Buddhahood. Norman connects this to Ryokan, who bowed to pictures of farmers in the fields, and notes that people are disgusted by the monk and dismiss his predictions as vain and irresponsible.

title: TATB 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up verses 6 through 15 of the text under study, which continue the discussion of the eighth consciousness, the alaya vijnana. Before getting into the technicalities, Norman backs up to ask why a Buddhist account of consciousness is worth studying at all. Norman describes these teachings as dialectical antidotes to the mistaken ideas of reality that everyone carries, since "everybody is a philosopher," whether or not a book was ever read. The test of those ideas is suffering, and the Buddhist remedy is to set an opposing idea against them until nothing remains but zero, neutrality, and the freedom to live. The passage closes on the claim that what a person is and what consciousness is differ from what we think.

title: Basic Zen Ethics 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Buddhist ethics through the Maha-assapura Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 39) and Mumonkan case 2, Hyakujo's Fox. Starting from a listener's alarm at a group's confession practice and a joke about Jewish and Catholic guilt, Norman sets Mount Sinai beside the sutra's thirteen steps, which begin with healthy shame about wrongdoing. Karma stays indelible even for an arhat, as the Buddha's stomachaches and Angulimala's stoning show. In the fox case, the old abbot's 500 fox lives turn out to be enjoyable, and Norman pairs this with Garrison Keillor's story of a town sandbagging a flooding river for days. Norman ends with Issa's haiku at the grave of Issa's daughter: "and yet, and yet."

title: Basic Zen Ethics 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the relationship between meditation and ethical conduct, arguing that sitting practice is the ground that conduct grows from. Norman describes how sitting opens a spaciousness in which the sense of "me" fades, and recalls a toothache that showed how the thought "this shouldn't be happening" makes pain worse. Ajahn Sumedho's instruction "it's just like this" and Les Kaye's comparison of sitting to brushing your teeth anchor the point. Norman then turns to the difficulty of judging right and wrong, especially in other people, and closes by inviting groups of three to share what they were taught about right and wrong as children.

title: Precepts 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer opens a series of three talks on the sixteen bodhisattva precepts by laying out background, drawing on Banjin Dotan's eighteenth-century commentary. Norman describes the precepts as everyday common sense and also as the blood lineage handed down in the midnight Dharma transmission ceremony, and sorts bodhisattvas into kings, boatmen, and shepherds. A mother yanking a child back from a busy street shows how strictness can grow from loving-kindness. Using the first precept, don't kill, Norman walks through three levels: the literal, the compassion level, where a Green Gulch farmer tallies the creatures he killed in one morning of organic farming, and the ultimate, where life and death are one. The ultimate level shows up only inside the literal acts of daily life.

title: Precepts 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads a 1995 talk by Sojun Weitsman from a Berkeley Zen Center newsletter, which fits the retreat's theme of taking refuge in the Triple Treasure. Before reading, Norman describes Mel as a plain priest met while raking leaves, who gave Norman a spare room in a hard season and shared quiet lunches under a plum tree. The reading names the teacher as one leg beside Dharma and Sangha, urges seeing a teacher's faults along with abilities, and ends with Joshu's willingness to listen to a seven-year-old girl. Norman then returns to the bodhisattva precepts, covering the three pure precepts and the ten grave precepts in brief. The closing instruction is to sit easily and let the body melt into the cushion.
